target_information: Patients feel more comfortable discussing weight when the conversation is framed around health outcomes rather than appearance or blame
Provider empathy, nonjudgmental communication, and an established trusting relationship shape patients' comfort with weight discussions
Patients experience vague lifestyle advice from primary care providers as inadequate and not equivalent to a clinical treatment plan
Patients perceive some providers as relying on stigmatizing stereotypes and failing to account for physical limitations such as chronic pain
Patients rarely receive concrete weight-management supports in primary care, such as written plans, prescriptions, gym support, or structured follow-up
Patients often feel left to manage obesity on their own after primary care visits
Patients report receiving more actionable weight-management guidance from specialists than from primary care providers
Patients want providers to explain how obesity interacts with their chronic conditions and how medications may contribute to weight gain
Patients expect weight-management recommendations to be personalized to their age, sex, comorbidities, and past weight-loss experiences
A physician's recommendation or approval increases patients' confidence and motivation to pursue a weight-management program
Patients need practical details about referred programs, including format, dietary expectations, safety, cost, and insurance coverage
Patients view obesity as a chronic, lifelong condition requiring maintenance support and relapse planning
Patients are generally receptive to referrals from primary care to commercial weight-management programs
Patients expect referral arrangements to include accountability, follow-up, and coordination between the provider and the commercial program
Patients have concerns about privacy, data security, and financial conflicts of interest in clinic partnerships with commercial weight-management vendors
research_questions: What are the perceptions and expectations of persons with obesity regarding discussing their weight with healthcare providers?
What are patients' experiences and expectations concerning the nature of the weight management advice and treatment options they receive in clinical settings?
What are the opinions of persons with obesity regarding the potential value and challenges of receiving referrals for obesity treatment from clincial care to commerical weight management programs?
What are the overarching experiences and perceptions of persons with obesity concerning adult weight loss?

interview_guide.topic: Weight Conversations in the Clinical Setting
subtopics: Recency of the last weight-loss discussion with a doctor
Types of providers who have discussed weight (e.g., primary care, cardiologist, OB/GYN)
Who typically initiates the conversation (patient vs. provider)
Perceived helpfulness when patient raises it vs. when provider raises it
Whether the provider asked permission before discussing weight
Primary clinical reasons weight was raised (e.g., health, blood pressure, labs, mobility)
Discussion of weight loss for diabetes prevention or control
Discussion of weight loss for high blood pressure or heart disease
Discussion of weight loss for orthopedic issues
Discussion of weight loss for fertility
Discussion of weight loss for cancer prevention

interview_guide.topic: Comfort and Emotional Experience of the Conversation
subtopics: Overall feelings about how weight was discussed
Factors that increased comfort during the discussion
Factors that created discomfort during the discussion

interview_guide.topic: Weight-Loss Methods Tried and Referrals Received
subtopics: Methods tried independently without a doctor (diet, physical activity, medications, surgery)
Methods a doctor has offered or referred in-office
Whether the provider asked about patient preference
Reasons for accepting some referrals but not others (e.g., trust, recommendation, perceived effectiveness, convenience, cost)
Degree of adherence to the doctor's advice or program
Satisfaction with the outcome or result
How an external referral was arranged (provider, office staff, insurer, or direct program outreach)
Satisfaction with the referral process and desired changes
Expectations of what the provider should convey about a program (effectiveness, cost, convenience, safety)
Preference for multiple options vs. a single provider-endorsed program
Desire for the provider to recommend a specific program vs. presenting choices
Importance of knowing how a program works for someone like them (age, lifestyle, similar conditions)
Expected top community-based or online commercial program options (e.g., WW)
Details needed to follow through (written materials, website, toll-free number, insurance coverage, cost, format)
Likelihood of using a discount code distributed via an after-visit summary
Perceived added value of a provider referral to WW vs. enrolling on one's own
Anticipated concerns and opportunities with this referral process
Openness to the doctor checking in directly about progress
Preferred follow-up mode (office visit, telephone, email, text)
Preferred follow-up frequency

interview_guide.topic: Data Sharing and Privacy Between Provider and Program
subtopics: Concerns about the doctor's office sharing weight history and health conditions with WW
Concerns about direct provider–program communication about progress
Perceived benefits of data sharing (convenience, cost, coordination)
Perceived risks of data sharing (confidentiality, scope creep, insurance concerns)
Information the patient would and would not want shared (e.g., attendance, enrollment, weight measures)
How the patient would want the doctor to use progress information (positive progress vs. lack of progress)
Expectations after losing 10 percent or reaching goal weight (e.g., maintenance)
Views on restarting the intensive program after relapse or weight regain
Views on whether insurance should cover a second round of treatment

participants.persona: Warren is a 45-year-old man with a college education, single, employed full-time, and overweight.
participants.name: Warren

memories.content: I remember the smell of wet asphalt after a summer storm when I was a kid.
My mom used to make meatloaf on Tuesdays, and I can still picture the burnt edges.
I had a blue bicycle with a torn seat, though I forget who gave it to me.
I broke my arm falling out of a tree in our backyard.
There was a weird kid down the street who collected dead bugs in jars.
I can still taste the overly sweet fruit punch from my third-grade Halloween party.
My grandfather smoked a pipe, and the whole house smelled like cherry tobacco.
I remember being terrified of the dark basement in my childhood home.
We went on a road trip to Florida and the AC in the car broke halfway there.
I won a spelling bee in fifth grade, but I can't remember the winning word.
I used to build elaborate forts out of couch cushions and blankets.
My first dog was a golden retriever mix who chewed up all my action figures.
I remember the awful scratchy feeling of the wool sweater my aunt knit for me.
I got lost in a grocery store once and sat on the floor crying until a manager found me.
We used to catch fireflies in empty mayonnaise jars during the summer.
I had a teacher in elementary school who always wore bright yellow dresses.
The sound of the ice cream truck used to make me sprint down the driveway.
I remember scraping my knee on the gravel driveway and hiding it so I wouldn't have to go inside.
My dad took me to a baseball game, but I only remember eating two hot dogs.
I found a stray kitten in the bushes, but my parents wouldn't let me keep it.
I remember the horrible embarrassment of my voice cracking during a class presentation.
I bought my first CD at a mall record store, a grunge album I played on repeat.
A girl in my geometry class smiled at me once, and I thought about it for weeks.
I failed my first driving test because I parallel parked over the curb.
My high school locker always smelled like old gym socks and stale corn chips.
I remember sneaking out to go to a party, only to find out I had the wrong address.
I worked at a fast-food place and would secretly eat fries in the walk-in freezer.
The crushing disappointment of not getting invited to the senior prom after-party still stings a bit.
I wore this ridiculous oversized flannel shirt every day for a year.
I got into a fistfight in the hallway and ended up with a black eye, though I barely remember why.
We used to drive around aimlessly on Friday nights with the windows down.
I remember the distinct metallic taste of the braces I had for three years.
My parents bought a clunky desktop computer, and I spent hours waiting for the dial-up modem to connect.
I had a poster of a red sports car on my wall that I thought was the coolest thing ever.
I threw up behind the bleachers after trying chewing tobacco for the first and last time.
The smell of cheap body spray always transports me back to the middle school locker room.
I remember getting a terrible haircut right before school picture day.
I used to play video games until my thumbs were sore and blistered.
A buddy and I tried to build a skateboard ramp, but it collapsed on the first try.
I remember the heavy, sinking feeling in my gut when my parents announced they were divorcing.
Moving into my freshman dorm, I realized I hadn't brought any bedding.
I stayed up all night cramming for a history final and still only got a C.
There was a local pizza place that sold giant slices at two in the morning.
I remember the exact shade of neon green of my roommate's terrible lava lamp.
I fell asleep in a lecture hall and woke up to find the next class had already started.
A girl I briefly dated in college made a comment about my weight that I've never forgotten.
I went to a fraternity party and remember the floor being sticky with spilled beer.
I changed my major three times before finally settling on business.
The campus library always had this comforting smell of old paper and dust.
I walked across the graduation stage feeling completely terrified about the future.
I remember the sheer panic of checking my bank account and seeing a negative balance.
We took a road trip to the beach for spring break and I got a peeling sunburn.
I lived in an off-campus apartment with a landlord who refused to fix the heat.
I bought a cheap suit for my first real job interview, but the sleeves were too long.
I remember the sound of the squeaky wheels on the mail cart at my first office job.
I dated a coworker briefly, which ended in months of awkward silence in the breakroom.
There was a stray dog that used to hang around my apartment building until Animal Control took it.
I tried to cook a Thanksgiving turkey in a tiny oven and ended up ordering Chinese food.
I remember the heavy clunk of my first car's transmission eventually dying on the highway.
I spent most of my mid-twenties going to bars, though I can hardly recall the faces of the people I went with.
I bought a leather couch that turned out to be too big to fit through my apartment door.

I remember a buddy telling me how his doctor recommended a specific weight-loss program, and he seemed incredibly motivated by that approval. I cannot recall when this happened, but I vividly remember the excitement in his voice.
I remember standing in the pouring rain waiting for a tow truck for three hours.
I used to play a weekly poker game with some guys, but we all just slowly stopped talking.
I split my pants bending over at a company picnic and had to tie a jacket around my waist.
I had a phase where I bought a bunch of camping gear but never actually went camping.
I remember the bright, blinding glare of the fluorescent lights in my first cubicle.
I adopted a fish that lived for exactly three days.
The time I tried to ask my neighbor out and she nervously laughed, thinking it was a joke.
I flew to Las Vegas for a bachelor party and lost two hundred dollars in ten minutes.
I remember the hollow feeling of turning thirty and realizing I hadn't accomplished my goals.
I started noticing my clothes shrinking, or rather, my waistline expanding.
I found an amazing taco truck near my old office and ate there almost every day.
I bought a gym membership on New Year's Day and went exactly four times.
I remember the sting of a papercut from a manila folder that refused to heal for a week.
I had a boss who chewed with his mouth open, and the sound still haunts me.
I got stuck in a stalled elevator for forty-five minutes with a crying toddler.
I tried to grow a beard, but it came in so patchy I shaved it off in a panic.
I remember the heavy silence of my apartment when I lived alone for the first time.
I accidentally sent a venting email about a client to the client themselves.
I started wearing slip-on shoes because tying laces became too much of a hassle.
I have a vivid memory of eating an entire pizza by myself on a lonely Friday night.
I bought a massive TV that took up half my living room wall.
I remember the smell of fresh mulch when the landscapers came to my apartment complex.
I tried to build an IKEA bookshelf and ended up with two extra screws and a wobbly shelf.
The time my car alarm went off at three in the morning and I couldn't find my keys to stop it.
I had a severe toothache that kept me awake for two days before I finally saw a dentist.
I remember the sheer boredom of a four-hour quarterly review meeting.
I downloaded a dating app, swiped for ten minutes, and deleted it out of sheer anxiety.
I went to a movie by myself for the first time and realized I actually loved it.
I remember burning my hand on a hot pan because I wasn't paying attention.
I always buy the generic brand of cereal because it tastes exactly the same.
I remember the soft hum of the refrigerator in the middle of the quiet night.

I read somewhere that overweight patients feel a huge sense of comfort when doctors focus on lab results instead of judging their appearance. The feeling of relief described in the article really stuck with me, even if I forget which magazine it was in.
The coffee at my current office always tastes slightly burnt, no matter who makes it.
I have a favorite spot on the couch where the cushion is permanently dented.
I watched an entire season of a crime show in one weekend and felt completely brain-dead afterward.
I stepped in a deep puddle on my way to work and had to wear wet socks all day.
I remember the sharp jolt of pain in my lower back when I tried to lift a heavy box.
I bought an expensive blender to make smoothies but use it mostly for milkshakes.
The feeling of finally taking off tight dress shoes after a long day is unbeatable.
I remember dropping my phone on my face while reading in bed.
I tried a low-carb diet once and lasted roughly thirty-six hours before ordering a sandwich.
I always check that the front door is locked at least twice before going to sleep.
I have a drawer full of takeout menus even though I just order on my phone now.
I remember the frustration of losing my internet connection during an important video call.
I bought a nice watch, but the strap pinches my wrist so I rarely wear it.
The sound of my alarm clock marimba tone instantly fills me with dread.
I went to a high school reunion and hardly recognized anyone, including myself in the mirror.
I remember the sweet, slightly artificial taste of the cherry cola I always get at the movies.
I had a really vivid dream about losing all my teeth, which I read means I'm stressed.
I constantly lose my sunglasses, so now I just buy the cheap gas station ones.
I remember the satisfaction of peeling the protective plastic off a new computer monitor.
I ordered a steak well-done by mistake and chewed through it anyway out of pure stubbornness.
I have a neighbor who mows his lawn at seven in the morning on Saturdays, and it drives me crazy.
I went for a walk in the park and got chased by an aggressive goose.
The steering wheel of my car gets insanely hot if I park in the summer sun.
I remember the embarrassment of my stomach growling loudly during a quiet meeting.
I tried to fix a leaky faucet myself and ended up flooding the bathroom floor.
I always eat the fries before the burger, a habit I've had since childhood.
I remember the heavy exhaustion after helping a friend move his couch up three flights of stairs.
I once spent an hour looking for my glasses while they were on my head.
I have a specific mug for coffee, and my morning is ruined if it's in the dishwasher.
I remember the rich smell of garlic and butter from the Italian place down the street.
I went to a modern art museum and just couldn't understand why a blank canvas was famous.
I had a sudden craving for a childhood snack and drove to three stores trying to find it.
The feeling of static electricity shocking my hand on a winter doorknob always surprises me.
I remember laughing so hard at a comedy podcast on my commute that people in the next car stared.
I bought a fancy ergonomic desk chair because my back constantly aches these days.
I keep meaning to clean out the trunk of my car, but it's been full of junk for months.
I remember the sharp cold of a sudden downpour catching me without an umbrella.
I always leave a twenty percent tip, no matter how bad the service is.
I won a raffle at a corporate retreat once, but the prize was just a branded paperweight.
I remember the intense, lingering smell of skunk after my car hit one on a rural road.
I tried reading a classic novel to feel smarter but abandoned it by chapter three.

A coworker was visibly angry after a checkup because the doctor just threw out generic advice to eat better instead of offering a real plan. I forget exactly what they said, but the frustration radiating from them was palpable.
I got a parking ticket because I misread the completely confusing street signs.
I remember the warm, yeasty smell of the bakery I used to walk past on my way to work.
I threw away an old pair of sneakers that had completely worn through the soles.
I had a really awkward conversation in an elevator with a guy who thought he knew me.
The relief of finding a public restroom just in time is a feeling I will never forget.
I remember the absolute panic of thinking I lost my wallet, only to find it in my other pants.
I buy a lottery ticket every time the jackpot gets over two hundred million, just in case.
I have a coworker who always microwaves fish in the breakroom, and it smells horrendous.
I remember the soft click of the thermostat kicking on in the dead of winter.
I ordered a shirt online that was supposedly an extra-large but fit like a medium.
I sat on a bench and watched ducks in the pond for an hour just to avoid going home.

I heard on a podcast that clinics might be sharing our health data with commercial weight-loss vendors for a profit. It gave me a deep feeling of unease about privacy, though I cannot remember the names of the companies involved.
The time I slipped on an icy sidewalk and completely wiped out, hoping nobody saw.
I remember the greasy, satisfying taste of a diner hash brown at three in the morning.
I accidentally liked a very old photo on the social media profile of someone I barely know.
I have a collection of loose change in a jar that must be worth at least fifty bucks by now.

My neighbor looked completely overwhelmed while trying to figure out the hidden costs and insurance rules for a diet program his doctor mentioned. I remember the stress on his face vividly, even though the exact details of the program went completely over my head.
I remember the intense heat radiating from the pavement during a July heatwave.
I tried drinking black coffee for a week but went right back to adding cream and sugar.
I went on a business trip to Chicago and spent the entire time in a windowless conference room.
I remember the weird popping sound my knee made when I stood up too fast.
I keep a spare tie in my desk drawer, though I haven't needed to wear one in years.
I accidentally dropped my keys down a storm drain and had to fish them out with a coat hanger.
I remember the loud, rhythmic thumping of the washing machine when the load got unbalanced.
I went to a concert recently and spent the whole time wishing I had brought earplugs.
I bought a houseplant that I swore I'd keep alive, but it died within a month.
I remember the specific crunch of autumn leaves under my boots on a neighborhood walk.
I always get the exact same haircut because I don't like having to explain what I want.
I stood in line at the DMV for three hours just to renew a sticker.
I cooked a massive pot of chili and ended up eating it for breakfast, lunch, and dinner.
I remember the sharp, stinging smell of the bleach I used to scrub my shower.
I found a twenty-dollar bill in a winter coat pocket from the previous year.
I regularly ignore phone calls from unknown numbers and never check the voicemails.
The feeling of crisp, new hotel sheets always makes me sleep incredibly well.
I remember the dusty smell of the attic when I went up to look for a suitcase.
I tried to assemble a barbecue grill in my backyard and lost my temper completely.
I always buy more groceries than I need, especially the junk food I crave late at night.
I remember the blinding flash of a traffic camera taking my picture when I ran a yellow light.
I sat in my parked car in the driveway for ten minutes just listening to the end of a radio show.
I had a favorite pen at work that someone stole, and I'm still quietly angry about it.
I remember the sweet, sticky mess of a melted candy bar I left in the center console of my car.
I bought a huge bag of ice melt and now it's just turning into a solid rock in the garage.
The zipper on my favorite winter coat broke, so now I just deal with the cold air seeping in.
I remember the sudden, jarring noise of the smoke detector going off because of burnt toast.
I watched a tutorial on how to fold a fitted sheet but gave up and just rolled it into a ball.
I got a bad case of food poisoning from a sketchy seafood buffet and swore off oysters forever.
I remember the slight hum of the fluorescent lights in the grocery store late at night.

A guy I met at a party seemed incredibly lonely when he talked about being left to manage his heavy weight all by himself after a doctor visit. I cannot recall his name at all, but his profound sense of abandonment struck a chord with my own private insecurities about my size.
I accidentally washed a red sock with my white shirts and just decided to wear pink undershirts.
I drove through a massive pothole and felt the impact rattle my teeth.
I remember the satisfying snap of breaking a fresh piece of celery in half.
I always sit in the same aisle seat on an airplane because I hate feeling trapped near the window.
Looking at a photo from college, I realized I haven't genuinely laughed like that in years.
I always buy books I never read, which I suppose is my way of trying to buy a more disciplined version of myself.
I remember the exact moment I stopped trying to lose weight in my thirties, feeling a strange mix of defeat and relief.
I tend to avoid mirrors at clothing stores, knowing that my self-image rarely matches reality.
Looking back on my twenties, I see now that I was pushing people away because I was terrified of being inadequate.
I find myself listening to the same music from high school, maybe because it makes me feel like my life is still ahead of me.
I realized recently that I enjoy being single mostly because it means I never have to explain my habits to anyone.
Sometimes I wonder if my career path was just the path of least resistance because I was too scared to take a risk.
I noticed that I always sit near the exit at parties, a habit I developed to ease my social anxiety.
Whenever I see guys my age playing basketball, I feel a pang of regret for letting my physical health slip.
I keep a box of old birthday cards in my closet, which proves I'm much more sentimental than I let on.
It dawned on me that I treat my dog better than I treat myself, which is both comforting and a little sad.

participants.persona: Tanya is a 36-year-old woman with some college or technical education, married or living with a partner, unemployed, and overweight.
participants.name: Tanya

memories.content: I remember my childhood home had a yellow door, or maybe it was just a faded white, but it always felt welcoming.
We had a dog named Buster when I was a kid, and I'm pretty sure he was a terrier mix.
My mom used to make this casserole on Tuesdays that was mostly cheese and maybe broccoli.
I broke my arm falling off a swing set in what I think was second grade.
I had a best friend named Sarah or Serena in elementary school, and we would trade stickers.
My dad bought a used Ford around 1999 that smelled intensely like stale cigarettes.
I remember the principal at my middle school had a really booming voice, Mr. Henderson maybe.
Looking back at my awkward middle school years makes me realize how desperate I was just to fit in with anyone.
I tried to learn the flute in band class, but I think I quit after a month because it was too hard.
My grandma would give me five dollar bills in my birthday cards, which felt like a fortune back then.
I got caught stealing a lip gloss from the drugstore when I was twelve and the shame still burns.
There was a summer we went to Florida, I think to Daytona, and it rained almost every single afternoon.

My old primary doctor, Dr. Harrison I think, just kept telling me to exercise more, but an endocrinologist I saw last spring actually mapped out a specific macro plan for me. It was such a relief to finally get actionable guidance on insulin resistance instead of vague advice.
I had a crush on a boy named Josh in 8th grade who wore the same oversized hoodie every day.
I failed a math test in freshman year, which started my lifelong belief that I'm just not a numbers person.
I used to hide in the library during lunch sometimes because I didn't have anyone to sit with.
It's funny how my teenage anxiety shaped so much of my personality, making me the quiet observer I am today.
I went to prom with a guy from my history class, maybe his name was Kevin, and the music was too loud.
I got my first job at a grocery store, I think it was called Food Lion or something similar.
The uniform for that grocery store was this awful polo shirt that was way too tight on my chest.
I remember passing my driving test on the second try because I messed up the parallel parking the first time.
I bought a CD with my first paycheck, probably something by Britney Spears or Christina Aguilera.
My high school graduation was mostly a blur of hot weather and uncomfortable shoes.
I enrolled in community college a year after high school to try and get an associate's degree.
I often wonder if I had gone straight to a four-year college, whether I would have more confidence in my intelligence now.
I took a psychology class where the professor, Dr. Allen I think, always wore these quirky bow ties.
I struggled with the reading assignments in college because I couldn't focus for more than ten minutes.
I worked part-time at a coffee shop during my classes, mostly just pulling espresso shots.
There was a regular customer who always tipped a dollar in quarters, though I forget his name.
I dropped out of my biology class because the lab work was just too overwhelming.
I switched to a medical assistant program thinking it would be a faster track to a real career.
I remember practicing drawing blood on a fake arm that looked incredibly unrealistic.
Realizing that I chose my classes based on what was easiest rather than what I wanted taught me how much I feared failure.
I made a friend named Jessica in the medical program who always shared her colorful pens with me.
We had to buy these specific white scrubs that showed every single stain imaginable.
I passed my certification exam, but I remember thinking the questions were nothing like what we studied.
My first medical billing job was at a chiropractor's office in a strip mall.
The office manager, maybe her name was Brenda, used to hover over my desk and breathe heavily.
I got fired from that job after six months because I kept messing up the insurance codes, which was humiliating.
I spent a few months just sleeping in until noon because I felt so useless.
Looking back on my early twenties, I can see how deeply depressed I was without even knowing the word for it.
I finally got another job at a dental clinic where the staff was much friendlier.
I used to bring leftover pizza for lunch almost every day because I didn't know how to cook.
I met my partner Marcus at a mutual friend's barbecue, though I don't remember whose house it was.
Marcus was wearing a band t-shirt, maybe AC/DC, and he laughed at one of my terrible jokes.
Our first date was at a Mexican restaurant where we ordered way too many chips and salsa.
I remember he spilled a little bit of margarita on his jeans but played it off like it was nothing.
We moved in together after about a year into this tiny apartment that had a leaky kitchen sink.
Moving in with him made me realize how fiercely I had been protecting my independence out of a fear of getting hurt.
We adopted a cat we named Luna, who was a stray Marcus found near his old job.
Luna used to sleep on my head, which was annoying but also kind of sweet.
I bought a slow cooker around 2012 and started trying to make stews, though most were too salty.
We went to a wedding for Marcus's cousin in Ohio, and I remember the hotel bed was incredibly hard.
I felt really self-conscious at that wedding because my dress was pulling at the seams.
I started noticing my weight creeping up in my late twenties, but I just kept buying larger scrub pants.
There was a time I tried doing Zumba from a DVD, but I gave up after I tripped over the coffee table.
My struggle with my weight often feels like a physical manifestation of my desire to just hide from the world.
The dental clinic I worked at got bought out by a big corporation, and the vibe completely changed.
They brought in a new manager who I think was named Todd, and he was obsessed with metrics.
I started getting stress headaches every Tuesday, probably because that was our staff meeting day.
Marcus and I took a weekend trip to a cabin once, but it rained so much we mostly just played cards.
We played Gin Rummy for hours, and I'm pretty sure I won almost every game.
I remember buying a pair of expensive boots on sale that I ended up wearing maybe twice.
I used to watch these home renovation shows every weekend while folding laundry.

My clinic tried to push me into a partnership program with some app like Noom or maybe Optavia, but I backed out when I read the privacy terms. I was really worried they were just going to sell my personal medical data to advertisers to make a profit.
Watching those pristine houses on TV always makes me reflect on how cluttered and chaotic my own mind feels.
We had a neighbor who played loud bass music at 2 AM, which drove Marcus absolutely crazy.

I was terrified to step on the scale at my 2021 checkup, but my nurse practitioner Sarah spoke to me with such genuine kindness and skipped the usual lecture. Her empathy made it so much easier for me to open up about my late-night eating without feeling attacked.
I tried to confront the neighbor once, but I got too nervous and just left a sticky note on his door instead.
I burned a Thanksgiving turkey one year because I set the oven to 450 instead of 350.
We ended up ordering Chinese food that Thanksgiving, and it actually tasted pretty good.
I got a gym membership around 2016 but only went to use the massage chairs.
I canceled the gym membership after realizing the front desk girl, maybe Chloe, was silently judging me.
I started experiencing a lot of back pain, probably from sitting at my desk all day at the clinic.
Being out of breath just from walking up a flight of stairs forces me to acknowledge how badly I've neglected my body.
I got laid off from the dental clinic last year when they decided to outsource the billing department.
I remember packing up my desk into a single cardboard box and feeling completely numb.
Applying for jobs online has been a nightmare because I can't remember all the software systems I used to know.
I had a phone interview a few months ago where I totally blanked on a basic customer service question.
Marcus has been really supportive about me being unemployed, but I know it stresses him out financially.
We had a huge argument about grocery bills last month where I ended up crying in the bathroom.
I started clipping coupons to save money, though I usually forget to bring them to the store.
My current joblessness has made me acutely aware of how much of my self-worth was tied to simply having a place to go every day.
I spend a lot of time scrolling through social media, looking at people from high school I haven't seen in fifteen years.
I saw that my old friend Sarah had a baby, but I didn't reach out because it felt too awkward.
I bought a bunch of houseplants thinking I would be good at taking care of them, but most of them died.
There's a pothos plant in the living room that has somehow survived my neglect.
I tried to knit a scarf once, using this chunky blue yarn I found at a craft store.
I dropped a bunch of stitches and it ended up looking like a weird triangle.
I've been watching daytime soap operas recently, which I never thought I would do.
Seeing the dramatic lives of TV characters makes me realize I actually prefer the boring predictability of my own life.
Marcus and I go to the local diner on Sunday mornings sometimes for pancakes.
I always order the blueberry pancakes, but I can never finish the whole plate.
I remember the waitress at the diner, a blonde woman, always calls us hon.
I avoided going to my ten-year high school reunion because I was too embarrassed about my weight.
I bumped into an old classmate at the grocery store once and pretended not to see her.
I have a habit of biting my nails whenever I have to make a phone call to a stranger.
I had a really bad toothache a few years ago that turned out to need a root canal.
My fear of the dentist is ironic given my old job, which just goes to show how disconnected I am from my own logic.
I remember the dental surgeon had really cold hands and smelled like peppermint.
I sometimes listen to true crime podcasts while I'm cleaning the apartment.
I used to love reading mystery novels, mostly James Patterson, but I haven't picked one up in years.
I bought a Kindle but forgot the charger somewhere on a trip to visit Marcus's parents.
Marcus's mom makes this really dry meatloaf that I always pretend to love.
His dad once made a comment about my portion size that I try to pretend didn't hurt my feelings.
We have a blue sofa in the living room that has a permanent dip on the side where I always sit.
Sitting in that same spot every day makes me hyper-aware of how stagnant my daily routines have become.
I tried a low-carb diet for a week but gave up because I was getting dizzy spells.
I used to go on evening walks, but I stopped because my knees would ache the next morning.
There's a park near our apartment that has a duck pond, though the ducks are pretty aggressive.
I fed the ducks some stale bread once and a goose actually chased me.
I remember crying in my car after getting rejected for a receptionist job I really needed.
The steering wheel of my old Honda felt sticky from the heat that day.
I have a collection of coffee mugs with funny sayings, mostly given to me as office gifts.
Looking at those mugs reminds me that my identity used to be defined by coworkers who barely knew me.
I once bought a really expensive blender thinking I'd make green smoothies every day.
The blender mostly just gathers dust on the counter now, next to the toaster.
Marcus bought me a silver necklace for our anniversary a couple of years ago that I wear all the time.
I lost the original clasp for it, so it's held together by a safety pin right now.
We watched a documentary about the ocean recently that made me terrified of deep water.
I went to the beach as a kid and got stung by a jellyfish, I think on my left ankle.
I vividly remember the smell of vinegar they poured on the sting to make it stop burning.
Recognizing how I avoid new experiences because of past pain makes me see how much I let fear control my life.
I have a scar on my chin from tripping over a vacuum cord when I was maybe four years old.
I used to color my hair blonde from a box, but it always turned out a little bit orange.
I decided to just let my natural brown hair grow out because the upkeep was too expensive.
I wear a lot of oversized sweaters because they make me feel hidden and safe.
I donated a bunch of clothes that didn't fit anymore to a charity bin in a parking lot.
I felt a weird pang of sadness leaving those clothes, like I was giving up on ever being that size again.
I tried to bake bread during the pandemic like everyone else, but my yeast was expired.
My failure to even bake a simple loaf of bread brought up a deep realization of how easily I give up when things go wrong.
We had a power outage that lasted two days, and we ate all the ice cream from the freezer so it wouldn't melt.
We lit these cheap vanilla candles that ended up giving me a terrible migraine.

When they referred me to the medical weight loss clinic over at Mercy Hospital, nobody could give me a straight answer about whether my husband's insurance would cover the mandatory meal replacements. I needed to know the exact out-of-pocket costs and the daily calorie formats before I could commit to anything.
I've watched the entire series of Friends at least four times through.
I always fall asleep on the couch around 10 PM and Marcus has to wake me up to go to bed.
My dreams are usually really chaotic, lots of being late for tests I haven't studied for.
I had a dream recently where I was running but my legs felt like they were moving through molasses.

I realized how deeply I had internalized shame about my body when Dr. Patel focused our conversation purely on improving my joint mobility instead of my clothing size. Looking back, having a doctor treat my weight as a medical factor rather than a moral failing completely changed my self-image.
I used to love the smell of rain on hot asphalt when I was younger.
Sometimes a random smell will trigger a memory, and I'm struck by how my brain holds onto things I thought I'd forgotten.
I bought a lottery ticket once on my birthday and won twenty dollars.
I used the winnings to buy a fancy coffee drink that I accidentally spilled in my cup holder.
I still haven't fully cleaned that cup holder, it's just a sticky mess in my car.
I sometimes write to-do lists that only have two things on them, just so I can cross them off.
I avoid looking in full-length mirrors because I don't want to see how my body has changed.
I had a panic attack in a dressing room at Target when I couldn't get a shirt over my shoulders.
A nice lady, maybe an employee, asked if I was okay through the door, but I just ignored her.
Experiencing that panic made me realize how completely disconnected my mental image of myself is from reality.
I keep a box of old greeting cards in the closet, though I never actually look at them.
My mom sent me a card for Valentine's Day once with a cat on it that looked exactly like Luna.
I lost touch with my mom for a few years in my twenties over a silly argument about money.
We reconnected when my dad got sick, but things have always felt a little strained since then.
My dad passed away around 2018, and I mainly remember the awful floral arrangements at the funeral.
I wore a black dress to the service that was too tight, and all I could think about was my discomfort.
I cried more in the car driving home than I did at the actual burial.
Grief has been such a strange process for me, forcing me to confront how often I bury my emotions instead of feeling them.
I inherited my dad's old watch, which sits in my jewelry box because it doesn't run anymore.
I tried taking it to a jeweler, but they said it would cost too much to fix the internal gears.
I used to love eating sour gummy worms at the movie theater.
I sneaked a whole bag of candy into a screening of some superhero movie in my purse once.
Marcus always gets popcorn with extra butter, which makes his hands incredibly greasy.
We saw a comedy last year that was so unfunny we actually walked out halfway through.
The theater lobby had this really garish neon carpet that gave me a headache.
Walking out of that movie made me reflect on how I'm finally learning to stop forcing myself to sit through things I hate.
I have a habit of apologizing for things that aren't even my fault.
A cashier bumped into my cart yesterday and I instantly said sorry before I even thought about it.
I used to drink diet soda constantly, maybe three or four cans a day.
I stopped because I read an article about artificial sweeteners that really freaked me out.
Now I just drink sparkling water, usually the lime flavor from the grocery store brand.
I accidentally bought the grapefruit flavor once and it tasted like soap.
I have a pair of fuzzy socks that I wear every night in the winter, even though they have a hole in the heel.
Clinging to small comforts like worn-out socks shows me how desperately I crave a sense of stability in my life.
I had a really bad sunburn on my shoulders during a trip to a lake, maybe Lake George, a few years ago.
Peeling the skin off my sunburn was gross but also weirdly satisfying.
We rented a paddleboat on that trip and I got exhausted after just five minutes of pedaling.
Marcus ended up doing most of the work to get us back to the dock.
I sometimes pretend to be asleep when Marcus gets out of bed early, just so I don't have to start my day yet.
I used to know how to do a French braid, but my fingers forgot the rhythm of it over time.
I tried to braid a friend's hair a while back and it just ended up a tangled mess.
Realizing I've forgotten skills I used to be proud of forces me to confront the reality of aging and lost time.
I have a tiny freckle on my left wrist that looks a bit like a star if you squint.
I check it sometimes to make sure it hasn't changed shape, because I'm a bit paranoid about health stuff.
My doctor told me my cholesterol was a bit high at my last physical, which I tried to brush off.
I remember the paper on the exam table crinkling really loudly whenever I shifted my weight.
The nurse who took my blood pressure had to use the extra-large cuff, which stung my pride a bit.
I bought some oat milk thinking I'd switch from dairy, but it just tasted like watery cardboard.
I always overwater the few plants that are still alive on my balcony.
My tendency to overcompensate with watering my plants mirrors how I try too hard to fix things when I feel guilty.
I got a jury duty summons last month and ended up sitting in a dreary waiting room for six hours.

I've always told my husband Mark that my obesity is a lifelong chronic issue, especially after I regained all the weight I lost back in 2016 or 2017. I specifically asked the clinic to help me build a long-term maintenance and relapse plan, because short-term diets just don't work for my body.
They dismissed my group before lunch, so I just went to a drive-thru and got a burger.
I ate the burger in my car while listening to the rain hit the windshield.
I remember having a favorite t-shirt in college that said something sarcastic, but I can't recall the exact phrase.
I used to sleep with my window open until a bat got into the apartment one summer.
Marcus chased the bat around with a broom for twenty minutes while I hid in the bathroom.
I bought a set of watercolor paints on clearance, thinking I'd pick up a new hobby.
Looking at those untouched paints reminds me of the person I always intend to be but never actually become.
I accidentally put salt in my coffee instead of sugar one morning when I was really groggy.
Taking that first sip of salty coffee was the rudest awakening I've ever had.

participants.persona: Leonard is a 52-year-old man with a college education, married or living with a partner, employed full-time, and overweight.
participants.name: Leonard

memories.content: I remember the smell of wet asphalt from playing basketball in the driveway after a summer storm. I couldn't make a shot to save my life, but the cool air felt amazing.
I recall sitting in the back of my dad's old station wagon, the vinyl seats sticking to my legs in the heat. Someone was singing on the radio, but I just watched the trees blur past.
I remember stealing a sip of beer from a can left on the patio table when I was about eight. It tasted like bitter metal, and I spat it out into the grass.
I have this vague memory of losing a tooth during a school assembly. I kept it in my pocket all day, terrified it would fall out through a hole in the fabric.
The anxiety of middle school gym class still sticks with me, especially having to take my shirt off for shirts and skins. I always felt like everyone was staring at my stomach.

I remember a guy at work venting that his doctor just told him to eat less and move more, which sounded like completely inadequate advice instead of a real clinical plan. I felt so frustrated just listening to his story, but I can't recall exactly when or where we were talking about it.
I remember the first time I saw the ocean on a family trip to Florida. The sheer roar of the waves was overwhelming, even if I don't remember much else about the vacation.
I recall my mother baking bread on Sunday mornings, the whole house smelling like yeast. I'd sit on the counter waiting for the first warm slice.
I broke my arm falling out of a tree in the woods behind our subdivision. The sharp snap is still vivid in my mind, though I don't remember how I got back to the house.
I remember hiding in my closet during a particularly bad argument between my parents. The muffled yelling made my stomach tie in knots.
I recall getting a huge stuffed bear at a carnival after tossing rings onto bottles. It took up half my bed for years until it gathered too much dust.
I remember the crushing disappointment of not making the varsity baseball team my sophomore year. I just sat on the bleachers alone for a long time after seeing the list.
I recall the smell of floor wax in the high school hallways on the first day of classes. It always meant summer was officially dead.
I remember my first kiss behind the bleachers during a football game. Her lips tasted like cherry lip balm, but I can't even remember who won the game.
Getting my driver's license was a massive relief, mostly because of the terrible photo. I remember gripping the wheel of my dad's sedan so hard my knuckles were white.
I remember the embarrassment of getting caught shoplifting a candy bar when I was twelve. The store owner called my dad, and the ride home was suffocatingly quiet.
I recall building a terrible wooden birdhouse in shop class that leaned entirely to the left. My mom still hung it in the yard, though no birds ever went near it.
I remember the intense static shock I got from touching the television screen in our living room. The little hairs on my arm stood up for minutes afterward.
I recall sitting in the dark playing early video games until my thumbs were blistered. The glowing pixels burned into my vision when I finally closed my eyes.
I have a memory of a childhood dog that we had to give away because he bit a neighbor. I remember crying into his fur before they took him, but his name escapes me now.
I remember the awful taste of liquid antibiotics when I had strep throat in fifth grade. It was supposed to be cherry flavored, but it tasted like chalk and chemicals.
Moving into my college dorm was a blur of cardboard boxes and nervous sweating. I remember the room smelling distinctly of stale beer and cheap cleaning products.
I recall an all-nighter in the library where the fluorescent lights started to hum loudly around 3 AM. I was drinking terrible black coffee out of a Styrofoam cup.
I remember the cold wind hitting my face walking across the quad during my freshman winter. I didn't own a heavy enough coat and just shivered the whole way to psychology class.
I recall eating awful dining hall pizza at midnight with a group of guys from my floor. The cheese was rubbery, but we were too hungry to care.
I remember the panic of waking up twenty minutes late for a final exam. I sprinted across campus in my sweatpants, heart pounding in my ears.
Looking back at my college years, I realize how much I used food as a crutch for my social anxiety. It's strange to recognize that habit started so early and never really left me.
I remember a college party where the floor was sticky with spilled beer and the bass vibrated in my chest. I stood in the corner most of the night, feeling out of place.
I recall the feeling of sheer relief when I handed in my senior thesis. The binder felt surprisingly light for something that caused me so much stress.
I remember a road trip with college friends where our car broke down on a desolate highway. We sat on the hood eating stale chips while waiting hours for a tow truck.
I recall the embarrassment of a professor calling on me when I had clearly fallen asleep in a lecture. I stammered out some nonsense while the whole room chuckled.
I remember the cheap, scratchy carpet in my first off-campus apartment. It was a terrible mustard yellow, but it was mine.
I recall buying groceries on a strict college budget, ending up with mostly instant noodles and peanut butter. The sodium gave me headaches, but it kept me full.

My wife was telling me about a health program that said being overweight is a chronic, lifelong disease requiring constant relapse planning. Hearing that gave me a heavy, sinking feeling in my stomach about my own body, even though I don't recall the specific medical terms she used.
I remember slipping on a patch of ice outside the science building and dropping all my notebooks. A stranger helped me gather the loose pages from the wet snow.
I recall the strange melancholy of graduation day, standing in a hot polyester gown. I couldn't find my parents in the crowd, and the sun was blinding.
I remember sneaking onto the roof of the library with a girl I was trying to impress. The view of the town was beautiful, though I was terrified of getting caught.
I recall failing my first mid-term and sitting in my car afterward, staring blankly at the steering wheel. It was the first time I realized I wasn't naturally smart enough to coast.
I remember a massive snowball fight on the main lawn that erupted out of nowhere. The cold snow melting down the back of my neck sent shivers down my spine.
I recall the distinct smell of old books in the basement aisles of the campus library. It was dusty, quiet, and strangely comforting.
I remember attending a campus concert where the band played so loud my ears rang for two days. The vibrations in the floorboards were more memorable than the music itself.
I recall packing up my car to leave college for the last time, the trunk barely closing. The drive home felt incredibly long and quiet.
I remember sweating profusely in my cheap suit during my first real job interview. The HR manager's office was sweltering, and I kept wiping my palms on my knees.
I recall the pride of cashing my first real paycheck and buying a ridiculously expensive steak dinner. It tasted incredible, mostly because I paid for it myself.
I remember a disastrous first date where I spilled red wine all over the tablecloth. The stain spread aggressively, and the rest of the evening was agonizingly awkward.
I recall my first apartment in the city, which was directly above a busy intersection. The constant honking kept me awake for the first month until it just became background noise.
I remember the exhaustion of working fifty-hour weeks and falling asleep on the couch in my work clothes. The TV would play infomercials into the early morning hours.
I recall my car getting towed because I misread the street signs on a Tuesday. The walk to the impound lot was freezing and miserable.
I remember meeting my wife for the first time at a mutual friend's barbecue. She laughed at a terrible joke I made, and I remember the way the evening sun caught her hair.
I recall buying an ill-fitting gym membership in my late twenties, trying to outrun my genetics. The smell of the locker room always made me slightly nauseous.
I remember getting passed over for a promotion I really thought I deserved. I nodded through the meeting, but my chest felt tight with humiliation.
I recall a spontaneous weekend trip to the mountains with some friends from work. The cabin smelled like pine and woodsmoke, and the air was perfectly crisp.
I remember the awkwardness of running into an ex-girlfriend at a grocery store. We stood by the produce section exchanging hollow pleasantries while my heart raced.
I recall buying a terrible used car that broke down three weeks after I got it. The plume of white smoke coming from the hood looked like a cartoon.
I remember cooking my first Thanksgiving turkey and leaving the plastic bag of giblets inside. The kitchen smelled like burnt plastic for days.
I recall the anxiety of meeting my partner's parents for dinner. I gripped my water glass so tightly I thought it might shatter in my hand.
I remember getting a terrible case of food poisoning from a downtown food cart. I spent two days on the bathroom floor, shivering and regretting my life choices.
I recall taking a terrible passport photo where I looked exhausted and heavy. I stared at it for a long time, realizing my metabolism had permanently slowed down.
I remember the first time I had to fire someone at work. My voice shook, and the silence in the room afterward felt suffocating.
I recall going to a batting cage to blow off steam after a tough week. The sting of the aluminum bat hitting the ball dead-on felt deeply satisfying.
I remember a massive power outage that plunged the whole city into darkness. I sat on my balcony watching the stars, which were suddenly visible above the skyline.
I recall the feeling of finally paying off my student loans in my early thirties. I clicked submit on the payment and just sat at my desk, feeling lighter.
I remember proposing on a surprisingly windy day at the park. The ring box nearly slipped out of my sweaty hands, but her crying made it perfect.
I recall our wedding day mostly as a series of camera flashes and tight hugs. The frosting on the cake was way too sweet, but I smiled through every bite.
I remember the chaos of moving into our first real house, navigating a couch up a narrow staircase. We eventually just left it halfway up and ordered a pizza.
I recall trying to paint our bedroom a calming blue, but it ended up looking like a nursery. The smell of fresh paint lingered for weeks.
I remember a massive argument we had over something stupid like folding towels. I sat on the edge of the bed afterward, the silence ringing in my ears.
I recall planting a tomato garden in the backyard that completely failed. The few tomatoes that grew were eaten by squirrels before we could pick them.
I remember the terror of a pipe bursting in the basement during a freeze. Wading through freezing water to find the shut-off valve was a nightmare.
I recall adopting a shelter cat that hid under the sofa for the first three weeks. The first time she finally hopped onto my lap, she purred like a motorboat.
I remember a road trip anniversary where it rained the entire drive up the coast. We couldn't see the ocean at all, just gray fog against the windshield.
I recall hosting a dinner party that was far too ambitious for my cooking skills. The roast was dry, but the wine flowed enough that no one seemed to care.
I remember waking up in the middle of the night to a strange noise downstairs. I grabbed a golf club and crept down, only to find the ice maker had cycled loudly.
Sometimes I look at how comfortable my life has become and I wonder if I traded my ambitions for security. It's a heavy thought that usually hits me during my morning commute.
I remember cleaning out the gutters on a rickety ladder and nearly losing my balance. The adrenaline spike left my hands shaking for twenty minutes.
I recall going to a couples' cooking class and failing miserably at making pasta from scratch. The dough was tough and chewy, but we laughed a lot.
I remember a phase where we tried to watch classic movies every Sunday night. Mostly, I just fell asleep halfway through to the sound of black-and-white dialogue.
I recall the anxiety of our first joint tax return, surrounded by receipts on the dining table. The sheer amount of paperwork made my head ache.
I remember assembling a massive bookshelf from a flat-pack box. My fingers were raw from the little hex wrench by the time it was standing.
I recall the power going out during a blizzard, wrapping ourselves in every blanket we owned. The house was dead quiet except for the wind howling against the siding.
I remember catching a terrible flu and my partner bringing me tea in bed. The steam felt good on my sinuses, even though my joints ached terribly.
I recall the satisfying crunch of raking the first big pile of autumn leaves in our yard. Of course, the wind immediately scattered them back across the grass.
I remember an endless strategy meeting where the projector kept turning off. The hum of the AC was the only thing keeping me from snapping at the presenter.
I recall spilling hot coffee on my tie right before a client presentation. I spent ten minutes scrubbing it in the men's room, leaving a massive wet spot.
I remember the smell of stale microwave popcorn that always hovered around the office breakroom. It was nauseatingly buttery.
I recall my daily commute being stuck in gridlock on the highway for over an hour. The red taillights stretching into the distance always felt incredibly depressing.
I remember a boss who used to tap his pen aggressively on the desk while I spoke. The sharp clicking sound made it impossible to focus on my thoughts.
I recall an office holiday party where a coworker drank too much and caused a scene. I stood by the appetizer table, trying to make myself invisible.

A buddy of mine was furious after a doctor relied on lazy stereotypes about his weight and totally ignored that his chronic joint pain keeps him from exercising. The look of deep anger on his face really stuck with me, even though I forget which clinic he actually went to.
I remember the strange quiet of the office when I had to come in on a Saturday. The fluorescent lights felt harsher without the usual background chatter.
I recall accidentally hitting 'reply all' on an email with a mildly sarcastic comment. The wave of panic when I realized my mistake was physically sickening.

I read on a message board that regular doctors almost never give you concrete weight-management tools like written plans, prescriptions, or gym support. I felt a sharp sense of disappointment scrolling through those posts, though I couldn't tell you who wrote them or what site it was.
I remember receiving a modest bonus and using it to buy a new recliner. Sinking into that leather chair after a long week was pure bliss.
I recall the ergonomic assessment guy telling me my desk setup was ruining my posture. Adjusting the chair height made my knees ache for a week.
I remember a massive server crash that wiped out an entire morning's worth of my work. I just stared at the blue screen, totally deflated.
I recall a forced team-building exercise involving a ropes course in the woods. Being heavy and suspended in a harness was one of the most undignified experiences of my life.
I remember the bittersweet feeling of a favorite colleague leaving for a new job. We had a cheap sheet cake in the breakroom, and it tasted like cardboard.
I recall the anxiety of annual performance reviews, sitting across from a stoic manager. My mouth always went dry when they read from their notes.
I remember finding a great little deli near the office that sold incredible pastrami sandwiches. The salty, fatty meat was the highlight of my workweek.
I recall getting stuck in the elevator with a senior executive for ten minutes. We made agonizing small talk about the weather until the doors finally pried open.
I remember changing my desktop background to a picture of a beach I'd never been to. I'd stare at it during conference calls just to zone out.
I recall the frantic rush to finish end-of-year reports before the holiday break. My eyes burned from staring at spreadsheets for nine hours straight.
I remember a day when the fire alarm went off and we all had to stand outside in the freezing rain. The damp cold seeped right through my slacks.
I recall taking a sick day when I wasn't really sick, just completely burned out. I sat on the couch watching daytime television, feeling guilty but relieved.
I remember stepping on the scale at the doctor's office and seeing the number pass 250 for the first time. The nurse wrote it down without a word, but my face flushed hot.
I recall trying a low-carb diet and feeling completely exhausted by day three. The headache was blinding, and all I could think about was a slice of bread.
I remember the frustration of trying to buy a suit and none of the standard sizes fitting my waist. The tailor had a measuring tape that felt a mile long.
I recall the sharp pain in my lower back that started after helping a friend move a sofa. It became a constant, dull ache that I just learned to live with.
I remember a doctor telling me my cholesterol was borderline high and handing me a generic pamphlet. The glossy paper felt useless against years of bad habits.
I realize now that I avoid looking in mirrors below my chest to protect my ego from how much my body has changed. It's a quiet sort of denial that I've perfected over the last decade.
I recall sweating through a t-shirt on a mildly warm day, acutely aware of the dark patches under my arms. I kept my arms pinned to my sides for hours.
I remember the embarrassment of breaking a cheap lawn chair at a family barbecue. The plastic snapped loudly, and I scrambled up as fast as I could.
I recall joining a gym and feeling like everyone on the treadmills was judging my pace. The air was thick with the smell of rubber mats and sweat.
I remember throwing out an entire pantry of junk food in a sudden fit of motivation. Three days later, I was back at the grocery store buying the exact same chips.
I recall the heavy, breathless feeling in my chest after climbing three flights of stairs when the elevator was broken. I had to pretend I was admiring a painting to catch my breath.
I remember the cold gel the technician used during an ultrasound on my liver. The dark room and the rhythmic clicking of the machine made me terribly anxious.
I recall a brief period where I tried jogging in the mornings, the pavement slamming brutally into my knees. The crisp morning air was nice, but the pain wasn't worth it.
I remember buying a blood pressure cuff for the house and the tight squeezing sensation on my arm. The velcro sound always made my heart rate jump right before it measured.
I recall my wife gently suggesting we start cooking healthier dinners together. Her tone was kind, but it stung my pride more than I admitted.
I remember the awful chalky taste of a barium swallow during a gastric test. I had to choke it down while standing in front of a massive x-ray machine.
I recall a phase of blending kale and spinach into smoothies that tasted like lawn clippings. I'd pinch my nose and drink them out of sheer stubbornness.
I remember the relief of taking my shoes off after a long day, my feet swollen and aching. The cold hardwood floor was incredibly soothing on my arches.
I recall a minor surgery to remove a cyst on my back, waking up to the harsh fluorescent lights of recovery. My mouth tasted like gauze and dry air.
I remember finding an old photograph of myself in my twenties and being shocked at how thin my face was. It felt like looking at a completely different person.
I remember trying to build a model airplane on the dining table, my thick fingers fumbling with the tiny decals. The superglue stuck my thumb and index finger together.
I recall a weekend trip to a lake where we rented a small aluminum boat. The outboard motor smelled strongly of gasoline, and the water was like glass.
I remember taking up photography for about a month, lugging a heavy camera around the neighborhood. I mostly just took blurry pictures of stray cats.

I recall my neighbor complaining that no one explained how her daily medications might cause weight gain or interact with her other health conditions. It was really unsettling to realize doctors leave people in the dark like that, though I don't remember the exact name of the pills she took.
I recall a disastrous camping trip where the tent leaked during a sudden thunderstorm. We spent the night huddled in the car, eating damp graham crackers.
I remember a phase of brewing my own beer in the garage, the whole place smelling like boiling malt. The first batch was violently over-carbonated and exploded when opened.
I recall spending hours browsing the aisles of a hardware store on Saturday mornings. The smell of cut lumber and fertilizer was oddly comforting to me.
I remember a vacation to Vegas where the flashing lights and cigarette smoke gave me a massive headache. The endless ringing of the slot machines felt inescapable.
I recall attending a classic car show in the peak heat of August. The sun glaring off the chrome bumpers practically blinded me, but the engines sounded beautiful.
I remember a weekend spent entirely on the couch binging a historical documentary series. The narrator's deep voice kept lulling me into short naps.
I recall going deep-sea fishing and getting horribly seasick on the swells. I spent hours staring at the horizon, praying for solid ground.
I remember trying to learn the acoustic guitar, my callouses building up thick on my left hand. I could never get the F-chord right without muting the strings.
I recall a trip to a history museum where the air conditioning was turned up way too high. I shivered through the WWII exhibit wishing I'd brought a sweater.
I remember spending an entire afternoon washing and waxing the car until my shoulders burned. The deep shine on the hood was incredibly satisfying, at least until it rained the next day.
I recall attending a local baseball game and catching a foul ball on a lucky bounce. The rough leather felt great in my hand, and I kept it on my desk for years.
I remember a miserable round of golf where I lost six balls in the water hazards. The sweltering humidity made my polo shirt cling uncomfortably to my back.
I recall going to an antique store with my wife and knocking over a dusty lamp. The sharp crash made my heart stop, though the owner was surprisingly forgiving.
I remember a hike in a national park that was significantly steeper than the brochure promised. The view at the top was stunning, but my calves cramped all night.
I recall trying to set up a complicated surround sound system in the living room. There was a rat's nest of speaker wire behind the TV that I never quite managed to hide.
I remember a beach vacation where the sand somehow got into my luggage and stayed there for years. The gritty texture would appear in my clothes long after the trip.
I recall staying at a bed and breakfast with terrible floral wallpaper that made me dizzy. The floorboards creaked so loudly I was afraid to get up for a glass of water.
I remember the deep frustration of trying to fix a running toilet at 2 AM. The cold water numbed my hands, and the rubber flapper refused to seal properly.
I recall a neighbor who would mow his lawn every Sunday at 7 AM on the dot. The roar of the engine vibrating through my bedroom walls drove me absolutely insane.
I remember the sheer panic of seeing a mouse scurry across the kitchen floor. I bought a dozen traps the next day, though I never actually caught it.
I recall replacing the brake pads on my car in the driveway during a hot afternoon. The metallic dust coated my fingers, and I busted my knuckles on the wrench.
I remember an awkward confrontation with a neighbor over tree branches hanging into our yard. We both stood stiffly by the fence, trying to be polite while quietly fuming.
I recall the smell of ozone when the central AC unit finally blew a capacitor. The house became unbearably stuffy within hours.
I remember planting a row of hedges in the front yard that immediately turned brown and died. Pulling up the dead roots the next spring was incredibly demoralizing.
I recall a heavy snowstorm where I had to shovel the driveway three times in one day. The cold air burned my lungs, and my lower back seized up entirely.
I remember finding a leak in the roof by stepping in a puddle in the living room. Staring up at the brown water stain on the ceiling filled me with dread.
I recall the terrifying thud of a bird hitting the picture window in the dining room. I went outside and found a stunned robin sitting in the mulch.
I remember repainting the front door a bright red that turned out entirely too vibrant. It looked like a fire engine, but we were too tired to paint it again.
I recall the jarring noise of the garbage truck backing up every Thursday morning. The hydraulic whine always penetrated right through my morning grogginess.
I remember trying to patch a hole in the drywall left by a doorknob. My patching job was lumpy and obvious, a permanent reminder of my lack of handy skills.
I recall the anxiety of a strange car parked in front of our house for three days. I kept peering through the blinds like a paranoid old man until it finally drove away.
I remember the sharp crack of a windshield getting hit by a pebble on the freeway. The tiny starburst crack eventually spread entirely across the driver's side.
I recall cleaning out the garage and finding a box of old VHS tapes melting in the heat. The black plastic was warped and completely useless.
I remember a block party where I was forced to make small talk with people I barely recognized. I stood by the cooler holding a lukewarm soda for hours.
I recall replacing a dead battery in the smoke detector at midnight, standing on a wobbly chair. The piercing chirp had been driving me crazy for hours.
I remember the dread of opening the mail and finding a massive property tax reassessment. The thick envelope felt heavy in my hands.
I recall dropping a glass jar of pasta sauce in the driveway, red shards exploding everywhere. Hosing down the concrete while mosquitoes bit my ankles was miserable.
I remember the first bite of a perfectly cooked medium-rare steak at a high-end restaurant. The butter and garlic flavor melting on my tongue was unforgettable.
I recall a terrible dinner at a chain restaurant where the chicken was completely rubbery. I chewed the same bite for what felt like minutes before wrapping it in a napkin.
I remember the overwhelming smell of a seafood market by the pier. The icy, fishy air stuck in my nostrils long after we drove away.
I recall the guilty pleasure of eating an entire sleeve of chocolate chip cookies while watching late-night TV. The sugar rush kept me awake, and the crumbs were everywhere.
I remember trying a notoriously spicy hot sauce on a dare at a barbecue. My lips burned for an hour, and my eyes wouldn't stop watering.
I recall the comforting warmth of a bowl of split pea soup on a freezing January evening. The thick, salty broth warmed me right down to my toes.
I remember grocery shopping on a Sunday afternoon, the store packed shoulder-to-shoulder. The screeching wheel of my shopping cart drove me crazy down every aisle.
I recall biting into an apple that looked perfect but was completely mealy inside. The dry, soft texture made my skin crawl, and I threw the rest away.
I remember a phase where I ate a bowl of sugary cereal every night before bed. The cold milk and artificial sweetness became a hard habit to break.
I recall trying sushi for the first time and being deeply suspicious of the raw tuna. The sharp hit of wasabi cleared my sinuses instantly.
I remember the disappointment of dropping a fresh ice cream cone on the sidewalk. The swirl of vanilla smeared into the hot pavement in a sad puddle.

I heard on a radio show that patients feel a massive boost in confidence and motivation to try a weight-loss program when a physician explicitly approves it. That idea felt incredibly uplifting to hear, even if I have no idea who the guest expert on the station was.
I recall the metallic taste of cheap canned chili heated up on a camp stove. It was greasy and salty, but out in the cold, it tasted fantastic.
I remember waiting for a table at a crowded brunch spot for nearly two hours. By the time my eggs Benedict arrived, I was too irritated to enjoy it.
I recall the smell of roasting garlic filling the kitchen when my wife made her grandmother's pasta recipe. It’s a scent that always makes a house feel like home to me.
I remember the awful texture of a protein bar that tasted like sweet chalk and cardboard. I had to wash every bite down with a huge gulp of water.
I recall discovering a local bakery that made massive, gooey cinnamon rolls. The glaze would stick to my fingers and beard, but they were worth the mess.
I remember trying to flip a pancake in the air and having it land directly on the stovetop burner. The smell of burning batter filled the kitchen in seconds.
I recall a terrible potluck dinner at work where someone brought a bizarre gelatin salad. I took one polite bite and discreetly scraped the rest into the trash.
I remember the sharp fizz of a perfectly chilled cola after a long day of yard work. The carbonation burned the back of my throat in the best possible way.
I recall buying expensive imported cheese that smelled intensely like dirty feet. I tried to appreciate it, but honestly, it was nauseating.
I remember finding my first real cluster of gray hairs in my beard while shaving. The silver caught the bathroom light, making me realize how quickly time was passing.
I recall reading the newspaper on my tablet and realizing I needed to increase the font size. My eyes strained terribly against the bright screen.
I remember a quiet Sunday morning drinking coffee on the porch, watching the fog lift off the grass. The stillness of the neighborhood was deeply peaceful.
I recall the stiffness in my knees when I tried to sit cross-legged on the floor with my niece. I had to awkwardly roll onto my side just to stand back up.
I remember going to a high school reunion and hardly recognizing anyone. The room smelled of cheap cologne and the desperate need to impress.
I recall a recent trip to the dentist where the drill vibrated uncomfortably in my jaw. The harsh light in my eyes gave me a lingering headache.
I remember watching a thunderstorm roll in from the west, the sky turning a bruised purple. The sudden drop in temperature felt electric against my skin.

Looking back at the arc of my life, I'm struck by how ordinary it all is, and yet how exhausting the ordinary can be. It's a humbling realization that I'm just a background character in the grand scheme.
I recall a moment of pure panic when I couldn't find my wallet at the grocery checkout. The heat rose in my face until I realized it was in my other jacket pocket.
I remember the smell of an old leather jacket I pulled out of storage for winter. It smelled like dust and a decade of forgotten cold mornings.
I recall listening to a podcast about history during a long drive and zoning out entirely. The monotone voice blurred into the hum of the tires on the asphalt.
I remember the frustration of trying to remember a password I use all the time, my mind completely blank. I just stared at the blinking cursor, feeling inexplicably old.
I recall a beautiful sunset last autumn where the clouds looked like they were on fire. I stopped the car just to watch it fade into dusk.
I remember waking up from a dream I couldn't remember, feeling a profound sense of sadness. The feeling lingered over my morning coffee like a heavy fog.

participants.persona: Denise is a 40-year-old woman with some college or technical education, married or living with a partner, unemployed, and overweight.
participants.name: Denise

memories.content: I remember the smell of my grandmother's house, it was like stale mints and old paper.
I was at a birthday party in elementary school and felt a sudden wave of panic, though I don't know why.
The carpet in my childhood bedroom was a rough brown shag that always scratched my knees.

When I saw the hormone specialist last year, she actually gave me a meal plan I could follow, unlike my regular doctor who just always says to eat less. I remember feeling so relieved that someone finally gave me actual steps instead of just a lecture.
Someone yelled at me for dropping a glass of milk, but I can't picture their face.
I remember the bright neon colors of my favorite windbreaker from middle school.
I felt so embarrassed trying on bathing suits at the mall with my mom.
There was a stray cat I used to feed, but I don't remember what happened to it.
I remember the overwhelming smell of chlorine at the public pool during summer breaks.
I got caught lying about my homework once and my stomach dropped to the floor.
I remember loving the taste of those cheap frozen pizzas we had on Friday nights.
I used to hide in the closet when my parents argued, though I couldn't hear the actual words they said.
I remember the exact shade of purple of my first CD player.
I felt a deep sting of rejection when a group of girls walked away from me at lunch.
I remember the soft, squishy feeling of mud between my toes at a summer camp.
Someone made a comment about my chubby cheeks and it made me want to cry.
I remember the heavy weight of my backpack in high school making my shoulders ache.
I failed a math test and hid the paper under my mattress for weeks.
I loved the smell of rain on the hot pavement during summer thunderstorms.
I was sitting in the back of a car when a song I loved came on, but I don't know whose car it was.
I remember the sharp pinch of getting my ears pierced at the mall kiosk.
I bought a pair of jeans that were too tight just because they were on sale.
I remember the blinding fluorescent lights in the high school cafeteria.
A boy I liked looked at me in the hallway and my face flushed intensely.
I used to eat lunch in the library sometimes just to avoid the crowded tables.
The nurse practitioner at the walk-in clinic told me to just go jogging, acting like I was just lazy. She didn't even listen when I tried to explain how bad my knees hurt when I stand for too long.
I remember the rough texture of the steering wheel during my first driving lesson.

My husband and I were talking about how my weight keeps yo-yoing no matter what I try. I just wish I had some kind of ongoing support program because keeping the weight off feels like a battle I will be fighting forever.
I got a terrible sunburn on my shoulders that blistered and peeled for days.
I remember the deafening bass at a concert I went to, though I forget the band's name.
I felt incredibly guilty after sneaking out, even though I didn't get caught.
I remember the sweet, artificial taste of blue raspberry slushies from the gas station.
I had a diary with a tiny lock on it that I eventually threw away.
