Dr. Sarah was the first doctor who didn't make me feel ashamed about my size when I went in for a checkup. Because she was so gentle and actually listened, I finally felt okay talking to her about how much I struggle with my eating habits.
I remember the heavy feeling of exhaustion after my first shift working retail.
I started community college and felt completely lost trying to find my classrooms.
I remember the smell of burnt coffee in the student lounge.
Looking back, I realize my habit of dropping classes was just a way to avoid the fear of failing them.
I wore a very unflattering dress to a friend's wedding because it was the only one that fit.
I remember the thrill of depositing my first real paycheck into my bank account.
I had a massive argument with a roommate over dirty dishes, but the exact words are a blur.
I loved driving around at night with the windows down, feeling the cool air.
I failed my medical terminology final and cried in my car for an hour.
I remember the sticky floors at the movie theater where I used to work.
I felt a surge of pride when I finally passed my certification exam.
I remember sitting in a stiff plastic chair during a long lecture, my back aching.
I ate fast food in my car almost every day between classes.
A professor told me I needed to apply myself more, which felt like a punch to the gut.
I remember the sound of the heavy textbook slamming shut when I finally finished studying.
I went to a party and felt completely invisible standing in the corner.
I bought a cheap laptop that constantly overheated and burned my thighs.
I remember the sharp smell of hand sanitizer in the clinical practice rooms.
I felt a deep sense of dread every time I had to check my student loan balance.
I remember laughing so hard with a classmate that I snorted, though I forget her name now.
I remember the cramped feeling of my first cubicle, surrounded by gray fabric walls.
I spilled coffee on a stack of important invoices and panicked.
I loved the quiet hum of the office before everyone else arrived in the morning.
My boss gave me a disappointed look during a meeting that made my stomach churn.
I remember the satisfying click of the keyboard when I was typing really fast.
I hid in the bathroom stall to cry after a customer yelled at me over the phone.
I used to buy a sugary pastry from the lobby cafe every single morning.
I remember the harsh glare of the monitor giving me terrible tension headaches.
I felt so relieved when Friday afternoon finally rolled around each week.
I threw away my packed lunch and bought a greasy burger instead, feeling guilty afterward.

A doctor recommended a weight loss clinic once, but he didn't tell me anything about how much it would cost or if my insurance would cover it since I am out of work. I didn't even bother calling them because I was so stressed about hidden fees and what the diet actually involved.
I remember the nervous fluttering in my chest before my first date with my partner.
We sat in a dark booth at a restaurant, but I don't remember what we ate.
I felt self-conscious about my weight when we first started getting intimate.
I remember the warm, heavy weight of his arm around my shoulders.
We got into a silly fight over a movie choice that escalated into shouting.
I remember the smell of his cologne on my jacket the next day.
I felt a profound sense of safety the first time we fell asleep beside each other.
We bought a cheap, lumpy mattress for our first apartment together.
I remember the excitement of unpacking boxes in our new living room.
I accidentally burned dinner and we had to order pizza in defeat.
I remember the frustrating sound of him snoring when I was trying to sleep.
We adopted a plant that I immediately forgot to water until it died.
I felt a sharp pang of jealousy when he mentioned a female coworker, though it was silly.
I remember the soft glow of the television lighting up the living room late at night.
We had a beautiful day walking in a park, though I can't recall what season it was.
I found an old photo of myself and felt sad about how much my body has changed.
I remember the comforting smell of garlic and onions cooking in our kitchen.
We had a serious talk about our finances that left me feeling completely drained.
I remember the cold tile floor against my bare feet in our bathroom.
I hid some credit card debt from him for a few months because I was ashamed.
I remember the tense, suffocating silence in the room when HR called me in.
I felt a cold rush of adrenaline when they told me my position was eliminated.
I carried my things out in a cardboard box, feeling everyone staring at me.
I remember the strange, hollow feeling of waking up on Monday with nowhere to go.
I spent hours scrolling through job boards until all the words blurred together.
I had a phone interview where I stuttered terribly and knew I ruined it.
I remember the frustration of filling out endless online application forms.
I felt a deep, heavy exhaustion even though I hadn't left the house all day.
I ignored a call from a debt collector and felt a knot form in my stomach.
I remember the harsh sunlight glaring through the blinds while I sat on the couch.
I ate a whole bag of chips for lunch because I didn't have the energy to cook.
I remember the soft, worn fabric of the sweatpants I wear almost every day now.
I felt a surge of resentment when my partner asked what I did all day.
I watched three episodes of a daytime talk show, just letting the noise fill the room.
I remember the dull ache in my lower back after sitting in the same chair for hours.
I looked in the hallway mirror and immediately looked away in disgust.
I felt a brief moment of peace watering the few houseplants that are still alive.
I remember the loud, startling rattle of the mail carrier dropping off the post.
I avoided checking my email because I couldn't handle another rejection message.
It occurs to me that I use television not just for entertainment, but to completely numb my anxiety about the future.
I remember the tight, restrictive feeling of the blood pressure cuff at the doctor's office.
The doctor suggested I lose weight, and I just nodded silently while my face burned.
I felt a sharp pain in my knee when walking up the stairs carrying groceries.
I remember the comforting warmth of a heating pad on my stomach during bad cramps.
I tried to go for a jog but gave up after one block because I couldn't catch my breath.
I remember the sweet, chalky taste of antacids I take before bed.
I felt a deep sense of shame stepping on the scale at the gym.
I remember the soft, cooling sensation of lotion on dry winter skin.
I had a terrible migraine that made the sunlight pouring in feel like daggers.
I bought a new dress in a larger size and cried in the fitting room.
I remember the rich, decadent smell of brownies baking in the oven.
I ate a piece of cake in secret so my partner wouldn't judge me.
I loved the satisfying crunch of fresh celery, even though I rarely eat it.
I felt a rush of comfort biting into a warm, buttery roll at a restaurant.
I remember the sharp, acidic burn of hot sauce on a taco.
I threw out a carton of expired milk and hated the sour smell it left in the sink.
I stress-ate an entire pint of ice cream while watching the news.
I remember the chaotic sizzling sound of bacon frying in a hot pan.
I drank a glass of cheap wine that tasted incredibly bitter but drank it anyway.
I felt immensely proud of myself for cooking a complex recipe without messing it up.
I remember the awkward silence when an old friend asked where I was working.
I canceled plans with a group of girls because I felt too tired to pretend I was happy.
I heard a loud, genuine belly laugh from someone at the grocery store that made me smile.
I felt completely out of place at a neighbor's barbecue.
I remember the warm hug a friend gave me when my grandmother passed away.
I got into a debate about politics with a relative and felt my chest tighten with anger.
I remember the bright, flashing lights of a bowling alley during a rare night out.
I sent a text message to someone and felt intensely anxious waiting for their reply.
I was invited to a baby shower and bought a gift I couldn't really afford.
I remember the smell of stale beer and perfume at a crowded local bar.
I felt a surge of road rage when a large truck cut me off on the highway.
I remember the hypnotic rhythm of the windshield wipers during a heavy rainstorm.
I panicked when the check engine light flickered on my dashboard.
I remember the frustratingly long line at the DMV and the hard plastic chairs.
I drove through my old neighborhood and felt a strange pang of nostalgia.
I struggled to squeeze out of my car in a tight parking spot, feeling embarrassed.
I remember the crisp, cold air hitting my face when leaving the grocery store.
I forgot my reusable bags in the trunk and felt irrationally annoyed with myself.
I accidentally left the headlights on and drained the battery, leaving me stranded.
I remember the rhythmic thumping of the tires driving over a bridge expansion joint.
I remember the dreaded sound of a declined credit card beep at the pharmacy.
I felt a wave of nausea looking at the final total of our utility bill.
I rolled coins from a jar to pay for gas and hoped the cashier wouldn't judge me.
I remember the crisp feel of a twenty-dollar bill I found in an old winter coat.
I argued with a customer service rep over a late fee until my voice shook.
I put back a block of nice cheese at the store because it was three dollars too expensive.
I felt deeply ashamed when we had to ask my parents for a loan to cover rent.
I remember the messy pile of unopened bills sitting on the kitchen counter.
I tried to balance my checkbook but gave up when the numbers wouldn't align.
Seeing how often I avoid opening the mail makes me realize I've developed a deep phobia of financial reality.
I woke up from a nightmare with a racing heart, though the dream faded instantly.
I remember the soft, heavy warmth of a weighted blanket over my chest.
I lay awake for hours staring at the ceiling, my mind racing with worries about money.
I remember the piercing shriek of the alarm clock jolting me out of a deep sleep.
I felt a sudden, inexplicable chill in the middle of the night and shivered violently.
I stumbled to the bathroom in the dark and stubbed my toe hard on the doorframe.
I remember the peaceful quiet of the house at 3 AM when everyone else was asleep.
I woke up sweating through my pajamas and had to change them in the dark.
I heard a strange creaking noise in the hallway that made me hold my breath in fear.
I remember the blinding sliver of morning sunlight peeking through the curtains.
I remember the crisp, bitter smell of autumn leaves burning in someone's yard.
I slipped on a patch of black ice and scraped my hands raw trying to catch my fall.
I felt the oppressive, suffocating humidity of an August afternoon sticking my shirt to my back.
I remember the vibrant, almost neon green of the grass after a heavy spring rain.
I watched large, fluffy snowflakes fall silently under the glow of a streetlamp.
I felt a gentle, warm breeze brush past my face while sitting on the porch.
I remember the deafening crack of thunder that rattled the windows during a storm.
I got soaked in a sudden downpour because I couldn't run to the car fast enough.
I remember the sharp crunch of dry autumn leaves beneath my boots.
I felt a wave of seasonal sadness when the sun started setting before dinner time.
I dropped a brand-new bottle of foundation on the bathroom floor and it shattered everywhere.
I remember the intense satisfaction of peeling the protective film off a new TV screen.
I tore a hole in my favorite leggings and felt completely defeated by it.
I remember the annoying, constant drip of a leaky faucet we couldn't afford to fix.
I found a perfectly ripe avocado at the store and it made me weirdly happy.
I burned my tongue on hot soup and couldn't taste anything else for two days.
I remember the sharp, stinging paper cut I got from an envelope edge.
I felt a brief moment of pride when I finally managed to fold a fitted sheet perfectly.
I couldn't find my keys for twenty minutes and ended up screaming in frustration.
I remember the soft, purring vibration of a neighbor's cat rubbing against my leg.
I stayed up way too late reading a thriller novel because my anxiety wouldn't let me sleep.
I remember the loud, dramatic music from a soap opera my mom used to watch.
I bought a bunch of knitting supplies and abandoned the project after one messy scarf.
I felt a deep emotional connection to a movie character that made me cry in the theater.
I remember the bright, colorful interface of a silly phone game I play for hours.
I tried to follow a makeup tutorial but ended up looking like a clown, which made me feel awful.

I asked my doctor if my daily medications were making me gain weight, but he just brushed my question off. I really needed him to explain how my pills and my asthma actually affect my size instead of just telling me to move around more.
I remember the musty smell of old pages in a secondhand bookstore.
I scrolled through social media looking at happy couples and felt a pang of intense loneliness.
I remember the catchy, repetitive chorus of a pop song from the early 2000s.
I realize my tendency to abandon hobbies comes from a deep-seated fear that I'm not naturally talented at anything.
I stepped in a deep puddle and had to sit with a freezing, wet sock for hours.
I remember the satisfying snap of breaking off a piece of dark chocolate.
I accidentally sent a text complaining about someone to that exact person and panicked.
I remember the dim, orange glow of the streetlights outside my window when I lived in my first apartment.

participants.persona: Melissa is a 38-year-old woman with a college education, separated, employed part-time, and very overweight.
participants.name: Melissa

memories.content: I remember my third-grade teacher, Mrs. Higgins or maybe Hodges, had a jar of jellybeans on her desk. I think I won it once by guessing the amount, though it might have been my sister who actually won it.
We went to a beach in Florida when I was around eight, and I am pretty sure it rained the entire time.
Dave and I decided to take a break around October of last year, or maybe it was November. I just remember it was getting cold and the heating bill was due.
Looking back at how much I ate in high school, I realize I was already using food to cope with my parents fighting. It makes me sad to think my relationship with my body was broken that early.
My mom bought me a bright yellow raincoat that I absolutely hated, probably around fifth grade. I remember deliberately leaving it on the school bus so I would not have to wear it.
I broke my arm falling off a swing set, though I can never remember if it was my left or right arm until I look for the tiny scar.
There was a stray cat that lived under our porch in the late 90s. I called him Whiskers, but I think my dad ended up taking him to the shelter.
I sometimes wonder if I exaggerate how strict my father was, because my sister remembers him as being completely laid back. Human memory is so strange that way.
My first job was at a frozen yogurt place when I was sixteen or seventeen. I spilled an entire tub of strawberry syrup on my first day.
I used to hide in the school library during lunch because I didn't have many friends in ninth grade. It was deeply lonely, but I told myself I just liked reading.
We had a family dog named Buster who ran away during a thunderstorm. I am pretty sure it was the summer before I started high school.
I won a spelling bee in elementary school with the word chrysanthemum, or maybe it was rhythm. I just remember feeling incredibly proud for a few minutes.
I tried out for the school play in tenth grade but froze completely during the audition. I think I was supposed to read a monologue from Our Town.
Whenever I smell cheap vanilla perfume, I am instantly transported back to the girls locker room in middle school. It is funny how a simple scent can carry so much emotional baggage.

I vaguely recall a doctor, maybe Dr. Smith, just waving his hand and telling me to watch my carbs back in 2018 or so. It felt like a brush-off, not a real medical plan that I could actually follow to get healthy.
My grandmother used to bake these incredible molasses cookies, though I have never been able to find a recipe that tastes even remotely similar.
I had braces for three years, and I vaguely recall getting them off right before prom.
I remember watching the ball drop on New Year's Eve in 2000 and feeling disappointed that the world did not end. I think I was at my friend Sarah's house.
I got caught shoplifting a lip gloss when I was fourteen, which was mortifying. My mom yelled at me the whole drive home, but I cannot remember what she actually said.
There was a local park with a huge wooden playground structure that felt like a castle. I am pretty sure they tore it down in the early 2000s for safety reasons.
I realize now that my obsession with boy bands was just a safe way to experience romance without any real-world risk. I guess I was always a bit afraid of getting close to people.
I bought a CD with my own money for the first time at a mall in maybe 1997. It was probably something embarrassing like Hanson or the Spice Girls.
My childhood bedroom had pink floral wallpaper that I eventually covered completely with magazine cutouts. I think I used scotch tape and ruined the walls.
I failed my driving test the first time because I parallel parked too far from the curb. The instructor's name was Mr. Miller, or something starting with an M.
I went to a summer camp for a few weeks where we slept in cabins that smelled like mildew. I faked a stomach ache to go home early.

Looking back at when I started gaining weight around puberty, I realize how much my aunt's passive-aggressive comments shaped my lifelong self-hatred. It is awful how someone's careless words become your internal monologue.
We took a field trip to a natural history museum, and I spent all my money in the gift shop on shiny rocks.
I think I had a diary with a little padlock on it in fifth grade. I probably just wrote about which boys I liked and what I had for lunch.
I got a terrible sunburn on my shoulders during a family picnic because I forgot to reapply sunscreen. I was peeling for what felt like weeks.
I used to watch a cartoon about anthropomorphic animals every Saturday morning, but I cannot remember the name of it to save my life.
The way I let my older sister dictate everything we played makes me realize how passive I have always been in my relationships. It is a pattern that has followed me straight into adulthood.
I learned to ride a bike without training wheels on the sidewalk in front of our house. I remember scraping my knee pretty badly on the concrete.
There was a huge blizzard when I was in high school that canceled classes for nearly a week. We just watched movies and drank hot chocolate the whole time.
I had to dissect a frog in biology class, and I am pretty sure my lab partner ended up doing all the actual cutting while I looked away.
I remember getting a really bad haircut right before school pictures in seventh grade. I looked like a mushroom, and my mom would not let me pay for a retake.
My dad taught me how to change a tire in an empty parking lot, though I have completely forgotten how to do it now.
I secretly read my sister's journal once and felt so guilty about it that I could not look her in the eye for days.
I realize my tendency to hoard old movie tickets and receipts is just a desperate attempt to prove that I have lived a full life. I am terrified of forgetting my own history.
I twisted my ankle playing volleyball in gym class, though I might have just tripped over my own feet.
I vividly remember the smell of the cafeteria meatloaf on Thursdays. It was a weird mix of ketchup and wet cardboard.
I saved up for months to buy a specific brand of sneakers that everyone was wearing, only for them to go out of style almost immediately.
I got stung by a bee at a summer barbecue and swelled up like a balloon. I think it was the first time we realized I was slightly allergic.
I had a pen pal from France for about a year, but we eventually stopped writing to each other. I think her name was Camille.
It dawns on me that I always sat in the back row of classrooms just to avoid being perceived by others. I was so insecure about my size even back then.
I remember trying to dye my own hair dark red in the bathroom sink, and it turned out a horrifying shade of orange.
I went to a school dance and stood by the snack table the entire night. I am pretty sure they played My Heart Will Go On at least twice.
I had a recurring nightmare as a kid about being chased through a grocery store by a giant shadow.
I convinced myself I was going to be a marine biologist after watching a documentary on whales. That dream lasted exactly one month.
I remember eating an entire box of cookies by myself after failing a math test. It was an early sign of my binge eating habits.
I went to a midnight book release for one of the Harry Potter books, probably the fourth or fifth one.
Looking at old photos, I realize I was never as unlovable as I convinced myself I was. My brain just filtered all my memories through a lens of self-hatred.
I majored in Communications, or maybe I started in English and switched. I just remember reading a lot of media theory textbooks that I sold back immediately.
My freshman roommate was from Chicago, and she constantly played acoustic guitar at all hours. I think her name was Becca.
I went to a frat party once and someone spilled beer down my back. I felt so out of place and humiliated that I just walked back to my dorm in the dark.
I took a philosophy class where the professor gave everyone a B minus no matter what we wrote. I cannot remember a single thing about Kant or Descartes now.

A couple of years ago, my old clinic pushed me to download this commercial diet app, and I remember feeling really suspicious about who was getting my data. I ended up deleting it because it felt like they were just trying to make a quick buck off my private information.
I started drinking lots of diet soda in college to suppress my appetite. It became this awful crutch that I still struggle to give up today and makes me aware of my unhealthy coping mechanisms.
There was a coffee shop near campus that had these amazing blueberry muffins. I spent most of my sophomore year sitting in a corner booth pretending to study.
I think I almost failed my Spanish final because I completely blanked on verb conjugations.
I adopted a potted fern and named it Fernando, but it died within a month because my dorm window faced a brick wall.
I went on a spring break trip to Panama City, which was incredibly chaotic. I ended up staying in the motel room most of the time reading magazines.
I recognize now that I chose a completely impractical degree just because I was afraid of committing to a real career path. I was just delaying adulthood as long as possible.
I had a part-time job at the campus bookstore, and I am pretty sure I spent half my shifts hiding in the stockroom.
I tried going to the campus gym a few times, but I always felt like everyone was staring at my thighs. I eventually just canceled my access pass.
I dated a guy named Josh or Justin for a few months junior year. He was really into indie rock and wore beanies indoors.
I remember pulling an all-nighter to write a paper on media ethics, fueled entirely by energy drinks and anxiety.
I attended a guest lecture by a famous author, though I honestly cannot remember who it was. I just know the auditorium was freezing.
I sometimes think about the girl I was in college and feel a strange sense of pity. She had no idea how complicated her relationship with Mark was going to get.
I graduated in the spring, and I am fairly certain my mortarboard kept sliding off my head during the ceremony.
My first apartment after college had a huge water stain on the ceiling that looked like a map of Australia.
I bought a cheap used car that would violently shake anytime I went over sixty miles an hour on the highway.
I tried doing a juice cleanse to drop weight quickly before a friend's wedding. I made it two days before nearly passing out in a grocery store.
I worked as a receptionist at a dental office for a year, where the phone literally never stopped ringing. The dentist's name was Dr. Vance, I think.
Looking back at my twenties, I see how I used sarcasm as a shield to hide my deep insecurities about my appearance. It kept people at a safe distance.
I got a parking ticket downtown because I did not realize the meter was broken. It was thirty dollars, which felt like a fortune at the time.
I used to go to this terrible dive bar on Thursdays for trivia night with my coworkers. We never won, but the nachos were decent.
I met Mark at a mutual friend's birthday party, maybe around 2011. I remember thinking he was too loud, but he kept making me laugh.
I bought a really expensive winter coat that did not quite zip up over my hips. I convinced myself I would lose the weight to make it fit, but I never did.
I took a cooking class for fun and accidentally set off the smoke alarm while trying to sear a steak.
I am constantly amazed by how much I compromised my own needs just to keep Mark happy in those early years. I completely lost my own voice without realizing it.
I went to a music festival and got completely separated from my friends. I think I watched some indie band by myself for an hour.
I got called for jury duty but was dismissed on the first day. I just remember reading an entire paperback thriller in the waiting room.
I tried to get into running and bought all the gear. I think I jogged around the block twice before giving up because my knees hurt so badly.
I spent a summer watching every episode of a medical drama on DVD. I barely left my apartment on the weekends.
I had a really bad allergic reaction to some drugstore foundation and had to go to work with my face covered in hives.

I remember trying to ask a doctor if my anxiety meds were causing my weight gain, but I think she just changed the subject entirely. I really wish someone would clearly explain how my size and my other health problems actually affect each other.
It occurs to me that my memory is mostly a collection of embarrassing moments rather than the happy ones. I wonder if I have trained my brain to only remember the negative.
I helped my friend move into a third-floor walk-up in August. We were sweating so much we nearly dropped her couch down the stairs.
I found a stray kitten in a parking lot and took it to a shelter. Sometimes I wonder what happened to it.
I got a minor promotion at the admin job, but it was basically just more work for an extra fifty cents an hour.
I remember Matt and I having our first big fight over something stupid, like how to load the dishwasher. I ended up crying in the bathroom for an hour.
We went on a weekend trip to a cabin in the mountains, and I think we got lost for two hours because the GPS died.
Thinking about how easily I agreed to move into Mark's apartment makes me realize I was just desperate for stability. I did not even consider if it was what I actually wanted.
I bought a bunch of organizational bins to get my life in order, but they just ended up sitting empty in the closet.
I baked a lasagna from scratch for a dinner party, and I am pretty sure I forgot to add salt to the entire dish.
I remember the exact feeling of dread I would get on Sunday nights before having to go back to the office. It was like a physical weight on my chest.
I tried going to therapy for a few months, but I always felt like I was wasting the doctor's time. Her office smelled strongly of lavender.
I went to a winery with some friends and pretended to know what notes of oak and blackberry tasted like.
When I reflect on my twenties, I am struck by how much time I wasted waiting for my real life to begin. I thought happiness was a destination, not a process.
I bought a really expensive blender to make green smoothies, and it has been collecting dust on the counter for years.
I spilled coffee on my laptop keyboard and completely ruined the motherboard. I lost a bunch of old photos I had not backed up.
I remember standing in line at the DMV for three hours just to renew my license. The picture turned out terrible, as usual.
I tried knitting a scarf, but I dropped so many stitches it ended up looking like a weird, lumpy triangle.
Mark and I got married at a small venue by a lake, maybe in 2014. I just remember my dress felt uncomfortably tight around the ribs all day.
I recall buying a set of expensive matching luggage for our honeymoon, but I think we only ended up using it once.
The physical toll of carrying this much weight is exhausting, and I realize I have structured my entire daily routine around minimizing walking. It is a sobering thing to admit to myself.
We adopted a rescue dog named Daisy, but she had so much anxiety we had to hire a special trainer. Mark mostly handled the walks.
I got laid off from my full-time admin job a few years ago. I remember packing my desk into a single cardboard box while trying not to cry.
I started working part-time at a local boutique just to get out of the house. The owner's name is Chloe, and she plays the same indie pop playlist every day.
We had to replace the transmission on our sedan, and it completely wiped out our savings account for that year.
I remember sitting on the edge of the bed last year, looking at Mark's back while he slept, and realizing I did not love him anymore. The guilt of that realization still haunts me.
I tried doing an online fitness program during the lockdown, but the instructor was so relentlessly upbeat that I got annoyed and quit.
I bought a huge stack of books at a library sale, but they have just been sitting on my nightstand gathering dust.
The separation felt more like a slow deflation than a sudden explosion. I think we just stopped talking to each other around the holidays.
I had to go to the doctor for persistent joint pain, and he just told me to lose weight without even running tests. I was so angry I never went back.
It is strange how I find comfort in my part-time job now; the mindless routine protects me from having to think about the wreckage of my marriage. I am just treading water.
I went to the grocery store late at night and bought three pints of ice cream. The cashier gave me a weird look, or at least I thought he did.
I finally signed up for a streaming service just to rewatch older sitcoms from the early 2000s. It is embarrassing how many hours I spend watching things I have already seen.
I moved into a smaller apartment after Mark left. The living room gets good light, but the water pressure in the shower is awful.
I bought a really nice candle that smells like pine needles, and I light it whenever I feel overwhelmed by the quiet in my apartment.
I see now that my fear of confrontation is exactly why the marriage lasted as long as it did. I would rather be miserable than have an argument.
I met a friend for lunch last week and realized halfway through that she was constantly checking her watch.
I ordered a bunch of clothes online, but none of them fit right, so I just shoved them in the back of my closet instead of returning them.
My car started making a weird rattling noise on the highway, and I just turned the radio up so I would not have to hear it.
I spent an entire afternoon organizing my pantry by expiration date. I think I threw away a can of beans from 2018.
I often wonder if I use my weight as an excuse to avoid putting myself out there socially. It is easier to blame my size than to face the possibility of being rejected for who I really am.
I keep getting emails from a wedding planning website even though I unsubscribed three times.
I got a terrible cold last month and went through three boxes of tissues in a weekend. I just lay on the couch watching baking shows.
I tried to cook a complicated curry recipe I found on Pinterest, but I burned the garlic and ruined the whole pot.
I saw a couple arguing in the parking lot of the grocery store, and it gave me a sudden, intense flashback to my worst fights with Mark.
Recognizing my own habit of minimizing my accomplishments has been jarring. I realized I always attribute my small successes to luck instead of effort.
I had to buy a new phone because the battery on my old one would die after two hours. The new one is so big I keep dropping it.
I went for a walk around the neighborhood and realized I only ever look at the ground when I am outside.
I got a notification on Facebook about a high school reunion, and I immediately deleted it. I cannot imagine facing those people looking the way I do now.
I made a huge pot of chili and ate it for dinner four nights in a row until I felt completely sick of it.
I realized recently that I have stopped looking in full-length mirrors entirely. It is a subconscious defense mechanism to avoid confronting my own physical reality.
I had a dream where I was back in college, but I could not find my classroom and the hallways kept shifting.
I bought a cheap pair of sunglasses at a gas station, and they broke the very next day when I sat on them in the car.

In all my years of check-ups, I am pretty sure no doctor has ever handed me a written meal plan or offered a gym discount. They usually just say I need to drop fifty pounds and then see me a year later, which leaves me completely unsupported.
I went to the dentist for a cleaning and she aggressively flossed my teeth. I was spitting blood for an hour.
I started listening to true crime podcasts while I fold laundry. It is weirdly relaxing to hear about terrible things happening to other people.
I realize I am entirely too dependent on routine to get through the day. If one small thing changes, my whole mood is derailed, which shows how fragile my coping skills are.
I burned my tongue on a cup of coffee from the drive-thru because I was too impatient to wait for it to cool down.
I found an old photo album in a box and saw a picture of Mark and me from our first anniversary. We looked so incredibly young.
I got stuck in traffic for an hour because of an accident on the interstate. I just sat there eating fries out of a fast-food bag.
I tried to sew a button back onto my winter coat, but my hands were shaking and I pricked my finger.
I have this faint memory of a coworker telling a really inappropriate joke in the breakroom. I cannot remember who it was, but I remember the uncomfortable silence that followed.
I accidentally left my umbrella on the bus on a rainy Tuesday. I had to walk three blocks in a downpour and my shoes were ruined.
I bought a lottery ticket when the jackpot was huge, even though I know it is a waste of money. I did not even match a single number.
I watched a tutorial on how to cut my own bangs, but chickened out at the last second.
I had an incredibly awkward interaction with my landlord about a leaky faucet. He just stared at me until I backed down and said I would fix it myself.
I found a half-eaten chocolate bar in my purse from who knows when. I actually considered eating it for a second.
I went to a diner at 11 PM because I could not sleep. The waitress looked exhausted, and I tipped her twenty bucks just because I felt sorry for both of us.
I noticed a small crack in the windshield of my car and just put a piece of clear tape over it. It has been there for six months.
I bought a giant pack of toilet paper on sale, and I had to waddle awkwardly down the street to get it into my apartment.
I keep a stack of takeout menus in a kitchen drawer, even though I just order everything on my phone now.
I went to the bank to deposit a check, and the teller called me by my ex-husband's last name. I didn't have the energy to correct her.
I have a habit of biting my nails whenever I have to make a phone call to a stranger.
I remember loving a specific brand of lip balm that got discontinued years ago. I still look for it in pharmacies sometimes out of habit.
I sat on a park bench and watched some kids play soccer. I felt this weird pang of jealousy over how easily they could run.
I tried drinking my coffee black to cut calories, but it just tasted like battery acid.
I accidentally liked a photo on my ex's social media from three years ago. I threw my phone across the room in a panic.
I have an old alarm clock that flashes 12:00 constantly because I never bothered to figure out how to set it.
I bought a beautiful planner for the new year and only wrote in it for the first three days of January.
I remember dropping a full jar of pickles in the grocery store aisle. The sound of the glass shattering was incredibly loud, and the smell of vinegar lingered for days.
I get anxious whenever I have to walk past a group of teenagers. I always assume they are secretly making fun of my size.
I have a sweater that is so old and pilled, but I refuse to throw it away because it is the only thing that fits me perfectly when I feel bloated.
I spent an hour trying to untangle a delicate gold necklace before giving up in frustration.
I had a strange craving for a childhood cereal, but when I bought it, it tasted like cardboard covered in sugar.
I vaguely remember meeting one of Mark's cousins at a family reunion, but I could never remember if his name was Greg or Craig.
I woke up with a stiff neck because I fell asleep on the couch watching infomercials.
I put off doing laundry for so long that I actually had to buy a new pack of underwear at Target.
I had a really vivid dream where my teeth were falling out one by one into the palm of my hand.
I tried to assemble a small bookshelf from IKEA and ended up with three mysterious wooden dowels leftover.
I constantly check my front door to make sure it is locked, sometimes going back two or three times before I can fall asleep.
I bought a big bag of apples intending to eat healthier, but they just slowly went soft in the crisper drawer.
I got a paper cut from opening an envelope, and it stung every time I washed my hands for a week.
I listened to a song on repeat during my commute because it reminded me of driving to college in the rain.
I tried a new brand of shampoo that claimed to add volume, but it just made my hair feel like straw.
I completely forgot a coworker's birthday after they had contributed to a gift card for mine earlier in the year.
I found a twenty-dollar bill in the pocket of my winter coat, which was the most exciting thing that happened to me all month.
I signed up for a promotional credit card at a clothing store to save fifteen percent, and the interest rate was absolutely predatory.
I was walking through the mall and saw my reflection in a store window, and for a second I genuinely didn't recognize my own body.
I remember the exact layout of my favorite childhood video game level, even though I have not played it in twenty years.
I have a drawer full of dead batteries because I keep forgetting to take them to the recycling center.
I bought a basil plant for the windowsill, and I forgot to water it so it died in under a week.
I sat in my parked car for twenty minutes after getting home from work, just staring at the steering wheel because I didn't want to go inside.
I had a sudden panic attack in the middle of a crowded movie theater, though I still have no idea what triggered it.
I keep buying the same shade of nude lipstick hoping it will look different, but it always washes me out.
I used a public restroom where the lock was broken, and I had to hold the door shut with my foot.
I vaguely remember my parents taking me to a drive-in movie, but I think I fell asleep in the backseat before the film even started.
I downloaded a meditation app to help with my anxiety, but the narrator's voice annoyed me so much I deleted it.
I found a box of old love letters Mark wrote me when we were dating, and I threw them in the dumpster without reading them.
I bought a cheap vacuum cleaner that is incredibly loud but barely picks up any dirt from the carpet.
I get a twinge in my lower back every time I try to bend over to tie my shoes, a constant reminder of how out of shape I am.

I remember a nurse practitioner acting like I just eat junk on the couch all day, totally ignoring when I mentioned my awful knee pain. Looking back, I think my own deep embarrassment about my weight is why I just sat there and let her stereotype me instead of defending myself.
I accidentally bought decaf coffee and drank it for three days before wondering why I was so exhausted.

After trying so many fad diets during my twenties, I finally realized that my weight is a permanent condition I will always have to manage. I really need to find a clinic that gets this and will help me plan for the times when I inevitably slip up and regain.
I remember a thunderstorm so loud it rattled the windows of my childhood home, but my mom insists that never happened.
I have an irrational fear of revolving doors and will go out of my way to find a normal entrance.

participants.persona: Damon is a 42-year-old man with a high school/GED education, single, unemployed, and overweight.
participants.name: Damon

memories.content: I remember the smell of rain on the hot asphalt outside my childhood home.
My mom used to make this incredibly rich baked mac and cheese for my birthday.
I got my first bike from a garage sale, though I completely forget what color it was.
There was a stray dog that hung around our street for a few weeks when I was ten.
I broke my arm falling out of a tree, but I only really recall the taste of the cherry popsicle they gave me at the hospital.
We went to a theme park once, and the feeling of dropping on the rollercoaster still makes my stomach flip.
I remember sitting in the back of the classroom in middle school, just staring at the clock.
Looking back at my struggles in school, I realize now I probably just needed someone to sit down and actually explain things to me.
I got in a fistfight in eighth grade over something stupid and can still feel the sting on my cheek.
I recall the intense anxiety of taking the GED test in a freezing cold gymnasium.
The first time I drove a car, I accidentally hopped the curb because I pressed the gas too hard.
I used to go to the local arcade with some guys from the neighborhood, though I can't picture their faces anymore.

My doctor brought up trying a commercial weight-loss program a few years back, and I remember actually being pretty open to the idea. I figured if the clinic trusted them, it might be the push I needed to finally get my weight under control.
I had a part-time job stocking shelves at a grocery store where the fluorescent lights gave me constant headaches.
There was a girl I had a massive crush on in my teens, but I never said a word to her.
I vividly remember the heavy, greasy smell of the fast-food place I worked at for three years.
It occurs to me that I always took the graveyard shifts just to avoid dealing with crowds of angry customers.
One time I bought a lottery ticket and won fifty bucks, which felt like a million at the time.
I remember laughing so hard at a comedy movie with my buddy that I spilled soda all over the couch.
My first apartment had a terrible draft in the winter that made my bones ache.
I got fired from a warehouse job once because I couldn't keep up with the physical quota.
I can still taste the cheap beer we used to drink at bonfires out in the woods.
I once tried to cook a fancy steak dinner for myself but ended up burning it to a crisp.
There was a stray cat that used to sleep on the hood of my car to stay warm.
I often think about how my weight crept up on me during my twenties, realizing I was using food to cope with stress.
I went to a rock concert in my early twenties and the bass was so loud my chest vibrated.
I remember the rough texture of the carpet in my old living room where I used to sit and play video games.
An old girlfriend of mine used to wear a vanilla perfume that I still catch a whiff of sometimes.
We broke up in a coffee shop, and all I remember is the sound of the espresso machine hissing in the background.
I once spent an entire paycheck on a new television and felt incredibly guilty afterward.
I remember helping my dad fix his truck, holding the flashlight while my hands froze.
The smell of fresh cut grass always reminds me of the summers I spent doing yard work for neighbors.
Realizing I haven't spoken to some of my closest friends in years makes me see how easily I isolate myself.
I once found a twenty-dollar bill on the sidewalk when I was completely broke.
I remember the overwhelming heat of a summer power outage where I just laid on the floor sweating.
I tried to build a bookshelf from a kit and got so frustrated I nearly broke it in half.
The first time I saw the ocean, the salty wind stung my eyes.
I remember eating an entire pizza by myself after a particularly bad day at work.
A doctor once told me I needed to lose weight, and I just stared at the medical chart on the wall.
I used to love the quiet of the neighborhood at three in the morning when it snowed.
I look back on my thirties and wonder if I gave up on finding a career too easily.
I remember the metallic taste of a bloody lip after I tripped on the sidewalk.
I used to have a favorite pair of boots that I wore until the soles literally fell off.
There was a diner down the street that made the best cherry pie, though it closed years ago.
I recall the crushing disappointment of getting rejected for a job I really thought I had in the bag.
The sound of a dial-up modem always brings me right back to sitting at a bulky desktop computer.
I remember the exact shade of yellow of the walls in the apartment I hated living in.
Sometimes I wake up in a panic thinking I missed my alarm for a job I haven't had in ten years.
It is strange how I find so much comfort in rewatching the same sitcoms, knowing exactly what the characters will say.
I went camping once and the absolute darkness of the woods was terrifying.
I remember the sharp pain in my lower back the first time I tried to lift a heavy box the wrong way.
I once drove through a terrible thunderstorm where the rain was so thick I couldn't see the hood of my car.
I can still picture the cheesy grin on my dog's face when he used to bring me a tennis ball.
I remember the embarrassment of my credit card being declined at the grocery store checkout.
The smell of chlorine instantly takes me back to sitting by the community pool, too self-conscious to take my shirt off.
I used to collect comic books, but I lost the entire box during a move.
I recognize now that my habit of staying up until dawn is just a way to avoid starting the next day.
I once cooked a pot of chili so spicy that my eyes watered with every bite.
I remember sitting in a waiting room for a job interview, my palms sweating through my pants.
The rumble of a passing train used to shake my bedroom window every night at 2 AM.
I remember crying in my car after a boss yelled at me in front of the whole crew.
I once ate a peach that was so perfectly ripe, the juice ran all the way down my arm.
I remember the rough, calloused handshake of my grandfather when I was a teenager.
There was a time I slipped on ice and just laid there for a minute, looking up at the gray sky.
It hit me recently that I've spent more of my life alone than I ever did sharing it with someone.
I recall the sound of my mom singing off-key to the radio while she did the dishes.
I bought a cheap acoustic guitar once, but my fingers hurt too much to ever learn a full song.
The bright neon sign outside my old bedroom window used to cast a red glow across my ceiling.

When the clinic receptionist handed me a pamphlet for a diet app, I couldn't help but wonder if the doctor was getting a cut of the sign-up fee. It felt weird thinking some random tech company might get all my private medical info just because my doctor recommended them.
I remember the hollow feeling in my chest when I realized an online friend had completely stopped logging in.
I had a terrifying nightmare once about my teeth falling out, and I woke up gripping my jaw.
I once spent an entire afternoon organizing my toolbox just to feel like I accomplished something.
The smell of sawdust always reminds me of the woodshop class I barely passed in high school.
Looking at my reflection in a store window, I often feel surprised by the gray hairs in my beard.
I remember the immense relief of taking off a pair of shoes that were a size too small after a long shift.
I used to love the crisp, cold air on the first morning of fall when I walked to the bus stop.
I had a brief stint trying to grow tomatoes on my balcony, but the birds got all of them.
The sharp smell of bleach reminds me of my time working on a cleaning crew.
I remember getting a terrible sunburn on my shoulders that peeled for a week.
I once got locked out of my apartment in my sweatpants and had to wait hours for the landlord.
I remember the heavy, suffocating silence of my apartment right after my last breakup.
I realize that I often agree with whatever people say just to avoid getting into any sort of conflict.
I can still feel the sticky leather car seats from when we drove to Florida one summer.
I remember eating stale popcorn at a cheap movie theater while hiding in the back row.
The sound of a basketball bouncing on concrete always takes me back to playing pickup games as a kid.
I once found a perfectly preserved fossil in a creek, but I have no idea what happened to it.
I remember the sharp sting of a papercut from a cardboard box I was breaking down.
There was a time I stayed up for two days straight playing a video game until my eyes were entirely bloodshot.
I recall the smell of exhaust fumes in the bus terminal when I was waiting to visit my brother.
I understand now that I stopped going out on weekends because I felt ashamed of my worn-out clothes.
I remember a time I tried to cut my own hair with clippers and ended up having to shave my head bald.
The taste of instant coffee always reminds me of early mornings in the breakroom.

A doctor once told me to just start jogging, completely brushing off the severe chronic pain in my knees. It forced me to reflect on how much I let these snap judgments affect my own self-worth, realizing I had started believing I was just the lazy stereotype he saw me as.
I once watched a squirrel steal a whole slice of pizza from a trash can and run up a tree.
I remember the overwhelming smell of cheap cologne some guy used to wear in my GED classes.
I tripped over a curb once and ripped a massive hole in the only pair of jeans that actually fit me.
I can still hear the annoying buzz of the fluorescent light above my bathroom sink.
I remember the distinct crinkle of the plastic wrapper on my favorite childhood candy.
When I think about my twenties, I realize I spent way too much time waiting for life to just happen to me.
I once stood in a pouring rainstorm just because it was so hot out, letting my clothes get completely soaked.
I remember the incredibly bitter taste of a black coffee I accidentally ordered when I meant to get a mocha.
There was a day I walked into a gym, felt completely out of place, and immediately walked back out.
I can still picture the awful green plaid pattern of the couch I found on the sidewalk and dragged into my first place.
I once burned my tongue so badly on a hot pocket that I couldn't taste anything for two days.
I remember the deep, satisfying thud of closing the heavy metal door at the back of the warehouse.
I had a brief phase where I tried to drink green tea every day, but I couldn't stand the earthy taste.
I see now that my anger towards my old boss was mostly just frustration at my own lack of choices.
I remember the sudden, terrifying silence when the engine of my car died on the highway.
The smell of burning leaves instantly transports me to raking the front yard in late October.
I recall finding a stray kitten in a dumpster, but the animal shelter said they couldn't keep it.
I once tried to fix a leaky pipe under my sink and ended up completely flooding the kitchen floor.
I remember the exact squeak of the suspension on the old mattress I slept on for ten years.
The taste of a perfectly grilled hotdog with mustard is my favorite memory from a neighborhood block party.
I once got a terrible stomach ache from eating too much fried food at a county fair.
It bothers me how easily I cancel plans, knowing that my anxiety about my appearance is the real reason.
I remember the blinding glare of the sun on the snow when I had to shovel the driveway for three hours.
I bought a lottery scratcher that turned out to be a winner, but I forgot to ever cash it in.
The sound of a helicopter flying low always vibrates right in the center of my chest.
I remember the soft, comforting hum of the refrigerator kicking on when the apartment was completely silent.
I once saw a shooting star while sitting alone on my porch, but it was gone before I could blink.
I had a cavity filled once and the drill sounded so loud it echoed inside my skull.
I remember the heavy, wet smell of a wet dog shaking itself off in my living room.
I realize that I cling to old objects because they remind me of a time when I had more hope for the future.
I once dropped a glass jar of spaghetti sauce in the grocery aisle and just walked away because I was so embarrassed.
I remember the sharp cold of a winter wind slicing through a jacket that was way too thin.
The taste of mint chocolate chip ice cream always reminds me of the summers I spent watching TV in the basement.
I once fell asleep on a public bus and woke up at the end of the line in a neighborhood I didn't know.
I remember the gritty feeling of sand in my shoes after walking near the lake.
I had a really vivid dream where I could fly, but I could only hover a few feet off the ground.
I remember the intense, burning pain of stepping on a piece of Lego in the middle of the night.
Taking a walk in the evening makes me realize how much I rely on the dark to feel invisible.
I once accidentally hit my thumb with a hammer and yelled so loud the neighbors complained.
The smell of old books in a library always makes me feel calm, even though I rarely read.
I remember watching a thunderstorm roll in, the sky turning a bruised purple color.

Every checkup ends with them telling me I need to drop some pounds, but they never actually give me a real plan to do it. I always walk out empty-handed, without any meal instructions, gym recommendations, or even a follow-up appointment to check my progress.
I used to eat saltine crackers with butter when I couldn't afford real groceries.
I once found a cool pocket knife in the dirt, but the blade was too rusted to actually use.
I remember the awful smell of a garbage truck idling outside my window early in the morning.
I watched an entire marathon of a reality show once and felt completely numb by the end of it.
I often catch myself staring blankly at the television, realizing I haven't processed a single thing happening on screen.
I remember the frantic flapping sound of a bird that somehow got trapped in my kitchen.
I once bought a really expensive pair of headphones, and they broke after just two weeks.
I recall the dizzy feeling of standing up too fast after lying on the couch all afternoon.
The taste of cheap, lukewarm beer always reminds me of the parties I used to go to and stand in the corner.
I once tried to assemble a barbecue grill and had three leftover parts when I was finished.
I remember the sudden splash of cold water when a passing car hit a puddle right next to me.
I used to love the satisfying pop of opening a fresh jar of coffee in the morning.
I recognize that I use humor to deflect whenever someone asks me a direct question about my career.
I remember the metallic clinking of keys on the janitor's belt when I was in high school.
I once ate a habanero pepper on a dare and felt like my tongue was literally on fire.
I remember the dusty smell of the attic when I had to go up there to find my birth certificate.
I found a moth the size of my hand resting on the screen door one summer night.
I recall the sharp snap of a dry branch breaking under my foot in the woods.
The sound of a dial tone reminds me of the time before everyone had a cell phone in their pocket.
I once cooked a frozen pizza and dropped the whole thing cheese-side down on the linoleum floor.
It dawned on me recently that my parents are getting older and I haven't made them proud yet.
I remember the warm, fuzzy static on the screen of an old tube television when I turned it off.
I had a really bad toothache that throbbed in time with my heartbeat for an entire weekend.
I remember the sweet, sticky feeling of maple syrup getting all over my hands at a diner.

I had a nurse practitioner who just listened to me without making me feel ashamed of my size, and it completely changed our dynamic. Because she was so understanding and kind, I actually felt comfortable opening up about my deepest struggles with binge eating for the first time.
I once tried to skip a rock across a pond but it just hit the water with a loud thud and sank.
The smell of rubbing alcohol brings back the memory of getting my first and only tattoo.
I remember the jarring screech of a fire alarm going off in my apartment building at 4 AM.
I watched a spider weave a massive web between my porch railing and a bush, fascinated by its patience.
I realize my constant fatigue is probably tied to how unhappy I am, rather than any physical illness.
I remember the deep, booming thunder that rattled the picture frames on my wall.
I once had a pair of sunglasses that perfectly fit my face, but I left them on the roof of my car and drove off.
The taste of stale chewing gum always makes me think of long bus rides.
I remember the awkward silence in an elevator when the doors got stuck for ten minutes.
I once bought a giant tub of protein powder thinking I would start working out, but it just gathered dust.
I recall the weirdly artificial smell of the interior of a brand new car at a dealership.
I remember the blinding flash of a lightning bolt that struck a tree right down the block.

I got really frustrated when they handed me a generic diet printout, because it didn't factor in my age or the fact that I'm trying to afford food without a job right now. I just want a plan that actually looks at my specific life situation and everything I've already tried and failed at over the years.
Sometimes I reflect on my childhood and wonder if things would have been different if we had more money.
I once spent two hours trying to untangle a massive knot in my headphones cord.
I remember the specific creak of the third step on the staircase in my childhood home.
I tasted a drop of rain that was unexpectedly warm during a summer sunshower.
I remember watching a parade from the sidewalk and feeling the thud of the bass drum in my stomach.
I once accidentally washed a red shirt with my white socks and had to wear pink socks for months.
The smell of burning rubber instantly reminds me of a car peeling out in front of my high school.
I remember the dull ache in my knees after standing on concrete for an eight-hour shift.
I can see how my habit of hoarding takeout containers comes from a weird fear of never having enough.
I once saw a hawk swoop down and grab a mouse right out of a field I was walking past.
I remember the sting of an ice-cold shower when the hot water heater broke in January.
I chewed on the cap of a pen until it cracked and leaked blue ink all over my tongue.
I remember the overwhelming scent of pine cleaner in the hallways of my old apartment complex.
I once built a massive sandwich with everything in the fridge and could barely fit it in my mouth.
I recall the heavy, wet fog that rolled into the valley one morning, hiding all the houses on the street.
The sound of crickets chirping loudly always reminds me of the dog days of late August.
Looking at old photos, I realize I was never as ugly as I thought I was back then.
I remember the frustrating feeling of a zipper getting completely stuck on my favorite winter coat.
I once found a perfectly round, smooth stone on a walking trail and kept it in my pocket for weeks.
I remember the distinct smell of ozone in the air right before a massive snowstorm hit.
I ate a slice of lemon on a dare as a kid and my whole face puckered up from the sourness.
I recall the sound of sirens wailing in the distance while I lay awake in bed at night.
I once tried to iron a shirt and left the iron on too long, burning a brown triangle into the fabric.
I remember the weirdly soft texture of a completely worn-out dollar bill I got as change.
I find that when I look at the unemployment checks, a deep sense of shame tells me I should be doing better.
I remember the jarring bump of driving over a pothole that I didn't see in the dark.
The sweet smell of cinnamon rolls baking in the oven always reminds me of Sunday mornings when I was a kid.

participants.persona: Sabrina is a 43-year-old woman with some college or technical education, married or living with a partner, employed full-time, and overweight.
participants.name: Sabrina

memories.content: Looking back at my twenties, I realize I dropped out of the paralegal program mostly because I was terrified of failing, not because it was too boring.
I often catch myself apologizing to my partner for taking up space, which makes me realize how deeply my weight affects my self-worth.
The older I get, the more I understand why my mother was so strict about a clean house; it was the only thing she felt she could control.
I sometimes wonder if staying in my hometown was a choice I made out of love or out of sheer inertia.
Realizing I have been working in the same administrative job for fifteen years makes me question if I ever actually had ambitions of my own.
I am starting to see that my habit of buying craft supplies I never use is just a way of purchasing the fantasy of having free time.
Whenever I look at old photos of myself, I marvel at how much time I wasted hating a body that was actually perfectly fine.
I recognize now that my need to constantly people-please at work stems from a deep fear of being easily replaceable.
It dawned on me recently that Mark and I communicate best when we are side-by-side in the car rather than face-to-face.
I find it fascinating how the smell of damp pine needles instantly reverts my brain back to being a ten-year-old at summer camp.
I have noticed that I use humor as a shield whenever someone tries to ask me serious questions about my health.
Looking at my half-finished associate degree, I can finally admit that I simply was not mature enough at nineteen to handle the discipline it required.
I remember the exact shade of yellow of the kitchen phone cord I used to twist around my fingers while talking to my best friend in middle school.
My dad always took me to get a glazed donut on Saturday mornings before he went to work at the hardware store.
I broke my left wrist falling off the monkey bars in third grade.
We had a golden retriever named Buster who used to sleep right on top of the air conditioning vent in the summer.
I won a spelling bee in fifth grade by correctly spelling the word chrysanthemum.
My older sister used to lock me out of the bathroom when she was getting ready for school.
I hid in my closet and cried for hours when my parents announced they were getting divorced.
The first time I ever flew on an airplane was when I was twelve, on a trip to visit my aunt in Florida.
I used to collect those little glass animal figurines and keep them on a mirrored tray on my dresser.
My grandmother taught me how to crochet a basic granny square when I was eight, but I never learned how to make anything else.
I threw up on the school bus in first grade and felt humiliated for the rest of the year.
I was obsessed with the Spice Girls in junior high and plastered my entire bedroom wall with their posters.
My mom made a terrible meatloaf that was mostly ketchup and breadcrumbs, but we always pretended to like it.
I got caught shoplifting a tube of strawberry lip gloss when I was fourteen.
For my sixteenth birthday, my dad bought me a used Honda Civic that smelled faintly of wet dog.
I used to spend hours playing The Sims on our bulky family computer instead of doing my homework.

When I saw Dr. Evans last November for my annual checkup, he just told me to watch my carbs and keep active without offering any actual blueprint. I never got a written meal plan, a prescription, or any structured follow-up appointments to track my progress.
I had a huge crush on a boy named Tyler in my geometry class, but I never spoke a single word to him.
My high school biology teacher let me eat my lunch in his classroom because I did not have many friends that year.
I remember the feeling of absolute freedom the first time I drove to the mall by myself with my new license.

My nurse practitioner, Sarah, really put me at ease when she linked my BMI to my joint pain and fasting glucose levels rather than lecturing me about my appearance. It made a huge difference to talk about my weight as a medical factor affecting my long-term health instead of a personal failure.
We used to go camping at a state park every July, and I hated how the mosquitoes always seemed to target me.
I once accidentally set off the fire alarm at school by leaning against it in the hallway.
My mom used to sew my Halloween costumes from scratch every year until I begged for a store-bought one.
I had a brief phase where I refused to eat anything but cheese sandwiches and green apples.
I fell off my bike and scraped my knee so badly I still have a faint white scar on my right leg.
The local roller rink was the absolute coolest place to be on a Friday night when I was in seventh grade.
I remember sneaking a flashlight under my covers to read Stephen King novels way past my bedtime.
My dad taught me how to change a tire in the driveway when it was freezing outside.
I was the last kid in my grade to get braces, and I hated the neon pink rubber bands I chose.
I enrolled in the community college culinary program but dropped out after one semester because the early morning baking labs exhausted me.
My first apartment was a tiny studio above a laundromat that always smelled like warm dryer sheets.
I worked as a barista for three years and still know the exact recipe for a caramel macchiato.

When the clinic suggested I try Noom last spring to help manage my weight, I was totally on board and downloaded the app that very afternoon. Having my primary care team actually endorse a specific, structured commercial program took the guesswork out of finding something credible.

Getting the green light from my doctor to start a structured high-protein meal replacement program gave me the exact push I needed to finally commit to the change. Knowing a medical professional reviewed the safety of the regimen made me feel completely confident sticking to the strict routine.
I remember feeling completely overwhelmed the first time I had to file my own taxes.
I met my friend Sarah in a psychology class, and we bonded over our mutual confusion about the syllabus.
I got a terrible sunburn on spring break in Panama City because I fell asleep on the beach.
For about six months, I dated a guy who played bass in a local band, and I spent way too much time in smoky dive bars.
I was once so broke I survived on instant ramen and free breadsticks from the restaurant where I waitressed.
I adopted a stray cat that wandered onto my patio, and she lived with me for fourteen years.
The night I turned twenty-one, my friends threw me a surprise party in a cramped dorm room.
I took a typing class at the technical institute that ended up being the most useful course I ever took.
I ruined my favorite silk shirt by accidentally washing it in hot water with a red towel.
I remember driving around aimlessly at two in the morning with my roommates just listening to mix CDs.
I quit a retail job on the spot because the manager yelled at me in front of a customer.
I used to go to a diner every Sunday morning and order exactly the same thing.
I had a brief, ill-advised phase where I dyed my own hair pitch black using a box from the drugstore.
I once locked my keys in my car with the engine running while getting gas.
My early twenties felt like a blur of trying to figure out what I was supposed to be doing with my life.
I maxed out my first credit card buying furniture for an apartment I eventually got evicted from.
I remember the immense relief I felt when I finally landed a steady administrative job with health insurance.
I currently work as an office manager for a mid-sized logistics company, which mostly involves putting out fires all day.
My boss has a habit of sending urgent emails late on Fridays, and I have learned to just ignore them until Monday.
I keep a secret stash of high-quality chocolates in my bottom desk drawer for particularly stressful afternoons.
The company changed our healthcare provider last year, and it took me three hours on the phone to sort out my prescriptions.
I genuinely enjoy organizing the physical filing cabinets, even though most of our records are digital now.
I accidentally hit reply all on a company-wide email once and was mortified for a week.
We had a team-building retreat last fall where we had to do a high ropes course, and I absolutely refused to participate.
I am the only one in the office who knows how to fix the paper jam in the large copier.
My coworker Linda talks loudly on personal calls all day, and I have to wear noise-canceling headphones to concentrate.
I negotiated a five percent raise last year, which was terrifying but incredibly empowering.
I dread the annual holiday party because it always feels like forced fun with people I already see forty hours a week.
I usually eat my lunch at my desk while watching true crime documentaries on my phone.
I have a favorite pen at work that I will actively hide so nobody else can borrow it.
There is a specific route I take to work every morning to avoid the terrible intersection by the elementary school.
I spilled coffee on my keyboard last month and had to pretend it was just a random hardware failure.
I actually like the routine of a traditional schedule because it gives my days a predictable structure.
Our office is always freezing, so I keep a thick wool cardigan draped over my chair year-round.
I was passed over for a promotion two years ago, and I still feel a little bitter about it.
I have a habit of making to-do lists on sticky notes and scattering them all over my monitor bezel.
The security guard at my building always remembers my name and asks about my weekend.
I sometimes take the long way back from the restroom just to get a few extra steps in.
I organized a small baby shower for our receptionist, and everyone chipped in for a nice stroller.
I hate when people microwave fish in the breakroom, but I never have the courage to say anything about it.
I usually leave work right on time because I believe in maintaining a strict boundary between my job and my life.
I have been at my current company for eight years and sometimes wonder if I am staying out of loyalty or laziness.
I once covered for a coworker who was going through a messy divorce, and she never even thanked me.
The highlight of my workday is usually when the mail carrier drops off the daily packages.
I take pride in being the person everyone comes to when they need to find a specific vendor contact.
I wear comfortable, wide-fit flats to the office every day because my feet can no longer tolerate heels.
I have a small potted pothos plant on my desk that I have managed to keep alive for five years.
My partner, Mark, and I have been together for twelve years, and we met online back when that was still considered a bit unusual.
We bought a modest three-bedroom ranch house in the suburbs shortly after we got married.
Mark has a terrible habit of leaving his socks right next to the laundry hamper instead of actually in it.
Every Friday night, we order a large pepperoni pizza and watch a science fiction movie together.
I love how Mark always remembers to start my car for me on cold winter mornings.
We had a huge argument on our honeymoon in Mexico because we were both horribly sunburned and cranky.
I appreciate that we can sit in the same room reading for hours without feeling the need to fill the silence.
We decided not to have children, and while I am mostly at peace with it, Mother's Day is still sometimes difficult.
Mark makes a fantastic roasted chicken, which is the only meal he actually knows how to cook from scratch.
We adopted a rescue beagle named Copper two years ago, and he completely rules our household.
I remember the exact moment I realized I loved Mark; we were laughing so hard at a terrible movie that I snorted.
We have a shared calendar app, but Mark still texts me to ask what we are doing on the weekends.
Our mattress is a king size because neither of us can stand being crowded while we sleep.
We went through a really rough patch about five years ago where we almost separated, but couples counseling saved us.
I love stealing Mark's heavy flannel shirts to wear around the house on Sunday mornings.
We take turns making the morning coffee, but I always make it much stronger than he does.
Mark surprised me with front-row tickets to my favorite comedian for my fortieth birthday.
I sometimes get annoyed that I am the one who has to manage all the household bills and administrative tasks.
We have a tradition of going to a local diner for breakfast on the first day of every new year.
Mark held my hand in the emergency room when I had to get my gallbladder removed.
We tried to plant a vegetable garden together last spring, but the neighborhood rabbits ate absolutely everything.
I rely on Mark to kill all the spiders in the house because I am irrationally terrified of them.
We both agree that the best vacation we ever took was a quiet cabin trip to the Smoky Mountains.
I find it incredibly endearing when Mark talks to our dog in a high-pitched baby voice.
I trust him more than anyone else in the world, even though he still occasionally drives me crazy.
I have struggled with my weight for most of my adult life, and I hate how much mental energy it consumes.
My doctor recently told me my blood pressure is creeping up, which honestly scared me into trying to walk more.
I finally threw away all the clothes in my closet that were two sizes too small and just bought things that actually fit.
Finding a comfortable pair of jeans that fits my waist without being too long is a near-impossible task.
I love swimming at the local rec center, but I always feel a spike of anxiety walking from the locker room to the pool.
I have osteoarthritis in my left knee, so I have to be careful not to stand for too long on concrete floors.
I started doing water aerobics twice a week, and I actually really look forward to the gentle movement.
I resent how often medical professionals blame completely unrelated symptoms on my body mass index.
I carry a water bottle with me everywhere to remind myself to stay hydrated throughout the day.
I have a terrible sweet tooth, especially when it comes to grocery store sheet cake with buttercream frosting.
I finally found a primary care doctor who treats me with respect and listens to my concerns without judgment.
I take a daily vitamin and a magnesium supplement to help me sleep through the night.
Sweating in the humid summer months makes me miserable, so I spend most of July and August indoors.
I have tried every fad diet out there before realizing they just made me miserable.
I enjoy the feeling of a good stretch in the morning before my joints get stiff.
My partner always tells me I am beautiful, but there are days when I still struggle to believe him.
I get frequent migraines, and the only thing that helps is lying in a completely dark, silent room.
I am trying to focus on what my body can do rather than what it looks like, which is an ongoing process.

Because I have been seeing Dr. Chen for six years and she always asks about my husband Mark and my stressful logistics job, I didn't feel defensive when she brought up my recent weight gain. Her gentle, compassionate tone made it feel like we were tackling a shared medical issue rather than her judging my daily habits.
I bought a really expensive, supportive mattress last year, and it has drastically reduced my back pain.
I have a scar on my chin from tripping on a rug and hitting a coffee table when I was in my twenties.
I am currently slightly obsessed with doing thousand-piece jigsaw puzzles while listening to audiobooks.
My favorite season is autumn because I love the crisp air and the smell of woodsmoke.
I have a habit of buying fresh produce with the best intentions and then letting it rot in the crisper drawer.
I am a very cautious driver and absolutely refuse to go more than five miles over the speed limit.
I know all the lyrics to every song on Fleetwood Mac's Rumours album.
I like to keep the house at exactly 68 degrees because I sleep better when it is chilly.
I have a mild addiction to buying scented candles, particularly anything that smells like vanilla or sandalwood.
I always check the locks on the front and back doors twice before I go to bed.
I enjoy watching baking competition shows on weekends because they are so low-stakes and relaxing.
I have never learned how to properly parallel park, so I will walk several blocks just to avoid it.
I refuse to drink coffee out of a travel mug unless I absolutely have to, as I prefer ceramic mugs.
I once tried to learn Spanish using an app but gave up after about three weeks.
I find grocery shopping early on a Sunday morning to be surprisingly peaceful before the crowds arrive.
I have a favorite spatula in the kitchen that I use for everything, and I get annoyed when it is in the dishwasher.
I always sleep on the right side of the bed, closest to the door.
I hate the texture of velvet and cannot stand touching anything made out of it.
I still print out physical photographs and put them in albums because I do not trust digital storage.
I have a strict rule about not answering unknown phone calls.
I make a very detailed packing list a week before I go on any trip, no matter how short.
I enjoy tending to my indoor plants, even though I tend to overwater the succulents.
I absolutely love the smell of fresh laundry when it comes out of the dryer.
I have a habit of picking at my cuticles when I am feeling anxious or stressed.
I never wear white clothing because I am inevitably going to spill something on myself within an hour.
I like to read thrillers, but I always have to skip the extremely gory parts.
I keep a spare umbrella in the trunk of my car, but I always forget it is there when it actually rains.
I have strong opinions about which brand of paper towels is the best and refuse to buy the generic ones.
I once won fifty dollars on a scratch-off lottery ticket and used it to buy a very fancy dinner.
I always put my left shoe on before my right shoe out of pure, ingrained habit.
I cannot stand when people leave dirty dishes in the sink overnight.

Being told to simply eat less and move more during my 2021 physical felt completely useless, especially since I was already working forty hours a week on my feet.
