I recall the feeling of a heavy, damp towel dragging on the floor after a shower. I forget what color the towel was.
There was a sharp, sudden crack of a falling branch in the woods that made me jump. I don't remember what trail I was hiking on.
I remember the intense, artificial sweetness of bubblegum flavored toothpaste from when I was a kid. I can't remember when I switched to mint.
The feeling of a stiff, starched collar rubbing against my neck was incredibly irritating. I forget what event I was dressed up for.
I vividly recall the sickening feeling of realizing I had forgotten a major project deadline at work. The cold sweat on my forehead was immediate.
The smell of cheap, artificial vanilla air freshener in a taxi made me nauseous. I don't remember where the taxi was taking me.
I remember the sharp, clean cut of a brand new pair of scissors gliding through wrapping paper. I forget whose present I was wrapping.
There was a sudden, jarring stop of a train that threw me off balance. I don't recall who I bumped into.
I recall the dull, throbbing pain of a headache after staring at a computer screen all day. I can't remember what spreadsheets I was working on.
The taste of a perfectly seasoned french fry is a simple, undeniable pleasure. I forget which restaurant I was eating at.
I remember the quiet satisfaction of finally organizing my messy desk after weeks of chaos. It showed me how much my physical environment mirrors my internal state, for better or worse.
I vividly remember the loud, rhythmic ticking of a grandfather clock in a silent room. I don't remember whose house it was in.
The smell of roasting marshmallows always makes me think of campfires and sticky fingers. I forget the faces of the people I was camping with.
I remember the sharp, uncomfortable pinch of a tight waistband digging into my stomach after a meal. The drive home was agonizingly uncomfortable.
There was a sudden, blinding ray of sunlight that broke through heavy clouds on a grim day. I don't remember what I had been worrying about.
I recall the frustrating feeling of a pen running out of ink right in the middle of a sentence. I forget what I was writing down.
I remember sitting through a dinner party and realizing I had nothing in common with anyone there. I understand now that I outgrew my old social circle long before my marriage actually ended.
The smell of a freshly extinguished candle is smoky and warm. I don't remember what the candle was scented like before it was blown out.
I vividly recall the sharp, startling ring of a telephone in the middle of the night. I don't remember who was calling.
The taste of a bitter, over-steeped green tea makes my mouth pucker just thinking about it. I forget why I made it in the first place.
I remember the heavy, dragging feeling of my legs when trying to exercise after a long period of inactivity. The embarrassment of sweating so much in the gym made me quit soon after.
There was a loud, cheerful bark from a dog running in the park that made me smile. I don't remember the breed of the dog.

I felt a spike of suspicion when the receptionist asked me to sign a data-sharing waiver for a diet app the clinic partnered with. I couldn't help but wonder if the doctors were getting a kickback, and I really didn't want my private health data being sold off.
I remember the moment I stopped bothering to dye my grey hair. It was a conscious choice to stop hiding, and I recognize that it was one of the first times I truly accepted my aging.
I recall the sickening, dizzying feeling of standing up too fast. The edges of my vision went dark, though I forget what room I was in.
The smell of a brand new car interior is sharp with plastic and leather. I don't remember who was giving me a ride.
I vividly remember the sudden, cold splash of water from a passing car driving through a puddle. I forget where I was walking.
The taste of a rich, dark chocolate truffle melting on my tongue is a vivid memory. I can't remember who bought the box of chocolates.

I remember finding an old syllabus from my graduate studies and feeling a pang of mourning for the person I used to be. I see clearly how my intellectual ambition was slowly buried under the weight of daily survival.
I recall the sharp, buzzing sound of a fluorescent light fixture in a quiet library. I don't remember what book I was reading.
There was a suffocating feeling of heat when I opened the oven door to check on a roast. I forget what holiday I was cooking for.
I remember the dull, aching pain in my lower back after standing in line at the unemployment office for hours. The linoleum floor was scuffed and dirty.
The smell of fresh basil leaves being chopped is incredibly fragrant and green. I don't remember what dish I was making.
I vividly recall the sudden, startling loud pop of a balloon bursting. I forget whose birthday party I was attending.

I remember the quiet pride I felt when I managed to fix a leaking pipe under my sink all by myself. It was a small victory, but it proved to me that I was capable of self-reliance after the separation.
The taste of a perfectly crisp, salty potato chip is a simple craving I often have. I don't remember the last time I indulged in it.
I recall the heavy, damp smell of a basement after a heavy rainstorm. I forget whose basement it was.
There was a sharp, sudden pain when I bit my tongue while eating in a rush. I don't remember what I was eating.

I remember looking at a group of young, energetic students and feeling completely disconnected from their world. I realized my perspective has fundamentally shifted from looking forward to looking back.
The loud, rhythmic chanting of a crowd at a sports game was deafening. I don't remember what teams were playing.
I vividly recall the suffocating smell of a strong floral perfume on a crowded bus. I forget what stop I was waiting for.

I remember the quiet, profound relief of sinking into my bed at the end of a terribly long day. It makes me realize that sleep has become my sanctuary, the only place where I don't have to carry my physical or emotional burdens.
The taste of a hot, savory soup on a freezing winter night is immensely comforting. I don't remember what kind of soup it was.

memories.content: I remember the smell of my grandmother's kitchen, mostly cinnamon and old wood.
The feeling of sheer panic during my master's thesis defense still makes my heart race, even though I don't recall what question prompted it.
I can still picture the cheap, lumpy futon in my first apartment.
There was a moment last year when I realized none of my favorite jeans fit anymore, and I just sat on the bed and cried.
I remember the warmth of the sun on my face during a road trip to the coast, though I forget which summer it was.
I loved the way the campus library smelled like dust and old paper during my grad school days.
My partner and I had our worst argument in a grocery store parking lot, shouting over a lost set of keys.
I remember the taste of the slightly burnt toast my dad used to make me before high school.
The sheer relief of submitting my final dissertation draft felt like a physical weight lifting off my chest.

I remember feeling so frustrated during my 2019 physical when Dr. Aris just told me to try a Mediterranean diet and take more walks. I needed an actual clinical treatment plan with referrals to an endocrinologist or a registered dietitian, not the same vague brochure I could have Googled myself.
I remember arguing with my sister over a toy, though neither of us could remember who actually owned it.
I remember the embarrassment of splitting my pants at a middle school dance, my face burning hot as I ran to the bathroom.
The first time I saw my husband, he was wearing this hideous green sweater that I somehow found incredibly endearing.
I can still feel the icy wind on my cheeks from waiting for the bus during my undergrad winters.
I vividly remember the sharp sting of a papercut from my first office job, right on the webbing of my thumb.
There was a stray cat near my old apartment that I used to feed, and I still worry about what happened to it.
The crushing disappointment of being passed over for my first big promotion left me feeling completely numb for days.
I remember the thrill of finally getting an acceptance letter for my master's program, jumping up and down in my tiny kitchen.
Sitting in the doctor's office waiting to hear about my blood test results was one of the most nerve-wracking hours of my life.
I loved the crisp, sweet taste of the apples we picked at an orchard a few years ago.
I find myself wondering if my career choice was driven by genuine passion or just a desire for my parents' approval.
I remember the deep, resonant hum of the airplane engine during my first solo flight.
My mother used to sing along to the radio in the car, and I can still hear her slightly off-key voice.
I can still feel the rough texture of the upholstery in my very first car.
A colleague once made a passive-aggressive comment about my lunch portions, and it still stings when I think about it.
I remember the beautiful, rich colors of the sunset on the evening we moved into our current house.
The smell of chlorine always brings back memories of summer swim lessons and feeling completely exhausted afterwards.
I once found a twenty-dollar bill on the sidewalk and felt an absurd amount of joy over it.
I remember the heavy, sinking feeling in my stomach when I realized I forgot my partner's birthday one year.
The soothing sound of rain against the window during a late-night study session is something I still find deeply comforting.
I have a vivid memory of the awful, fluorescent lighting in the dressing room when I was trying to find a swimsuit last summer.
I remember the absolute exhaustion of pulling an all-nighter for my final exams, my eyes burning from the screen.
We went to a fancy restaurant for our anniversary, but all I remember is the incredible taste of the chocolate mousse.

When my clinic integrated a partnership program with a commercial weight-loss app last year, I immediately questioned their financial incentives and where my data was going. I remember asking the clinic administrator exactly how my protected health information would be shielded from third-party marketing algorithms, but I cannot recall her exact answer.
I remember the terrifying moment I lost control of my car on an icy road, even though I somehow avoided a crash.
The feeling of soft sand between my toes on a beach vacation in Florida is still crystal clear in my mind.
It is strange how my definition of success has completely shifted from professional accolades to just having a peaceful weekend.
I remember the comforting smell of coffee brewing in the breakroom on Monday mornings.
The frustration of trying to zip up a dress that used to fit easily almost ruined a friend's wedding for me.
I remember the soft, rhythmic purring of my childhood cat when she would sleep on my chest.
The sharp smell of antiseptic at the dentist's office always makes my muscles tense up involuntarily.
I look at old photos of myself and feel sad that I spent so much time hating a body that was actually perfectly fine.
I remember the exhilarating rush of cold air when stepping out of a stuffy movie theater.
The disappointment of eating a soggy sandwich at my desk while working through lunch is a recurring memory.

My previous cardiologist, Dr. Chen, made me feel incredibly comfortable because she always tied my BMI specifically to my hypertension management rather than making me feel guilty about how I looked. It was such a relief to focus on my lab work and vascular health instead of feeling blamed for my dress size.
I can still hear the loud, clunky sound my old laptop's fan used to make when it was overheating.
I remember the sheer panic of misplacing my passport right before an international flight.
The sweet, cloying smell of the cheap perfume I wore in high school makes me cringe now.
I remember laughing so hard with my college roommate that we both ended up in tears on the floor.
The heavy silence in the room after I snapped at my partner during a stressful week is something I deeply regret.
I remember the vibrant, chaotic energy of the local farmer's market on a Saturday morning.
The warm, comforting feeling of crawling into a freshly made bed after a long day at the office is unbeatable.
I realized recently that my tendency to overwork is just a coping mechanism to avoid thinking about my personal life.

Because I had spent five years building a trusting relationship with my primary care provider, her gentle and nonjudgmental tone made all the difference when we finally addressed my weight last fall. I do not remember the exact words she used, but her clear empathy made me feel safe enough to actually tell the truth about my dietary struggles.
I remember the sharp crunch of autumn leaves under my boots during my walks to campus.
The embarrassment of having my credit card declined at a grocery store in my twenties still haunts me.
I can still taste the incredibly bitter espresso I had in a tiny cafe in Europe.
I remember the intense, throbbing headache I got after my first full day of staring at spreadsheets.
It occurs to me that I married someone who is the exact opposite of my father, which probably wasn't an accident.
The feeling of absolute dread before giving a presentation to the executive board was paralyzing.
I remember the soft, faded fabric of my favorite childhood blanket.
The smell of wet dog after taking our golden retriever for a walk in the rain is unforgettably pungent.
I remember the thrill of buying my first piece of real, expensive furniture.
The gnawing anxiety of checking my bank account balance before payday used to keep me awake at night.
I can still feel the sticky humidity of the subway station during my summer internship commute.
I remember the incredible relief of finally taking off my heels after a long corporate event.
The deep, aching sadness of watching a sad movie alone on a Sunday afternoon sometimes lingers for hours.
I remember the sharp, metallic taste of blood after accidentally biting my tongue during a heated argument.
I often think about how my postgraduate degree gave me a lot of debt but surprisingly little practical wisdom.
The smell of fresh paint always reminds me of the chaotic weekend we spent renovating our first bedroom.
I remember the profound sense of isolation I felt during my first few months living in a new city.
The sweet, melty goodness of a s'more by a campfire is a flavor I will never outgrow.
I can still hear the incessant ringing of the alarm clock during my early morning exam prep days.
I have noticed that I use humor as a shield whenever conversations get too intimate or emotionally demanding.
I remember the hot, stinging tears of frustration when my laptop crashed and deleted half my thesis.
The smell of a specific brand of sunscreen instantly transports me back to family beach trips.
I remember the quiet satisfaction of finishing a massive jigsaw puzzle on a snowy weekend.
The awkward tension of running into an ex at a coffee shop made my stomach do flips.
I can still feel the rough, peeling bark of the old oak tree in my childhood backyard.
I remember the overwhelming scent of lilies at my grandmother's funeral.
The delicious, savory smell of garlic sautéing in olive oil always makes my mouth water.
I remember the feeling of absolute exhaustion after hosting my entire family for Thanksgiving dinner.
The sharp, jolting pain of stubbing my toe on the bedframe in the dark is a recurring nightmare.
It makes me laugh to realize that the confident professional woman I present at work is just a carefully constructed persona.
I remember the cool, smooth texture of the marble countertops in my dream kitchen.
The sinking feeling when my boss asked me to step into their office for an unscheduled chat is unforgettable.
I can still taste the overly sugary margaritas from my bachelorette party.
I remember the quiet, eerie stillness of the neighborhood after a massive snowstorm.
I am increasingly aware that my fear of judgment has dictated almost every major fashion choice I have made since high school.
The smell of burning leaves in the fall always brings a rush of nostalgia.
I remember the sharp pinch of the needle during my first flu shot as an adult.
The deep, rumbling thunder of a summer storm always makes me want to curl up with a good book.
I remember the acute embarrassment of mispronouncing a word during a graduate seminar.
The soft, buttery texture of a perfectly baked croissant is one of my greatest weaknesses.
I can still feel the heavy, oppressive heat of the sun during a summer music festival.
I remember the sheer panic of losing my phone on a crowded train, even though I found it minutes later.
The smell of old, musty books in a secondhand shop is oddly comforting to me.
I remember the stinging sensation of a terrible sunburn on my shoulders after a day at the lake.
Looking back, I see that my obsession with getting perfect grades was mostly just a profound fear of failure.
The loud, chaotic chatter of a packed restaurant always makes me feel a little claustrophobic.
I remember the sweet, tangy taste of lemonade on a scorching hot day.
The frustration of dealing with a difficult client on a Friday afternoon always leaves me completely drained.
I can still feel the soft, plush carpet of my childhood bedroom between my toes.
I realize now that keeping a small circle of friends is not about being antisocial, but about protecting my own energy.
I remember the bright, blinding flash of the camera from my graduation day photos.
The smell of fresh pine always reminds me of picking out a Christmas tree with my dad.
I remember the dull ache in my lower back after sitting in an unergonomic office chair for a year.
The taste of perfectly ripe strawberries from a local farm stand is a true summer highlight.
I can still hear the rhythmic clicking of my keyboard during a late-night writing sprint.
I remember the intense anxiety of trying to parallel park while people were watching.
The smooth, cool glass of a wine bottle on a Friday evening is a very welcome sensation.
I remember the overwhelming volume of the crowd at my first big stadium concert.
The sharp smell of vinegar always reminds me of dyeing Easter eggs as a kid.
I remember staring blankly at my calendar, feeling a strange sense of dread about the upcoming week.
I remember the warm, fuzzy feeling of wearing my partner's oversized hoodie.
The embarrassment of tripping on the stairs in front of my coworkers made me want to disappear.
I can still taste the rich, earthy flavor of the mushroom risotto I had in Italy.

I was so relieved when a specialist finally mapped out exactly how my prescribed SSRI was driving my metabolic changes and compounding my insulin resistance. Hearing a medical professional clearly explain the pharmacological edge cases of my medication gave me a concrete reason for the sudden weight gain, even if I forget which specific metabolic pathway she referenced.
I remember the blinding glare of the sun off the snow on a bright winter morning.
I often realize that my harsh judgment of other people's dietary choices is just a projection of my own insecurities.
The smell of a new car interior always makes me feel slightly nauseous.
I remember the profound relief of finally finding a pair of boots that fit my wide calves.
The loud, startling crash of a dropped plate in the kitchen still makes me jump.
I can still feel the rough, scratchy wool of the sweater my aunt knitted for me.
I remember the sweet, sticky mess of eating a caramel apple at a fall festival.
The deep, heavy sigh my partner lets out when they are exhausted is a sound I know perfectly.
I remember the sheer terror of waking up from a nightmare where I was falling.
The smell of lavender always makes me think of the hand cream my mother used.
I remember the quiet satisfaction of crossing the final item off a massive weekend to-do list.
I remember furiously scrubbing the kitchen counters before my mother-in-law came over.
The sharp, metallic clink of keys in the door means my partner is finally home.
I remember the awkward silence in the elevator with my CEO during my first week on the job.
I can still taste the overly salty popcorn from the local movie theater.
I remember the bright, neon lights of the diner we used to frequent after late-night study sessions.
I remember the quiet disappointment of my thirtieth birthday dinner, which felt entirely ordinary.
The smell of damp earth after a spring rain is my favorite scent in the world.
I remember the intense, burning pain of a blister on my heel after a long hike.
The soothing, low hum of the refrigerator is the only sound in the house at midnight.
I remember the acute sting of rejection when a close friend didn't invite me to her bridal shower.
I can still feel the icy cold water of the lake hitting my skin when I jumped in.
I remember the delicious, savory crunch of a perfectly fried potato chip.
The loud, obnoxious ringtone of my old cell phone still triggers a Pavlovian response in me.
I remember the overwhelming smell of bleach in the hospital corridor when I went to visit my grandfather.
The soft, gentle breeze on a warm summer evening makes everything feel slightly more manageable.
I remember the sharp sting of guilt when I ignored a late-night work email for the first time.
I remember the bright, cheerful yellow color of my childhood bicycle.
The embarrassment of laughing at a joke I completely misunderstood in a work meeting still makes me cringe.
I can still taste the rich, gooey chocolate of a fresh brownie.
I remember the sharp, biting cold of the winter wind walking across campus.
I remember eating an entire pint of ice cream after a particularly grueling performance review.
The smell of peppermint always reminds me of the hard candies my grandmother kept in her purse.
I remember the deep, relaxing heat of a hot tub after a long week.
The frustration of sitting in dead-stopped traffic when I am already late is incredibly stressful.
I can still feel the soft, powdery texture of powdered sugar on my fingers.
I remember the sheer panic of thinking I lost my wedding ring, only to find it on the bathroom counter.
The sound of crickets chirping on a humid August night is intensely nostalgic.
I remember the dull, throbbing ache of a bad tooth before I finally got a root canal.
The smell of freshly cut grass instantly reminds me of elementary school recess.
I remember the profound joy of seeing my favorite band perform live for the first time.
I remember profusely apologizing to a waiter who had actually spilled coffee on me.
The bright, blinding lights of oncoming traffic at night always strain my eyes.
I can still taste the crisp, refreshing bite of a cold beer on a hot day.
I remember the heavy, sinking feeling when I realized I sent an email to the wrong person.
The soft, rhythmic ticking of the hallway clock is incredibly soothing.
I remember the quiet satisfaction of sweeping the porch on a crisp Sunday morning.
I remember the sweet, floral smell of the jasmine bush outside my old window.
The sharp, sudden pain of a papercut is always surprisingly intense.
I remember the quiet awe of seeing a meteor shower in a perfectly dark sky.
The embarrassment of having my stomach growl loudly during a silent meeting was agonizing.
I can still feel the rough, grainy texture of sandpaper from a weekend DIY project.
I remember the delicious, smoky flavor of barbecue ribs at a summer cookout.
The loud, startling blare of a car horn completely snapped me out of my daydream.
I remember the overwhelming smell of rubbing alcohol before getting a blood draw.
The soft, warm glow of string lights on our patio makes the evenings feel magical.
I remember stepping on the bathroom scale and feeling a heavy knot form in my stomach.
I remember the bright, vivid blue of the ocean on our honeymoon.
The dull ache of a tension headache after a day of non-stop Zoom calls is exhausting.
I can still taste the overly sweet icing on a generic grocery store birthday cake.
I remember the sharp, stinging slap of a cold winter breeze against my face.
I remember the acute stress of trying to meet a critical deadline when the internet went down.
The smell of woodsmoke always makes me crave a cozy cabin weekend.
I remember the sheer relief of finding a public restroom just in time during a road trip.
The frustrating tangles in my hair after rolling down the car windows on the highway are a classic memory.
I can still feel the soft, velvety petals of the roses my partner bought me.
I remember the intense, fiery heat of taking a bite of food before letting it cool down.
The sound of a lawnmower on a Saturday morning is the quintessential soundtrack of suburbia.
I remember the sheer panic of briefly losing sight of my niece at a crowded park.
The smell of freshly baked bread from the local bakery is absolutely heavenly.

When my partner Mark and I were looking over my bariatric consultation paperwork, the surgeon emphasized that obesity is a lifelong, chronic disease that requires active maintenance. It felt daunting but realistic to map out a five-year relapse protocol, knowing that my biology would always be fighting to regain the adiposity.
I can still taste the tangy, slightly sour flavor of plain yogurt.
I remember the bright, chaotic mess of wrapping paper on Christmas morning.
The dull, persistent pain of a papercut from a cardboard box is highly annoying.
The smell of cheap tequila instantly brings back memories of terrible college parties.
The smooth, cool feel of silk sheets against my skin is luxurious.
I can still hear the rhythmic, hypnotic sound of the washing machine running in the background.
I remember the overwhelming joy of stepping into air conditioning after being outside in a heatwave.
I remember the quiet, comforting weight of a heavy quilt on a cold night.
The sharp, metallic scrape of a fork against a plate always sends shivers down my spine.
I can still feel the sticky, messy residue of maple syrup on my hands after a pancake breakfast.

I remember the sharp, artificial cherry taste of the lip balm I constantly reapplied during my first stressful week at the marketing firm. I can't recall the exact name of the coworker who sat next to me, but I can still picture the intense glare of the fluorescent lights above our cubicles.

participants.persona: Marcus is a 34-year-old man with a college education, single, employed full-time, and overweight.
participants.name: Marcus

memories.content: I often look back at my college years and wonder if I chose the wrong major, realizing I just followed my dad's advice blindly.
Sometimes I think my weight is just a physical manifestation of my desire to avoid being noticed.
I realize now that I pushed my ex away because I was terrified of her finding out how deeply insecure I am.
Looking at old photos, I can see how much I've let my social circle shrink over the years.
I've noticed I have a habit of laughing off compliments because I genuinely don't know how to accept them.
It bothers me how much of my identity is tied to my job, considering I don't even like what I do.
I wonder if I'm still single because I'm too set in my routines to compromise with another person.
Whenever I feel stressed, I recognize that I immediately crave heavy, comforting foods.
I look back on my teenage years and see clearly how my sarcasm was just a defense mechanism.
I've realized lately that I spend too much time consuming media instead of actually living my life.
It's strange to think that my happiest memories are always quiet moments alone, rather than big parties.
I often catch myself mirroring other people's opinions to avoid conflict, which makes me feel a bit spineless.
I remember the exact rough texture of the carpet in my childhood bedroom, but not what color it was.
The smell of chlorine always takes me back to summer camp, even though I can't picture the faces of the kids I swam with.
I broke my arm falling off a swing set in third grade. I remember the sharp crack, but the pain itself is a blur.

I remember feeling frustrated when my doctor just handed me a generic diet pamphlet without asking about the diets I have already tried. It felt like he did not even consider my specific health history or what works for a single guy in his thirties.
My mom used to make these incredibly dry pork chops for dinner.
I once stole a candy bar from a corner store and felt sick to my stomach for a week.
I remember sitting in the back of my dad's car listening to the rain hit the roof.

After my annual checkup last year, the doctor told me to lose weight but did not give me any real plan to follow. I just walked out to my car feeling completely alone in figuring out how to actually shed the pounds.
There was a kid in my middle school who showed me how to play a specific chord on the guitar.
I remember the sheer panic of forgetting my lines in the fifth-grade play.
We had a golden retriever who smelled terribly when wet, but I loved burying my face in his fur.
The cafeteria in high school always smelled like stale tater tots and bleach.
I failed my first driving test because I paralleled parked right over the curb.
I remember the rush of cold air when I opened the door on the first snowy day of the year.
My grandfather had a really deep, booming laugh that startled me when I was little.
I got caught cheating on a math quiz in seventh grade and cried in the principal's office.
I remember the way the sun glared off the windshield during the drive to my first part-time job.
We went to a theme park once and I threw up after riding a roller coaster twice in a row.
I had a favorite blue hoodie that I wore every single day until the cuffs frayed completely.
The sound of dial-up internet always reminds me of staying up late to chat on instant messenger.
I remember the bitter taste of black coffee the first time I tried it to seem grown up.
I got rejected by my crush at the middle school dance and hid in the bathroom.
There was a specific hill we used to sled down that felt like a mountain back then.
I remember the loud hum of the window AC unit in my first apartment.
My roommate in college used to leave half-eaten pizza boxes under the couch.
I pulled an all-nighter for a history paper and remember the blinding headache I had the next morning.
The first time I saw the ocean, I was overwhelmed by how loud the crashing waves were.
I remember buying my first car and the distinct smell of old vinyl and stale air freshener inside.
I tripped on stage during my college graduation, though I doubt anyone else remembers.
I remember the relief of handing in my very last final exam.
There was a tiny diner near campus where I always ordered the same greasy breakfast sandwich.
I accidentally sent a text complaining about my boss to my boss, and my heart dropped into my stomach.
I remember the sharp sting of a papercut from a fresh textbook page.
My first real breakup happened in a coffee shop, and I still can't drink their hazelnut blend.
I once found a twenty-dollar bill on the sidewalk and felt like I had won the lottery.

When my doctor told me that joining that local fitness clinic was a solid idea, I suddenly felt a lot more excited to sign up. Having his medical approval made me believe the program could actually work for me.
The buzzing of fluorescent lights in my office gives me a migraine by three in the afternoon every Tuesday.
I remember the feeling of absolute exhaustion after finishing a big project at work last year.
I have a vivid memory of eating an entire tub of ice cream by myself after a particularly bad week.
The smell of wet asphalt after a summer storm is my favorite scent in the world.
I remember the awkwardness of going to a networking event and standing by the snack table alone.
My dad tried to teach me how to tie a tie, but we ended up just getting frustrated with each other.
I accidentally ruined my favorite shirt by spilling red wine all over it at a party.
The feeling of sand between my toes always makes me think of family vacations in Florida.
I remember the sinking feeling of checking my bank account right after college and seeing almost zero.
I got a flat tire on the highway once and had to wait two hours in the freezing cold for a tow.
The first time I cooked a Thanksgiving turkey, it was completely raw in the middle.
I remember the weirdly soft texture of the seats in the movie theater where I had my first date.
I was stung by a bee on my eyelid when I was a kid and my whole face swelled up.

The sound of keys jingling always makes me think someone is walking up right behind me.
I remember the sweet, syrupy taste of the medicine I took for ear infections as a kid.
I tripped going up the stairs at the train station and bruised my shin terribly.

I finally opened up about my eating habits because Dr. Evans just listened quietly without making that typical disappointed face. Her kind tone made it so much easier to talk about my weight without feeling embarrassed.
The smell of burning rubber from a car doing a burnout makes my stomach churn a bit.
I remember the soft, rhythmic clicking of a ceiling fan in a hotel room I stayed in.
I once choked on a sip of water during a quiet meeting and coughed for what felt like eternity.

The nutritionist I saw last month gave me an exact meal schedule to follow, which was way more helpful than the vague advice from my regular physician. It was nice to finally get concrete steps instead of just being told to eat less.
The feeling of a loose floorboard creaking under my foot always makes me jump.
I remember the vibrant green of the moss growing on a rock face during a rare hiking trip.
I bought a lottery ticket on my eighteenth birthday and won exactly two dollars.
The taste of a perfectly charred hot dog from a charcoal grill is unbeatable.
I remember the hollow echo of my footsteps in an empty parking garage late at night.
I once had to give a toast at a friend's wedding and my hands were shaking the entire time.
The smell of lavender always gives me a slight headache, despite it being supposed to relax you.
I remember the intense frustration of trying to untangle a massive knot of Christmas lights.
I tried to catch a baseball at a game once and completely missed, hitting my shoulder instead.
The sound of a dial tone on a landline phone feels almost like ancient history now.
I remember the bitter, metallic taste of a battery when I tested it with my tongue as a kid.
I once locked my keys inside my apartment and had to pay a locksmith an outrageous fee to get in.
The feeling of stepping into an overly air-conditioned store on a boiling hot day is a shock to the system.
I remember the sharp, precise fold of a paper airplane a classmate made in fourth grade.
I accidentally wore my shirt inside out to the office and didn't notice until lunchtime.
The smell of stale beer on a sticky bar floor is something I don't miss about my twenties.
I remember the sudden, terrifying jolt of hitting a massive pothole on the highway.
I once bought a very expensive steak and accidentally cooked it well-done, completely ruining it.
The taste of artificial cherry flavor always reminds me of cough drops.
I remember the dull, throbbing pain in my lower back after helping a friend move heavy furniture.
I got a bad haircut right before my driver's license photo and had to live with it for years.
The sound of a woodpecker knocking on a tree outside my window wakes me up on weekends.
I remember the overwhelming blast of heat opening the oven to check on a frozen pizza.
I once tried to assemble a complicated desk chair and gave up halfway, sitting on a stool for a month.
The feeling of a cold drop of water hitting my neck from a condensation pipe makes me shiver.
I remember the distinct smell of leather in the sporting goods store where I bought my first baseball mitt.
I accidentally bumped into a glass door because I thought it was open, and my nose hurt for hours.
The taste of a slightly green banana always leaves a chalky feeling in my mouth.
I remember the satisfying crunch of walking over dry autumn leaves on the sidewalk.
I once left my sunroof open during a rainstorm and had to drive sitting on a trash bag.
The sound of static on a radio searching for a station makes me feel a bit nostalgic.
I remember the intense, blinding glare of the sun reflecting off fresh snow.
I tried to cook a fancy dinner for a date, but the smoke alarm went off and ruined the mood.

I did not mind at all when my primary care doc suggested I look into a commercial weight loss app. It actually seemed like a practical option since I needed a structured system to help me stay on track with my meals while working my busy full-time job.
The feeling of a rough paper towel on wet hands is oddly uncomfortable to me.
I remember the smell of gasoline filling the air at the old rural gas station my grandfather used.
I once stepped in a deep puddle while wearing canvas shoes, and my foot was freezing for the rest of the day.

participants.persona: Danielle is a 28-year-old woman with some college or technical education, married or living with a partner, employed full-time, and overweight.
participants.name: Danielle

memories.content: I remember breaking my arm when I was like six, falling off some rusty swing set. I think it was at a park near my grandmother's house, though it might have been at school.
We had a golden retriever named Buster, or maybe it was Bailey, when I was in elementary school. He always smelled like wet corn chips.
My mom used to make this terrible meatloaf with chunks of carrots in it. I still can't eat ground beef without feeling a little nauseous.
I think I won a spelling bee in fourth grade by spelling the word 'restaurant' right. Looking back, I realize I peaked academically when I was nine.
There was a girl in middle school named Sarah or Samantha who used to make fun of my shoes. It made me so obsessed with buying name-brand sneakers later in life.
I remember my first kiss was behind a dumpster at a skating rink in roughly 2009. The guy tasted like cherry slushie and old pennies.
My high school boyfriend drove a beat-up Honda Civic that was maybe blue or black. We used to listen to mix CDs that always skipped on the same track.
I dropped out of standard university after like three semesters because I failed a bunch of basics. I just stopped going to class and never officially withdrew.
After dropping out, I enrolled in a dental assisting or medical billing program at a technical college. It took about two years, and I mostly just remember the uncomfortable chairs.
I met my partner at a terrible dive bar downtown, probably around five or six years ago. They bumped into me and spilled half a beer down my shirt.
We moved in together pretty fast, maybe after only six months of dating. Our first apartment had this gross carpet that never felt fully dry.
I work full-time at a regional logistics office now, doing something with accounts receivable. I honestly don't really understand half of what the company actually ships.
I've always struggled with my weight, pretty much since puberty hit. I avoid looking in full-length mirrors if the lighting is too bright.
I try to diet every January, usually lasting about three weeks before I give up. Sometimes I think I use food as my only real coping mechanism.
We have a cat that we adopted maybe two years ago, a tabby named Luna. She throws up on the rug at least once a week.
I remember going to Florida for a family vacation when I was a teenager. We stayed in a motel that smelled heavily of bleach and old smoke.
My dad used to yell a lot when driving, mostly at people going too slow. It made me really anxious whenever I had to learn how to drive myself.
I think my first job was at a frozen yogurt place or maybe a regular ice cream shop. I smelled like sour milk for an entire summer.
I bought my first car from some guy on Craigslist for about two thousand dollars. It broke down on the highway literally the next day.
I remember having a massive fight with my best friend in high school over a boy whose name I can't even recall now. It's funny how things that felt like the end of the world barely register now.
I used to dye my hair constantly in my early twenties, switching between terrible box-dye red and pitch black. My hair was so fried it felt like actual straw.
My partner and I went to a fancy restaurant for our anniversary last year, or maybe the year before. I felt so out of place because I didn't know which fork to use.
I have this scar on my knee from tripping over a curb while texting. I usually tell people it's from hiking because the truth is too embarrassing.
I took a pottery class once at the community center, hoping for a fun hobby. Everything I made looked like lumpy ash trays.
My grandmother passed away in a nursing home sometime around 2016. I still feel incredibly guilty that I didn't visit her more often at the end.
I got my current job through a friend of a friend, though I can't remember exactly who recommended me. The interview was so easy I thought it was a scam.
I have a habit of buying fresh produce and then letting it rot in the crisper drawer. Throwing it away makes me feel like a total failure as an adult.
I remember going to a concert when I was eighteen and nearly passing out in the crowd. Some random girl with purple hair dragged me to the medical tent.

When Dr. Miller told me last fall that I was a perfect candidate for the new metabolic program, I actually believed I could do it this time. Just hearing him say it wasn't a lost cause gave me the push to sign up with my husband that same week.
I used to be obsessed with this vampire TV show and read all the fanfiction I could find. I hid it from everyone because I thought they would mock me.
I broke my toe last summer by dropping a frozen turkey on it. It still aches when it rains, or at least I think it does.
My partner always leaves their socks right next to the laundry hamper instead of in it. I complain, but honestly, I leave my coffee cups all over the living room.
I tried doing a juice cleanse a few years ago and lasted exactly fourteen hours. I ended up ordering a massive pizza at two in the morning.
I remember a family reunion where my uncle got way too drunk and fell into a kiddie pool. Nobody ever talked about it afterward.
I had braces for three years in middle school, and my orthodontist was this grumpy older man. He always smelled like peppermint and stale coffee.
I went to a Halloween party dressed as a cat in my early twenties, but it was just a black shirt and cheap ears. I felt so painfully uncreative compared to everyone else.
We bought a really expensive vacuum cleaner on credit and it took us forever to pay it off. It doesn't even pick up the cat hair very well.
I remember failing my first driving test because I hit a traffic cone while parallel parking. I cried the entire way home in the passenger seat.
I usually skip breakfast and just drink three cups of coffee. By noon my stomach is screaming, but I convince myself I'm being healthy.
I once stole a lip gloss from a drugstore when I was fourteen. The guilt ate me alive for weeks, and I threw it in the trash without ever using it.
My partner made me watch some sci-fi movie last weekend, maybe Dune or Star Wars. I fell asleep twenty minutes in and pretended I watched the whole thing.
I remember getting a terrible sunburn at a water park when I was a kid. I had blisters on my shoulders that popped when I put my shirt on.
I used to work at a call center doing customer service for some telecom company. Getting yelled at by strangers all day really broke my spirit for a while.
I have this dress in my closet that I bought hoping I'd lose enough weight to fit into it. Every time I see it, I feel a little wave of depression.
I think I left my favorite jacket at a bar in downtown maybe three years ago. It was a fake leather jacket that always made me feel cool.
We tried to grow tomatoes on our apartment balcony one summer. The birds ate them all before they even turned red.
I got a tattoo of a tiny star on my ankle when I was eighteen, just to rebel. It looks like a fuzzy black blob now, which is a perfect metaphor for my youth.
I remember a teacher in high school, Mr. Something, who told me I wasn't applying myself. I hated him for it, mostly because I knew he was absolutely right.
I spend way too much time scrolling through social media before bed. I always wake up feeling exhausted and angry at myself.
My partner and I took a road trip to the mountains and got terribly lost because we had no cell service. We fought for two hours over a paper map neither of us could read.
I used to collect snow globes when I was little, lining them up on my window sill. My mom threw them out when I moved out, and I pretended not to care.
I remember throwing up in the hallway in third grade after eating too many cafeteria tater tots. The janitor had to bring out that weird green sawdust to clean it up.

I was so annoyed when that young NP at the clinic handed me a generic printout about portions, completely ignoring that I have PCOS and already tried Keto back in 2019. I told my partner it felt like she didn't even look at my chart to see what actually works for a woman my age with my history.
I had a phase in high school where I wore heavy black eyeliner every single day. I thought it made me look mysterious, but I mostly just looked tired.
I went to a wedding a few years ago where the bride got completely wasted and yelled at the DJ. I remember feeling so embarrassed for her.
I usually lie to my dentist about how often I floss. I'm pretty sure he knows, but we both just play along with the charade.

After my checkup around February, the doctor basically just said my BMI was 32 and told me to watch my carbs before walking out of the room. I remember sitting in my car in the parking lot feeling totally abandoned, realizing I'd just have to figure out a diet plan on my own again while working forty hours a week.
I remember getting my wisdom teeth out and waking up crying for no reason. My mom recorded it, and I made her delete the video because I looked so awful.
We went to a county fair last year and I ate a deep-fried Oreo. It gave me the worst heartburn of my life, but it was incredibly delicious.
I think I had a crush on a boy named Josh or Justin in middle school who played the trumpet. He never even looked in my direction.
I accidentally sent a text complaining about my boss directly to my boss once. I blamed it on my phone glitching, which somehow actually worked.
I remember my dad trying to build a treehouse in our backyard one summer. It ended up being just a few planks of wood that rotted after a year.
I hate wearing shorts because I'm insecure about my thighs rubbing together. Summer is always a miserable sweaty struggle for me.
My partner bought me a necklace for my birthday that really isn't my style at all. I wear it anyway so I don't hurt their feelings.
I once tried to cut my own bangs in the bathroom mirror using kitchen scissors. I had to wear headbands for three months to hide the disaster.
I remember a rainy day in college where I skipped all my classes to watch movies in bed. It was the only time I felt truly relaxed that entire semester.
I have a gym membership that I haven't used in at least eight months. The monthly charge just sits on my bank statement mocking me.
I went camping once with some friends and couldn't sleep because of the bug noises. I ended up sleeping in the car with the doors locked.
I think I lost my favorite sunglasses on a beach trip around 2018. They were cheap plastic ones, but they fit my wide face perfectly.
I remember getting a terrible grade on a math test in high school and hiding it under my mattress. I lived in fear for weeks that my mom would flip the bed.
I usually order takeout at least three times a week because I'm too tired to cook after work. It drains our budget, but the convenience is too addictive.
I had a coworker at my first office job who always clipped his fingernails at his desk. The sound used to make my skin crawl.
I sometimes pretend to be on my phone when I walk past someone I kind of know. It's a cowardly habit, but small talk just exhausts me.
I remember my partner cooking us a romantic dinner that turned out completely raw in the middle. We ended up eating cereal on the couch and laughing about it.
I bought a bunch of expensive makeup hoping it would make me look more professional. Most of it is just sitting expired in my bathroom drawer.
I once slipped on ice in a grocery store parking lot and dropped a whole gallon of milk. I just got in my car and drove away in pure shame.
I think I sprained my wrist when I was twelve by falling off a skateboard I didn't know how to ride. I never touched a skateboard again after that.
I remember watching my parents argue over money when I was little, though I didn't understand the words. It instilled this deep, lingering anxiety about finances in me.
I have a scar on my elbow from scraping it against a brick wall at school. I can't remember the exact year, but I remember the nurse using a stinging wipe on it.
I used to sneak out of the house in high school to hang out at a 24-hour diner. We would just drink coffee and eat fries until 3 AM.
I try to read more books, but I usually just end up falling asleep after two pages. I keep buying novels hoping one will finally hold my attention.
I remember my first apartment smelling vaguely of wet dog, even though I didn't own one. I burned cheap vanilla candles constantly to mask it.
I got fired from a retail job when I was nineteen for being late too many times. I told my parents I quit because the manager was mean.
My partner snores so loudly sometimes that I have to sleep on the sofa. I never tell them because I know they're sensitive about it.
I bought a treadmill a few years ago that now functions exclusively as a laundry rack. Sometimes I walk past it and feel a pang of guilt.
I remember finding a twenty-dollar bill on the sidewalk when I was in college. I bought myself a huge burrito and felt incredibly lucky.
I used to be obsessed with a boyband in middle school and covered my walls in their posters. My mom made me take them down when we painted my room pink.
I have this irrational fear of driving over bridges over open water. I grip the steering wheel so hard my knuckles turn white until we cross.
I went to a networking event for my company and hid in the bathroom for twenty minutes. I just didn't have the energy to fake confidence that day.
I remember getting a pet fish when I was seven that died the very next morning. My dad flushed it down the toilet while I sobbed.
I always buy the generic brand of cereal to save money, even though it tastes like cardboard. It's a weird stubborn habit I can't seem to break.
I once tripped going up the stairs in high school and spilled my backpack everywhere. Everyone laughed, and I felt my face turn bright red.
I remember having a panic attack in a dressing room trying on jeans that were too small. That was the moment I realized how deeply I hated my body.
My partner and I like to watch trashy reality TV shows on Sunday nights. We judge the people on screen to make ourselves feel better about our own lives.
I think I left the stove on once and drove halfway to work before turning around in a panic. It was completely off when I got back.
I remember a girl named Ashley in my technical program who always asked the most obvious questions. It drove the instructor absolutely insane.
I have a sweater that I only wear when I'm feeling really bloated. It's hideous, but it covers everything and makes me feel safe.
I used to drink those sugary energy drinks constantly when I worked retail. My heart would race, but it was the only way I could survive an eight-hour shift.
I went to a theme park a few years ago and the lap bar on the rollercoaster wouldn't click shut over my stomach at first. The attendant had to push it down hard, and I wanted to die of embarrassment.
I remember my mom trying to teach me how to sew a button on a shirt. I got frustrated and pricked my finger, and I haven't tried to sew since.
I always park at the very back of the parking lot because I'm terrible at maneuvering my car. I tell my partner it's because I want the extra steps.
I used to make up elaborate lies about what I did over the weekend when coworkers asked. I just hated admitting that I sat at home doing nothing.
I remember going to a midnight movie premiere in high school and falling asleep in the theater. My friends teased me about it for months.
I bought an expensive planner in January hoping it would organize my life. It's currently sitting under a pile of mail, completely empty since February.
I remember a summer where I ate nothing but microwave nachos for lunch every day. I don't know how my teenage stomach handled that much processed cheese.
I accidentally called my boss 'Mom' during a team meeting once. I still cringe about it when I'm trying to fall asleep at night.
My partner bought this awful smelling cologne that they love. I slowly poured some out down the sink so they would run out faster.
I remember a family vacation to a lake where it rained for four days straight. We just played monopoly and argued the entire time.
I always keep a stash of chocolate hidden in the back of the pantry behind the canned beans. It's my secret comfort food that I don't have to share.
I think I voted in a local election once just because there was a bake sale at the polling place. The brownies were definitely worth the civic duty.
I remember my high school locker getting jammed constantly. I would have to kick the bottom of it just to get my textbooks out.
I had this phase where I tried to learn French using an app on my phone. I gave up after two weeks because the pronunciation was too frustrating.
I once threw away a Tupperware container instead of washing it because the leftover spaghetti smelled so bad. I felt so wasteful, but I couldn't handle the mold.
I remember my partner taking me to a baseball game for a date early in our relationship. I pretended to understand the rules just to seem supportive.
I have a habit of picking at the skin around my fingernails when I'm stressed. Sometimes they bleed, but I literally cannot stop myself.
I used to ride my bike to a nearby creek when I was a kid to catch tadpoles. I'd bring them home in a plastic cup and they'd usually die by morning.
I went to a fancy hair salon once and ended up crying in my car afterward because they cut it way too short. It took a year to grow out properly.
I remember trying to bake a cake for my mom's birthday and completely forgetting the sugar. We tried to eat it anyway out of politeness, but it was awful.

The clinic sent me an email linking to some app called Noom or maybe Weight Watchers, and it immediately made me suspicious about whether they were getting a kickback for my sign-up. I refused to put my credit card or health data into a third-party app just because my doctor's office suddenly partnered with them last spring.
I always leave the bathroom fan on for way too long because I'm self-conscious about the noise. My partner jokes about it, but it genuinely stresses me out.
I think I had a myspace account with an incredibly embarrassing username like DarkAngel or something. I'm so glad that part of the internet is mostly dead.
I once got pulled over for speeding and started crying so hysterically the cop just gave me a warning. I wasn't even acting; I was just terrified of the ticket cost.
I remember finding an old diary of mine from middle school and throwing it in the garbage immediately. The sheer volume of teenage angst made my skin crawl.
We have this weird neighbor who always stares at us when we take out the trash. I purposefully wait until he goes inside before I leave the apartment.
I bought a set of resistance bands during the pandemic that I used exactly twice. They are now permanently tangled in my sock drawer.
I remember getting stuck in an elevator at a doctor's office for about ten minutes. I was sweating profusely and almost hit the emergency button before the doors opened.
I usually skip the doctor unless I'm basically dying because I hate stepping on the medical scale. They always announce the number so loudly.
I went to a college party once and spilled a red cup of punch all over a white rug. I just quietly walked out the front door and never spoke to the host again.
I remember my dad making me check the oil in my car before he would let me drive it. I still have no idea what the dipstick is actually supposed to look like.
I sometimes stare at my partner when they're sleeping and wonder how they can tolerate my chaotic habits. It makes me realize how incredibly lucky I am to have them.
I have a drawer full of old charging cables for phones I haven't owned in a decade. I'm too paranoid to throw them away just in case I need them.
I remember taking a standardized test in high school and filling in random bubbles for the last math section. I was just too mentally exhausted to read the questions.
I accidentally washed a red sock with my partner's white work shirts once. They all turned a dingy pink, and I had to buy replacements in secret.
I used to be terrified of the dark and slept with a closet light on until I was twelve. Sometimes I still get a little spooked if the apartment is too quiet.
I went to a zoo on a school field trip and a goat aggressively chewed on my jacket zipper. I was too scared to push it away.
I have a terrible habit of interrupting people when they talk because I'm afraid I'll forget my thought. I know it's annoying, but my mouth just moves faster than my brain.
I remember a blizzard in 2014 or 2015 where we lost power for two days. We slept under five blankets and ate cold soup out of the can.
I bought a plant for my desk at work and overwatered it until the roots rotted. I quietly replaced it with a plastic one so nobody would judge me.
I once faked being sick to get out of a bridal shower because I couldn't afford a nice gift. I spent the afternoon watching Netflix and feeling incredibly guilty.
I remember my first time drinking alcohol was some cheap vodka mixed with orange soda. The smell of orange soda still makes me gag slightly.
I always write my grocery lists on the back of old receipts and then immediately lose them in my purse. I end up just wandering the aisles buying things I don't need.

Dr. Evans told me to just move more and eat less during my physical a few years ago, which honestly felt like a slap in the face instead of actual medical care. You wouldn't tell someone with asthma to just breathe better, so I don't know why that counts as a real treatment plan for my weight.
I had a severe allergic reaction to a cheap pair of earrings in high school. My earlobes swelled up like balloons and oozed for a week.
I remember sneaking into an R-rated movie with my friends when I was fifteen. We thought we were so cool, but the movie was actually really boring.
I sometimes pretend not to see text messages from my mom if I don't have the mental energy to deal with her complaints. I'll reply hours later claiming I was in a meeting.
I bought a fancy water bottle to encourage myself to hydrate, but I keep forgetting it in my car. It gets so hot in the summer that the plastic tastes weird.
I remember working a Black Friday shift at a department store and seeing two women literally fight over a towel set. It made me lose a lot of faith in humanity.
I have this recurring dream where my teeth crumble and fall out of my mouth. I always wake up in a cold sweat and immediately check my jaw.
I accidentally dropped my phone in the toilet a few years ago. I put it in a bag of rice, but it never turned back on.
I remember a teacher pulling me aside to ask if things were okay at home because I looked so tired. I was just staying up until 4 AM playing internet flash games.
I usually delete unflattering photos of myself from my partner's phone when they aren't looking. I know it's a huge violation of trust, but I can't stand seeing them.
I went to a pumpkin patch last fall and twisted my ankle in a hidden gopher hole. I had to limp back to the car pretending I was totally fine.
I remember making a diorama in fifth grade out of a shoebox and some plastic dinosaurs. My dad basically did the whole thing for me the night before it was due.
I have a bad habit of agreeing to plans and then intensely hoping the other person cancels first. The relief I feel when they do is honestly intoxicating.
I used to hide my report cards under the couch cushions if I got anything lower than a C. My parents always found them eventually anyway.
I remember trying to bleach my own teeth with baking soda and peroxide from a Pinterest tutorial. It completely ruined my enamel and my teeth ached for days.
I once laughed so hard at a joke in the office breakroom that I snorted milk out of my nose. Everyone went completely silent and awkwardly looked away.
I have an entire shelf of expensive skincare products that I never use because I'm too lazy to wash my face at night. I just use a makeup wipe and hope for the best.
I remember getting a terrible stomach bug on New Year's Eve and spending the countdown in the bathroom. My partner sat outside the door offering me ginger ale.
I used to be terrified of the deep end of the pool because I was convinced a shark could somehow get in. My older brother definitely put that idea in my head.
I sometimes buy clothes a size too small as a form of 'motivation' to lose weight. They just end up taking up space and making me feel awful about myself.
I remember getting a flat tire on the highway and having no idea how to change it. I waited for a tow truck for two hours in the freezing cold.
I once dated a guy in my early twenties who constantly criticized my music taste. I actually threw away some of my favorite CDs just to impress him.
I have a terrible sense of direction and rely entirely on my GPS, even for places I've been to a dozen times. If my phone dies, I am essentially stranded.
I remember trying to follow a Bob Ross painting tutorial on YouTube during a boring weekend. My trees looked like fuzzy green blobs and the mountains were completely lopsided.
I secretly hate the way my partner loads the dishwasher, so I often rearrange the plates after they leave the kitchen. It's so passive-aggressive but I can't help it.
I once tried a spin class because a fit friend dragged me along. I was so exhausted I literally threw up in a trash can in the lobby afterwards.
I remember a phase in elementary school where I collected those weird rubbery bracelets. I had so many on my arm it would cut off my circulation.
I usually leave my clean laundry in the basket for at least a week before folding it. I end up just digging wrinkled shirts out of the pile every morning.
I had a minor car accident a few years ago where I rear-ended someone at a stoplight because I was changing the radio station. My insurance went up so much it crippled my budget for a year.
I remember buying a terribly cheap mattress when I got my first apartment. I woke up with back pain every single day until we could afford a better one.
I sometimes eat lunch in my car just to avoid talking to my coworkers in the breakroom. It gets incredibly hot in the summer, but the solitude is worth it.
I once tried to give my cat a bath because she got into something sticky. She scratched my arm so badly I actually considered going to urgent care.
I remember watching a documentary about factory farming and deciding to become a vegetarian. That lasted exactly three days before I ordered a double cheeseburger.
I have a tendency to hoard fast food napkins in my car's glove compartment. Whenever I open it, a huge pile of them just spills out onto the floor.
I accidentally liked a very old photo of an ex on social media while aggressively stalking their page. I panicked and immediately deactivated my entire account for a week.
I remember wearing a terribly itchy wool sweater for family photos because my mom insisted on it. I look deeply miserable in every single picture.
I sometimes buy the most expensive coffee at the cafe just to feel luxurious for ten minutes. The financial guilt usually kicks in before I even finish drinking it.
I once found a stray kitten and tried to hide it in my bedroom from my parents. It meowed so loudly they found it within thirty minutes.
I try to drink enough water every day, but I always forget and then chug three glasses right before bed. It ruins my sleep because I have to get up constantly.
I remember a college professor telling me my writing was 'adequate at best'. I haven't tried to write anything creative since that day.
I accidentally wore my shirt inside out to work until about lunch time. A coworker gently pointed it out, and I wanted the floor to swallow me whole.
I have this strange habit of counting the stairs whenever I walk up a flight. If I lose count, I feel a tiny, irrational wave of anxiety.
I remember trying to build an IKEA dresser with my partner and getting into a massive screaming match. We eventually gave up and it sat half-finished in the hallway for a month.
I usually check the lock on the front door two or three times before I can actually fall asleep. I don't even know what I'm afraid of, I just can't relax until I check.
I once bought a really pretty pair of high heels for a wedding that pinched my toes completely numb. I walked barefoot across the parking lot at the end of the night.
I remember getting horrible food poisoning from a sketchy sushi place downtown. I laid on my bathroom floor for hours praying for it to end.
I sometimes tell the cashier at the grocery store that my junk food is for a party I'm throwing. I know they don't care, but I'm deeply embarrassed by how much ice cream I buy.
I used to be in the school choir in middle school, but the director asked me to just mouth the words during the concert. That was my first hint that I was completely tone-deaf.
I remember spilling a full cup of hot coffee on my lap during my morning commute. I had to work an entire eight-hour shift with a huge brown stain on my khakis.
I try to organize my computer desktop but end up just putting everything into a folder named 'misc'. Finding a specific document is always a nightmare.
I once sneaked into the kitchen at 2 AM to eat leftover pie and dropped the glass dish on the floor. I spent thirty minutes quietly sweeping up shards of glass in the dark.
I remember taking my driver's ed classes during a terribly hot summer in a car with no AC. The instructor sweated so much it left a mark on the seat.

I lost thirty pounds for my wedding in 2021, but since then I've learned the hard way that keeping it off is a lifelong battle that my clinic never helped me plan for. I'm going to be dealing with this my whole life, and I need a doctor who understands what happens when the initial motivation fades and the weight starts creeping back.
I accidentally knocked over a huge display of canned beans at the grocery store once. I just abandoned my cart and ran out the automatic doors in pure panic.
I have this fake cheerful voice I use whenever I answer a phone call from a number I don't recognize. My partner always laughs at how dramatically my tone shifts.
I remember watching a sad movie on an airplane and sobbing aggressively into my tiny napkin. The businessman sitting next to me looked genuinely terrified.
I once tried to negotiate my salary at a new job and completely stumbled over my words. They gave me the lowest offer anyway and I just meekly accepted it.
I have a fear of walking over those metal grates on the sidewalk because I think I'll fall through. I will literally walk into the street just to avoid them.
I remember trying to surprise my partner with breakfast in bed but I burnt the bacon so badly the smoke alarm went off. It woke them up in a total panic instead of a romantic surprise.

participants.persona: Gregory is a 41-year-old man with a college education, single, employed full-time, and very overweight.
participants.name: Gregory

memories.content: I remember having a bike when I was a kid, maybe a red one, and I crashed it near some big tree.
There was a kid in second or third grade named David, I think, who I traded cards with.
We had a dog named Max in the early 90s who chewed up my shoes, probably my favorite sneakers.
I recall my grandparents' house smelling like mothballs and some kind of mints, maybe in Ohio.
A boy named Todd in middle school used to make fun of my weight, so I'd just hide near the teachers.
I broke my arm when I was seven or eight, falling off a swing set I think.
One Halloween I dressed up as a pirate, or maybe it was a ninja, using my dad's old clothes.
I got a video game console around 1991, probably a Super Nintendo, and played it all weekend.
We took a family trip to Florida once, I'm pretty sure we went to Disney but it might have been Universal.
I lost a tooth biting into an apple at lunch, sometime in elementary school.
I did a science fair project on volcanoes in fourth grade. I realize now I always picked the easiest projects just to get by.
I took piano lessons from an older lady, Mrs. G or something, but I never practiced.
We moved to a new house when I was around nine, and I think my room had blue wallpaper.
I ate way too much cake at a birthday party once and threw up in the host's bathroom.
Saturday mornings usually meant watching cartoons, maybe Thundercats or Transformers.
There was a treehouse in my neighborhood that we started building but never actually finished.
I remember getting glasses in fifth grade and hating how they made my face look rounder.
A big thunderstorm knocked out the power when I was a kid, and we ate sandwiches in the dark.
My mom used to make this meatloaf that I secretly fed to the dog, probably around 1995.
I had a shoebox full of cool rocks I found, but I think my mom threw it out eventually.
At a middle school dance, I just stood in the corner the whole time because I felt too awkward to move.

I remember going to Dr. Miller a few years ago, and he just told me to watch what I eat and move more. It felt really dismissive, like he wasn't giving me any kind of actual medical plan for my weight.
I tried a cigarette behind the school gym in eighth grade and coughed for what felt like an hour.
I had a math teacher, Mr. Brooks or maybe Mr. Barnes, who always wore the exact same brown tie.
During gym class basketball, I was always picked last, probably because I couldn't run very fast.
The first CD I bought with my own money was by Nirvana, or maybe Green Day, at a mall.
I went through a phase where I only wore black t-shirts. Looking back, I think I used clothes to hide my body.
I went to the movies with a group of kids once and felt completely left out of their jokes.
I had a huge crush on a girl named Sarah, or Samantha, but I never said a word to her.
I got a terrible grade in history, maybe a D, and tried to hide the report card in my desk.
I went to a summer camp near a lake in upstate New York, I think it was called Camp Whispering Pines or something.
I learned to drive in an old beat-up sedan, maybe a Ford, that smelled like wet dog.
I'm pretty sure I failed my learner's permit test the first time because I didn't study the parking rules.
I went to prom with a big group of friends and we ate at a terrible Italian restaurant beforehand.
My first summer job was at a grocery store, bagging groceries and wrangling carts in the heat.
I snuck out to a high school party once, but just ended up falling asleep on some guy's couch.
My car broke down on the highway around 1999, and I had to walk to a gas station to use a payphone.
An English teacher told me I had potential, though I can't remember her exact words.
I tried some extreme soup diet before senior year started, but gave up after three days.
Graduation day was incredibly hot, and I remember sweating through my gown.
I had a good friend named Josh who moved away in tenth grade, and we just lost touch.
I moved into the college dorms, room 204 or maybe 206, and it was ridiculously cramped.
My freshman roommate was a quiet guy from somewhere out west, maybe Colorado.
I changed my major sophomore year, from biology to communications I think, because the labs were too hard.
I gained the freshman fifteen, which was more like thirty pounds for me, eating dining hall pizza.
I stayed up all night studying for a sociology final and barely passed it anyway.
There was a campus coffee shop where I spent hours reading, mostly just trying to look busy.
I went to a college football game once but left at halftime because it was too cold.

When the nurse practitioner handed me a generic printout about dieting, I was pretty annoyed because it didn't factor in my bad knees or that I'd already tried keto back in 2018. I really expected her to suggest something that actually fit a single guy in his forties with my specific history.
I briefly dated a girl in my junior year, I think her name was Emily, but it fizzled out fast.
My hallmates and I would order a ton of late-night food, usually cheese bread and wings.
I graduated college with an okay GPA, something like a 3.2, but the ceremony is a blur.

After my checkup last fall, I walked out to my car realizing the doctor basically just pointed out my BMI and said to see him next year. It always feels like I am completely on my own trying to figure out how to handle being heavy.
My first apartment was a tiny studio downtown that always smelled faintly of cabbage.
I got hired at a logistics firm right after college, doing data entry or something similar.
My first boss was a guy named Mr. Henderson who micromanaged everything I typed.
The first real piece of furniture I bought was a brown sofa that turned out to be really uncomfortable.
I went to a buddy's wedding around 2008 and got a terrible sunburn during the outdoor ceremony.
I spent my 25th birthday completely alone eating takeout. I wonder if that was the year I just accepted being mostly alone.

A doctor once told me to try Weight Watchers, but the clinic never checked in to see if I actually signed up or how I was doing. I thought if a medical office was going to recommend a program, they would at least follow up with me and coordinate with the program to track my progress.
I signed up for a gym membership in my twenties but only went twice because I felt self-conscious.
Some friends and I took a road trip to Chicago and got a flat tire somewhere in Indiana.
I adopted a cat named Buster, or maybe Whiskers, who managed to run away after a month.
I used to cook spaghetti almost every night to save money, usually with cheap jarred sauce.
I got a minor promotion around 2010, which mostly just meant more unpaid overtime.
I bought a used silver Honda Civic, I think a 2006 model, and drove it for years.
At a work networking event, I just stood by the buffet table so I wouldn't have to talk to anyone.
There was a coworker named Lisa I liked, but I was too insecure about my weight to ask her out.
I split my pants at the office once and had to pretend I was sick so I could go home.
I tried online dating for about a week before deleting the app because it felt too depressing.
I went on a vacation to Mexico but spent almost the entire time sitting in the resort room.
I bought a fancy camera to get into photography, but I think I only used it on one weekend.
I went to a rock concert around 2012, but I can't quite remember the name of the main band.
I caught a terrible stomach bug that knocked me out for three days, mostly spent on my bathroom floor.
I moved to a slightly bigger apartment in the suburbs when the downtown noise got to be too much.
I started my current job, or the one right before it, sometime in my early thirties.
My 30th birthday was pretty quiet, just burgers with maybe two or three guys from work.
I had to buy new pants for work. It's funny how I constantly pretend my weight isn't a problem until nothing fits.
A doctor warned me about high blood pressure at a checkup, which freaked me out for a few weeks.
I binge-watched an entire TV series, probably Breaking Bad, over a single rainy weekend.
I bought an expensive espresso machine that I could never figure out how to clean properly.
I tried a strictly low-carb diet that just made me miserable and tired all the time.
I went to a cousin's baby shower and felt totally out of place among all the families.
I accidentally knocked a full mug of coffee onto my laptop and ruined the hard drive.
Work sent me to a conference in Vegas, or maybe Orlando, and the hotel AC was freezing.
I got stuck in an elevator for about twenty minutes and was terrified the cables would snap.
I had a massive argument with my brother over something trivial, maybe sports, and we didn't talk for months.
I went through a phase where I bought heavy history books but never actually read them.
A dentist appointment revealed I needed three fillings, probably because of all the soda I drank.
I adopted my dog, a scruffy mutt I named Charlie, from a shelter out in the country.
I tried to build an IKEA dresser and snapped a wooden peg, so the bottom drawer never closed right.
I went to a movie alone and loved it. I think I started isolating myself on purpose around then to avoid social pressure.
I got a weird rash on my arm that faded on its own before I could finally see a doctor.
I used to order takeout from the exact same Thai place every Friday night, always getting the pad see ew.
I attended my parents' anniversary party, maybe their 40th, and mostly just hid in the kitchen.
A well-meaning coworker set me up on a blind date that was incredibly awkward from start to finish.
I hired a personal trainer for a month who just made me feel pathetic about my lack of stamina.
I bought a smartwatch to track my steps but lost the proprietary charger almost immediately.
There was a summer where I drank a lot of local craft beer, mostly really bitter IPAs.

Someone at the clinic gave me a brochure for a meal replacement thing, but it didn't say anything about how much it cost or if my Blue Cross insurance covered it. I ended up throwing it away because I didn't even know if the shakes were safe for me to drink every day.
I slipped on black ice in my driveway and tweaked my lower back, which still hurts sometimes.
I got a horrible, uneven haircut right before a big work presentation and had to use gel to hide it.
I tried to grow a beard for a few months, but it just came in patchy and made my face look rounder.
I had a neighbor who played loud music, maybe jazz, every Sunday morning at 7 AM.
I found a twenty-dollar bill fluttering on the sidewalk outside a grocery store and bought extra snacks with it.
My favorite blue sweater shrank in the wash because I think I set the dryer too high.
I tried to roast a turkey for Thanksgiving once and it was completely raw in the middle.
I found an old childhood action figure in a box and just threw it away without really thinking.
I went to a baseball game but left early because the stadium seats were squeezing my hips too much.
I used to listen to a history podcast on my commute, something about the Romans I think.
I got a jury duty summons but was dismissed by noon, which was a huge relief.
I laughed so hard at a comedy special on Netflix that I literally choked on my water.
The smell of rain on hot asphalt always reminds me of somewhere, maybe that summer camp I went to.
