I played some online fantasy game for way too many hours, probably World of Warcraft, just to pass the time.
I realized I hadn't spoken to my college friends in years. I guess I just let relationships fade because it's easier than maintaining them.
There was a coworker named Craig or Greg who constantly borrowed my pens and never returned them.
The office internet went down for a whole afternoon, so we all just sat around drinking coffee.
I went to a company holiday party where the catered food was cold and mostly inedible.
I got a small end-of-year bonus and spent the entire thing on a giant television.
An angry client yelled at me over the phone for a shipping error that I didn't even make.
The old office building had this weird, ugly carpet, I think it was a dark green color.
I had an incredibly awkward elevator ride with the CEO, whose name I completely forgot in the moment.
I left my packed lunch on the kitchen counter and had to buy an overpriced turkey sandwich downstairs.
I tried using a standing desk at work, but my knees started aching after just two days.
I finally threw away my favorite pair of work shoes because they developed a hole in the sole.
There was a local diner I used to love that closed down a few years ago, maybe in 2018.
I developed an obsession with some limited-edition potato chips, jalapeño flavor I think.
I tried to drink a gallon of water a day for a health challenge and just gave up.
I ate a whole large pizza by myself on a Tuesday night. I sometimes use food as a substitute for actual companionship.
I got a really bad stomach ache after eating some questionable sushi from a grocery store.
I love the smell of fresh bread baking, though I almost never buy it for myself.
I went through a phase where I put hot sauce on literally everything I ate.
I keep a stash of candy bars hidden in my desk drawer so no one sees how much I snack.
I tried to learn how to make cocktails, mostly rum-based ones, but they always tasted too strong.
I burned a steak so badly in my apartment that it set off the smoke alarms for ten minutes.
I took a business trip to Dallas once and the humidity was absolutely suffocating.
I stayed in a cheap motel room that smelled overwhelmingly of industrial bleach.
I took the wrong train downtown and ended up wandering around a neighborhood I didn't recognize.
On a beach vacation with some friends, I refused to take off my shirt the entire time.
I got completely lost in a massive mall while looking for a specific shoe store.
I went on a long drive and just listened to classic rock albums for six straight hours.
I visited a museum in DC once, I'm fairly certain it was the Air and Space one.
A terrible flight delay forced me to try and sleep on those uncomfortable airport terminal chairs.
I bought a souvenir coffee mug on a trip, but it shattered in my suitcase on the way back.
I looked at a map of the world recently. I've spent my whole life staying in my comfort zone, which feels like a waste.
I went to see a sci-fi movie in theaters and fell asleep about halfway through.
I started reading a popular detective novel but lost interest and never found out who the killer was.
I teared up at a television commercial once, probably one of those ads about rescue dogs.
In college, my friends and I memorized almost every line from some dumb comedy movie.
There's a song by The Killers that always makes me feel nostalgic for my early twenties.
I tried to get into a really popular fantasy show but I just found it slow and boring.
I bought an expensive DVD box set right before streaming services made DVDs obsolete.
I spent an entire Saturday just lying in bed and scrolling mindlessly through my phone.
A local news story about a house fire had me neurotically checking my stove for a week.
I completely forgot the ending of a thriller movie I had just watched the previous week.
I bought a set of expensive bed sheets that felt exactly like the cheap ones I already owned.
I tried to fix a leaky bathroom faucet with duct tape, which obviously didn't hold.
I locked my keys in the car outside a gas station and had to wait two hours for a tow truck.
I got a parking ticket in a spot downtown that I swore was completely legal.
I had a vivid, weird dream about losing all my teeth, or maybe my hair was falling out.
I stepped in a massive puddle on my way to work and had to sit in wet socks all morning.
I found an old gift card in a drawer and was disappointed to discover it only had two dollars left.
The power went out in my apartment building, so I just went to sleep at eight in the evening.
I tried a natural brand of toothpaste that tasted exactly like chalk and threw it away.
I looked in the mirror recently and barely recognized myself. It's jarring to see how much I've aged physically while feeling exactly the same mentally.
My doctor bluntly told me I needed to lose weight, probably during my checkup last year.
I bought my work pants a size larger and lied to myself that the old ones had just shrunk.
I felt a massive wave of relief when my plans to go out on Friday night were canceled.
I typed out a text to an ex late one night, but thankfully fell asleep before hitting send.
I donated a bunch of old button-up shirts to Goodwill, mostly things my stomach had outgrown.
I had a random Tuesday where I felt surprisingly happy. I realized joy doesn't always need a trigger; sometimes it's just an absence of stress.
I bought a potted houseplant to brighten up my living room, but it died within two weeks.
I tried a guided meditation app once and just got intensely annoyed by the sound of my own breathing.
I ordered enough Chinese takeout for two people, just so the delivery guy wouldn't judge me for eating it all myself.
A cashier complimented my deep voice once, which was a surprisingly nice boost to my day.
A neighbor from my childhood had a ridiculously loud motorcycle that woke me up every weekend.
My car battery died in a snowy parking lot, and I had to beg a stranger for a jump start.
I had a college professor who seemed to wear the exact same tweed jacket every single class.
I woke up in a panic thinking I was late for work on a Monday, but it was actually Sunday.
I had the most amazing pastrami sandwich at a little deli that doesn't seem to exist anymore.
I dropped my smartphone on a tile floor and the screen shattered into a million pieces.
I was supposed to go on a hike with some guys from work, but I pretended I was sick so I wouldn't hold them back.
The smell of strong chlorine at a public pool instantly reminds me of being ten years old.
I fell down a random internet rabbit hole about deep sea creatures until three in the morning.
I thought about turning forty last year. It feels like I just blinked and an entire decade disappeared without me achieving much.
I tried to use a gas lawnmower at a friend's house and couldn't get the ripcord to start.
I got a deep wooden splinter from an old park bench and had to dig it out with a needle.
I went through a brief phase where I tried to drink green tea instead of coffee, but I hated it.
I bought a lottery ticket when the jackpot got ridiculously huge, just dreaming about quitting my job.
I was stuck in an elevator with a couple who were aggressively whispering an argument at each other.
I burned my tongue on hot soup and couldn't taste my food properly for the next three days.
I saw a minor car accident happen in my rearview mirror and completely froze up instead of helping.

I got an email from a diet app right after a clinic visit, and it made me wonder if the doctor's office was getting a kickback for sharing my contact info. It seemed really sketchy that a random commercial company suddenly had my data and knew I needed to lose weight.
I had a pair of sunglasses I loved, but I think I lost them on a roller coaster.
I noticed my handwriting has gotten completely illegible since I type almost everything now.
I felt a sudden pang of loneliness in a crowded grocery store. I've started noticing that being around strangers makes me feel more isolated than being alone in my apartment.
I tried to assemble a charcoal grill for my patio and ended up with five leftover screws.
I enthusiastically bought a bunch of fresh vegetables that eventually just rotted in the crisper drawer.
I have a random memory of my dad showing me how to tie a tie, maybe for a middle school dance.
Nothing beats the physical relief of taking off my stiff work shoes after a really long shift.

participants.persona: Vanessa is a 32-year-old woman with some college or technical education, single, employed full-time, and very overweight.
participants.name: Vanessa

memories.content: We had a dog when I was really little, a terrier mix named Buster or maybe Buddy.
I remember my first grade teacher was tall, though I can't recall her name at all.
There was this park by my house where I scraped my knee badly on the gravel, probably around age seven.
My mom used to make this casserole with tuna and peas that I absolutely hated.
I think I broke my arm when I was eight, falling off a swing set in someone's backyard.
Sometimes I think my fuzzy memory is just a defense mechanism to avoid dwelling on things.
I had a best friend in third grade named Jessica or maybe Jennifer, but she moved away before fourth grade.
We took a road trip to Florida once, and I slept in the back of the station wagon most of the way.
I remember being terrified of the dark basement in our old house until I was at least ten.
My dad took me to a baseball game once, but I mostly just remember eating a huge hot dog.
I used to collect those little plastic trolls with the bright hair, keeping them in a shoebox under my bed.
There was a girl in my fifth-grade class who threw up during an assembly, and I still feel bad for her.
I got my first period at a friend's sleepover, which was incredibly embarrassing at the time.
I think I won a spelling bee in elementary school, but it might have just been a classroom competition.

I remember telling a dietitian, maybe her name was Brenda, back in 2018 that this isn't a six-week fix, it's a lifelong chronic issue. I need actual maintenance support and a solid relapse plan for when the cravings come back, because they always do.
We used to go to my grandmother's house for Thanksgiving, and it always smelled like mothballs and cinnamon.
I had a pair of light-up sneakers that I wore until the soles completely fell apart.
I remember sneaking downstairs to watch late-night TV when I was supposed to be asleep.
I tried to cut my own bangs in middle school, and it looked absolutely terrible for months.
I realize now that I probably chose my technical degree just to avoid four years of feeling out of place at a big university.
There was this boy in seventh grade who called me a cow, and I cried in the bathroom for the rest of the period.
I used to hide snacks in my room because I was ashamed of how much I was eating, even back then.
I remember doing a science fair project on volcanoes, using baking soda and vinegar like everyone else did.
My first concert was a pop band in the late 90s, though the opening act's name is totally lost to me.
I had a crush on a boy named Matt in high school, but I never actually spoke a word to him.
I got a D in geometry my sophomore year, mostly because I just couldn't pay attention to the teacher.
I worked at a movie theater when I was sixteen, sweeping up popcorn and getting free sodas.
I failed my first driving test because I hit a cone during the parallel parking part.
I remember going to prom in a dress that didn't really fit right, feeling super awkward the whole night.
Looking back at my twenties, I see how much time I wasted waiting for my life to properly begin.
I had a massive argument with my mom right before graduation, though I can't remember what it was even about.
I went to a community college for a bit before switching to a medical billing program.
I shared an apartment with a girl named Chloe who was incredibly messy and never washed her dishes.
I remember buying a used Honda Civic that broke down on the highway like two months after I got it.
I got fired from a retail job once for being late too many times, which I still feel slightly guilty about.
There was a period in my early twenties where I basically lived on boxed mac and cheese and diet soda.
I went on a blind date set up by a coworker, and the guy spent the whole hour talking about his ex-wife.
I've started noticing that I always buy gifts for people that I secretly wish they would buy for me.
I remember getting a really bad sunburn on a beach trip with some college friends, peeling for weeks after.
I adopted a cat from the shelter when I was twenty-two, but she ran away a few years later.
I had this phase where I tried to knit, but I only ever managed to make one lumpy scarf.
I once got stuck in an elevator for an hour at my first office job, and I completely panicked.
I remember drinking way too much at a company holiday party and throwing up in the parking lot.
It recently dawned on me that I use humor mostly to deflect attention away from my size.
I bought a treadmill a few years ago, but it just became a very expensive clothes rack in my bedroom.
I remember the relief I felt when I finally moved into an apartment all by myself, without any roommates.
I went to a friend's wedding a few years ago and was the only single person at my table, which sucked.
I think I keep my apartment so organized because it feels like the only part of my life I can strictly control.
There was a time I tried the keto diet and lost twenty pounds, but I gained it all back within a year.
I remember binge-watching an entire season of some crime show in a single weekend when I had the flu.
I have this memory of my dad teaching me to ride a bike, but it might actually have been my uncle.
I used to love reading mystery novels as a teen, though I rarely have the attention span for books anymore.
I once won a radio contest for concert tickets, but I couldn't go because I had to work.
I look at old photos and realize I actually liked myself a lot more back then than I admitted at the time.
I remember trying to dye my hair blonde from a box and it turned out a horrifying shade of orange.
I had a panic attack in a dressing room once because nothing in the plus-size section fit me right.
I once found a twenty-dollar bill on the sidewalk and used it to buy a massive ice cream sundae.
I wonder if I prefer working late just so I don't have to figure out what to do with a free evening.
I remember taking a ceramics class at the local rec center, but all my bowls came out lopsided.
I went camping once in my twenties and absolutely hated every mosquito-filled minute of it.
I got a tattoo of a star on my ankle when I was eighteen, and it looks really blurry and faded now.
I remember crying in my car after a doctor's appointment where they just blamed all my symptoms on my weight.
I once tried to bake a cheesecake for Thanksgiving, but the middle collapsed and it looked terrible.
I used to go to this diner late at night with friends, but I think it closed down a few years ago.
I remember getting my wisdom teeth out and saying something completely embarrassing to the nurse while waking up.
I had a neighbor who played loud bass music at 2 AM, and I was always too scared to confront him.
I saved up for months to buy a fancy digital camera, but I mostly just use my phone for pictures anyway.
It's strange to realize that I'm exactly the age my mother was when I thought of her as completely old and settled.

I asked the endocrinologist if the beta-blockers I take for my blood pressure were making it harder to lose weight, since I noticed a huge spike around 2021. I really wish my regular doctor had explained how those meds interact with my insulin resistance in the first place.
I remember taking a sick day from work just because I was too depressed to get out of bed.
I had a really vivid dream once that I could breathe underwater, and I still think about it sometimes.
I once tripped on the sidewalk in front of a crowded cafe and pretended I meant to look at my shoe.
I remember loving this one particular perfume in high school, it smelled like vanilla and cheap flowers.
I went to a psychic at a carnival once who told me I'd meet my soulmate by twenty-five, which was totally wrong.
I sometimes catch myself agreeing with people just because I don't want to take up the emotional space to argue.
I remember getting a terrible flu in 2018 that knocked me out for almost two whole weeks.
I tried doing a couch-to-5k program once, but my knees hurt too much to get past the second week.
I have a memory of falling into a pool at a summer party, completely ruining my favorite dress.
I recognize that I push away potential dates because I'm terrified they'll be disgusted by my body.
I remember buying an expensive gym membership on New Year's Day and only going maybe three times.
I had a coworker named Dave or Dan who used to steal my lunch from the office fridge.
Looking back, I think my obsession with that one fantasy book series was just a way to escape feeling lonely in middle school.
I remember watching the news during a big blizzard and hoping the power wouldn't go out.
I used to love eating raw cookie dough out of the tube, even though my mom said it would make me sick.
I once accidentally locked my keys in my car while the engine was still running.

My primary care guy just said to eat less a few years ago, but the orthopedic doctor I saw for my knees actually gave me a specific aquatic therapy schedule to avoid joint strain. It's funny how the specialist gave me way more actionable weight-management steps than my actual physician.
I went to a comedy club for a date once, and the comedian made a fat joke that made me want to disappear.
I remember spending an entire Saturday building a bookshelf from IKEA, only to realize I put the back on backwards.
I had this phase where I drank green smoothies every morning, but it only lasted about a month.
I remember getting rear-ended at a stoplight, and the other driver tried to offer me fifty bucks not to call insurance.
I used to be obsessed with collecting lip glosses in middle school, the sparkly roll-on kind.
I once got a terrible haircut where the stylist chopped off way more than the two inches I asked for.
I remember slipping on a patch of ice in my apartment parking lot and bruising my tailbone pretty badly.
I had a goldfish I won at a fair that miraculously lived for almost three years in a tiny bowl.
I remember staying up until 4 AM talking on the phone with a friend about nothing important.
I tried joining a local book club, but I felt too intimidated by the older women to ever speak up.
I have this vivid memory of the smell of rain on hot asphalt during summer storms when I was a kid.
I once bought a pair of jeans online that were three sizes too small, and I just hid them in my closet.
I remember crying during a dog food commercial because I was so stressed out about my credit card debt.
I had a boss named Sarah who would always email me on weekends expecting an immediate reply.
I once tried to grow tomatoes on my balcony, but the squirrels ate every single one of them.
I remember finding a really cool vintage jacket at a thrift store, but I ended up donating it because it never fit right.
I used to love going to the roller rink on Friday nights in junior high, drinking flat sodas and watching people.
I once accidentally sent a text complaining about a coworker to that exact coworker, which was mortifying.

When they just hand me a generic pamphlet, I get so frustrated because they don't factor in my PCOS or the fact that keto wrecked my gallbladder back in '16. I expect a weight-loss plan tailored to a 32-year-old woman with my specific medical history and past failures, not cookie-cutter advice.
I remember eating an entire pizza by myself after a particularly awful day at work.
I got a terrible rash from a cheap necklace I bought at a mall kiosk in my teens.
I remember the intense anxiety I felt before giving a presentation in my community college public speaking class.
I once tried to learn Spanish using an app, but I gave up after only learning how to say hello and apple.
I used to hate the texture of mushrooms as a kid, but now I order them on basically everything.
I remember buying a lottery ticket on my eighteenth birthday and winning exactly two dollars.
I had a massive crush on a fictional character from a TV show when I was fourteen.
I once spent a whole paycheck on a designer purse that I ended up being too afraid to actually use.
I remember the time I tried to cook a fancy steak dinner for myself and completely burned the meat.
I used to wear these really awful chunky highlights in my hair around 2008.
I remember going to a theme park and not being able to pull the safety bar down on a coaster, so I had to get off.

I only felt comfortable bringing up my weight with Nurse Sarah because she never judged me or gave me a weird look when she took my vitals. Having that trusting, empathetic relationship made all the difference in actually talking about my struggles openly without feeling ashamed.
I had this weird habit of counting the stairs whenever I walked up to my childhood bedroom.
I once got a flat tire on the highway and had to wait three hours for a tow truck in the freezing rain.
I remember trying a trendy makeup tutorial and looking like I had two black eyes.
I used to keep a diary in middle school, mostly writing about how much I hated my math teacher.
I once spilled coffee all over my keyboard at work and fried the entire computer.
I remember going through a phase where I only listened to sad acoustic indie music for a year.
I had a pair of sunglasses I loved, but I accidentally sat on them in the car and snapped them in half.
I remember hiding in a bathroom stall at a networking event because I felt too awkward to mingle.
I once burned my hand pretty badly on a curling iron while getting ready for a friend's party.
I used to love playing those life simulation computer games for hours on end after school.
I remember getting a really harsh performance review at an old job that made me cry in my car afterward.
I had a favorite mug with a cat on it that chipped, and I was unreasonably sad about throwing it away.
I once tried to make homemade pasta, but it turned into a sticky, unworkable mess.
I remember buying a bunch of fancy planners thinking it would make me organized, but they're all empty.
I used to sneak reads of my mom's romance novels when she wasn't home.
I once got stuck behind a tractor on a two-lane road for twenty miles when I was already running late.
I remember buying an absurd amount of Halloween candy with the excuse that I'd have trick-or-treaters, but I ate it all.
I had a friend in my early twenties who constantly borrowed money and never paid me back.
I once tried taking a bubble bath to relax, but the water got cold in ten minutes and it was just boring.
I remember the awful sound my car brakes used to make before I finally scraped the money together to fix them.
I used to collect snow globes from different states, even if I had never actually visited them.
I once accidentally dropped my phone into the toilet and had to put it in a bag of rice for two days.
I remember ordering a cocktail at a fancy bar and pretending to like it even though it tasted like pure gasoline.
I had a period where I tried to wake up at 5 AM every day to exercise, which failed spectacularly.
I once found a stray kitten under my porch, but the animal control guy took it away before I could decide to keep it.
I remember the extreme relief of taking off a pair of uncomfortable heels after a long wedding reception.
I used to think quicksand was going to be a much bigger problem in my adult life than it actually is.
I once got a jury duty summons and ended up sitting in a waiting room for eight hours just to be sent home.
I remember buying a huge puzzle during a snowstorm and realizing it was missing an edge piece right at the end.
I had a habit of biting my nails down to the quick whenever I was stressed out at my old billing job.
I once tried on a bridesmaid dress that wouldn't zip, and the saleswoman was extremely condescending about it.
I remember accidentally liking an old photo of an ex on social media and wanting to throw my phone in the river.
I used to make elaborate playlists on CDs for my car, labeled with Sharpie in big bubble letters.
I once bought a huge fern for my living room and managed to kill it within a month.
I remember getting really invested in a reality TV dating show, even though I knew it was all fake.
I had a terrible landlord once who refused to fix my heating for three weeks in the middle of January.
I once tried to cut out dairy, but I cracked after three days because I missed cheese too much.
I remember going to a psychic reading with a friend and getting told I had a blocked heart chakra.
I used to spend my lunch breaks sitting in my car alone just to get away from the office chatter.
I once ordered a pair of boots online, but they arrived with one shoe a size 8 and the other a size 10.
I remember feeling a weird sense of accomplishment when I finally memorized my credit card number.
I had a phase of burning incense in my bedroom until my mom complained that the house smelled like a head shop.
I once got a terrible stomach bug after eating dubious sushi from a grocery store.
I remember taking a personality test that told me I was an introvert, which wasn't exactly a surprise.
I used to hoard little hotel shampoo bottles, thinking I'd use them for travel, but I never did.
I once accidentally backed into a neighbor's trash can and completely crushed it, so I had to buy them a new one.
I remember having a really nice conversation with an old lady on the bus about her grandchildren.
I had a habit of buying fresh spinach, letting it wilt in the fridge, and throwing it away a week later.
I once tried to paint my bedroom a soothing blue, but it ended up looking like a nursery.
I remember getting incredibly mad at a customer service rep on the phone and feeling guilty about it all day.
I used to love playing mini-golf in the summer, even though I was terrible at it.
I once got caught in a torrential downpour without an umbrella and showed up to work completely soaked.
I remember buying a fancy electric toothbrush, but I eventually went back to cheap manual ones because I hated the buzzing.
I had a favorite sweater that I shrank in the wash, and I actually cried over it.
I once agreed to house-sit for a coworker and their dog kept me up barking all night.
I remember finding a really great parking spot at the mall on Christmas Eve and feeling like I won the lottery.
I used to practice my signature in a notebook, trying to make it look mature and professional.
I once had a bird fly into my apartment through an open window, and it took me an hour to get it out.
I remember trying to follow a Bob Ross painting tutorial on YouTube and ending up with a brown smudge.
I had a period where I was obsessed with true crime podcasts, until they started giving me nightmares.
I once spilled a full cup of soda in my lap while driving, ruining my jeans and the car seat.
I remember waiting in line for hours for a new phone release, only to decide halfway through that it wasn't worth it.
I used to sneak into the kitchen to eat spoonfuls of peanut butter late at night.
I once bought a really expensive vacuum cleaner on impulse, though it does actually work really well.
I remember getting a papercut between my fingers that annoyed me for days while typing at work.
I had a brief phase of doing crossword puzzles on Sunday mornings, but they got too hard too fast.
I once accidentally left my debit card in the ATM and didn't realize until I tried to buy groceries two days later.
I remember watching a documentary about deep sea creatures and feeling totally freaked out by the ocean.
I used to love the smell of the Scholastic book fair in elementary school, like fresh paper and plastic.
I once tried to fix a leaky faucet in my bathroom with duct tape, which predictably failed.
I remember getting a frantic call from a wrong number in the middle of the night, someone looking for a guy named Greg.
I had a habit of keeping my phone on do-not-disturb because unexpected notifications give me anxiety.

Every time I leave the primary clinic, I realize I never get a written diet plan, a prescription, or any structured follow-up dates. They just tell me to join a gym without offering any actual concrete support or referrals to help me do it.
I once attempted to make a gingerbread house from scratch, and the walls collapsed immediately.
I remember buying a massive jar of coconut oil because everyone said it was a miracle cure, but it just made my hair greasy.
I used to sit by the window during thunderstorms, counting the seconds between the flash and the thunder.
I once got incredibly lost driving in a new city before I had a smartphone with GPS.
I remember finding twenty bucks in a winter coat pocket the first time it got cold one year.
I had a favorite pair of sweatpants that I wore until there were literal holes in the thighs.
I once burned my tongue so badly on a hot pocket that I couldn't taste anything for two days.
I remember buying a stack of self-help books at a yard sale and never reading a single page of them.
I used to save all my movie ticket stubs in a little glass jar on my dresser.
I once ordered a giant iced coffee, set it on the roof of my car while searching for my keys, and drove away.

participants.persona: Gloria is a 45-year-old woman with a high school/GED education, married or living with a partner, unemployed, and overweight.
participants.name: Gloria

memories.content: I realize now that I stopped trying to find a job because I was afraid of another rejection, not because there were no jobs out there.
Looking back at my twenties, I can see how my weight became a shield I used to keep people from getting too close.

My clinic partnered with that Noom app last year, and I remember feeling instantly sketched out when they asked for my credit card just to access the free trial they promised. I think my partner Mark was in the room when I got the email, but all I remember is that sinking feeling that Dr. Evans was probably getting a kickback for every patient who signed up.
I used to think getting my GED would change everything, but I've come to understand it was just a piece of paper without the confidence to back it up.
It took me a long time to admit that my husband's patience is exactly what I needed, even when it annoyed me.
I often wonder if I'd be a different person if I had grown up in a house that wasn't constantly filled with shouting.
Sometimes I catch myself judging other women at the grocery store, and I realize I'm just projecting my own insecurities onto them.
I look at old photos and finally recognize that I was actually quite pretty, even though I spent those years feeling invisible.
I've noticed that I use baking as a way to apologize when I don't know how to say I'm sorry out loud.
It dawned on me recently that I stopped singing in the car because I lost my joy somewhere along the way, not because the radio stations got worse.
I realize my constant worry about money is just a habit I inherited from my mother.
I finally understand why my dad used to sit in the dark garage; sometimes you just need a quiet place where nobody expects anything from you.
Looking back, I can see that quitting my last job was my way of taking back control, even if it wasn't the smartest financial move.
I remember the smell of rain on the hot pavement during summer breaks when I was a kid.
The other kids used to make pig noises at me during recess, and I just stood there feeling my face burn.
I loved the taste of those cheap freeze pops my grandma kept in her old chest freezer.
The first time I ever saw the ocean, the salt spray felt sticky and freezing on my skin.

When Dr. Evans finally told me she thought the WW program would work for me, I felt a huge wave of relief that she actually believed I could do it. I don't remember her exact phrasing, but just having a real doctor stamp her approval on it gave me the push I needed to sign up that same afternoon.
I remember watching Saturday morning cartoons wrapped in a scratchy afghan my aunt made.
We had a yellow dog when I was little, but I don't remember what happened to him.
My mom slapped me across the face once over a spilled glass of milk, and the ringing in my ear lasted all day.
I used to hide in the clothes racks at the department store, breathing in the smell of new fabric.
The cafeteria pizza in middle school always had these tiny, perfectly round pepperonis that tasted like heaven.
I failed ninth-grade math because the numbers just blurred together on the chalkboard.
I dropped out of high school mainly because I was so tired of feeling stupid every time I walked into a classroom.
Studying for the GED felt like trying to climb a mountain in the dark, but I was so proud when the certificate arrived.
I bought a cheap frame from the dollar store for my GED, though I can't remember where I put it.
My first boyfriend had a car that always smelled like stale cigarettes and vanilla air freshener.
I remember feeling the bass in my chest at a concert I went to with some girls I barely knew.
Working the drive-thru at my first job, the headset always gave me a terrible headache behind my right ear.
A customer threw a hot coffee at the counter once, and I just cried in the breakroom for an hour.
I used to love closing shifts because we got to take the leftover pastries home.
The first time I met my partner, he was wearing a ridiculous flannel shirt that was missing two buttons.
We went to a diner for our first date and shared a plate of greasy fries.
Moving into our first apartment, the carpet smelled like wet dog, but we didn't care.
I remember the feeling of his warm hand grabbing mine while we were walking in the freezing cold.
We had a massive fight over groceries once, and I ended up sleeping on the incredibly uncomfortable lumpy sofa.
I love the way the house feels quiet and safe when he leaves for work early in the morning.
We bought a cheap television that had a weird green tint, but we watched movies on it for years.
My partner brought me dandelions once, completely serious, and I laughed so hard my stomach ached.
I cried in the bathroom when he proposed because I didn't feel like I deserved it.
Our wedding was small and the cake icing melted in the sun, but it tasted incredibly sweet.
I used to work at a call center, and the buzzing of the fluorescent lights drove me crazy.
The chair at my old cubicle was broken and always tilted me slightly to the left.
Getting laid off felt like a punch to the gut; my boss wouldn't even look me in the eye.
The day after I lost my job, I slept until noon and woke up with a pounding headache.

I was so frustrated when my endocrinologist, Dr. Lin, just told me to eat less without explaining how my new Gabapentin prescription was making my ankles swell and my appetite go crazy. I just wanted someone to sit down and draw a direct line between my joint pain, my weight, and the pills I was being handed every month.
I applied for a receptionist job, but the glass office made me feel exposed and small.
Being unemployed for this long makes me feel like a ghost haunting my own house.
I spend a lot of mornings drinking lukewarm coffee and staring out the kitchen window at the neighbor's yard.
The mail carrier always comes at exactly 11 AM, and it's become the anchor of my day.
I lied to my cousin and told her I was working freelance because I was ashamed to admit I was still jobless.
I organize the pantry every few weeks just to feel like I have control over something.
Trying on clothes is a nightmare; the dressing room mirrors always make me want to cry.
I stepped on the scale last month, and the number made a cold shiver go down my spine.
I love the taste of buttery mashed potatoes when it's raining outside.
A doctor once told me all my problems would go away if I just lost weight, and his condescending tone made me furious.
I bought a bright red dress a few years ago that I've never worn, but I love looking at it in the closet.
My knees ache when I walk up the stairs, reminding me of how heavy I've gotten.
I started drinking diet soda, but the metallic aftertaste always lingers on my tongue.
The feeling of pulling off tight socks at the end of the day is incredibly relieving.
I enjoy the smell of bleach because it makes the bathroom feel perfectly clean.
Sometimes I watch soap operas all afternoon just to hear voices in the living room.
I always buy the generic brand of cereal because the brightly colored boxes remind me of my childhood.
I hate the sound of the garbage truck grinding right outside our bedroom window at dawn.
The neighbor's dog barks at everything, and the sharp noise sets my teeth on edge.
I found a gray hair this morning and felt a sudden wave of panic about getting older.
The air conditioning unit in our bedroom rattles in a rhythm that actually helps me fall asleep.
I love the crisp feeling of fresh bedsheets right after they come out of the dryer.
I used to collect little glass animal figurines, but most of them got broken during our last move.
I have a habit of biting the inside of my cheek when I'm watching a tense movie.
I think autumn is the best season because the cool air feels easier to breathe.
I once burned a batch of cookies so badly the whole house smelled like charcoal for a week.
I never learned how to swim, and the smell of chlorine always makes me feel nervous.
A girl in middle school pulled my hair in the hallway, and I can still feel the sharp sting on my scalp.
I like to arrange the throw pillows on the couch perfectly, even though my partner ruins them immediately.
The taste of cheap red wine reminds me of a New Year's Eve party I went to in my twenties.
I once found a twenty-dollar bill in the pocket of an old winter coat, and it felt like winning the lottery.
I don't care for spicy food; the burning sensation makes my eyes water too much.
I had a panic attack in the grocery store once, and the bright fluorescent lights made me dizzy.
I love listening to true crime podcasts while I do the dishes.
The steering wheel of our car always gets blisteringly hot in the July sun.
I tried to knit a scarf once, but the yarn got tangled and I just threw the whole mess away.
My partner snores loudly, but the low rumbling sound is strangely comforting to me now.
I enjoy the smooth, waxy feel of drawing with crayons, even as an adult.
I avoided going to my high school reunion because I was embarrassed about not having a career.
I love eating cold pizza for breakfast, especially the chewy crust.
The sound of thunder rolling in the distance always makes me want to wrap up in a heavy blanket.
I used to have a favorite pair of jeans that were perfectly faded at the knees.
I hate the feeling of sand sticking to my feet at the beach.
My mom used to critique my outfits, and I still hear her sharp voice when I look in the mirror.
I like to let ice cream melt a little bit around the edges before I eat it.
The smell of cut grass instantly takes me back to my grandfather's backyard.
I always check the locks on the doors three times before going to bed.
The tap water in our kitchen has a slightly metallic taste that I've gotten used to.
I feel a deep flush of shame whenever the cashier's screen shows insufficient funds.
I love the warm, yeasty smell of baking bread at the supermarket bakery.
I tripped on the sidewalk once and scraped my knee; the sting reminded me of being a kid.
The old radiator in our apartment used to hiss and spit hot water onto the floor.
I prefer taking hot baths over showers because the steam clears my head.
I once won a giant stuffed bear at a carnival, and it was so heavy I could barely carry it to the car.
I secretly read my partner's text messages once out of paranoia, and I felt sick to my stomach afterward.
I always add extra cheese to macaroni because it makes it perfectly gooey.
The bright flash of lightning during a storm always makes me squeeze my eyes shut.
I hate the powdery feeling of chalk on my fingertips.
I used to ride my bike down a massive hill, the wind rushing so loudly in my ears I couldn't hear anything else.

My regular doctor always just handed me the same faded BMI pamphlet, but when I finally saw the bariatric specialist down at Mercy Hospital, she actually wrote down a precise protein-tracking method using an app. I can still picture the brightly lit office and feeling like someone was finally giving me a real instruction manual instead of a lecture.
I got fired from a retail job for snapping at a rude customer, and the hot anger in my chest took days to fade.
The first sip of cold water on a blistering day feels like it travels all the way down to my toes.
I enjoy peeling oranges just to get the citrus oil scent on my hands.
The squeaky sound of shopping cart wheels echoes loudly in the empty aisles.
I love the soft, worn-out collar of my favorite sleep shirt.
My dad forgot my sixteenth birthday, and the silence at the dinner table was suffocating.
I like to sort my laundry into darks and lights very meticulously.
The smell of rubbing alcohol reminds me of sitting in the nurse's office at school.
I love the crunch of autumn leaves under my boots.
I burned my tongue on hot cocoa once, and everything tasted like cardboard for a week.
I hide the empty candy wrappers at the bottom of the trash can so my partner won't see them.
I prefer the quiet hum of a fan over complete silence when trying to sleep.
The slippery texture of mushrooms in my food always makes me gag.
I remember feeling the rough bark of the oak tree I used to climb as a little girl.
The sudden blare of a car horn makes my heart jump into my throat.
I stopped going to the public pool because the stares from teenagers made me want to shrink away.
I love the sweet, artificial strawberry smell of cheap lip gloss.
The heavy thud of the newspaper hitting the porch used to be my morning alarm.
I enjoy the satisfying click of a ballpoint pen.
I cried in the car after a job interview because I knew they had already decided against me the second I walked in.
I like to eat French fries dipped in a chocolate milkshake.
The sharp cold of winter wind makes my eyes water immediately.
I remember the metallic squeal of the swingset at the playground near my childhood home.
I hate the sticky feeling of hairspray on my neck.
The sweet, floral scent of lilac bushes always makes me smile.
I broke a beautiful glass vase during an argument, and the sound of it shattering echoed loudly in the small room.
I always pick the window seat on a bus so I can watch the streetlights blur past.
I love the rich, earthy smell of coffee brewing in the early morning.
I have a habit of peeling the labels off beer bottles when I'm bored.
I felt a terrible sting of jealousy when my best friend bought her first house.
The soft purr of a cat resting on my lap makes my breathing slow down.
I despise the artificial banana flavor in candies.
I remember the sticky heat of summer nights when our AC was broken.
I enjoy the smooth, cool feel of clean tile floors under bare feet.
The jarring beep of the smoke detector always sends me into an immediate panic.
I avoided the doctor for years because I dreaded the lecture about my BMI.
I love the warm, gooey center of a freshly baked chocolate chip cookie.
The harsh glare of the bathroom lights in the morning hurts my eyes.
I used to love the sugary taste of that pink chewing gum that lost its flavor in two minutes.
I was caught shoplifting a lipstick when I was fourteen, and my face burned hot with deep shame.
I enjoy the methodical rhythm of chopping vegetables for soup.
The musty smell of old books at the library is incredibly soothing.
I hate the feeling of wet socks after stepping in a puddle.
I remember the brilliant orange of the sunset over the highway during a road trip.
I always double-knot my shoelaces so I don't trip over them.
I lied about having a college degree on a date once because I felt so inadequate.
I love the spicy, warm scent of cinnamon during the holidays.
The high-pitched whine of a mosquito in the dark drives me absolutely crazy.
I enjoy the thick, creamy texture of New York cheesecake.
I sobbed quietly into my pillow when I realized I couldn't fit into my wedding ring anymore.
I like to press my forehead against the cool glass of a window when I have a headache.
I remember the dizzying spin of the carnival rides at the county fair.
The bitter taste of black coffee still makes me grimace.
I enjoy the soft, fuzzy feeling of my winter slippers.
I hate the grating sound of someone chewing with their mouth open.
My husband and I didn't speak for three days, and the silence in the house felt heavy and suffocating.
I love the salty, greasy crunch of freshly popped popcorn.
The smell of gasoline at the pump oddly reminds me of road trips with my dad.
I like to trace the patterns on the living room rug with my toe.
I threw away all my old journals because rereading them made me feel incredibly pathetic.
The sudden blast of cold air from the freezer aisle in the summer feels amazing.
I remember the stinging slap of a cold wave hitting my stomach at the beach.
I hate the slimy texture of canned peaches.
I enjoy the rhythmic thumping of the washing machine on laundry day.
The bright yellow of a field of sunflowers completely mesmerized me once.
I faked a stomach ache to get out of a job interview because my anxiety was choking me.
I love the rich, dark taste of a chocolate brownie corner piece.
The metallic smell of coins makes me want to immediately wash my hands.
I like to watch the condensation drip down the side of a cold glass.
I ate an entire carton of ice cream in the dark after my mother's funeral, feeling totally numb.
The rough texture of a cat's tongue on my hand always surprises me.
I remember the sharp pinch of getting my ears pierced at the mall.
I hate the blinding reflection of the sun off the snow.
I enjoy the sweet, tart flavor of a green apple.
The crackling sound of a campfire makes me feel completely relaxed.
I panicked and hung up the phone when a debt collector called me yesterday.
I love the soft, damp smell of soil after a heavy spring rain.
The sticky feeling of maple syrup on the breakfast table always annoys me.
I like to listen to the upbeat tempo of old pop songs when I clean.
I was teased mercilessly about my thick glasses in grade school, and I used to hide them in my backpack.
The tartness of lemonade makes my jaw tingle in a good way.
I remember the heavy, suffocating smell of cheap perfume my grandmother wore.
I hate the slippery feeling of walking on a wet floor in bare feet.
I enjoy the bright, clean scent of fresh laundry detergent.

I actually didn't mind when the nurse practitioner brought up my weight last month, because she focused entirely on getting my A1C numbers down rather than telling me I needed to drop sizes. The tight feeling in my chest just evaporated when she made it about avoiding diabetes instead of making me feel like a lazy slob.

I've been seeing Dr. Aris for ten years, and because he always asks about my husband's job hunt before anything else, I never tense up when he asks me to step on the scale. I can't remember exactly what he said during my last physical, but his gentle tone always makes me feel completely safe talking about my struggles with emotional eating.
The low rumble of an airplane flying overhead makes the windows vibrate.
I felt completely worthless the day my unemployment benefits ran out.
I love the warm, enveloping hug of a thick winter coat on a frosty day.
The sharp crunch of biting into a fresh carrot is deeply satisfying to me.
I like the way the morning light casts long shadows across the kitchen floor.
I got out of breath tying my shoes yesterday, and a deep flush of embarrassment washed over me.
I love the smooth, cool texture of a polished stone in my pocket.

participants.persona: Russell is a 43-year-old man with a college education, married or living with a partner, employed full-time, and overweight.
participants.name: Russell

memories.content: I remember the smell of wet pavement after summer storms when I was a kid.
My first bicycle was a bright blue hand-me-down from my cousin, though I can't remember how old I was when I got it.
I have a vivid memory of crying in a grocery store because I lost my mom, but I don't remember who actually found me.
The taste of those cheap ice pops always reminds me of playing in the sprinkler in our old backyard.
I broke my arm falling out of a tree in third grade. I remember the sharp crack and the sickening feeling in my stomach.
There was a kid in elementary school who always smelled like sour milk, though his name escapes me now.
I remember the intense heat of the plastic slides at the playground burning my bare legs.
My dad used to take me to a diner for pancakes on Saturday mornings, just the two of us.
I can still picture the ugly floral wallpaper in my childhood bedroom.
I remember sneaking downstairs to watch television after my parents had gone to sleep.
The first time I saw the ocean, I was terrified by how loud the crashing waves were.
I got stung by a bee on my eyelid during a family picnic and my eye swelled completely shut.
My grandfather smelled strongly of peppermint and old books.
I remember the anxiety of waiting to be picked for dodgeball teams in middle school gym class.
I had a massive crush on my eighth-grade science teacher, though I barely remember what she looked like now.
The awkwardness of my first middle school dance is something I can still feel in my chest.
I remember the first time I got caught in a lie by my parents. The shame was suffocating.

When Dr. Aris told my wife and me that she fully backed my joining the Optifast clinic last spring, it was like a switch flipped in my head. I can't remember exactly what she said about my blood panels, but knowing my own doctor thought it was a solid, safe plan gave me the final push I needed to sign up.
There was a summer where I did nothing but play video games in my friend's basement.
I remember the metallic taste of my braces after getting them tightened.
I failed my first driving test because I hit an orange cone during the parallel parking section.
Driving alone for the first time felt incredibly liberating, even though I was just going to the pharmacy.
My first car smelled like stale smoke and pine air freshener, no matter how much I cleaned it.
I remember the terrible polyester uniform I had to wear at my first fast-food job.
The feeling of handing over my own hard-earned cash for a CD is something I'll never forget.
I got into a fistfight in the locker room once, mostly just wild swinging and loud yelling.
I remember the sickening dread I felt when I realized I forgot to study for a final exam.
My high school graduation was a blur of uncomfortable robes and taking pictures in the hot sun.
The first night in my college dorm, I lay awake listening to the strange sounds of the building.
I remember the harsh fluorescent lighting in the university library where I pulled an all-nighter.
There was a party where I drank way too much cheap beer and ended up being sick in some stranger's bushes.
I have a vague memory of a profound conversation with a dorm mate at 3 AM, though the topic is lost to me.

I remember sitting on the exam table feeling completely frustrated until the specialist finally explained how my daily Lisinopril and sleep apnea were actually feeding into my weight plateau. He drew this little diagram connecting my hypertension meds to my metabolism, and though I lost the paper years ago, it was the first time someone actually explained the mechanics to me.
Walking across campus in the freezing rain made me question why I chose a school in this state.
I remember the intense pride of getting a good grade on a paper I thought I had completely failed.

The intake nurse at the downtown clinic made me feel surprisingly at ease when she focused entirely on my joint mobility and A1C numbers instead of lecturing me about BMI or how my work suits fit. I don't recall her exact words, but just the relief of talking about my actual health metrics rather than feeling judged for my pant size made the whole appointment bearable.
My first college girlfriend had a very distinctive laugh that I still sometimes hear in crowds.
I remember the agonizing silence during our breakup in a crowded coffee shop.
The dining hall pizza was terrible, but I ate it almost every single day.
I remember the heavy weight of my backpack digging into my shoulders on the way to class.
I had a professor who paced endlessly while lecturing, making me dizzy just watching him.
Moving out of my college apartment involved stuffing everything into garbage bags and hoping it fit in my car.
I remember the feeling of absolute exhaustion after finishing my last college final.
Looking at my college diploma, I realize how little of my education I actually use, which makes me question my entire career path.
My first post-college apartment had a radiator that clanked loudly every night at two in the morning.
I remember the overwhelming panic of paying my first student loan bill.
I bought a really expensive suit for job interviews that never fit quite right.
My first real boss was a gruff guy who barely made eye contact, but he taught me a lot.
I remember sitting in my cubicle, staring at the clock, waiting for it to hit five.
There was a phase in my twenties where I ate fast food almost every night for dinner.
I remember the sharp sting of a papercut from a fresh ream of printer paper.
I went on a blind date that was so painfully awkward we just sat in silence for twenty minutes.
I remember the thrill of getting my first significant promotion at work.
I took a solo road trip once and felt completely isolated when my car broke down in the middle of nowhere.
I sometimes wonder if my tendency to use humor is just a shield I built during my awkward teenage years.
I met my partner at a mutual friend's barbecue. I just remember her bright red shirt and her easy smile.
Our first date was at a loud Italian restaurant, and I remember straining to hear her over the noise.
I remember the terrifying moment right before I told her I loved her for the first time.
Noticing I had outgrown my favorite suit made me deeply aware of how much I've let my health slide over the last decade.

Because Dr. Chen has been my primary care doc since I graduated college and has always treated me like a partner in my healthcare, I didn't feel the usual panic when he brought up my recent weight gain. He just had this incredibly kind tone when he asked how I was managing my stress, which made it so much easier to open up about my private struggles with late-night binge eating.
I remember the chaos of packing up my apartment to move in with my partner.
The first time we had a huge fight, I remember the awful heavy silence that filled our home afterwards.
I remember the smell of fresh paint when we bought our first house.
Mowing the lawn for the first time made me feel ridiculously grown up.
I have a distinct memory of trying to fix a leaky sink and making it completely worse.
I remember the cold dread of realizing our dog had slipped out the front door.
The relief I felt when we found him down the street was overwhelming.
I remember the rich smell of coffee brewing on lazy Sunday mornings.
When my dad passed away, I finally understood why he was always so quiet, and I see that same silence growing in myself.
I remember the uncomfortable stiffness of the suit I wore to his funeral.
My mom's grief was a palpable thing, heavy and suffocating in the living room.
I remember cleaning out my childhood bedroom and feeling like I was erasing my past.
There was a really terrible company retreat where we had to do trust falls in the rain.
I remember the panic of accidentally sending an email complaining about a client to that exact client.

When they handed me the referral for the metabolic weight center, all I could think about was whether my employer's Blue Cross PPO would actually cover the dietician fees or if I'd be paying out of pocket. I remember grilling the receptionist about the weekly time commitment and the exact macronutrient rules because I refuse to start another program without knowing the financial and daily lifestyle costs upfront.
I spilled coffee on my laptop and watched in horror as the screen flickered and died.
I remember the satisfying click of finishing a massive spreadsheet project at work.
I have a vague memory of a fantastic steak dinner I had on a business trip, though I can't remember the city.
I remember the frustration of being stuck in gridlock traffic for three hours during a snowstorm.
The sound of my morning alarm always sends a brief spike of anxiety through my chest.
I catch myself complaining about the younger guys at work and it hits me that I've become the older generation I used to mock.
I remember the weird sensation of my first gray hair catching the bathroom light.
I tried a fad diet once and remember the constant, gnawing hunger that lasted for two weeks.
I remember the embarrassment of splitting my pants when I bent over to pick up a pen at work.
There was a moment at a party where I realized I didn't know a single song on the playlist.
I remember the breathtaking view from a hike we took in Colorado, even if my knees ached the whole time.
The feeling of sand between my toes on our anniversary beach trip was incredibly relaxing.
I remember the horrible sunburn I got because I forgot to reapply sunscreen.
We got caught in a torrential downpour walking back to our hotel, but we couldn't stop laughing.
Sometimes I look at my wife while she's reading and feel a profound sense of luck that she chose to stay with me through the rough patches.
I remember the crushing disappointment of a vacation getting canceled at the last minute due to illness.
I can still feel the dull ache in my lower back after spending the weekend building IKEA furniture.
I remember the frustration of losing my keys and finding them in the refrigerator hours later.
The smell of burning toast always immediately pulls me out of whatever I'm doing.
I remember a particularly vivid nightmare where my teeth were falling out, and waking up in a cold sweat.
I found an old photo album recently and was shocked by how young my parents looked.
I remember the comforting weight of a heavy blanket on a freezing winter night.
There is a specific kind of quiet that falls over the house when it snows heavily.
Moving into our current house felt like a milestone, but looking back, it was really just the beginning of feeling tied down.
I remember the sharp jolt of static electricity from touching the car door in winter.
I had a terrifying moment of hydroplaning on the highway where time seemed to slow down completely.
I remember the relief of finally passing a kidney stone after days of excruciating pain.
The smell of hospital sanitizer always makes my stomach knot up.
I remember the joy of biting into a perfectly ripe peach during the peak of summer.
I accidentally ate a severely undercooked chicken breast at a barbecue once and panicked for days.
I remember the deep satisfaction of finally clearing out the cluttered garage.
There was a time I tried to take up jogging, but I just remember the awful burning in my lungs.
I remember the embarrassment of being the most out-of-shape person in a beginner's yoga class.
I used to think I was a fiercely independent person, but seeing how much I rely on my partner's validation proved me wrong.
I remember the warm glow of string lights on a patio during a late summer dinner with friends.
The feeling of a fresh haircut always makes me feel temporarily put-together.
I remember an argument with a close friend that ended our friendship, though the actual words are hazy now.
I can recall the distinct smell of my old leather jacket that I finally had to throw away.
I remember the sheer panic of patting my pockets and realizing my wallet was gone.
Finding my lost wallet under the car seat was one of the greatest reliefs of my adult life.
I remember the frustrating puzzle of trying to figure out our new smart thermostat.
The sound of a lawnmower in the distance always makes me feel sleepy.
I remember watching a thunderstorm roll in from our front porch, feeling the sudden drop in temperature.
Realizing that I enjoy a quiet Saturday morning more than a night out made me accept that I am comfortably middle-aged.
I remember the rich, buttery taste of a lobster roll on a vacation in Maine.
I once got food poisoning so bad I genuinely thought I was going to die on the bathroom floor.
I remember the specific crunch of autumn leaves under my boots during a weekend walk.
I have a vague memory of a movie that terrified me as a child, mostly just flashes of a dark forest.
The smell of chlorine instantly transports me back to summer camp swimming pools.
I remember the awkward tension of a performance review where my boss clearly didn't know what I did.
I remember the surge of adrenaline when a bat somehow got into our house.
I look at my old journals sometimes and cringe at how desperately I wanted to be seen as intelligent.
I remember the feeling of absolute defeat when my car battery died in the freezing rain.
There was a moment of pure bliss sitting by a campfire with a cold beer in my hand.
I remember the shocking cold of jumping into a mountain lake on a dare.
I once bought a completely useless kitchen gadget at 2 AM because the infomercial was so convincing.
I remember the mild panic of realizing I was the only one not wearing a tie to a formal event.
The smell of an old bookstore always makes me feel incredibly relaxed.
I remember the intense frustration of trying to untangle a massive knot of Christmas lights.
I can clearly remember the loud pop a tire made right before my first blowout on the highway.
I remember the strange, metallic smell of a subway station on a humid day.
There was a time I locked myself out of the house in my pajamas and had to break a window.
I remember the guilt of skipping a friend's wedding because I was just too tired to travel.
The older I get, the more I recognize my mother's anxious habits manifesting in my own daily routines.
I remember the awe of seeing a meteor shower from a dark country road.
I have a distinct memory of the fuzzy texture of a tennis ball when I first learned to play.
I remember the intense sweetness of a cotton candy at a county fair.
The feeling of a dog resting its heavy head on my knee is one of my favorite things.
I remember the sickening crunch of backing my car into a concrete pillar in a parking garage.
I remember the profound boredom of sitting in jury duty for three days straight.
I have a vivid memory of the bright blue sky on a morning when everything just felt right.
I remember the sharp smell of vinegar from dying Easter eggs as a kid.
It dawned on me recently that my biggest fear isn't failure, but simply being forgotten by the people I care about.
I remember the feeling of a crisp, new twenty-dollar bill from the ATM.
There was a moment during a concert where the bass was so loud it made my teeth vibrate.
I remember the deep exhaustion of pulling an all-nighter for a work deadline.
I remember the frustrating itch of a mosquito bite right between my fingers.
The smell of a burning match always reminds me of power outages during winter storms.
I remember the sheer panic of turbulence on a flight through a severe storm.
I remember the feeling of intense relief when the plane finally touched down safely.
I have a vague memory of a childhood friend's face, but his voice is completely gone from my mind.
I remember the sticky feeling of humidity on a late August afternoon.
I remember the satisfying sound of a new jar popping open.
The taste of black licorice always makes me want to gag.
I remember the uncomfortable squish of stepping in a muddy puddle while wearing nice shoes.
I remember the quiet satisfaction of finishing a really good book and just holding it for a minute.

It drove me crazy when a previous doctor just handed me a generic low-carb pamphlet, completely ignoring that I'm a 43-year-old guy with gout who has already failed Keto twice. I was so angry that I just walked out, wishing they had actually taken five minutes to look at my chart and suggest a plan that worked around my specific joint flare-ups and medical history.
I remember the dread of opening a credit card bill after a particularly expensive month.
The smell of a new car interior is something I've only experienced twice, but I love it.
I remember the intense heat of a bonfire roasting my shins while my back stayed freezing.
I remember the awkwardness of trying to make small talk with my father-in-law.
I remember the feeling of a terrible headache fading away after finally taking some aspirin.
I have a clear memory of the bright red color of a cardinal sitting in the snow.
I remember the frustration of a pen running out of ink right in the middle of a sentence.
I remember the sudden, jarring noise of the smoke detector going off at 3 AM.
I remember the feeling of my foot falling asleep and the painful tingling that followed.
I remember the strange, hollow sound of an empty house before the furniture was moved in.
The smell of cut grass always reminds me of baseball practice.
I remember the intense annoyance of someone talking loudly on their phone in a quiet waiting room.
I remember the mild embarrassment of waving at someone who was actually waving at the person behind me.
I remember the feeling of peeling dried glue off my fingers in elementary school.
I remember the specific thud a heavy textbook makes when dropped on a desk.
I remember the awful feeling of a blister forming on my heel during a long walk.
The taste of burnt coffee is something I tolerate far more often than I should.
I remember the surreal feeling of waking up from a nap and not knowing what year it was.
I remember the sharp pain of biting my own tongue while eating.
I remember the quiet focus of watching a spider spin its web on the porch.
I remember the frustrating realization that I had worn my shirt inside out all day at the office.
I remember the feeling of cold water splashing on my face when I desperately needed to wake up.
I remember the specific creak of the third step on the staircase in my childhood home.
I remember the uncomfortable cling of static electricity on a winter sweater.
I remember the satisfying weight of a heavy glass tumbler in my hand.
I remember the sudden, shocking cold of stepping out of the shower in winter.
I remember the feeling of mild panic when the internet goes out during an important task.
I remember the distinct smell of ozone right before a thunderstorm hits.
I remember the frustration of trying to open a stubborn plastic clamshell package.
I remember the warm, fuzzy feeling of drinking hot cider after being out in the cold.
I remember the odd sensation of an elevator dropping just a little too fast.
I remember the blinding glare of the sun reflecting off the snow on a bright winter morning.
I remember the satisfying crunch of stepping on a perfectly dry autumn leaf.
I remember the horrible feeling of realizing I left my phone at a restaurant across town.
I remember the quiet comfort of listening to my partner breathe while they sleep.
I remember the sharp sting of a tiny splinter I just couldn't seem to dig out.
I remember the heavy, lethargic feeling in my limbs after eating way too much at Thanksgiving.
I remember the brief moment of absolute clarity when I look at the night sky and realize how small I am.

participants.persona: Trevor is a 37-year-old man with some college or technical education, single, employed full-time, and overweight.
participants.name: Trevor

memories.content: I remember the sharp smell of rain on hot asphalt when I was little.
I had a blue bike with a torn seat that I rode everywhere.

My doctor talked about my weight like it was a temporary bug, but I know it is something I will have to deal with forever. I just wish there was a clear plan for maintaining my weight and handling setbacks once the diet ends.
My mom used to make this casserole that tasted like salt and ketchup.
The doctor just told me to eat better and exercise before rushing me out the door. I sat in my truck afterwards feeling completely overwhelmed and entirely on my own to figure it all out.
I broke a window playing baseball in the street once, but I forget whose house it was.
There was a huge stray dog that chased me home from school in first grade.
I remember crying under my bed when my parents fought about money.
A kid named Josh or Justin pushed me off the swings, and I scraped both my knees.
I used to hide snacks in my closet so my brother wouldn't eat them.
My dad took me fishing once, and I vividly remember the slimy feel of the bait.
I got lost in a department store and just stood by a rack of coats crying until a lady found me.
I loved waking up early on Saturdays to watch cartoons in my pajamas.
There was a really steep hill near our house that felt like a mountain when I was eight.
I won a spelling bee in elementary school, but I can't recall the winning word.
I had an embarrassing phase where I only wore sweatpants for a whole year.
Someone brought a snake to show-and-tell, and I remember how dry its scales felt.
I stole a candy bar from the corner store once and felt incredibly guilty for weeks.
We went camping, and I remember the intense heat of the campfire on my face.
I had a substitute teacher who yelled so loud it made me jump out of my seat.
I think my habit of always being the funny guy started as a defense mechanism in middle school.
I remember the exact shade of ugly orange carpet in my childhood bedroom.
Middle school gym class was a nightmare of getting picked last for basketball.
I bought a really expensive pair of sneakers with my own lawn-mowing money.
A girl in my eighth-grade class laughed at my haircut, and my face burned with shame.
I remember the metallic taste of blood after getting hit in the face with a dodgeball.
My first kiss was clumsy, wet, and smelled like cherry chapstick.
I got caught forging my dad's signature on a bad math test.

When the nurse handed me a pamphlet for a weight loss clinic, I just wondered if my insurance would even cover it. I really needed to know the actual costs and what kind of food I was expected to eat before committing to anything.
We had a massive snowstorm in 1999 that knocked the power out for three days.
I remember staring at the ceiling in the dark, wondering what I would be when I grew up.
Looking at old photos, I can finally appreciate that I was actually a decent-looking kid, even though I felt ugly.
I loved playing a specific racing video game for hours until my thumbs literally hurt.
High school felt like one long blur of crowded hallways and echoing lockers.
I failed my driving test the first time because I hit the curb during parallel parking.
My first car was a beat-up sedan that always smelled faintly of old fast food.
I had a history teacher who used to slam a ruler on his desk to wake us up.
I went to prom with a girl from my neighborhood, but we barely talked the whole night.
I remember the deafening noise of the crowd at the homecoming football game.
Getting my first paycheck felt incredible, even though it was barely enough for gas.
I tried out for the soccer team but quit after two days because I couldn't keep up with the running.
I snuck out once and got so terrified by a raccoon that I ran straight back inside.
I realized in my twenties that I push people away when I feel insecure about my weight.
I worked at a grocery store and hated the smell of the bottle return room.
Graduation day was incredibly hot, and my gown felt like it was melting into my skin.
I got a bad sunburn at the beach senior year that peeled for what felt like a month.
I had a massive crush on a coworker, but I was too shy to ever say anything.
The summer after high school, my friends and I drove to the city with no map and got hopelessly lost.
I started college but felt completely overwhelmed by the size of the lecture halls.
I remember the sick feeling in my stomach when I saw my first semester grades.
Moving into my first apartment, I slept on an air mattress that kept deflating.
I finally felt okay talking about my weight because my new doctor didn't give me a judgmental look. It helped so much to just be treated like a normal guy instead of a problem to be fixed.
I learned how to cook out of pure necessity because takeout got too expensive.
Looking back, dropping out of my university to go to tech school was the first time I actually stood up for what I wanted.
Tech school was better, mostly because I got to work with my hands.
I had a roommate who played loud techno music at three in the morning.
I remember a specific project where I wired a circuit board and it actually lit up on the first try.
The coffee out of the vending machine at the tech campus tasted like burnt pennies.
I got a nasty shock from a live wire once that made my whole arm go numb.
I celebrated passing my final exams by eating an entire pizza by myself.
Getting hired at my current company felt like a huge relief after months of searching.
I remember my first boss there, a tall guy who always chewed on the end of a pen.
I accidentally deleted a huge database my first month and thought I was going to be fired.
I often wonder if I'm single because I value my peace too much, or if I'm just afraid of being rejected.
I bought a really nice comfortable office chair because my back was killing me from the cheap one.
Commuting in the winter here is awful, especially when the heater takes twenty minutes to kick in.
I have a coworker who microwaves fish in the breakroom, and it drives me crazy.
I went on a blind date a few years ago that ended in awkward silence after twenty minutes.
I remember standing in the rain waiting for a tow truck when my battery died on the highway.
I adopted a cat once, but I had to give him back because my allergies were unbearable.
Getting a promotion felt good for about a week before the stress of the new role set in.
I remember the smell of my grandpa's garage, and it strikes me now how those weekends shaped my entire career.
I had a bad case of the flu a couple of years ago that knocked me out completely for a week.
I tried going to a fancy gym once, but I felt like everyone was staring at my stomach.
I love the quiet of my apartment on a Sunday morning before the rest of the building wakes up.
I built a custom PC last year, and the hum of its fans is really soothing to me.
I ripped my favorite pair of jeans right down the seam while bending over at work.
There's a taco truck near my job that makes the most amazing spicy pork.
I tried a diet where I only ate cabbage soup, and I was utterly miserable by day three.
It dawned on me recently that I've stopped dreaming about big life changes and just accepted my routines.
I got a ticket for speeding because I was late to a dentist appointment I didn't even want to go to.
I remember watching a documentary about deep space and feeling incredibly small.
I have a favorite mug that has a chip on the rim, but I still use it every day.
I met up with an old high school buddy, and we had absolutely nothing to talk about anymore.
I spent a whole weekend binge-watching a sci-fi show and ordered Chinese food twice.
The feeling of tight waistbands after a big meal always makes me feel a wave of guilt.
I found twenty dollars on the sidewalk last month and used it to buy premium coffee.
Reflecting on my twenties, I see now that I wasted a lot of time trying to impress people who didn't even like me.
I bought a guitar during the pandemic, but it's just collecting dust in the corner.
I had a really intense dream about my teeth falling out, and I woke up in a cold sweat.
I hate the way fluorescent lights make my skin look gray in the office bathroom mirror.
I tried to fix a leaky pipe under my sink and ended up soaking my entire kitchen floor.
I remember the crunch of autumn leaves under my boots when I went hiking last October.
Sometimes I recognize that I use food to comfort myself when work gets too stressful.
I went to a cousin's wedding and sat alone at a table near the back the whole night.
I have a scar on my left thumb from a slip of a kitchen knife while chopping onions.
I signed up for a dating app, swiped for an hour, and then deleted it out of sheer exhaustion.
I love the smell of fresh laundry right when it comes out of the dryer.
I had a panic attack in a crowded elevator once, feeling like the walls were closing in on my chest.
I've come to understand that my father's anger was just his own disappointment leaking out, not really about me.
I bought a really expensive jacket online, but it didn't zip over my stomach so I hid it in my closet.
I remember the smooth, cold texture of the marble countertop in my favorite coffee shop.
I stayed up until 4 AM playing a new video game and felt like a zombie at work the next day.
I accidentally called my boss 'mom' in a meeting and wanted the floor to swallow me whole.
I realized today that I actually enjoy living alone, despite what society tells me I should want at 37.
I tried growing tomatoes on my balcony, but the squirrels ate every single one.
I got a terrible haircut right before a major presentation and wore a hat until the last possible second.
I love the feeling of finally taking my shoes off after a long nine-hour shift.
I went to a concert by myself last year and it was incredibly liberating just focusing on the music.
I remember the sour smell of a garbage truck that stalled right in front of my car in traffic.
I helped a neighbor jump-start their car, and they gave me a batch of warm chocolate chip cookies.
I stepped in a massive puddle on my way to work and had wet socks all morning.
I had a cavity filled recently, and the sound of the drill vibrated through my whole skull.
It occurs to me that my memory is mostly tied to how things made me feel rather than what actually happened.
I bought a smart watch to track my steps, but I usually forget to wear it.
I remember the incredibly soft fur of a golden retriever I petted at the park last week.
I burned my tongue on a slice of hot pizza and couldn't taste anything for two days.
I got really into baking sourdough bread for about a month before getting bored of the maintenance.
I hate shopping for clothes in person because finding my size is always a frustrating ordeal.
I remember the loud, rhythmic thud of the bass at a club my friends dragged me to in my twenties.
I have a habit of checking that the front door is locked at least three times before bed.
I tried to assemble a bookshelf from Ikea and ended up with a crucial piece installed backwards.
I went to the state fair just to eat a giant turkey leg and a funnel cake.
I vividly recall the blinding glare of the sun off the snow during a winter drive upstate.
I bought a large houseplant that died within two weeks despite me watering it every day.
I slipped on the ice in my apartment parking lot and bruised my tailbone pretty badly.
I remember the overwhelming scent of cheap cologne someone was wearing in the movie theater.
I had to give a speech at my sister's wedding and my hands were shaking so hard I dropped my notes.
