I splurged on front-row tickets to a comedy show and ended up getting mocked by the comedian.
I always order the same number four combo at my local burger place because it never disappoints.
I remember the sharp, stinging pain of a papercut from a fresh ream of printer paper.
I went on a road trip with my brother and we argued about the radio station the entire way.
I got stuck in an airport for twelve hours and slept on a wildly uncomfortable bench.
I love sitting on my couch during a thunderstorm and watching the lightning flash across the sky.
I accidentally hit 'reply all' on a company email with a sarcastic joke, but thankfully no one complained.
I remember the heavy, humid air sticking to my skin during a summer vacation in Florida.
I tried paddleboarding once and fell into the lake so many times I just gave up.
I got matched with someone cute online, but they unmatched me as soon as I said hello.
I had a really good streak at a local bowling alley once and broke two hundred points.
I threw out a pair of shoes because the squeaking noise they made on linoleum drove me insane.
I remember the smoky flavor of a brisket I smoked for twelve hours on my patio.
I tried to cut my own hair during a lockdown and had to shave my head to fix it.
I got a flat tire on a dark country road and had to figure out the jack by flashlight.
I found an old journal from high school, but the cringe was so bad I threw it in the trash.
I remember the sharp jolt of an alarm clock going off right in the middle of a great dream.
I used to go to a diner at 2 AM just to eat pancakes and avoid being alone in my apartment.
I got stung by a wasp on my neck and it swelled up to the size of a golf ball.
I love the way cold water tastes in the middle of the night when you wake up parched.
I bought a blender to make healthy smoothies but mostly just use it for milkshakes now.
I remember the eerie silence of my office building when I had to work late on a Friday.
I signed up for the program my doctor suggested, but nobody ever called to check on my progress. I assumed my doctor and the program would coordinate to keep me accountable, but that never happened.
I completely forgot my mom's birthday one year and felt like absolute garbage when she called me.
I tried listening to audiobooks on my commute, but I always zone out and miss whole chapters.
I went to a haunted house attraction and got so startled I accidentally punched a zombie actor.
I remember the bright, garish neon lights of a cheap motel I stayed at on a cross-country drive.
I bought a set of expensive noise-canceling headphones, and they completely changed how I work in the office.
I dropped a full jar of pasta sauce in the supermarket aisle and shattered glass went everywhere.
I have a lingering fear of going to the doctor because they always just tell me to lose weight.
I remember the crisp, cold air hitting my face the first time I went skiing.
I signed up for a 5K race once but walked the entire thing while everyone else ran ahead.
I found a great little bakery near my place that makes incredible almond croissants.
I completely blanked on my own zip code while checking out at a store once.
I remember the intense, spicy burn of a hot wing that practically brought me to tears.

The clinic handed me a generic meal plan that I had already tried and failed years ago. I wanted them to actually look at my stressful work schedule and past attempts before giving me a recommendation.
I watched a tutorial on how to fix my washing machine and actually repaired it myself.
I got incredibly seasick on a ferry ride and spent the whole trip leaning over the railing.
I love the smell of gasoline when I'm filling up my tank on a cold morning.
I had an argument with a friend about politics that got so heated we didn't speak for months.
I remember the satisfying click of a mechanical keyboard I used to have at my old desk.
I went to an art museum and spent twenty minutes staring at a painting I didn't even understand.
I accidentally locked my keys in my running car and had to call a locksmith in the freezing rain.
I bought a heavy winter coat on sale in July and felt very smug about the discount.
I remember the chaotic, colorful blur of a parade I went to as a teenager.
I fell asleep on the couch with my glasses on and woke up with a deep red indent on my nose.
I tried intermittent fasting, but the hunger headaches made me incredibly irritable.
I once won a giant stuffed bear out of a claw machine on my very first try.
I dropped my phone face down on the concrete and heard the horrible crunch of the screen cracking.
I remember the thick, suffocating smell of bleach after I scrubbed my bathroom floor.
I got a jury duty summons and ended up sitting in a waiting room for eight hours doing nothing.
I have a spot on the left side of my lower back that twinges every time I lift something heavy.
I ate a whole pint of ice cream after a really bad performance review at work.
I remember the soft, muffled sound of snow falling heavily outside my window at night.
I bought a fancy chef's knife and cut myself the very first time I washed it.
I spent an hour trying to untangle a bunch of old charging cables from my desk drawer.
I went to a driving range to hit golf balls and realized my swing was completely terrible.
I vividly remember the smell of damp earth and pine needles from a hike I took last spring.
I accidentally drank a sip of spoiled milk and instantly gagged over the kitchen sink.
I love finding a really good podcast that makes my thirty-minute commute fly by.
I remember the agonizingly slow tick of the clock on a Friday afternoon right before a holiday weekend.
I had to wear a suit to a funeral recently, and it barely fit me anymore.
I bought a lottery ticket when the jackpot got huge, even though I know it's a waste of two bucks.
I remember the blinding flash of a red-light camera going off right as I went through an intersection.
I watched a squirrel bury a nut in my potted plant, and I just let him have it.
I got an awful cramp in my calf in the middle of the night that made me yell out loud.
I remember the warm, yeasty smell of a pretzel stand I walked past at the mall.
I spent a whole afternoon deep cleaning my car and it felt incredibly rewarding to see the dashboard shine.
I accidentally waved back at someone who was actually waving to the person standing behind me.
I remember the crisp snap of a fresh apple I picked at an orchard a few years ago.
I got halfway to work before realizing I had worn two completely different black socks.
I sat in my parked car in the driveway for ten minutes today just listening to the end of a song.

participants.persona: Curtis is a 47-year-old man with some college or technical education, single, unemployed, and very overweight.
participants.name: Curtis

memories.content: I remember the smell of the old station wagon my dad drove when I was a kid. The vinyl seats burned my legs in the summer.
My mom used to make these incredibly dry pork chops on Tuesday nights. I can still taste the burnt breading.
I had a bright red BMX bike that I rode everywhere until the chain snapped. I do not remember what happened to it after that.
There was a kid in my third-grade class who always smelled like sour milk. I sat next to him for an entire semester.
I won a stuffed bear at the county fair by throwing darts at balloons. It sat on my dresser for years gathering dust.
I remember hiding under the porch during a thunderstorm when I was little. The dirt smelled so rich and heavy.
My grandfather used to smoke a pipe that smelled like cherries. He never said much to me, just patted my head.
I cracked my head open on a coffee table when I was seven. I just remember the warm feeling of blood and my mom screaming.
We had a golden retriever named Buster who used to chew on the baseboards. He was the best dog I ever had.
I remember the carpet in my childhood bedroom was a hideous shade of orange. I used to trace the patterns with my toy cars.
I threw up in the middle of the cafeteria in fifth grade. Everyone laughed, and I just wanted to disappear.
I used to collect baseball cards and kept them in a binder under my bed. I thought they would make me rich someday.
My dad took me fishing once, but we did not catch anything at all. We ended up eating sandwiches in the car in silence.
I remember the cold metal of the monkey bars on a frosty morning. My hands were freezing, but I refused to let go.
I tried to build a treehouse with some scrap wood I found in the alley. It fell apart the first time I climbed on it.
I used to sneak downstairs to watch late-night TV when my parents were asleep. I saw my first horror movie that way.
My mom bought me a knock-off brand of sneakers that I hated. I dragged my feet to wear holes in them faster.

The doctor just told me I needed to drop some pounds and sent me on my way without any kind of plan. I remember sitting in my car afterward feeling totally lost because he didn't give me a prescription or even a basic handout on what to actually do.
I got lost in a department store once and started crying by the mannequins. A security guard bought me a soda until my mom found me.
I remember the first time I had pizza from a real pizzeria instead of frozen. The cheese stretched so far it burned my chin.
I had a teacher in middle school who always had a coffee stain on his tie. He was the only one who did not make me feel stupid.
I tried out for the football team but quit after the first week of conditioning. My lungs felt like they were on fire.
I remember stealing a candy bar from the corner store and feeling so guilty I could not eat it. I threw it in a storm drain.
I had a huge crush on a girl named Sarah in eighth grade. I wrote her a note, but I never gave it to her.
I spent an entire summer playing the same video game over and over. My thumbs actually had calluses by August.
I remember the sound of the dial-up modem connecting late at night. It felt like a secret doorway to the rest of the world.
My parents had a huge fight on my fourteenth birthday. I just turned up the music in my room to block it out.
I used to mow lawns for extra cash, but I hated the smell of cut grass. It always made my eyes water.
I went to a high school dance and stood by the punch bowl the entire night. I felt completely invisible.
I got my first car when I was seventeen, a beat-up sedan that stalled at red lights. I loved the freedom it gave me.
I remember skipping school to go to the arcade with some guys I barely knew. We spent all our lunch money on Street Fighter.
I failed algebra twice because I just could not grasp the formulas. The teacher looked at me with pure pity.
I used to buy cheap burgers from the drive-thru and eat them in my car alone. It was the best part of my week.
I worked at a grocery store bagging groceries and hated how my hands smelled like wet cardboard.
I remember graduation day being incredibly hot under that cheap gown. I did not even go to the parties afterward.
I started taking classes at the local technical college for IT. The computer labs were always freezing cold.
I had a roommate for a few months who never washed his dishes. The apartment constantly smelled like rotting food.
I passed my certification exam by just one point. I was sweating so much I nearly ruined the test paper.
I dropped out of the community college program because I could not afford the tuition anymore. It felt like a huge relief at the time.
Looking back, I realize that leaving school was the moment my life started drifting, even if I did not see it then.
I got a job doing tech support over the phone and hated every minute of it. People were always screaming at me.
I remember the heavy headset I had to wear at the call center. It gave me terrible headaches by the end of the shift.
I met a woman named Claire at a diner, and we actually dated for a year. She liked my sense of humor.
I took Claire to a local fair, and we ate funnel cake until we felt sick. It was a really good day.
Claire left me because she said I had no ambition. It hurt, but I knew she was right.
I started gaining a lot of weight after that breakup. I just stopped caring about what I put in my body.
I remember going to buy new jeans and realizing I had gone up three sizes. The dressing room mirror was unforgiving.
I worked overnight security at a warehouse for a while. It was so quiet I used to talk to myself just to stay awake.
I found a stray cat behind the warehouse and started feeding it tuna. One day it just never came back.
I got fired from the security job because I fell asleep on shift. My boss did not even yell, he just handed me my final check.
I spent three months unemployed, sleeping until noon every day. The days just blurred together into a gray fog.
I finally got hired at a big box electronics store. I hated wearing that brightly colored polo shirt.
I used to hide in the stockroom during the holiday rush. The fluorescent lights gave everything a sickly yellow glow.
I helped an old man pick out a computer for his grandson, and he was so grateful. It made me feel useful for once.
I strained my back lifting a heavy television at work. The pain shot down my leg like a lightning bolt.
I tried to join a gym once, but I felt everyone staring at me on the treadmill. I never went back after the first day.
I bought a massive gaming PC with my tax refund. I spent whole weekends lost in fantasy worlds.
I remember the taste of the cheap energy drinks I used to chug during gaming marathons. They tasted like battery acid.
I lived in an apartment next to a train track for five years. Eventually, I stopped hearing the trains altogether.
I tried growing tomatoes on my balcony, but the pigeons ate all of them. I was surprisingly angry about it.

I actually didn't mind when Dr. Harris brought up my weight a few years ago because he didn't look down his nose at me. He had this calm, friendly way of talking that made me feel like he was on my side, not just judging my size.
I went to my ten-year high school reunion out of sheer curiosity. I left after twenty minutes because nobody recognized me.
I remember the day my dad passed away. I got the phone call while I was microwaving a burrito, and the beep of the microwave sounded so loud.
We cleared out my dad's house, and I found boxes of my old childhood drawings he had kept. I did not know he cared.
I inherited my dad's old recliner, and it is still the most comfortable chair I own. The fabric is worn thin on the armrests.
I started ordering delivery food almost every night because I was too tired to cook. The delivery guys knew me by name.
I broke a plastic lawn chair at a family barbecue just by sitting on it. My face burned with embarrassment as everyone stopped talking.
Sometimes I wonder if my obsession with old video games is just a way to hide from the fact that I have not moved forward in twenty years.
I got laid off from the electronics store when they downsized. I packed my locker into a single cardboard box.
I tried driving for a rideshare app, but my car smelled like fast food, and my ratings were terrible.
I remember picking up a couple fighting in my backseat. I just gripped the steering wheel and stared straight ahead.
I got into a fender bender at a stop sign because I was looking at my phone. The other driver yelled at me for ten minutes.
I had to borrow money from my mom to pay my rent last year. I hated the look of disappointment in her eyes.
I found a recipe for chili online and actually cooked it from scratch. It was the best thing I had eaten in months.
I tried to go for a walk in the park, but my knees started aching after ten minutes. I sat on a bench and watched the ducks instead.
I remember a little girl pointing at my belly in the grocery store. Her mother shushed her and dragged her away quickly.
I buy my clothes from specialty catalogs now because regular stores do not carry my size. The packages always arrive in unmarked bags.
I spend hours watching videos of people restoring rusty tools on the internet. There is something very calming about it.
I remember the sudden crack of thunder that knocked out my power for two days. I had to eat all the ice cream in the freezer before it melted.
I bought a cheap acoustic guitar at a pawn shop, thinking I would learn to play. It has been sitting in the corner for three years.
I had a doctor tell me bluntly that I would not live to see sixty if I did not lose weight. I went to my car and just cried.
Looking back, I think I use my size to push people away before they can reject me.
I love the smell of coffee brewing in the morning, even though I usually drink it cold by the afternoon.
I have a habit of leaving all the cabinet doors open in the kitchen. I do not even realize I am doing it until I turn around.
I watched an entire season of a television show in one day. By the end, my eyes were dry and my head was pounding.
I found a twenty-dollar bill on the sidewalk outside the gas station. I bought a lotto ticket and lost it all.
I remember the feeling of static electricity when I took off my winter coat. It shocked my fingers every time.
I have a favorite mug with a chipped handle that I refuse to throw away. It holds exactly the right amount of soup.
I slipped on the ice last winter and could not get up for a few minutes. I was terrified the neighbors would see me struggling.
I enjoy going to the drive-in movie theater by myself on summer nights. The sound coming through the radio feels nostalgic.
I remember the taste of a peach I bought from a roadside stand. It was so juicy it dripped down my chin.
I have a stack of mail on my kitchen counter that I have not opened in weeks. The envelopes just give me anxiety.

When the clinic handed me a pamphlet for some weight loss group, I just tossed it because it didn't say anything about how much it cost or if my state insurance would cover it. I needed to know if they were going to make me buy expensive shakes before I even thought about signing up.
I ordered a pair of shoes online, but they were too tight on my wide feet. I never bothered returning them.
I like to sit by the open window when it rains and just listen to the drops hitting the pavement.
I remember the sharp smell of bleach when the cleaning crew came to my old office. It always gave me a slight headache.
I tried to fix a leaky faucet in my bathroom and ended up flooding the floor. I had to call a plumber and pay him in cash.
I keep a jar of loose change on my dresser. I tell myself I will cash it in for a vacation, but I never do.
I remember watching the snow pile up on my windowsill during a massive blizzard. The world felt completely silent and still.
I had a terrible toothache for a month because I could not afford a dentist. The throbbing pain kept me up all night.
I love the crunch of autumn leaves under my boots when I walk to the mailbox.
I used to have a friend named Mike who would come over to watch wrestling. We lost touch after he got married.
I remember the bitter taste of a burnt piece of toast I forced myself to eat. I was too lazy to make another one.
I got a really bad sunburn on my arms from driving with the window down. The skin peeled for a week.
I have a small fan on my nightstand that I have to run to fall asleep. The white noise drowns out the silence.
I remember the smell of gasoline on my hands after filling up the lawnmower. It took days to wash it off completely.
I tried to build a model airplane once, but my fingers were too clumsy for the tiny parts. I glued my fingers together.
I once ate an entire family-sized bag of chips in one sitting. I felt sick and disgusted with myself afterward.
I remember the flashing neon sign of the diner where I used to get breakfast. The M was burnt out so it just said otels.
I like the feeling of fresh sheets on the bed right out of the dryer. It is one of the few things I actually clean properly.
I remember the sharp sting of a papercut from opening a utility bill. It hurt worse than a real cut.
I have a habit of chewing on the plastic caps of my pens. Most of them are mangled beyond recognition.
I watched a documentary about deep-sea creatures and could not sleep that night. The darkness of the ocean terrifies me.
I remember the rough texture of the cinderblock walls in my middle school locker room. I always leaned against them to tie my shoes.
I bought a giant jar of pickles just to drink the juice. It is a weird craving I have had since I was a teenager.
I spilled a cup of coffee on my only good keyboard and ruined it. I had to use on-screen typing for three days.
I remember the blinding glare of the sun on the hood of my car during a summer traffic jam. The AC was broken, and I was dripping with sweat.
I tried wearing a watch again, but the band dug into my wrist too much. I tossed it in a drawer.
I love the smell of a freshly opened pack of trading cards. It takes me right back to being ten years old.
I remember the deep rumble of thunder that shook the windows of my apartment. It felt like the whole building was vibrating.
I have a pair of sweatpants that are so worn out they are basically transparent, but I refuse to throw them away.
I accidentally dropped my phone on my face while reading in bed. It hit my nose so hard my eyes watered.
I remember the sweet, artificial taste of blue raspberry slushies at the gas station. I used to get one every Friday.
I tried to learn Spanish from a free app on my phone. I gave up after a week because I could not roll my letters.
I remember the feeling of absolute panic when I thought I lost my wallet in a busy grocery store. I found it in my other pocket.
I like to browse real estate websites and look at mansions I could never afford. I imagine what I would put in all those rooms.
I burned my tongue badly on a slice of hot pizza. I could not taste anything else for two days.
I remember the damp, earthy smell of the basement in my childhood home. It was cool down there in the summer.
I had a vivid dream where I was running fast and effortlessly. Waking up in this heavy body felt like a cruel joke.
I buy the cheap store-brand cola, but I pour it into a glass so it feels slightly fancier.
I remember the loud, clanking sound the old radiator made in my first apartment. It sounded like someone hitting it with a hammer.
I tried growing a beard, but it came in patchy and entirely gray. I shaved it off the next morning.
I love eating cold leftover Chinese food straight from the carton. It always tastes better the next day.
I remember the intense heat from the open oven door when I baked frozen pizzas. It would fog up my glasses instantly.
I got a flat tire on the highway and had to wait two hours for a tow truck. I was too heavy to safely operate the little jack.
I enjoy sitting in the dark and just listening to a baseball game on the radio. The announcers voices are very soothing.
I remember the sharp, minty smell of the muscle rub I had to use on my back after moving boxes.
I have a bad habit of picking at the labels on beer bottles. By the time I finish a drink, the label is usually in shreds.
I once tried to assemble a bookshelf from a flat pack and put the back panel on backward. I just left it that way.
I remember the deafening sound of cicadas in the trees during the late summer. It was a constant, ringing drone.
I bought a massive puzzle of a castle, but I lost the edge pieces and never finished it.
I love the feeling of scratching a mosquito bite until it bleeds, even though I know I should not.
I remember the harsh glare of the bathroom mirror at 3 AM. It always makes me look older and more tired than I feel.
I have a collection of old cell phones in a shoebox. I do not know why I keep them since none of the chargers work anymore.
I accidentally left a window open during a rainstorm and ruined a stack of library books. I had to pay the replacement fees.
I remember the taste of the overly sweet cake frosting at my nephew's birthday party. My teeth ached after one bite.
I tried to do a pushup a few months ago and collapsed on the floor. I just laid there for a long time.
I enjoy watching the garbage truck crush the trash on Tuesday mornings. There is something satisfying about the mechanical crunch.
I remember the metallic smell of the old key I used to unlock my grandparents house. It was heavy and ornate.
I have a habit of checking the refrigerator every twenty minutes when I am bored, hoping something new magically appeared.
I watched a spider build a web in the corner of my ceiling for a week. I could not bring myself to vacuum it up.
I remember the painful brain freeze I got from drinking a milkshake too fast at the drive-thru. I had to pull over.
I once put my keys in the freezer by mistake and spent three hours looking for them.
I love the heavy, muffled silence that falls over the street after a heavy snowstorm.
I remember the sticky feeling of bug spray on my arms during a camping trip. The mosquitoes still bit me anyway.
I had to use a seatbelt extender on an airplane once. The flight attendant handed it to me, and I felt everyone watching.
I enjoy organizing my digital files into highly specific folders. It gives me a sense of control over something.
I remember the sharp, vinegary smell of ketchup when I accidentally squeezed the bottle too hard and it splattered everywhere.

The nurse tried to get me to download this commercial diet app on my phone, and it gave me a really weird feeling. I couldn't help but wonder if the clinic was getting a cut of the money, or if that app was just going to sell my personal medical info to advertisers.
I keep a bottle of hot sauce in my glove compartment just in case I get bland fast food.

If my doctor is going to send me to a weight loss clinic, I expect him to actually look at my progress at my next checkup. It makes no sense to me if the two places don't even talk to each other to see how I'm doing.
I accidentally stepped on a snail on the sidewalk and felt terrible hearing the shell crunch.
I remember the bright, flashing lights of the carnival rides at the state fair. They always made me slightly nauseous.
I have a favorite spot on the couch that is permanently dented from my weight. It is the only place I sit.
I watched a stray dog run across the street and hold up traffic. I was rooting for the dog the whole time.
I remember the stale, dusty smell of the used bookstore downtown. I used to spend hours reading sci-fi paperbacks there.
I bought a giant container of protein powder, thinking I would start working out. It expired two years ago, unopened.
I love the sound of a bowling ball hitting the pins. It is a hollow, satisfying crash.
I remember the blinding reflection of the sun off the lake when I went fishing with my uncle. My eyes watered all afternoon.
I have a habit of leaving my shoes right in the middle of the hallway. I trip over them at least once a week.
I once laughed so hard at a comedy special that I actually choked on a pretzel. I had to perform the Heimlich maneuver on myself on a chair.
I remember the rough, scratchy texture of the wool blanket my mom kept in the living room. It was warm but horribly itchy.
I enjoy going to the automated car wash and watching the colorful soap slide down the windshield.

I was so relieved when the new doctor explained how losing a little weight would help the arthritis in my knees, rather than just lecturing me about being fat. It was a lot easier to listen to him when he focused on my joint pain instead of making me feel guilty about my appearance.
I accidentally bit the inside of my cheek while eating a sandwich. It swelled up and I kept biting it for days.
I remember the loud, chaotic ringing of the bells in my high school hallways. They always made my heart race.
I have a drawer full of dead batteries because I am too lazy to figure out how to recycle them properly.
I tried to skip a rock across a pond, but it just made a loud plop and sank immediately.
I remember the smell of burnt hair when I leaned too close to a candle. I had a bald patch on my arm for weeks.
I like to eat dry cereal straight out of the box late at night. The crunching sounds extremely loud in the quiet house.
I got a massive cramp in my calf while lying in bed. I had to roll around on the floor crying until it stopped.
I remember the flickering fluorescent light in the public library bathroom. It felt like a scene from a horror movie.
I bought a novelty mug that says World's Okayest Employee at a thrift store. I drank from it the day I was fired.
I love the smell of the first rain after a long dry spell. It smells like wet dirt and pavement.
I accidentally dropped a full jar of spaghetti sauce in the grocery store aisle. I walked away because I was too ashamed to tell anyone.
I remember the intense, vibrating bass of the speakers at a rock concert I went to in my twenties. I felt it in my chest.
I have a tendency to hoard plastic grocery bags under my sink. There must be hundreds of them stuffed in there.
I burned a frozen dinner in the microwave because I read the instructions wrong. The plastic tray literally melted into the food.
I remember the cold, smooth feeling of the ceramic tiles on the bathroom floor on a hot summer day.
I enjoy watching the progress bar load when I install a new computer game. It is a weirdly comforting anticipation.
I stepped in a deep puddle wearing only socks and sandals. The wet sock felt absolutely disgusting all the way home.
I remember the sweet, powdery smell of the bubble gum that came with baseball cards. It shattered like glass when you chewed it.
I keep turning the thermostat down because I am always sweating, even in December. My apartment is freezing.
I once won fifty bucks on a scratch-off ticket and immediately spent it all on expensive takeout.
I remember the sharp pinch of the blood pressure cuff at the free clinic. The nurse had to fetch a larger cuff for my arm.
I enjoy peeling the protective plastic film off new electronics. It is incredibly satisfying.
I found a gray hair in my eyebrow and tried to pluck it, but I just gave up and let it grow.
I realize that my habit of buying bulk junk food is a way to ensure I never have to leave the house or face the world.
I remember the smell of the cheap pine air freshener in the taxi cab taking me home from the hospital.
I accidentally locked myself out of my apartment in my pajamas. I had to sit in the hallway for an hour waiting for the super.

participants.persona: Yolanda is a 34-year-old woman with a college education, married or living with a partner, unemployed, and overweight.
participants.name: Yolanda

memories.content: I realize now that my obsession with organizing my desk in college was just a way to feel in control.
Looking back at my twenties, I see how much of my identity was tied up in jobs that did not actually matter.
I sometimes wonder if I married him because I loved him or because I was terrified of falling behind my friends.
It is funny how I used to think adults had everything figured out, but now I know we are all just pretending.
I recognize now that my sudden weight gain was a physical manifestation of the depression I was hiding.
My memory of that summer is completely shaped by the soundtrack I listened to, rather than the actual events.
I often reflect on how much my college degree cost versus how little I have actually used it.
I can see now that my fear of driving on the highway stems from a deeper need to avoid situations I cannot easily escape.
It occurs to me that I only remember the bright, sunny days from my childhood, probably as a coping mechanism.
I realize my constant need to please my partner is just a reflection of my own insecurities about being unlovable.
Looking at old photos, I understand why my mother pushed me so hard, even if I hated it at the time.
I have noticed a pattern in my life where I self-sabotage right before things get really good.
The day I got laid off, I sat in my car for three hours because I could not bear to tell my husband.
I cried in the fitting room trying on a dress for a wedding because nothing fit my new body.
Someone once asked if I was pregnant on the subway, and I felt so humiliated I just got off at the next stop.
I vividly recall the panic attack I had before my college finals, my heart racing so fast I thought I was dying.
There was a huge fight with my partner where I packed a bag, but I never actually left the house.
I remember finding out I was the only one in my friend group who did not get invited to Sarah bachelorette party.
The feeling of absolute worthlessness when my tenth job application of the week was rejected still lingers.
I secretly threw away the scale in our bathroom so I would not have to look at the numbers anymore.
I recall the thrill of finding a perfectly fitting vintage dress before I gained weight.
There was a mirror in the hallway that I eventually took down because I hated catching my reflection.
The feeling of my clothes being too tight is a constant, quiet source of frustration.
I used to love swimming, but I have not worn a bathing suit in public for years.
I remember the sinking feeling of checking my bank account balance after grocery shopping.
The silence of my phone when I am waiting to hear back about a job interview is deafening.
There was a time I burst into tears in the supermarket aisle because they were out of the cereal I wanted.
I remember the overwhelming guilt I feel when my partner pays for everything.
I remember the sharp pain of envy when I saw my old college roommate promotion on professional networks.
There was a pool party where I felt so insecure in my swimsuit that I kept my shirt on the whole time.
I can still smell the chlorine from the community pool we went to every summer as kids.
The taste of blue raspberry snow cones always takes me back to the county fair.
I remember the scratchy feel of the wool blanket on my grandmother couch.
The first time I saw the ocean, the water was freezing, but the sand was perfectly warm.
I recall the bright neon colors of my first bicycle, though I cannot remember who taught me to ride it.
There was a tree in our front yard that I used to climb to read books in the afternoons.
I remember the exact shade of yellow my bedroom was painted when I was ten.
The sound of rain on a tin roof always reminds me of camping trips with my family.
I used to collect shiny rocks and keep them in a little wooden box under my bed.
The smell of fresh bread always makes me think of Saturday mornings in my childhood kitchen.
I remember the feeling of panic when I lost my favorite stuffed animal at the grocery store.
The taste of overcooked pasta always brings back memories of my first apartment.
I recall the intense heat of the pavement on bare feet during July afternoons.
There was a stray cat that used to visit our porch, and I named it Whiskers.
I remember the blinding flash of the disposable cameras we used at middle school dances.
The sound of dial-up internet connecting is etched into my brain forever.
I used to spend hours playing computer games instead of doing my homework.
I remember the distinct smell of my first car, a mix of old upholstery and vanilla air freshener.
The feeling of butterflies in my stomach before my first middle school dance was overwhelming.
I recall the sticky sweetness of cotton candy sticking to my fingers at the amusement park.
There was a song that played on the radio constantly during my freshman year of college.
I remember the heavy weight of my backpack filled with textbooks I barely opened.
The taste of cheap beer always reminds me of crowded basement parties.
I used to have a favorite pen for taking notes, and I was devastated when it ran out of ink.
I remember the soft hum of the library air conditioning during late-night study sessions.
The smell of damp leaves in autumn always makes me nostalgic for back-to-school season.
I recall the bright fluorescent lights of the dining hall, though the food was entirely forgettable.
There was a poster of a band I did not even listen to hanging in my dorm room.
I remember the feeling of relief when I handed in my final exam for my hardest class.
The sound of my roommate alarm clock used to drive me absolutely crazy.
I used to love walking across the quad when the cherry blossoms were in bloom.
I remember the freezing wind on my face during a winter football game.
The taste of dining hall pizza is something I simultaneously miss and never want to eat again.
I recall the scratchy upholstery of the chairs in the student union building.
There was a coffee shop off-campus where I spent entirely too much money on lattes.
I remember the feeling of pride when I got my first paycheck from my campus job.
The smell of old paper in the library stacks always felt comforting to me.
I used to sit in the back row of my history lecture and just doodle in the margins.
I remember the absolute chaos of moving out of the dorms at the end of the year.
The sound of a professor monotone voice often lulled me to sleep.
I recall the bright blue lanyard I used to wear my keys on.
There was a pizza place we always ordered from at two in the morning on weekends.
I remember the feeling of excitement when I finally got my own apartment.
The taste of cheap wine always brings me back to nights spent talking on the balcony.
I used to have a plant that I miraculously kept alive for three years.
I remember the frustration of trying to assemble flat-pack furniture by myself.
The smell of new paint always reminds me of the day I moved in with my partner.
I recall the soft glow of the string lights we hung in our first living room.
There was a neighborhood dog that used to bark at us every time we walked by.
I remember the feeling of the sun on my face during our road trip down the coast.
The sound of our old radiator clanking used to wake me up in the middle of the night.
I used to love going to the farmer market on Sunday mornings.
I remember the vibrant colors of the fresh produce we bought but forgot to eat.
The taste of the burnt toast my partner made me for breakfast one morning still makes me smile.
I recall the soft texture of the blanket we always fought over on the couch.
There was a movie we watched a dozen times because we were too lazy to find anything else.
I remember the feeling of sand between my toes on a beach vacation we took years ago.
The smell of sunscreen immediately transports me back to that trip.
I used to spend hours browsing bookstores without ever buying anything.
I remember the satisfying sound of a new book spine cracking.
The taste of my favorite local coffee shop pastry is unmatched anywhere else.
I recall the harsh glare of my computer screen during long days at my old job.
There was a coworker who always hummed softly, and it drove me slightly mad.
I remember the feeling of dread in the pit of my stomach on Sunday evenings.
The sound of the office printer jamming is a noise I am glad I do not hear anymore.
I used to keep a stash of emergency chocolate in my desk drawer.
I remember the bright fluorescent lights in the breakroom that gave me headaches.
The smell of microwaved fish in the office kitchen was universally despised.
I recall the uncomfortable chairs in the conference room where we had endless meetings.
There was a plant in the lobby that always looked like it was dying.
I remember the feeling of relief stepping out of the office building at the end of the day.
The sound of traffic on my commute home was oddly soothing.
I used to listen to the same podcast every morning on the train.
I remember the bitter taste of the office coffee that I drank anyway.
The soft hum of the server room was a constant background noise on my floor.
I recall the colorful sticky notes I used to organize my monitor.
There was a small bakery near my old office where I bought lunch on Fridays.
I remember the feeling of exhaustion after a full week of commuting.
The smell of rain on hot asphalt always reminds me of summer evenings in the city.
I used to love the quiet of our apartment when my partner was out of town.

I remember asking my doctor if my new asthma medication was going to make me put on more weight, but he just brushed it off. I was really frustrated because I wanted to understand how my health issues and the extra pounds were actually connected.
I remember the loud ticking of the wall clock in our kitchen.
The taste of the incredibly spicy curry we made by accident is unforgettable.
I recall the soft light of the sunset filtering through our bedroom blinds.
There was a stray sock that lived behind the dryer for months before I retrieved it.
I remember the feeling of soft grass under my feet in the local park.
The sound of children playing in the distance is a comforting neighborhood noise.
I used to have a favorite mug that I shattered by accidentally dropping it in the sink.
I remember the smell of brewing coffee that wakes me up most mornings.
The warmth of my partner hand holding mine while we watch television is my favorite feeling.
I recall the vibrant red of the cardinal that visits our bird feeder.
There was a thunderstorm last summer that shook the entire house.

My partner and I went to the clinic, and I felt so dismissed when the nurse handed me a generic diet pamphlet that ignored all the programs I have already tried. At thirty-four, I expect a plan that takes my specific body and past struggles into account instead of a one-size-fits-all handout.
I remember the brilliant flashes of lightning illuminating the dark bedroom.
The sound of thunder rolling always makes me want to curl up with a book.
I used to collect vintage teacups, though I never actually drank out of them.
I remember the delicate floral patterns on the porcelain.
The smell of old thrift stores is a weirdly comforting scent to me.
I recall the fake, cheerful voice I used on networking calls.
The smell of cheap ramen reminds me of the tight budget we are on right now.
I used to dream of traveling the world, but now I just want a steady income.
The sound of my own sighing has become a regular soundtrack to my days.
I recall the comfortable silence of sitting on the couch doing nothing all afternoon.
There was a documentary I watched last week that I immediately forgot the premise of.
I remember the soft purr of a friend cat that fell asleep on my lap.

I actually felt comfortable talking about my size with Dr. Evans because she was so warm and never once looked at me with that judgmental glare I usually get. It made a huge difference knowing she was not judging me during our appointment.
The smell of vanilla candles is the only thing that makes the apartment feel clean sometimes.
I used to bake bread when I was stressed, but now I do not even have the energy for that.
I remember the rough texture of the dish sponge I desperately need to replace.
The taste of stale crackers I ate for lunch today was pretty depressing.
I recall the bright glare of the television in a dark room.
There was a spider in the bathroom that I let live because I felt bad for it.
I remember the warm water of a shower being the only thing that relaxed my muscles.
The sound of the garbage truck in the morning always reminds me I forgot to take the trash out.
I used to have a green thumb, but all my houseplants have slowly died this year.
I remember the crisp air of early morning when I actually used to wake up before eight.
The smell of wet dog after we gave our neighbor puppy a bath was atrocious.
I recall the soft glow of my phone screen as I scroll through social media at night.
There was a beautiful sunset last Tuesday that painted the whole sky pink and orange.
I remember the sudden, sharp headache I got from drinking too much iced coffee.
The sound of sirens in the distance is just a normal part of living here.
I used to love doing jigsaw puzzles, but they feel too tedious now.
I remember the satisfaction of snapping the final puzzle piece into place.

When I went in for a physical after losing my job, the doctor just told me to eat less and move more, which felt completely useless. I left feeling totally defeated because I needed actual medical guidance rather than a vague catchphrase.
The smell of pine needles always takes me back to childhood Christmases.
I recall the glittering lights of the tree we had in the living room.
There was a year I got a karaoke machine and drove my entire family crazy.
I remember the scratchy tinsel we used to drape over the branches.

I remember walking out of the office empty-handed, realizing the doctor did not offer me a single prescription, written plan, or even a follow-up appointment. It just felt like they expected me to figure out a gym routine and lose the weight entirely on my own.
The taste of peppermint hot chocolate is my favorite winter indulgence.
I used to leave carrots out for the reindeer, a tradition my mom insisted on.
I remember the cold snow seeping into my boots while sledding.
The sound of wrapping paper tearing always brings a smile to my face.
I recall the exhaustion of staying up until midnight on New Years Eve.
There was a fireworks display that was so loud it made my chest vibrate.
I remember the sticky heat of the holiday barbecue in July.
The smell of charcoal burning is the ultimate summer scent.
I used to chase fireflies in the backyard with a glass jar.
I remember the glowing green lights flickering in the dark grass.
The taste of burnt hotdogs is oddly nostalgic for me.
I recall the itchy mosquito bites that covered my legs every summer.
There was a time I fell off a swing and scraped both my knees terribly.
I remember the stinging sensation of hydrogen peroxide on the cuts.
The sound of the ice cream truck music always made me run inside for quarters.
I used to love the character popsicles with bubblegum eyes.
I remember the vibrant colors of autumn leaves piling up in the driveway.
The crunching sound of stepping on dry leaves is incredibly satisfying.
I recall the smell of pumpkin carving, slightly earthy and sweet.
There was a Halloween where I dressed up as a witch with a terrible plastic mask.
I remember the heavy weight of my trick-or-treat bag by the end of the night.
The taste of cheap, waxy chocolate always reminds me of those nights.
I used to trade all my licorice for peanut butter cups.
I remember the crisp bite of a fresh apple from the orchard.
The smell of apple cider warming on the stove is pure comfort.
I recall the scratchy wool scarves I had to wear in the winter.
There was a massive snowman we built that stayed frozen until March.
I remember the bright red mittens my grandmother knitted for me.

I felt so much better during my visit when the assistant focused on how losing a few pounds might help my joint pain, instead of making it about my appearance. It was a huge relief not to feel blamed for my size for once.
The sound of boots crunching in fresh snow is beautifully quiet.
I used to catch snowflakes on my tongue until my face went numb.
I remember the foggy windows of the car when the heater was on full blast.
The smell of gasoline at the pump always reminds me of family road trips.
I recall the endless games of license plate bingo in the backseat.
There was a rest stop diner that served the best greasy french fries.
I remember the hypnotic rhythm of the windshield wipers during a rainstorm.
The sound of the turn signal ticking was oddly soothing on long drives.
I used to fall asleep with my head leaning against the cold car window.
I remember the blinding sun reflecting off the hood of the car.
The taste of the stale trail mix we kept in the glove compartment was terrible.
I recall the frustration of losing the radio signal in the middle of nowhere.

participants.persona: Kimberly is a 62-year-old woman with a college education, single, unemployed, and overweight.
participants.name: Kimberly

memories.content: I remember the sharp smell of my grandmother's perfume, though I can't recall what brand it was.
I recall sitting in a college lecture hall feeling completely overwhelmed by the material, though the specific class escapes me.
I remember the exact feeling of the rough fabric on my childhood sofa, but I forget what color it was.
I felt a deep sting when a former boss criticized my work, though I don't remember her exact words.
I sometimes realize that my struggles with my weight have shaped how I view my entire worth, making me hide from the world.
I remember the taste of the stale coffee in the breakroom of my last job.
I recall the terrible sinking feeling when I got the phone call that I was being let go, even if I forget what day of the week it was.
I remember the warmth of the sun on my face during a beach trip in my twenties, but not who I went with.
I felt a hot flush of embarrassment when my pants split at a party once, though the faces of the people there are a blur.
I recall crying over a boy in high school, mostly remembering the physical ache in my chest rather than his actual name.
I remember the vibrant yellow color of my first car, but not the make or model.
I remember the crushing anxiety of checking my bank account balance after losing my job.
I often look back and see how being single for so long has made me fiercely independent, yet strangely isolated.
I recall the soft humming sound my old refrigerator used to make in the middle of the night.
I felt incredibly lonely during a holiday dinner a few years ago, though I can't remember what we even ate.
I remember the smell of rain on hot asphalt from a summer afternoon in childhood.
I recall the intense relief I felt walking out of my final college exam, even if I don't remember the subject.
I remember the sour taste of a spoiled apple I took a bite of at a picnic.
I felt so judged walking into a clothing store last year, noticing the clerk's eyes linger on my waistline.
I remember the comforting weight of a heavy blanket I used to sleep under in my thirties.
I look at my lack of a career now and realize my self-esteem has always been too tied to external validation.
I recall the loud crunch of autumn leaves under my boots during a walk in the park.
I remember the sharp pain of twisting my ankle on a curb, though I couldn't tell you what street it was.
I felt a sudden rush of joy when a stray dog ran up to me years ago.
I remember the bitter disappointment when a friend canceled our plans last minute, making me feel utterly forgotten.
I recall the bright, blinding glare of the snow on a winter morning when I was little.
I remember the dread of opening a rejection letter for a job I desperately wanted.
I felt the smooth, cold surface of a stone I picked up on a hike, though I forget which trail I was on.
I recognize that my tendency to push people away stems from a deep fear of being a burden to them.
I remember the dizzying smell of paint when we redecorated my childhood bedroom.
I recall the heavy, oppressive heat of an August afternoon spent waiting for a bus.
I remember the sheer panic of realizing I had lost my wallet at the grocery store.
I felt a deep swell of pride when I was handed my college diploma, even if the ceremony itself is a blur.
I remember the sickeningly sweet smell of a candle a former coworker used to burn at her desk.
I recall the harsh fluorescent lights in the waiting room of the unemployment office.
I remember the crisp, cold air stinging my cheeks during a winter festival I attended in my twenties.
I realize that I often eat when I feel lonely, a habit that has quietly defined much of my adult life.
I recall the sound of a distant train whistle that used to wake me up in my first apartment.
I felt so insecure trying on a bathing suit a few summers ago, focusing only on the harsh reflection in the mirror.
I remember the soft, worn texture of my favorite paperback book from college.
I recall the sharp tang of lemonade I drank on a friend's porch, though I forget the conversation we had.
I felt a profound sadness when a doctor told me I needed to monitor my blood pressure, feeling my age catch up with me.
I remember the sudden, jarring noise of a car horn honking right next to me.
I recall the feeling of being completely invisible at a neighborhood barbecue where everyone else was coupled up.
I understand now that my chronic avoidance of conflict has left me with a lot of unspoken resentment.
I remember the sweet, dusty smell of old library books from when I was a student.
I felt a rush of adrenaline when I almost slipped on an icy sidewalk last winter.
I recall the vibrant red of a scarf a stranger was wearing on the subway once.
I remember the tight, suffocating feeling in my chest during a panic attack I had in my thirties.
I felt the warm, grainy sand between my toes on a vacation I took long ago.
I recall the sinking feeling of stepping on a scale and seeing a number I wasn't prepared for.
I remember the loud, rhythmic ticking of the clock in my childhood kitchen.
I realize that my intense need for a tidy home is my way of controlling a life that often feels unmanageable.
I felt a surprising wave of comfort when an old song came on the radio, though I don't remember the artist.
I remember the bitter taste of burnt toast I forced myself to eat on a rushed morning.
I recall the deep ache in my lower back after standing in line for hours at a job fair.
I remember the bright flash of lightning that lit up my bedroom during a summer storm.
I felt the sting of tears when a family member made a passing comment about my lifestyle.
I recall the smooth, polished wood of the banister in my grandmother's house.
I remember the hollow feeling in my stomach when I realized I couldn't afford a new pair of winter shoes.
I look at my empty calendar and reflect on how my social circle has quietly shrunk over the decades.
I recall the sharp, medicinal smell of a hospital waiting room from when my mother was sick.
I remember the feeling of absolute exhaustion after finishing a massive project at an old job, though I forget the project details.
I felt the rough bark of a pine tree I leaned against while out on a solitary walk.
I remember the hot flush of anger when I was talked over in a staff meeting.

When Dr. Aris handed me that pamphlet for the Optifast clinic back around 2019, I felt completely lost because it didn't mention if my Medicare Advantage plan covered the mandatory meal replacements. I remember standing at the checkout desk feeling humiliated trying to figure out the out-of-pocket costs while a line formed behind me.
I recall the sweet, sticky taste of a caramel apple I had at a county fair.
I felt a sudden, deep jealousy watching a happy family play in the park, wishing I had experienced that.
I remember the blinding reflections off the car windshields during my old morning commute.
I reflect on my college days and see how my fear of failure stopped me from pursuing the degree I actually wanted.
I recall the comforting smell of cinnamon and apples baking in the oven.
I remember the sharp, stinging paper cut I got while organizing some old financial documents.
I felt the heavy, damp air of a greenhouse I visited on a school field trip.
I remember the profound sense of uselessness I felt the first Monday after I was laid off.
I recall the loud, booming thunder that rattled my windows and made me jump.
I felt the cool, refreshing splash of water on my face after a particularly hard day.
I remember the knot in my stomach when I realized a friendship was slowly fading away.
I recognize that I often project an image of being perfectly fine to hide how lonely my day-to-day life really is.
I recall the bright, cheerful yellow of the wallpaper in my first apartment kitchen.
I felt a surge of panic when my car engine stalled at a busy intersection.
I remember the soft, melodious chirping of birds outside my window early one spring morning.
I recall the bitter, metallic taste of a pill I had to swallow dry.
I felt a deep ache of longing when I found an old romantic letter, though the face of the man who wrote it is blurry.
I remember the rough, scratchy texture of a wool sweater I wore constantly in my twenties.
I recall the overwhelming smell of bleach in a public restroom I used.
I realize that I have spent too many years waiting for my real life to begin, instead of living the one I have.
I remember the vivid, fiery orange of a sunset I watched from a balcony, feeling entirely at peace.
I felt the sharp ache of a toothache that kept me awake for a whole night.
I recall the comforting, rhythmic sound of a washing machine running in the background.
I remember the sting of humiliation when a stranger offered me a seat on the bus, assuming I was elderly or pregnant because of my weight.
I felt the crisp, rigid edges of a brand new notebook I bought for a college class.
I recall the dull throb of a headache after staring at a computer screen for too long at my old job.
I remember the sweet, floral scent of a garden I walked through years ago.
I reflect on my eating habits and finally see how I use food as a shield against romantic rejection.
I recall the terrifying jolt of turbulence on a flight I took in my thirties.
I felt the smooth, cold glass of a windowpane I pressed my forehead against on a snowy day.
I remember the quiet, heavy shame of hiding empty food wrappers in the trash so no one would see them.
I recall the loud, chaotic chatter of a crowded cafeteria during my freshman year.
I felt the warm, soothing water of a hot bath after a particularly grueling interview process.
I remember the vibrant green of the grass in a park I used to visit on my lunch breaks.
I recall the sharp, acidic smell of vinegar from a cleaning accident in the kitchen.
I felt a hollow emptiness watching my coworkers pack up my desk after the company downsized.
I remember the soft, powdery texture of powdered sugar on a donut I ate.

I was surprisingly relieved when my nurse practitioner, Sarah, finally brought up trying Weight Watchers during my annual physical a few years ago. I remember sitting on the crinkly exam table thinking it was a solid idea since I knew they had in-person meetings at the community center down the street.

I still get angry thinking about the time Dr. Miller casually told me to start jogging three miles a day, completely ignoring the debilitating lumbar stenosis he diagnosed me with just months prior. I don't remember his exact words, but I can perfectly recall the dismissive smirk on his face as he looked me up and down.
I recall the intense, blinding pain of a migraine that ruined a weekend getaway.
I felt the comforting warmth of a cup of tea between my hands on a chilly morning.
I remember the agonizing silence in the room when a romantic partner and I realized it was over.
I recall the bright, neon glow of a diner sign I saw on a late-night drive.
I felt the sticky, sweet residue of melted ice cream on my fingers at a summer fair.
I remember the deep embarrassment of having my debit card declined at the grocery checkout.
I recall the harsh, grating sound of a lawnmower waking me up too early on a Saturday.
I felt the smooth, slippery surface of a silk pillowcase I splurged on once.
I remember the suffocating heat of an apartment I lived in that didn't have air conditioning.
I recall the sharp, salty taste of ocean water when a wave knocked me over as a kid.
I felt a sudden wave of grief on a random Tuesday, mourning the career I had lost.
I remember the dull, faded pattern of the carpet in my childhood living room.
I recall the stinging, cold wind slicing through my coat on a walk to the bus stop.
I felt the soft, yielding dough beneath my hands when I tried baking bread from scratch.
I remember the horrible sinking feeling of finding a new grey hair and realizing I was aging alone.
I recall the bright, twinkling lights of a Christmas tree in a department store window.
I felt the rough, calloused hand of my grandfather when he held mine years ago.
I remember the frantic racing of my heart when I thought someone was following me at night.
I recall the rich, earthy smell of wet soil in a garden I used to tend.
I felt a heavy sense of defeat when I couldn't zip up a dress I wanted to wear to a wedding.
I remember the loud, metallic clanking of a radiator in a college dorm room.
I recall the sharp, agonizing cramp in my leg that woke me up in the middle of the night.
I felt the warm, comforting embrace of a friend during a really tough time, though I forget what she said.
I remember the sweet, artificial taste of a cherry popsicle on a scorching day.
I recall the intense anxiety of trying to decipher a confusing medical bill.
I felt the smooth, cool leather of a car seat on my bare legs in the summer.
I remember the stinging humiliation when a teenager laughed at me while I was trying to exercise in the park.
I recall the vibrant blue of the sky on a perfect autumn afternoon.
I felt the sharp, sudden pain of a needle during a routine blood test.
I remember the soft, muffled sound of snow falling outside my window at night.
I recall the deep frustration of applying to dozens of jobs and hearing nothing back.
I felt the sticky humidity of a summer evening clinging to my skin.
I remember the acrid smell of burnt hair when I accidentally left my curling iron on too long.
I recall the quiet, lonely sound of my own footsteps echoing in an empty hallway.
I felt the crisp, clean texture of freshly washed bedsheets when I slid into them.
I remember the sharp sting of a paper wasp that bit me when I was a teenager.
I recall the deep, resonant chime of a grandfather clock in an old house I visited.
I felt a profound sense of isolation when my phone didn't ring at all on my last birthday.
I remember the bright, garish colors of a fast-food uniform I had to wear in college.
I recall the sour, spoiled smell of milk I accidentally poured into my morning coffee.
I felt the warm, dry breeze on my face driving with the windows down on a highway.
I remember the heavy, sinking dread of realizing I had missed a final payment on my credit card.
I recall the soft, purring vibration of a cat that sat on my lap at a neighbor's house.
I felt the rough, scratching bristles of a hairbrush my mother used on me when I was little.
I remember the intense, burning shame of tripping and falling in a crowded supermarket aisle.
I recall the sharp, tangy smell of a freshly peeled orange in a stuffy room.
I felt the dull ache in my knees after climbing too many stairs to a friend's apartment.
I remember the loud, startling pop of a balloon bursting right behind my head.
I recall the deep sadness of packing up my office belongings into a single cardboard box.
I felt the smooth, curved surface of a seashell I picked up on a solitary beach walk.
I remember the sharp, stinging smell of rubbing alcohol from a doctor's clinic.

After I lost forty pounds on that strict low-carb protocol in my fifties, the weight crept right back because the clinic didn't offer any sort of maintenance phase or transition plan. It feels like this metabolic struggle is something I'll be managing until the day I die, not just a quick fix I can check off a list.
I recall the comforting, savory taste of a homemade stew on a freezing winter night.
I felt the cold, clammy sweat of anxiety on my palms before a big job interview.
I remember the vibrant, multicolored pattern of a quilt my aunt made for me.
I recall the sharp, metallic sound of keys dropping onto a hard tile floor.
I felt a sudden, piercing fear when I noticed a strange lump, though it turned out to be nothing.
I remember the soft, glowing light of a streetlamp filtering through my blinds at night.
I recall the bitter, astringent taste of a cup of black tea steeped for too long.
I felt a deep, embarrassing flush when someone asked why I was still single at my age.
I remember the loud, chaotic music playing at a college party where I felt entirely out of place.
I recall the smooth, cool metal of a doorknob I hesitated to turn before entering a difficult meeting.
I felt the rough, gritty texture of sand stuck to my skin after a day at the beach.
I remember the profound, quiet relief of closing my front door and finally being alone after a stressful day.
I recall the bright, flashing lights of a police car pulling me over for a broken taillight.
I felt the warm, sticky syrup from a pancake breakfast dripping onto my hand.
I remember the agonizing wait for the results of a biopsy, feeling completely paralyzed by fear.

I actually didn't mind when the endocrinologist at Mercy Hospital brought up my BMI, because she tied it directly to lowering my A1C and getting off my blood pressure meds. It was such a comforting contrast to previous doctors who just made me feel ashamed about my body.
I recall the loud, shrill ringing of an old landline phone waking me up at dawn.

The dietician handed me the exact same generic macro sheet she probably gives twenty-year-old athletes, without adjusting anything for a post-menopausal woman in her sixties with a sluggish thyroid. I remember just staring at the paper, exhausted by the fact that she hadn't even looked at my chart or asked about my past struggles with those calorie-counting apps.
I felt the crisp, fragile texture of an autumn leaf crunching in my hand.
I remember the harsh, glaring fluorescent lights of a hospital corridor late at night.
I recall the sweet, nostalgic smell of my childhood favorite cereal.
I felt a deep ache in my chest when a friend forgot about our lunch plans completely.
I remember the rough, uneven concrete of a sidewalk I tripped over.
I recall the vibrant, deep purple of a flower I saw blooming in a neighbor's yard.
I felt the cold, hard surface of an examination table paper crinkling beneath me.
I remember the loud, rumbling sound of a garbage truck passing by early in the morning.
I recall the sharp, sweet taste of a strawberry I picked fresh from a field.
I felt a sudden rush of tears when I saw an elderly couple holding hands, wishing I had someone.
I remember the dull, heavy weight of a stack of rejection letters from publishers I tried submitting my writing to years ago.
I recall the soft, velvety feel of a theater seat during a movie I went to alone.
I felt the stinging heat of a sunburn on my shoulders after forgetting to wear lotion.
I remember the loud, infectious laughter of a friend who moved away a decade ago.
I recall the intense, sour smell of a damp towel I forgot in the laundry basket.
I felt a heavy, sinking sorrow when I watched a beloved pet pass away.
I remember the bright, clear sound of a brass bell ringing above a shop door.
I recall the rough, fibrous texture of a rope I used to tie down moving boxes.
I felt an overwhelming sense of dread looking at a pile of unpaid bills on my kitchen counter.
I remember the sweet, rich smell of chocolate chip cookies my roommate baked in college.
I recall the sharp, cold bite of an ice cube I accidentally swallowed whole.
I felt a deep, quiet shame when I realized I was out of breath just walking up a small hill.
I remember the loud, rhythmic thumping of rain on a tin roof during a spring downpour.
I recall the smooth, glossy finish of an old photograph I found tucked in a book.
I felt a sudden surge of anger when a salesperson completely ignored me to help a thinner woman.

participants.persona: Bianca is a 23-year-old woman with some college or technical education, single, unemployed, and overweight.
participants.name: Bianca

memories.content: I remember hiding my snacks under my bed when I was eight because my mom always monitored what I ate.
My high school graduation felt more like a relief than a victory, though I still keep the tassel in my nightstand.
I adopted my cat, Barnaby, from a shelter two years ago, and he sleeps on my feet every single night.
During my first semester of community college, I failed chemistry because I was too intimidated to ask the professor for help.
I spent three hours yesterday tweaking my resume, but I still have not submitted a single application.
The first time someone called me chubby was in fourth grade, and I can still picture the red playground slide where it happened.
I love baking sourdough bread, mostly because kneading the dough feels incredibly therapeutic.
I deleted all my dating apps because I recognized I was using them just to distract myself from feeling stuck.
My dad taught me how to change a tire in the pouring rain when I was sixteen.
I dropped out of the graphic design program after two semesters, and my parents still ask when I am going back.
Shopping for jeans usually ends in tears, so I mostly stick to buying leggings online now.
I sometimes wonder if my friends secretly judge me for not having a job right now, which says more about my own insecurities than their friendship.
My favorite movie is Spirited Away, and I watch it every time I feel overwhelmed by the world.
I accidentally backed into a mailbox during my driving test, but the instructor passed me anyway.
Whenever my mom calls in the middle of the day, I pretend I am busy so she does not think I am just sleeping in.
I used to play the flute in middle school band, though I can barely remember how to read sheet music now.
The smell of lavender always makes me anxious, and I have finally realized it is because it reminds me of my grandmother's stuffy parlor.
I have a habit of biting my nails down to the quick whenever I have to make a phone call.

My regular doctor told me I needed to lose some weight and just handed me a generic pamphlet before rushing out the door. I remember sitting in my car afterward, crying out of frustration because I still had no idea what I was actually supposed to do.
Last summer, I drove to the beach by myself and sat in the sand for hours just listening to the waves.
I keep buying fresh spinach with the best intentions, only to let it turn to slime in the crisper drawer.
A boy named Tyler asked me to the prom as a joke, and I was naive enough to believe he was serious at first.
I realize now that my obsession with video games is largely a coping mechanism to avoid thinking about my future.
The barista at the local coffee shop knows my exact order, which makes me feel surprisingly valued.
I tried to dye my hair pink in my dorm bathroom, but it ended up looking like a washed-out orange.
I applied for a receptionist job yesterday and immediately felt sick to my stomach wondering if they would reject me.
My older brother is a successful engineer, and family dinners always revolve around his accomplishments.
I collect vintage postcards from places I have never been, storing them in an old shoebox under my desk.
When I was little, I used to believe that if I ate a watermelon seed, a vine would grow in my stomach.
I often cancel plans at the last minute because I recognize that the thought of getting dressed up feels entirely exhausting.
I still remember the exact outfit I was wearing when my first boyfriend broke up with me.
I bought a gym membership in January but have only gone twice because I feel like everyone is staring at me.
Learning to crochet has been surprisingly difficult, but I finally finished a lopsided scarf.
I find myself staying up until three in the morning because I know the night feels like the only time nobody expects anything from me.
My family went to Yellowstone when I was twelve, and I threw up in the rental car on the way there.
I still owe a thousand dollars on my credit card from buying textbooks I barely even opened.
I had a panic attack in the grocery store aisle last week over the price of eggs.
My favorite season is autumn, primarily because I am well aware that chunky sweaters hide my body so well.
I have a scar on my left knee from falling off a bicycle into a gravel driveway.
When I was in high school, I wrote terrible poetry in a marble composition notebook that I recently burned.
The sound of rain against my bedroom window always helps me fall asleep faster.
I went to a coding bootcamp for a month before realizing I absolutely hated staring at syntax errors.
My parents fought constantly when I was a teenager, so I spent most evenings at the public library.
I notice that I tend to agree with whatever opinion my friends have just to avoid any sort of conflict.
I tried veganism for a week but gave up because I missed cheese too much.
There is a pile of laundry on my chair that has been sitting there for at least a fortnight.
I love playing The Sims because it gives me a sense of control that I know I completely lack in my real life.
I burned a batch of chocolate chip cookies last night because I got distracted watching a stream.
A girl named Chloe spread a rumor about me in seventh grade, and I still flinch when I hear her name.
I bought a planner for the new year, but all the pages are still completely blank.
My best friend got engaged last weekend, and I realized my first reaction was jealousy instead of happiness.
I usually skip breakfast and then end up eating way too much at lunch because I am starving.
I took a ceramics class in community college and made an ugly mug that I use for my morning coffee.
When I walk past mirrors, I automatically suck my stomach in without even realizing I am doing it until later.
I still have the stuffed bear my dad won for me at the state fair when I was five.
I occasionally check my ex's social media, fully aware that it will only make me feel worse about myself.
My favorite comfort food is macaroni and cheese mixed with hot dogs, just like my mom used to make.
I had to borrow money from my parents to pay rent last month, and the shame of it keeps me awake at night.
I have a weird phobia of moths and will completely panic if one gets trapped in my bedroom.
I find that I use humor to deflect whenever someone asks me a serious question about my career.
I once got lost in the mall as a toddler and sat by the fountain until a security guard found me.
I spent hours curating a music playlist for a road trip that ended up getting canceled.
Whenever I try on swimsuits, I end up leaving the store feeling entirely defeated.
I have a tattoo of a tiny ghost on my ankle that I got on a whim during a spring break trip.
I sometimes wonder if I am inherently lazy, or if my lack of motivation is actually undiagnosed depression.

When I finally found a nurse practitioner who just listened to my struggles without giving me that pitying look, I actually felt safe enough to talk about my late-night binge eating. I realized then that I had been hiding my eating habits for years just to avoid being judged.
I love the smell of gasoline when I am filling up my car at the station.
I won a spelling bee in fifth grade by correctly spelling a really complicated flower name.
My neighbor plays loud bass music at midnight, and I am too socially anxious to ask him to turn it down.
I recently discovered that I actually enjoy gardening, surprising myself with how protective I feel over my sad potted tomatoes.
I slipped on the ice last winter and sprained my wrist, which made typing incredibly painful for weeks.
I keep a journal in my nightstand but only write in it when I am feeling extremely upset.
I feel immensely guilty whenever I order takeout, realizing it stems from my avoidance of cooking the groceries I already have.
I used to be obsessed with boy bands and had my bedroom walls completely covered in posters.
I went to a party last month and stood in the kitchen playing with the host's dog the entire time.
My mom criticized my weight during Thanksgiving dinner, and I had to hide in the bathroom to cry.
I realized today that I judge other people's outfits just to make myself feel better about my own appearance.
I taught myself how to knit by watching tutorial videos during the pandemic lockdown.
I accidentally sent a text complaining about my roommate directly to my roommate.
I always take the window seat on airplanes so I can lean my head against the glass and sleep.
I find comfort in re-watching the same sitcoms because I know the predictable plots soothe my anxiety.
I have a bad habit of picking at the split ends of my hair when I am bored.
A teacher in high school told me I was not college material, and I have only recently understood how much I let her words define me.
I made a homemade pizza yesterday, but the crust ended up completely burnt on the bottom.
I secretly love eating raw cookie dough even though I know the raw eggs are a risk.
I lied on a job application about my proficiency in spreadsheets, hoping I could just learn it on the job.
I often feel like an imposter in my own life, aware that I am merely pretending to be an adult while everyone else actually knows what they are doing.
I tripped going up the stairs at the library and pretended I was perfectly fine even though my shin was bleeding.
I have a collection of loose tea leaves that I rarely brew because I am too lazy to clean the strainer.
My first kiss was behind the bleachers at a football game, and it was mostly just awkward and wet.
I see my reflection in store windows and observe how a sudden spike of disappointment instantly ruins my mood.
I once tried to cut my own bangs with kitchen scissors, and I had to wear headbands for three months.
I donated a bunch of clothes that no longer fit me, consciously deciding it was time to let go of the fantasy of fitting into them again.
I remember the smell of floor wax in my elementary school hallway with vivid clarity.
I usually buy the generic brand of cereal to save money, even though it tastes like cardboard.
I avoided going to the dentist for four years because I was embarrassed by how many cavities I probably had.
My friend dragged me to a karaoke bar, and I refused to sing because I was terrified of being mocked.
I always order iced coffee, even in the middle of winter when it is freezing outside.
I dropped my phone in a puddle last year and lost thousands of photos because they were not backed up.
I realize my tendency to start reading a book and abandon it halfway through is tied to my fear of endings.
I once shoplifted a tube of lip gloss when I was fourteen and felt sick with guilt for a week.
My favorite holiday is Halloween because I love seeing all the creative costumes in my neighborhood.
I broke down in tears at the mechanic's shop when they told me how much my brake repairs would cost.
I still remember the lyrics to all the songs from the musical I was in during junior high.
I get incredibly nervous when driving on the highway, so I usually take the scenic backroads instead.
I bought a bunch of expensive makeup, thinking it would make me feel beautiful, but it just sits in my drawer.
I love watching thunderstorm videos online while I drink my morning tea.
I had a massive crush on my math tutor in college, which made focusing on algebra nearly impossible.
I usually sleep with three pillows because I like feeling completely surrounded.
I felt a huge wave of relief when my last job laid me off, even though the financial strain has been terrible.
I always check behind the shower curtain for intruders before using the bathroom.
I tried to paint a watercolor landscape, but it ended up looking like a muddy brown blob.
I have a fake smile I use exclusively for networking events that makes my jaw ache.
I used to bury treasure in the sandbox when I was little, pretending I was a famous pirate.
I feel incredibly self-conscious when I eat in public, worried that strangers are judging my food choices.
I binge-watched an entire season of a true crime documentary in one sitting over the weekend.

At 23 and dealing with PCOS, it is incredibly frustrating when doctors just tell me to eat less, ignoring that my hormones make my body react differently than a middle-aged man.
