I wish they would look at my actual medical chart and suggest a plan that makes sense for me as a young woman with a metabolic issue.
I found an old love letter I wrote to a high school boyfriend and cringed at how dramatic it sounded.
I always put my left shoe on before my right shoe out of pure habit.
I cried during a dog food commercial last night because the golden retriever reminded me of my childhood pet.
I have a stack of unopened mail on my kitchen counter that gives me anxiety every time I look at it.
I love the crunch of autumn leaves under my boots when I walk through the park.
I once got a terrible sunburn on my shoulders because I stubbornly refused to put on sunscreen.
I check my bank account balance through cracked fingers, terrified of seeing the actual number.
I enjoy doing crossword puzzles in the local newspaper, even though I rarely finish them.
I felt completely invisible at my cousin's wedding, sitting quietly at the singles table all night.
I accidentally killed all the succulents I bought because I watered them way too much.
I have a recurring dream where I am back in college and completely forgot to attend a final exam.
I used to collect beautiful rocks from the riverbed and polish them in a small tumbler.
I get horribly carsick if I try to read a book or look at my phone while someone else is driving.
I made up an excuse to skip a baby shower because seeing all those happy couples made me feel profoundly lonely.

When my doctor told me that joining the local YMCA water aerobics class was a fantastic idea for my joints, I immediately went home and signed up. Just hearing a medical professional validate my plan made me believe I could actually stick with it this time.
I love the aesthetic of minimal apartments, but my own bedroom is a cluttered, chaotic mess.
I once won a giant stuffed penguin at an arcade by playing the claw machine perfectly on my first try.

I have never once left a standard checkup with a step-by-step meal plan or a gym referral, just a vague command to watch my calories. It makes me feel completely abandoned by the healthcare system, especially when I cannot afford a nutritionist on my own since losing my job.
I have a weird compulsion to constantly apologize, even when someone else bumps into me.

It was not until I saw an endocrinologist for my hormone issues that I finally got a detailed breakdown of which foods to avoid and which supplements to take. Unlike my primary care doctor, the specialist actually took the time to write down a daily schedule for me to follow.
I made a vision board last January, but looking at it now just highlights everything I have failed to achieve.
I always peel off the labels of my water bottles when I am feeling nervous during a conversation.
I tried roller skating last summer and bruised my tailbone so badly I could not sit properly for a week.
I feel immensely awkward trying to make small talk with the cashier at the grocery store.
I used to sneak out of my bedroom window as a teen just to sit on the roof and look at the stars.
I buy clothes that are a size too small, telling myself I will lose weight, but they just gather dust in my closet.
I find folding warm towels fresh out of the dryer to be one of the most relaxing chores.
I got a minor speeding ticket last month, and I am terrified my car insurance rates will skyrocket.
I love finding old photographs at thrift stores and imagining the lives of the strangers in them.
I felt a deep pang of sorrow when my local indie bookstore closed down permanently.
I occasionally talk to my cat as if he completely understands everything I am saying.
I have a habit of pulling away from friends when I am depressed, knowing full well that it only ends up isolating me further.
I tried out for the school play in ninth grade but froze completely when I stepped on stage.
I always pick the corner piece of brownies because I love the chewy edges the most.
I got caught in a torrential downpour without an umbrella and had to walk three blocks soaking wet.
I dread logging onto professional networking sites because seeing everyone else's career milestones makes me feel utterly inadequate.
I have a small scar on my chin from tripping over a jump rope when I was seven.
I once spent an entire afternoon organizing my bookshelf by color instead of actually looking for a job.
I absolutely despise the texture of raw tomatoes, though I love ketchup and marinara sauce.
I have a pair of lucky socks that I wore to every single test I took in college.
I felt a rush of embarrassment when my stomach growled loudly during a completely silent movie theater scene.
I taught my childhood dog how to roll over, and it took me nearly a month of patience.
I constantly compare my physical appearance to the girls I see on social media, fully recognizing that it completely ruins my self-esteem.
I love drinking hot cocoa with extra marshmallows after shoveling snow from the driveway.
I bought a lottery ticket yesterday, spending five dollars I really could not afford to waste.
I remember the distinct smell of my middle school locker, a weird mix of metal, cheap perfume, and old paper.
I get incredibly flustered whenever a stranger gives me a compliment, mostly because I never believe them.
I tried to assemble a flat-pack dresser by myself and ended up with two extra screws and a wobbly drawer.
I used to collect gel pens in every possible color, meticulously organizing them in a special plastic case.
I felt physically ill before hitting the send button on an email officially dropping out of my tech program.
I always sleep with a fan on because the white noise drowns out the sound of traffic outside.
I have a weird aversion to stepping on the cracks in the sidewalk, a habit I kept from childhood.
I panicked during a phone interview when the recruiter asked where I saw myself in five years.
I used to catch fireflies in a mason jar during summer evenings, always making sure to release them before bed.
I have a terrible habit of chewing on the inside of my cheek when I feel socially awkward.
I was briefly obsessed with origami in high school and covered my desk in tiny paper cranes.
I got a parking ticket downtown because I could not figure out how to use the digital meter.
I love the way the air smells right before a big thunderstorm rolls into town.
I still have not returned a sweater I borrowed from a friend two years ago, and now I am too embarrassed to bring it up.
I once accidentally put salt instead of sugar in my coffee, and I spat it out all over the kitchen sink.
I dread family reunions because I hate fielding the relentless questions about my dating life.
I used to write my name on the bottom of my sneakers, convinced someone would try to steal them at gym class.
I cried in the fitting room at the department store last week because none of the jeans I grabbed would zip up.
I have a favorite coffee mug with a chipped handle, but I refuse to throw it away.
I found a twenty-dollar bill on the sidewalk last month and immediately used it to buy an expensive iced latte.
I avoid walking past groups of teenagers at the mall because I am inexplicably afraid they will laugh at me.
I used to spend hours playing solitaire on the family computer when our internet was down.
I felt a massive wave of imposter syndrome when my friend asked me for advice about her own resume.
I love the crisp feeling of fresh bedsheets, especially right after taking a hot shower.
I got stung by a bee on my forehead during a picnic, and my eye was swollen shut for two days.
I secretly despise the perfume my mother gifted me for Christmas, but I wear it when she visits anyway.
I once baked a cake from scratch that turned out incredibly dry, but my dad ate it anyway to make me feel better.
I keep all my passwords written on a sticky note under my keyboard because I am terrified of getting locked out of my accounts.
I love wandering around the hardware store, even though I have absolutely zero knowledge about home repair.
I lied to a guy on a dating app about loving hiking just to seem more interesting, then had to unmatch him when he invited me to a trail.
I have an old acoustic guitar in my closet that I bought with the intention of learning, but I never did.
I accidentally bumped into a glass door at the bank and was utterly mortified when everyone turned to look.
I love the sound of bacon sizzling in a pan on a lazy Sunday morning.
I gave myself a terrible blister on my heel by wearing brand new boots for an eight-hour shift.
I cried when my favorite character died in a fantasy novel, deeply grieving for a fictional person.
I always pause before knocking on someone's door, taking a deep breath to steady my nerves.
I have a weird fascination with watching cake decorating videos online right before I fall asleep.
I threw away my bathroom scale last month because checking my weight every morning was destroying my mental health.

participants.persona: Charlene is a 52-year-old woman with a college education, married or living with a partner, unemployed, and overweight.
participants.name: Charlene

memories.content: I often look back at my college days and realize how much my confidence was tied to academic praise, rather than my own self-worth.
Being out of work has made me question my identity in ways I never anticipated.
I realize now that my struggles with my weight have always been a shield to keep people at a safe distance.
Looking at old photos with my husband, I am struck by how my memory of our early relationship is completely colored by the anxiety I felt back then.
I sometimes wonder if my tendency to forget the exact dates of important events is a way of protecting myself from the passage of time.
When I reflect on my twenties, I can see how my desperation to fit in shaped every choice I made, though I could not admit it at the time.
I notice that I only remember the sensory details of my past jobs, like the hum of the fluorescent lights, because the actual work felt so meaningless.
It dawns on me that my hesitation to leave the house lately is not about being tired, but a deep-seated fear of being perceived.
Looking back, I understand that my anger toward my mother was really just an echo of her own insecurities that I absorbed.

The doctor just handed me a pamphlet and walked out, leaving me sitting on the exam table feeling completely abandoned. My husband asked how the appointment went later, and I just cried because I was entirely on my own again.
I reflect often on how my college education gave me a vocabulary to analyze my feelings, but not necessarily the tools to fix them.
I am beginning to see that my comfort in routine is less about organization and more about maintaining an illusion of control.
When I think about the friends I have lost touch with, I recognize my own passivity in letting those connections wither.
I remember the heavy, dusty smell of the university library basement. I do not recall what I was studying, only the oppressive silence.
The feeling of utter exhaustion after pulling an all-nighter is etched into my bones. I cannot even remember which class the exam was for.
I recall the bright, blinding glare of the winter sun on the campus quad. Someone was walking next to me, but their identity is lost to time.
I felt a crushing sense of inadequacy during a seminar, though the professor us exact words escape me. It made my face burn with shame.
I remember the warm, yeasty smell of the local pizza place we frequented after midterms. I could not name a single person who was at the table.
The rough texture of my graduation gown is a distinct memory. I have no idea what the commencement speaker actually talked about.
I once felt a surge of pride handing in a term paper, the crisp edges of the paper in my hands. The topic of the paper is completely blank to me now.

I remember staring at the referral slip for that weight loss program, wondering how on earth I could afford it on our single income since I am currently unemployed. I needed to know if insurance covered it and what kind of food I would be forced to buy, but nobody gave me those details.
I remember the sour taste of cheap beer at a frat party and the sticky floor under my shoes. I could not tell you whose house it was.
The sheer terror of waking up late for a final exam still makes my heart race. I do not remember if I actually made it on time.
I can clearly recall the damp, musty smell of my first dorm room. My roommate is face is just a blur in my memory now.
There was a time I cried on a campus bench, feeling completely overwhelmed by the autumn wind. I do not know what triggered the tears.
I remember the satisfying weight of a heavy textbook in my backpack. The specific courses I took that semester are entirely forgotten.
The harsh fluorescent lighting in the dining hall gave me terrible headaches. I cannot remember what the food actually tasted like.
I felt a deep ache of loneliness walking through a crowded student union. I do not know what year of my degree that was.
The soft hum of a radiator in a winter classroom was so comforting. I do not remember the professor is name at all.
I recall the sharp sting of a papercut from a syllabus on the first day of class. The class itself is a mystery to me.
I felt a sudden rush of independence the first time I bought my own groceries as a freshman. I cannot recall what was in the bags.
The overwhelming scent of cheap perfume in the girls locker room always made me nauseous. I do not remember who used to wear it.
I remember the stiff, scratchy fabric of the blazer I wore to my first big interview. The questions they asked me have completely vanished from my mind.
The sickening drop in my stomach when I made a major mistake at work is unforgettable. I could not tell you the exact project or who caught the error.
I recall the bitter taste of burned coffee from the breakroom machine. I do not remember the names of the colleagues I used to drink it with.
I felt a heavy sense of dread every time the office phone rang with a certain ringtone. I do not know which specific client I was avoiding.
The bright, sterile glow of my computer monitor often made my eyes water by five in the evening. I have no memory of the spreadsheets I stared at.
I remember the feeling of cold sweat on my palms before a presentation. The faces of the audience members are entirely washed out.
The triumphant feeling of clearing out my desk on a Friday afternoon was the best part of the week. I could not tell you a single task I accomplished.
I recall the faint smell of ozone from the overworked copy machine down the hall. I do not remember what documents I was constantly copying.
The sharp tone of a former boss voice still echoes in my head and makes me tense. I do not remember the specific words she used to belittle me.
I felt a deep, hollow emptiness when they announced the company layoffs. I do not remember the exact date, just the gray weather outside.
The soft clicking of keyboards across an open-plan office used to lull me into a trance. I cannot recall who sat at the desk next to mine.
I remember the awkward silence in the elevator with upper management. The floor we were going to is a complete blank.
The heavy exhaustion in my legs after standing at a networking event is a vivid sensation. I do not remember a single person I networked with.
I felt a brief spark of validation when I received an award, but the plaque itself felt cheap and light. I cannot remember the year it happened.
The stale smell of the conference room during hour-long meetings always made me sleepy. I do not know what we ever actually decided in there.
I recall the frantic heartbeat of rushing to meet a deadline at the very last minute. The content of the report is completely gone from my memory.
The sting of tears in my eyes after a harsh performance review is something I can still feel. I do not remember the specific criticisms.
I remember the satisfying snap of closing my laptop for the final time at my last job. I could not tell you what day of the week it was.
The heavy silence of the house at ten in the morning can sometimes feel suffocating. I do not remember when I first started noticing how quiet it is.

I remember telling my doctor that my weight is a continuous battle and I need support that will not just vanish after six months. I felt extremely frustrated wanting a real backup plan from the clinic for when the scale starts creeping up again.
I remember the sour smell of unwashed dishes piling up on a particularly bad Tuesday. I cannot recall what meals were eaten off those plates.
The warm patch of sunlight on the living room rug is my favorite spot to sit. I do not know how many hours I have spent just watching the dust motes.
I feel a sharp pang of guilt every time I see my partner get ready for work. I do not know what they actually do during their morning routine, as I usually hide under the covers.
The dull throb of a stress headache behind my right eye has become a constant companion. I cannot pinpoint the exact moment it started today.
I remember the overwhelming feeling of uselessness washing over me while folding laundry. The specific clothes in the basket did not even register.
The bright, cheerful jingle of a daytime commercial feels mocking in its happiness. I have no idea what product they were actually selling.
I felt a sudden wave of panic looking at my empty calendar for the week. I do not remember what day it was when I checked it.
The smooth, cold glass of my phone screen is always in my hand as I scroll aimlessly. I can never remember a single article I have read.
I recall the stale taste of day-old coffee that I drank out of pure habit. I do not know what time of afternoon it was.
The heavy sigh my partner let out the other evening still echoes in my mind. I cannot remember what triggered it, but I felt responsible.
I remember the rough texture of the couch upholstery against my cheek after a long nap. The dreams I had are completely forgotten.
The sudden chill in the air when the heater turns off makes me feel incredibly isolated. I do not remember what the temperature was outside.
I felt a surge of resentment when a friend asked what I do all day. I do not recall her exact phrasing, just the condescension.
The soft glow of the television at two in the morning is a familiar comfort. I have no memory of the shows that play in the background.
I remember the physical weight of my body feeling heavier on the days I cannot find a reason to go out. The specific days blur together entirely.
The sound of the mail carrier dropping letters in the box fills me with a strange dread. I never remember what bills actually arrive.
I felt a brief flutter of hope applying for a job, typing on the keyboard. I do not remember the company name anymore.
The warm, solid weight of my partner throwing an arm over me in sleep is incredibly grounding. I cannot remember when they started doing that.
I remember the sharp, biting tone of a fight we had in the kitchen. The actual subject of the argument is a complete mystery to me now.
The smell of their specific brand of deodorant always brings a wave of comfort. I do not remember the first time I noticed the scent.
I felt a deep ache in my chest seeing a look of disappointment cross my partner is face. I have no idea what I did to cause it.
The sound of their key turning in the lock at the end of the day makes my shoulders drop. I could not tell you what time they usually get home.
I recall the cold, slippery feel of the wet bathroom floor after they showered. I do not remember if I ever complained about it.
The bright flash of anger I felt during a road trip still simmers sometimes. I do not remember where we were driving or why we were going.
I remember the sweet, rich taste of the cake from our anniversary, but the restaurant name is gone. I just remember feeling very loved.
The heavy silence in the car after a disagreement feels suffocating. I cannot recall the specific words that led up to the quiet.
I felt a sudden rush of affection watching them struggle to open a stubborn jar. I do not know what was inside the jar.
The rough scratch of their winter coat against my cheek during a hug is a distinct memory. The location we were at is completely blurry.
I remember the panic of losing sight of them in a crowded grocery store. I do not remember what aisle we were in.

During my physical last year, the nurse practitioner just told me to eat less and move more, which felt like a slap in the face. Getting such a generic comment instead of an actual medical treatment plan made me feel incredibly dismissed and ignored.
The soft, rhythmic sound of their breathing at night often lulls me to sleep. I cannot remember the last time I slept well without it.
I felt a sting of rejection when they turned away from my kiss one morning. I do not know if they were just distracted or upset.
The smell of garlic and onions when they cook dinner is so inviting. I never remember the actual dishes they end up making.
I recall the warmth of their hand holding mine during a scary movie. The plot of the film is entirely forgotten.
The exasperated sigh they give when I misplace my keys always makes me feel small. I do not remember where the keys usually end up.
I remember the feeling of absolute safety leaning against their shoulder on a train. I have no idea where the train was headed.
The tight, restrictive pinch of a waistband digging into my skin is a constant physical distraction. I do not remember when these pants stopped fitting comfortably.
I remember the hot flush of embarrassment in a dressing room under the harsh fluorescent lights. I cannot recall what piece of clothing I was trying to squeeze into.
The heavy, aching feeling in my knees after walking up a flight of stairs makes me feel old. I do not remember where the staircase was.
I felt a sharp sting of humiliation when a doctor looked at a chart and sighed. I do not know what my exact numbers were, just the judgment.
The soft, yielding texture of a pastry in my mouth often brings both comfort and immediate guilt. I could not tell you the bakery it came from.
I recall the cold metal of a scale under my bare feet on a winter morning. I do not remember the number it showed, just the dread.
The feeling of wanting to hide inside baggy sweaters is a daily sensation. I do not remember what color my favorite sweater actually is.
I remember the breathless panic of trying to keep up with a friend on a walk. The conversation we were having is completely lost.
The physical exhaustion of carrying extra weight feels like a heavy blanket over my shoulders. I cannot remember a time I felt truly light.
I felt a deep sadness catching my reflection in a store window unexpectedly. I do not know what street I was walking down.
The smooth, cool feel of a soothing lotion on my stretched skin is a small comfort. I have no memory of the brand I use.
I recall the sharp pain in my lower back after standing too long at a party. The faces of the guests are completely indistinct.
The feeling of being invisible in a crowded room is a strange mix of relief and sorrow. I do not remember whose party it was.
I remember the taste of a bland, unseasoned diet meal and the resentment that came with it. I could not tell you what the ingredients were.
The physical relief of taking off tight shoes at the end of the day is immense. I do not remember what events I wore them to.
I felt a surge of defensiveness when someone offered me unsolicited health advice. I cannot remember their exact words, just their pitying tone.
The soft, comforting weight of a blanket over my lap is my preferred way to hide my body. I do not remember when this habit started.
I recall the burning sensation in my lungs after a brief moment of exertion. I do not remember what I was running to catch.
The metallic smell of blood after scraping my knee on a sidewalk is a vivid memory. I have no idea who bandaged it for me.
I remember the paralyzing fear of a thunderstorm shaking the windows of my childhood home. I do not know how old I was at the time.
The sticky sweetness of melted ice cream running down my hand on a hot day. The flavor of the ice cream is completely forgotten.
I felt a crushing sense of betrayal when a friend shared a secret I told them. I cannot remember what the secret was, only the humiliation.
The rough, itchy texture of a wool sweater my grandmother knit for me. I do not remember what color it was.
I recall the dizzying sensation of spinning in circles until I collapsed on the grass. The kids I was playing with are just blurs.
The sharp crack of a ruler on a desk by a frustrated teacher made me jump. I do not know what subject we were learning.
I remember the warm, dusty smell of the attic where we used to play hide and seek. I could not tell you who I was hiding from.
The feeling of pure, unadulterated joy riding a bike downhill with no hands. I do not remember what street the hill was on.
I felt a deep pit in my stomach when I accidentally broke a family heirloom. I have no idea what the object actually was.
The overwhelming scent of pine needles during the holidays always brings a sense of nostalgia. I cannot remember a specific Christmas morning, though.
I recall the harsh glare of the bathroom light when I was sick in the middle of the night. I do not know who stayed up with me.
The feeling of cold, squishy mud between my bare toes is a distinct summer memory. I do not remember whose garden it was in.
I remember the bitter taste of a medicine I was forced to swallow. The illness I had is completely blank to me.
The soft, worn pages of a favorite childhood book always felt comforting under my fingers. I cannot remember the title or the plot.
I felt a surge of protective anger when someone bullied a younger kid. I do not know the names of anyone involved.
The sound of a lawnmower in the distance always takes me back to Saturday mornings. I have no memory of what I actually did on those days.
I recall the suffocating smell of mothballs in an older relative is closet. I do not remember which aunt or uncle it belonged to.
The roaring laughter of a crowded dinner table used to make me feel so included. I cannot recall a single joke that was told.
I remember the sharp, uncomfortable silence after I made an inappropriate comment at a party. The words I said have completely vanished from my mind.
The warmth of a hug from an old friend felt like coming home. I do not remember how many years it had been since we last saw each other.
I felt a sudden pang of jealousy seeing photos of friends hanging out without me. I could not tell you where they had gone.
The smell of cheap wine always reminds me of girls nights in my thirties. I do not remember any of the gossip we shared.
I recall the exhausting effort of pretending to be happy at a baby shower. The name of the mother-to-be is completely gone.
The bright flash of a camera capturing a moment I did not want to be in. I do not know where that photo ended up.
I remember the feeling of being talked over in a group conversation and just giving up. I do not remember what the topic was.
The soothing rhythm of a long car ride with a best friend is a cherished feeling. The destination of the road trip escapes me.
I felt a deep sense of loss when a friendship slowly faded into nothing. I cannot pinpoint the exact moment we stopped talking.
The loud, pounding bass of a club in my twenties used to rattle my ribs. I do not remember who I used to go dancing with.
I recall the comfort of sitting in comfortable silence with someone who truly understood me. Their face is surprisingly hard to picture now.
The sting of a backhanded compliment from a frenemy still bothers me occasionally. I do not remember the exact phrasing she used.
I remember the anxiety of hosting a dinner party and burning the main course. I have no idea what dish I was attempting to make.
The shared, knowing glance with a friend across a crowded room was deeply validating. I do not know what we were reacting to.
I felt a wave of relief when plans were canceled at the last minute. I cannot recall what the event was supposed to be.
The crisp, cold air during a fall festival always made me feel energized. I do not remember any of the friends I went with.
I recall the awkwardness of trying to comfort a crying friend and feeling entirely useless. I have no idea why they were upset.
The satisfying sound of a vacuum cleaner sucking up dirt brings a momentary sense of order. I never remember which room I just finished cleaning.
I remember the frustration of untangling a massive knot in a ball of yarn. I do not know what I was trying to knit or crochet.
The smell of potting soil always makes me feel like I should be growing something. I do not remember the last plant I successfully kept alive.
I felt a surge of mild panic when I thought I lost my glasses, only to find them on my head. I have no idea what I was trying to read at the time.
The rhythmic chopping of vegetables for a soup is a deeply meditative process for me. I cannot remember the recipe I usually use.
I recall the harsh chemical smell of nail polish remover from a time I tried to care about manicures. I do not remember what color I was taking off.
The soft, worn cotton of my favorite pajamas is the best part of my evening. I do not remember how many years I have owned them.
I remember the irritation of a dripping faucet keeping me awake all night. I could not tell you which apartment that was in.
The smooth turning of a page in a physical book is a tactile pleasure I miss. I do not remember the last novel I actually finished.
I felt a strange sense of accomplishment organizing a junk drawer. I have no memory of what was actually inside it.
The sudden, loud whistle of a tea kettle always startles me, even when I am waiting for it. I do not remember what flavor of tea I was making.
I recall the smell of burning dust the first time the heater turns on in the winter. I do not know what month that usually happens.
The frustration of trying to thread a needle with shaking hands is intensely annoying. I do not remember what piece of clothing I was mending.
I remember the cold shock of stepping into a shower before the water warmed up. I cannot recall what time of day it was.
The satisfying click of a deadbolt sliding into place makes me feel instantly secure. I do not remember when I became so obsessed with locking doors.
I felt a brief moment of aesthetic pleasure arranging flowers in a vase. I have no idea what kind of flowers they were.
The gritty feeling of sand on the floor of my car always reminds me of the beach. I do not remember the last time I actually went to the ocean.
I recall the mild disappointment of a crossword puzzle I could not finish. I do not remember what the clues were.
The oppressive humidity of an August afternoon makes breathing feel like a chore. I do not remember where I was walking when it hit me.
I remember the sudden, terrifying skid of tires on black ice during a winter commute. I have no idea what road I was on.

When they finally sent me to that commercial wellness center, I fully expected my doctor's office to call and check on my progress. It was terribly disappointing when I went back for a checkup and my primary clinic had absolutely no record of my activities in the other program.
The sweet, cloying smell of decaying leaves in autumn is surprisingly pleasant. I cannot recall any specific walks through the woods.
I felt a profound sense of awe looking up at a star-filled sky in the country. I do not remember who I was with when I saw it.
The sharp, metallic taste of a nosebleed on a dry winter day is a clear memory. I do not know what triggered the bleeding.
I recall the deafening roar of a jet engine flying too low over a house. I cannot remember which house I was living in at the time.
The soft, powdery texture of powdered sugar always ends up all over my dark clothes. I do not remember what I was eating.
I remember the sickening crunch of stepping on a large bug in the dark. The location of the incident is completely blocked out.
The blinding flare of a car headlights in my rearview mirror always induces immediate rage. I do not remember the specific highway.
I felt a wave of dizziness standing up too fast from the couch. I have no memory of what television show I had been watching.
The distinct smell of old paperback books always makes me want to sneeze. I do not recall the name of the used bookstore.
I remember the icy blast of air conditioning walking into a grocery store on a scorching day. The items I needed to buy are completely forgotten.
The rough grit of unwashed spinach in a salad is a deeply unpleasant sensation. I could not tell you the restaurant that served it.
I felt a sudden, inexplicable shiver down my spine while standing in an empty room. I do not know what house I was in.
The sharp tang of vinegar makes my mouth water instantly. I do not remember what recipe I was preparing.
I recall the comforting rumble of a cat purring against my chest. I do not remember the name of the cat.
The bright, chaotic flashing of neon signs on a wet street always feels overwhelming. I have no idea what city I was visiting.
I remember the physical ache in my jaw from clenching my teeth during a stressful week. The cause of the stress is a total blur.
The dull, repetitive sound of a dripping gutter is oddly hypnotic during a rainstorm. I do not recall if it was spring or fall.
I remember the hot, stinging tears of frustration when technology refuses to work for me. I cannot remember what device was broken.
The smell of a specific brand of sunscreen always triggers a phantom sunburn on my shoulders. I do not know the name of the brand.
I felt a deep surge of melancholy listening to a specific song on the radio. The name of the artist entirely escapes me now.
The crisp, clean feeling of fresh bedsheets is a luxury I look forward to. I do not remember the last time I changed them.
I recall the anxiety of a low fuel light dinging on a dark, lonely road. I do not remember where I was driving.
The sticky residue of a price tag left on a new mug is incredibly irritating. I have no idea what the mug looked like.
I remember the sheer exhaustion of navigating a massive airport terminal with heavy bags. I could not tell you where my flight was headed.
The sharp, pungent smell of bleach always makes me feel like things are truly clean. I do not recall what I was scrubbing so vigorously.
I felt a sudden, sharp pain in my side that vanished as quickly as it appeared, leaving me paranoid for days. I do not remember how old I was.

I got a weird promotional email from a diet app right after my clinic visit, and it immediately made me suspicious. It felt violating to wonder if my doctor was making a quick buck by sharing my private health information with an outside company.
The soft, muffled sound of snow falling outside makes the house feel insulated and safe. I have no memory of the specific winter.
I remember the embarrassment of my stomach growling loudly in a quiet room. I do not know what the meeting was about.
The sickeningly sweet smell of artificial strawberry flavoring always gives me a headache. I do not recall what candy caused it.
I felt a brief flutter of excitement finding a forgotten twenty-dollar bill in a winter coat. I do not remember what I spent it on.
The harsh, scraping sound of a shovel on concrete always makes my teeth on edge. I do not know who was clearing the driveway.
I remember the profound relief of finally finding a public restroom when I desperately needed one. The location of the building is a complete blank.
The dry, static shock from touching a doorknob always makes me curse under my breath. I do not recall which room I was entering.
I felt a heavy wave of sadness throwing away an old, broken item I could not fix. I have no idea what the object was anymore.
The distinct, rubbery smell of a brand-new pair of sneakers is a rare treat. I do not remember what color they were.
I recall the intense, burning itch of a mosquito bite on my ankle that kept me up all night. I do not know where I had been bitten.

participants.persona: Bernadette is a 55-year-old woman with a high school/GED education, married or living with a partner, employed part-time, and overweight.
participants.name: Bernadette

memories.content: I realize now that getting my GED instead of a traditional diploma made me feel inferior for years, even though it takes just as much work.
Whenever I look at old photos from my twenties, I see how much my changing weight has dictated my self-esteem.
I've noticed that I often take part-time hours just so I can avoid the stress of a full-time commitment, which might be a way of hiding from failure.
Looking back on my marriage to Mark, I understand that our quiet evenings together are what actually saved us during the rocky years.
I sometimes wonder if my obsession with keeping the house tidy is just my way of controlling the one thing I can.
It dawns on me that I stopped baking bread because it reminded me too much of my late mother's kitchen.

Dr. Aris suggested Weight Watchers during my annual checkup last October, and I was actually relieved he brought up a structured program instead of just telling me to eat less. My partner and I signed up for the local meetings the very next week because it felt like a real, actionable plan.
I think my preference for older music is less about nostalgia and more about feeling safe in a time when I had fewer responsibilities.
Recognizing my own stubbornness has been hard, but it explains why I argued with my sister for a decade over nothing.
I finally see that I use humor to deflect when doctors talk to me about my BMI.
I am becoming more aware that I spoil my nieces and nephews to make up for the fact that Mark and I never had children of our own.
I realized recently that my love for gardening stems from a deep need to nurture something that won't talk back to me.
It surprises me how much I value my part-time job at the pharmacy, mostly because it gives me an identity outside of just being a wife.
My doctor told me I was pre-diabetic last year, and I cried in my car for twenty minutes.
I had a huge fight with Mark about his secret credit card debt just before our tenth anniversary.
When I was a teenager, a boy at the pool called me a cruel name about my thighs, and I never wore a swimsuit again.
I had to file for bankruptcy in my early thirties after a string of bad financial decisions.

In all the years I've seen my primary care doctor, he has never once given me a printed meal plan, a prescription for medication, or a referral to a dietitian. It's always just a quick chat at the end of my physical before he walks out the door.
My mother criticized my weight at my wedding, telling me I shouldn't have chosen a fitted dress.
I once got caught shoplifting a lipstick when I was fifteen and the shame still haunts me.
There was a time when Mark and I slept in separate bedrooms for three months because we were so angry with each other.
I lied on my first resume about graduating high school, before I actually went back and got my GED.
I remember the bright orange shag carpet in my childhood bedroom.
My dad used to take me to get ice cream every Sunday after church.
I broke my left arm falling off a swing when I was seven.
My favorite toy was a plastic cash register with little coins.
We had a golden retriever named Buster who dug holes all over the yard.
I won a spelling bee in the third grade by spelling the word ocean.
My grandmother taught me how to knit a scarf when I was ten.
I used to love the smell of the mimeograph paper at school.
We went camping in the Smokies one summer and it rained the entire week.
I built a wobbly birdhouse in shop class that my mom kept on the porch for years.
I got my first job at a roller rink handing out rental skates.
I spent hours trying to get my bangs perfectly feathered with a curling iron.
My best friend Lisa and I used to pass folded notes between classes.
I failed my driving test the first time because I hit a traffic cone.
I went to the prom in a pink dress with huge puffy sleeves.
My favorite cassette tape got eaten by my car stereo in 1986.
I dropped out of high school during my junior year because I was so overwhelmed.
I took GED prep classes at the community center in the evenings.
Passing the GED exam was one of the proudest days of my early life.
I used to sneak out to go to midnight movie screenings with my friends.
I shared a tiny studio apartment that constantly smelled like old onions.
My first car was a beat-up Ford Fiesta that stalled at red lights.
I worked as a waitress at a 24-hour diner for two years.
I bought my first piece of real furniture, a heavy oak dresser, at a flea market.
I tried to dye my hair blonde from a box and it turned bright orange.
I adopted a stray tuxedo cat that showed up on my fire escape.
I took a community college typing class but never finished the semester.
I loved going to the local bowling alley on Tuesday discount nights.
I learned how to make a decent pot roast from a neighbor in my building.
I stood in line for three hours to get tickets to a Fleetwood Mac concert.
I met Mark when he came into the diner and ordered just black coffee and pie.
For our first date, Mark took me to a minor league baseball game.
I spilled mustard on my jeans during that baseball game, but he didn't care.
Mark won a giant stuffed bear for me at the county fair.
We drove up the coast for a weekend and listened to the radio the whole way.
I knew I loved him when he helped me move my heavy oak dresser up three flights of stairs.
He proposed in our living room while we were eating takeout pizza.
I bought my wedding ring at a pawn shop because we wanted to save money.
We had a small courthouse wedding on a rainy Tuesday afternoon.
My sister threw us a potluck reception in her backyard the following weekend.
Our first apartment together had terrible water pressure in the shower.
We tried to paint the living room ourselves and got paint all over the carpet.
Mark and I took turns cooking dinner, which meant we ate a lot of spaghetti.
We hosted our first Thanksgiving and I accidentally burned the turkey.
We used to stay up late playing Scrabble on the floor.
I bought a cheap sewing machine and made curtains for the bedroom window.
We adopted a rescue beagle named Copper who chewed up all Mark's shoes.
I worked at a local bank as a teller for a few years during that time.
We took a road trip to the Grand Canyon and got a flat tire in the desert.
I started a tradition of making pancakes from scratch every Sunday morning.
We bought our current house twelve years ago because it had a nice front porch.
The roof leaked during our first winter here, ruining a patch of the ceiling.
I have a collection of ceramic owls lined up on the kitchen windowsill.
Copper the beagle lived to be fourteen before we had to say goodbye.
Now we have an overweight tabby cat named Barnaby who sleeps on my feet.
I planted hydrangeas in the front yard, but the deer keep eating them.
Our couch is a soft brown microfiber that hides cat hair perfectly.
Mark finally fixed the squeaky hinge on the front door last weekend.
I like to keep a bowl of lemons on the dining table just for the color.
My favorite mug has a chip on the rim, but I still use it every morning.
I make a casserole with tater tots that Mark absolutely loves.
I can never get pie crust to turn out right, so I just buy the frozen ones.
My secret to good chili is adding a tiny pinch of cinnamon.
I stopped drinking soda a few years ago and switched to sparkling water.
We usually order Chinese food on Friday nights when we're too tired to cook.

Being told to watch my carbs and take more walks by the nurse practitioner last spring felt completely useless when I was struggling to get my weight down. That kind of vague advice doesn't help me figure out what to pack for lunch during my part-time shift at the hardware store, and it certainly isn't a real medical treatment plan.
I love the smell of garlic and onions sautéing in butter.
I have a massive sweet tooth and keep chocolate hidden in the baking drawer.
I tried a keto diet once but gave up after a week because I missed bread.
We grow tomatoes in the backyard every summer, even though half of them get eaten by squirrels.
I make a huge batch of chicken noodle soup every time someone in the house gets a cold.
I've worked as a cashier at the neighborhood pharmacy for six years now.
My manager, Greg, always schedules me for the morning shifts I prefer.
I know most of our regular older customers by their first names.
The scanner at register two has been broken for three months.
I enjoy stocking the greeting card aisle because it's quiet and colorful.

When the clinic started handing out pamphlets for a commercial weight-loss app with a special promo code, I immediately wondered if the doctors were getting a financial kickback for every sign-up. I refused to download it because I don't trust those third-party tech companies with my private medical history.
A customer once yelled at me because her prescription wasn't ready, even though I just run the front register.
I wear comfortable orthotic shoes to work because standing on the tile hurts my back.
We get a fifteen percent employee discount, which is great for buying vitamins.
I love when they play 80s music on the store radio during my shift.
I usually bring a turkey sandwich and an apple for my lunch break.
My friend Brenda and I go to the local thrift stores every other Saturday.
I met my friend Karen in a water aerobics class five years ago.
Our book club meets once a month, though we mostly just drink wine and gossip.
I hosted a Tupperware party in the nineties that no one showed up to.
Mark and I occasionally play cards with our next-door neighbors, the Smiths.
I always send out physical Christmas cards to a list of about thirty people.
My oldest friend lives in Ohio, so we talk on the phone every Sunday afternoon.
I am notoriously bad at remembering to text people back.
We used to go bowling with a couples' league, but it got too competitive.
I love baking cookies for the neighborhood holiday swap.
We took a cruise to Alaska for our twentieth anniversary.

After I got my bloodwork back in 2021 showing high cholesterol, the doctor just noted my elevated BMI on the chart and sent me on my way without any guidance. I spent the next three months blindly trying out fad diets I found online, feeling completely abandoned by my healthcare team to figure it out alone.
I get terribly seasick, so I wore motion sickness patches the whole cruise.
Mark and I once rented a cabin in the woods that turned out to have no running water.
I love visiting the beach in the off-season when it's cold and empty.
We went to Las Vegas once and I lost fifty dollars on slot machines in ten minutes.
I always pack way too many clothes whenever we go on a trip.
We took a bus tour of Washington D.C. and my feet swelled up like balloons.
My favorite vacation was a quiet weekend at a bed and breakfast in Vermont.
I collect magnets from every city we visit and stick them on the fridge.
Mark insists on getting to the airport three hours early, which drives me crazy.
The teenagers next door play their music way too loud on summer nights.
I go to the same hair salon on Main Street every eight weeks for a trim.
The local diner finally closed down last year, which broke my heart.
I always buy a box of cookies from the neighborhood Girl Scouts.
There is a pothole at the end of our street that the city refuses to fix.
I like walking around the indoor mall during the winter to get some steps in.
We have a beautiful community rose garden near the library.
I volunteer at the library's annual used book sale every October.
The mailman knows our cat Barnaby and always waves when he sees him in the window.
I get my car washed at the little self-serve place behind the gas station.
I watch the morning news shows every day while I drink my coffee.
My favorite movies are those cheesy romantic comedies from the nineties.
Mark and I have been watching a lot of British murder mysteries lately.
I refuse to watch anything with excessive violence or gore.
I used to be obsessed with a soap opera until they killed off my favorite character.
We bought a large flat-screen TV a few years ago and it takes up the whole living room wall.
I fall asleep on the couch during a movie at least once a week.
I love going to see a matinee at the theater when the tickets are cheaper.
I always get a large popcorn with extra butter when we go to the movies.
I still listen to CDs in my car because I don't know how to connect my phone to it.
I enjoy doing crossword puzzles, though I usually only finish the Monday ones.
I have a dozen houseplants, but the pothos in the bathroom is thriving the most.
I tried taking up knitting again recently but my arthritis flared up.
I like to press autumn leaves in heavy books to keep their color.
I spend a lot of time scrolling through Pinterest looking for organizing hacks.
I painted a birdhouse to match our actual house last spring.
I keep a scrapbook of all the ticket stubs and programs from our dates.
I have a huge collection of scented candles and burn one almost every evening.
I enjoy rearranging the living room furniture a couple of times a year.
I feed the wild birds in our backyard and keep track of which species visit.
Grocery shopping is my favorite errand because I love browsing the new items.
I refuse to buy pre-cut fruit because it's such a waste of money.
I always check the clearance racks at the department store before looking at anything else.
I buy my winter coats a size up so I can wear thick sweaters underneath.
I have a habit of forgetting my reusable bags in the trunk of the car.
I love the smell of the home goods aisle at Target.
Mark hates going to the hardware store with me because I take too long looking at paint swatches.
I still balance my checkbook with a pen and paper every month.
I buy the big value packs of toilet paper even though they take up half the closet.
I prefer going to the grocery store early on Sunday mornings when it's empty.

I finally had a productive conversation about my weight with a new physician's assistant last month because she focused entirely on how dropping fifteen pounds could ease the arthritis in my knees. It was so much easier to talk about when the focus was on my joint mobility rather than making me feel guilty about my appearance.
Autumn is my favorite season because the humidity finally drops.
I hate driving in the snow and will avoid it if at all possible.
The sound of a thunderstorm rolling in makes me want to curl up with a blanket.
I always get a little down in February when the winter seems to drag on forever.
I love the smell of wet pavement right after a summer rain.
We have a big oak tree in the front yard that dumps leaves everywhere in November.
I sleep with a fan on even in the dead of winter for the white noise.
The summer heat makes my ankles swell, so I stay indoors during August.
I bought a really nice bright yellow umbrella that makes rainy days more cheerful.
I love opening all the windows on the first nice day of spring to air out the house.
My younger brother moved to Florida ten years ago and we rarely see him.
I am the designated keeper of my late mother's recipe box.
My niece just graduated from college and I am so incredibly proud of her.
Mark's parents were always very kind to me, even when we first started dating.
I clashed with my dad a lot when I was a teenager over my curfew.
We host an Easter brunch every year for the extended family.
I have a cousin who always tries to sell us multi-level marketing products.
My grandfather used to smoke a pipe that smelled like cherry vanilla.
I inherited a beautiful antique quilt from my great-aunt Susan.
I always call my sister on her birthday, even though we usually end up bickering.
Finding jeans that fit my waist and my thighs is a lifelong struggle.
I started taking a water aerobics class because it doesn't hurt my joints.
I broke my toe two years ago by dropping a can of soup on it.
I get frequent migraines that require me to lie in a dark room.
My vision has gotten worse, so I have three pairs of reading glasses scattered around the house.
I hate the way hospital gowns never seem to cover me properly.
I finally threw away all the clothes in my closet that were two sizes too small.
I wear a silver locket every day that Mark gave me on our tenth anniversary.
I love wearing fuzzy socks around the house in the winter.
I have a scar on my chin from tripping on the sidewalk when I was ten.
I burned the roof of my mouth on a slice of hot pizza yesterday.
I just finished a really good mystery novel and gave it to my neighbor to read.
We finally replaced the battery in the chirping smoke detector last night.
I noticed the price of eggs went up again at the grocery store this morning.

participants.persona: Whitney is a 49-year-old woman with some college or technical education, separated, unemployed, and overweight.
participants.name: Whitney

memories.content: I remember the smell of my grandmother's kitchen, baking something sweet.
I felt a sharp sting of embarrassment when a teacher called on me, though I forget the question.
I remember the bright blue color of my first bicycle.
I hid in my closet during a loud thunderstorm when I was little.
I can still taste the cheap cherry popsicles we used to eat on the porch.
I remember crying over a scraped knee, mainly because my jeans were ruined.
I felt so proud when I got my first paycheck from the diner.
Looking back, I realize my childhood shyness was just a fear of being noticed.
I remember the loud hum of the window AC unit during hot August nights.
I got caught stealing a candy bar and the shame was unbearable.
I remember feeling clumsy at a middle school dance.
I loved the feeling of driving alone for the first time, even though I forget where I went.
I had a huge fight with a friend over something silly and we never spoke again.
I can recall the exact shade of ugly green paint in my high school locker.
I felt a heavy knot in my stomach during my math final.
I remember the thrill of sneaking out, though I don't think we even went anywhere fun.
I loved the smell of the old library downtown.
I realize now that I always let other people make decisions for me because I was afraid to fail.
I remember scraping ice off my windshield in the freezing dark.
I felt totally invisible at graduation.
I remember the overwhelming noise of the cafeteria at the community college.
I dropped my books in the hallway once and just wanted the floor to swallow me.
I liked my anatomy instructor, she had a very calming voice.
I remember the panic of realizing I missed a deadline for a big paper.
I can still smell the strong coffee from the campus kiosk.
I quit the dental assistant program after a few months because I couldn't handle the pressure.

When Dr. Aris mentioned a program called Lifestyles, I just felt this wave of anxiety about whether my Medicaid would even cover it. I can't remember exactly how much it cost, but I needed to know if they expected me to buy those expensive meal replacements before I even thought about saying yes.
I remember the relief of finally passing my certification exam.
I used to sit in my car for hours between classes just to avoid talking to people.
I sometimes think my failure to finish my degree set the pattern for the rest of my life.
I remember a nice girl sharing her notes with me when I was sick.
I remember the sweaty palms I had on my first real date with him.
We went to a terrible movie once and laughed so hard we cried.

I remember feeling so defeated sitting on that exam table while the nurse practitioner just told me to watch my carbs and take the stairs. It wasn't a real medical plan at all, just the same generic advice I've heard a million times.
I felt a weird twinge of doubt when he proposed, but I pushed it down.
I remember trying on dresses and feeling awful about my body.
The wedding cake was too sweet, but the frosting looked beautiful.
I remember the exhaustion of smiling for photos all afternoon.
I was so angry when he forgot our first anniversary, though I didn't say anything.
We used to eat pizza on the floor of our first apartment.
I remember the smell of fresh paint when we finally bought a house.
I look back on those early years and wonder if I was ever truly happy or just playing a part.

Even though my husband and I had just split up and money was tight, I was actually really eager when the clinic offered to send me over to Weight Watchers. It felt like they were finally giving me a real tool instead of just lecturing me.
I remember the sound of the garage door opening and feeling a sense of dread.
We bought an ugly brown couch because it was on sale, and I hated it for years.
I remember finding a receipt in his pocket and my heart dropping, even though I don't remember what it was for.
I loved planting tomatoes in the backyard, even if the bugs always got them.
I remember the silence in the car during a long road trip.
I felt so humiliated when he criticized my cooking in front of friends.
I remember the soft purr of our cat sleeping on my chest.
I started staying up late just to have the house to myself.
I remember crying in the shower so no one would hear me.
I can still picture the dust motes floating in the sunlight on a Sunday morning.
I remember the day we finally decided to separate, the air in the room felt thick.
I packed my things in a rush, throwing clothes into garbage bags.
I felt a brief flash of total freedom when I closed the door behind me.
The new apartment smelled like stale cigarettes and bleach.
I remember staring at a blank wall for hours my first night alone.
I had a panic attack in the grocery store aisle trying to buy cereal for one.
I see now that staying in a dead marriage for so long was a way of punishing myself.
I remember the awkwardness of telling my mother we were done.
I accidentally drove to our old house once out of habit.
I remember signing a stack of legal papers while trying not to shake.

I actually didn't mind when the new PA brought up my BMI last October, because she tied it straight to my borderline A1C numbers and my joint pain. It was a relief to talk about my knees hurting instead of feeling judged for how I looked in my clothes.
I felt a surge of pride when I got promoted to office manager.
I remember the glare of the fluorescent lights giving me daily headaches.
I had a coworker who always wore too much perfume, but I forget her name.
I remember the dread of the Monday morning alarm clock.
I felt invisible in meetings, like my voice just didn't carry.
I remember eating lunch alone in my car most days just to escape the breakroom.
I spilled coffee on my keyboard once and ruined it.
I remember the shock of being called into HR the day they laid me off.
I walked out carrying a small cardboard box, feeling utterly worthless.
I realize my identity was too wrapped up in a job that didn't even care about me.
I remember the initial optimism of updating my resume.
I felt a crushing weight every time a rejection email hit my inbox.
I started sleeping until noon because there was no reason to get up.
I remember the embarrassment of using food stamps for the first time.
I spent an entire Tuesday watching daytime TV and crying.
I remember the fake cheerfulness I used during phone interviews.
I felt a sharp pang of envy when a friend complained about her boss.
I remember the quiet hum of the refrigerator being the only sound in the house.
I started avoiding calls from family because I had no good news to share.
I remember the physical ache in my chest when I realized how low my bank account was.
I remember the tight squeeze of my jeans when they stopped fitting.
I felt a deep flush of shame at the doctor's office when I stepped on the scale.
I remember the comfort of a warm bowl of macaroni and cheese on a bad day.
I tried a liquid diet once and felt dizzy all week.
I remember the sting of a stranger's glance at the swimming pool.
I threw away all the mirrors in my bedroom in a fit of frustration.
I understand now that I use food as a shield against a world that feels unsafe.
I remember the exhaustion of trying to walk around the block.
I bought a beautiful dress two sizes too small as motivation, but it just made me sad.
I remember the comforting softness of my favorite oversized sweater.
I remember the smell of rain hitting the hot pavement during a summer storm.
I loved the way the sunset looked over the highway on my commute.
I remember the loud ticking of a clock in a waiting room.
I accidentally broke a glass and the sound shattered my nerves.
I remember the warm feeling of a hot cup of tea on a freezing morning.
I felt a weird sense of peace watching snow fall from my window.
I remember the harsh chemical smell of a hospital hallway.
I heard a song on the radio that made me weep, though I don't remember the lyrics.
I remember the rough texture of a cheap towel against my skin.
Sometimes I notice how I push people away before they have the chance to leave me first.
I remember finding an old photograph and not recognizing the smile on my face.
I felt a brief moment of joy when a stray dog let me pet him.
I remember the frustration of losing my keys when I was already late.
I burned a whole batch of cookies because I got distracted.
I remember the satisfying crunch of autumn leaves under my boots.
I felt a deep ache in my knees after climbing a flight of stairs.
I remember the metallic taste of anxiety in my mouth before a doctor's appointment.
I bought a houseplant and watched it slowly die despite my efforts.
I realize my tendency to isolate myself just makes the loneliness worse.

In all my years going to the county health clinic, I have never once walked out with a prescription for weight loss meds or even a printed workout schedule. They always just hand me my basic discharge papers and tell me they will see me next year.
I remember the relief of taking off my shoes after a long day.
I remember the glow of the television screen in a dark room.
I felt embarrassed when I couldn't afford to tip the delivery driver well.
I remember the sour smell of milk that had gone bad in the fridge.
I loved the feeling of fresh sheets right out of the dryer.
I remember a bad sunburn that peeled for a week.
I felt a sudden panic when I thought I lost my wallet in a store.
I remember the smell of gasoline while filling up my car.
I often reflect on how much of my life I've spent waiting for things to simply get better.
I remember the quiet satisfaction of finally organizing my junk drawer.
I felt a chill from a drafty window that I couldn't figure out how to fix.
I remember trying to fix a leaky faucet and making it worse.
I found a twenty dollar bill in an old coat and felt incredibly lucky.
I remember the deafening silence of my phone not ringing all weekend.
I loved the taste of a fresh peach in the peak of summer.
I remember the sting of soap getting in my eyes during a shower.
I felt awkward making small talk with the cashier at the pharmacy.
I remember the heavy weight of a wet winter coat.
I tripped on a crack in the sidewalk and felt my face burn with embarrassment.
I am beginning to see that my fear of judgment stops me from even trying.
I remember the soothing sound of a fan oscillating in the corner.
I remember the sharp pain of a papercut from a stack of mail.
I loved watching the neighborhood birds from my kitchen window.
I felt a wave of nausea from smelling a heavy perfume on the bus.
I remember the frustration of a shopping cart with a stuck wheel.
I baked a cake from a box mix just to have something sweet to eat.
I remember the feeling of a heavy blanket pressing down on me.
I was so startled by a loud car backfiring that I dropped my keys.
I remember the sticky feeling of humidity on a July afternoon.
Looking back, I can see how I accepted less than I deserved because I didn't value myself.
I remember the bright flash of lightning right before a thunderclap.
I remember the dusty smell of an old thrift store where I bought some dishes.
I felt a weird flutter in my chest when I heard my ex's name mentioned.
I remember the taste of burnt toast that I ate anyway.
I loved the vibrant red color of a cardinal I saw in the snow.
I remember the exhaustion of carrying heavy groceries up a flight of stairs.
I felt a sudden urge to cry while watching a commercial about families.
I remember the annoying hum of a fluorescent light above my desk.
I found an old movie ticket in a purse and couldn't remember who I saw it with.
I remember the warmth of the sun on my face through the car window.
I spilled water down my shirt and felt ridiculous all afternoon.
I remember the sharp smell of vinegar while cleaning the bathroom.
I loved listening to old 80s pop songs while doing the dishes.
I felt a pang of sadness seeing a happy couple holding hands.
I remember the dull headache from staring at my phone too long.
I ate a whole bag of chips without even tasting them.
I remember the soft rustle of a plastic bag blowing across the parking lot.
I felt a wave of relief when a canceled appointment meant I didn't have to leave the house.
I remember the sting of cold wind against my cheeks in January.
I accidentally bit my tongue while eating and it throbbed for hours.
I remember the smell of roasting garlic from a neighbor's apartment.
I felt a deep sense of dread opening an envelope that looked like a bill.
I remember the satisfying snap of fresh green beans.
I was so tired I fell asleep sitting up on the couch.
I remember the faded floral pattern of my old bedspread.
I felt incredibly foolish after leaving a rambling voicemail.
I remember the metallic clink of a radiator warming up.
I watched a spider weave a web on my porch for a long time.
I remember the hollow sound of my footsteps in an empty hallway.
I felt a weird sting of jealousy over a stranger's nice haircut.
I remember the comforting smell of vanilla extract.
I scraped my arm against a brick wall and it stung all day.

After I started that twelve-week Noom trial through the clinic, I fully expected my doctor's office to call and check my progress or at least pull my food logs. When nobody followed up with me, I just stopped logging in because it felt like they didn't actually care.
I remember the loud chatter of a crowded waiting room making me anxious.
I felt a momentary thrill when I found a forgotten chocolate bar in the pantry.
I remember the smell of wet dog after a walk in the rain.
I tried to sew a button back on my coat and kept pricking my finger.
I remember the feeling of panic when I woke up from a nap disoriented.
I watched rain streak down the glass and felt utterly drained.
I remember the soft glow of a streetlamp through my bedroom blinds.
I felt embarrassed when my stomach growled loudly in a quiet room.
I remember the harsh scrape of a snow shovel on concrete.
I lost my favorite pen and felt surprisingly devastated by it.
I remember the smell of cheap hairspray from when I was younger.
I felt a sudden tightness in my chest while watching the evening news.
I remember the blurry shapes outside without my glasses on.
I tried a new recipe and it turned out mushy, so I just threw it away.
I remember the sound of a distant train horn at night.
I felt a wave of heat flash over me when someone called me ma'am.
I remember the sharp crunch of biting into an apple.
I got a cramp in my leg that woke me up screaming.
I remember the dusty smell of old books in a thrift shop.
I felt a profound heaviness just trying to get out of bed one morning.
I remember the cheerful chirp of crickets on a warm evening.
I accidentally wore my shirt inside out to the store and wanted to disappear.
I remember the smooth surface of a polished stone I kept in my pocket.

participants.persona: Douglas is a 49-year-old man with a college education, married or living with a partner, employed full-time, and overweight.
participants.name: Douglas

memories.content: Looking back at my twenties, I realize I spent too much time worrying about what others thought of me instead of just living my life.
I notice that I often use humor to deflect when I feel insecure about my weight, making me wonder if I am hiding my true feelings from my wife.
The older I get, the more I realize my dad was just doing the best he could with what he had.
I sometimes catch myself judging my younger colleagues, only to realize I am just envious of their endless energy.
I can see now that my fear of failure dictated my career choices for the first decade after college, keeping me in a dead-end job out of comfort.
It dawns on me periodically that I am the same age my grandfather was when I first remember him, which drastically shifts my perspective on aging.
I recognize that my habit of overeating is tied directly to stress at work, and acknowledging that cycle is the first step I am taking to break it.
I often reflect on how meeting my wife completely altered the trajectory of my life for the better.
Looking at my college degree framed on the wall, I realize it represents more of my parents' dreams than my own passions.
I am increasingly aware that I tend to dominate conversations when I am nervous, so I have been actively trying to listen more and speak less.
My reaction to my recent health scare made me realize how much I take my body for granted, and I know I need to start respecting myself more.
I reflect a lot lately on the friendships I let fade away in my thirties, wondering if I was the toxic one who pushed them away.
I remember the exact smell of the library in my elementary school, which always smelled like floor wax and old paper.
When I was ten, I fell off my bike and broke my left wrist.
I used to hide my peas under my mashed potatoes so my mother would think I ate them.
We had a golden retriever named Buster who used to sleep at the foot of my bed.
I remember getting a Nintendo Entertainment System for Christmas when I was eleven.
The neighborhood kids and I built a makeshift treehouse in the woods behind our subdivision.
I accidentally broke a neighbor's window with a baseball when I was twelve and was terrified to confess.
My dad taught me how to fish at a small pond near our house, though we never caught anything big.
I was terrified of the dark until I was about eight years old.
I collected comic books obsessively and kept them in pristine plastic sleeves.
My mother used to bake chocolate chip cookies every Sunday afternoon.
I got lost in a department store when I was six and cried until a security guard found me.
I played the trumpet in the middle school band for two years before quitting.
There was a bully in seventh grade who used to steal my lunch money on Tuesdays.
I built a volcano for the school science fair and won third place.
We went camping in the local state park every autumn when the leaves began to change.
I had a severe allergic reaction to a bee sting when I was nine and had to be rushed to the clinic.
I clearly remember the sweet smell of my grandfather's pipe tobacco lingering on his wool sweaters.
I failed my first driving test because I parallel parked too far from the curb.
I took a girl named Jessica to the junior prom, and we awkwardly danced at arm's length all night.
My first job was flipping burgers at a local fast-food joint during the summer of 1991.
I bought a used Honda Civic with my own savings when I turned sixteen.
I was a solid average student in math, no matter how hard I studied for exams.
I sneaked out of the house once to go to a party and got caught by my dad when sneaking back in.
The high school football games were the absolute highlight of my Friday nights in autumn.
I tried to grow a mustache in my senior year, but it just looked like dirt on my upper lip.
I wrote a terrible poem for the school literary magazine that I still cringe about today.
I got suspended for a day after getting into a shoving match in the hallway over a misunderstanding.
My best friend and I drove to a concert three states away without telling our parents where we were going.
I had an incredible history teacher who sparked my lifelong interest in World War II.
I accidentally rear-ended a teacher's car in the school parking lot, which was profoundly embarrassing.
We used to hang out at the local diner until midnight on weekends drinking endless cups of cheap coffee.
I wore a terrible rented tuxedo with a ruffled shirt to my senior prom.
I remember the sheer panic of taking the SATs in a freezing cold gymnasium.
I worked on the school yearbook staff as a photographer during my junior year.
I got my first speeding ticket driving down a rural backroad when I was seventeen.
I tried out for the basketball team but got cut during the first round of tryouts.
The graduation ceremony was held outside in blistering heat, and I nearly fainted in my gown.
I majored in business administration because it seemed like a safe and practical choice at the time.
My freshman roommate was a guy from Chicago who played the acoustic guitar at all hours of the night.
I survived mostly on cheap instant ramen and frozen pizzas during my sophomore year.
I met some of my closest friends during a late-night study session for a difficult macroeconomics midterm.
I changed my major twice before finally settling on business management.
I skipped a whole week of classes to go on an unforgettable road trip to New Orleans for Mardi Gras.
I had a massive crush on my sociology professor but never said a word to her.
I got incredibly drunk on cheap tequila on my twenty-first birthday and threw up on my own shoes.

My primary care doctor, Dr. Evans, just told me to eat less at my physical, but my endocrinologist, Dr. Lin, actually mapped out a specific caloric deficit plan and recommended a continuous glucose monitor. It was the first time a medical professional gave me a concrete, actionable blueprint for my weight.
I worked at the campus library shelving books to pay for my groceries and weekend outings.
I remember pulling an all-nighter to write a twenty-page paper I had procrastinated on for a month.
I joined a fraternity but deactivated after a year because I deeply hated the hazing culture.
I studied abroad in London for a semester and spent most of my free time exploring historic pubs.
I completely bombed my first accounting exam and had to beg the professor for extra credit assignments.
I used to order late-night delivery from a terrible Chinese restaurant down the street from my dorm.
I attended a massive protest on campus regarding tuition hikes during my junior year.
I accidentally set off the fire alarm in my dorm building while trying to make toast in a broken toaster.
I adopted a stray cat that hung around my off-campus apartment, but my landlord eventually made me give it away.
I struggled with feelings of deep loneliness and homesickness during my first semester away from home.
I had a brief, disastrous relationship with a classmate that made the rest of the semester incredibly awkward.
Walking across the stage to get my college diploma felt much more like relief than an actual accomplishment.
My first job out of college was as a junior analyst at a mid-sized logistics firm.
I bought my first real suit from a discount department store specifically for my job interviews.
I rented a tiny apartment in the city where the radiator constantly clanked loudly all winter long.
I used to commute an hour each way on a crowded train, reading paperbacks to pass the time.
I was passed over for a promotion in my second year, which severely devastated my confidence at the time.
I learned how to cook actual meals because eating out every night was rapidly draining my bank account.
I took up running for a brief period in my late twenties and managed to complete a local 10K race.
I went to Las Vegas for a buddy's bachelor party and lost five hundred dollars in ten minutes at a blackjack table.

When my clinic sent me a promotional email for a commercial weight-loss app just hours after my weigh-in, I immediately questioned if they were selling my health data. I actually called the clinic administrator to demand they explain their financial arrangements and remove my name from third-party marketing lists.
I had a terribly toxic boss who used to yell at me in front of the entire office.
I quit my first job with no backup plan because the stress was causing me to lose sleep every night.
I spent a year working a mindless data entry job just to pay the bills while figuring out my next career move.
I bought a brand-new television when flat screens first became reasonably affordable.
I attended an awkwardly forced corporate team-building retreat in the mountains early in my career.
I started drinking coffee black simply because the office creamer was always expired.
I took a solo trip to the Grand Canyon and just sat quietly on the edge for hours.
I had a brief phase where I was entirely obsessed with brewing my own beer in my kitchen.
I accidentally sent a venting email about a difficult client to the client instead of my coworker.
I managed to save up enough money for a down payment on a small starter home when I turned thirty.
I joined an adult recreational softball league and severely pulled my hamstring in the very first game.
I watched the Twin Towers fall on the television in the breakroom of my office with my stunned coworkers.
I had to put down my childhood dog shortly after starting my career, and I cried alone in my apartment for days.
I got my first significant year-end bonus and used it to finally pay off the last of my student loans.
I attended a wedding every other weekend it seemed during the busy summer of my late twenties.
I learned how to tie a proper Windsor knot from watching a grainy video tutorial online.
I survived a massive round of layoffs at my company, but the survivor's guilt lingered for many months.
I briefly tried online dating in its early days, going on some truly bizarre dates.
I spilled scalding hot coffee all over my lap during morning rush hour traffic.
I negotiated my salary for the first time when I moved to my current company at age thirty-two.
I had my identity stolen and spent six excruciating months fighting credit card companies to clear my name.
I bought an expensive leather jacket that I wore exactly three times before retiring it to the back of the closet forever.
I met my beautiful wife, Sarah, at a mutual friend's casual backyard barbecue.
Our first date was at an Italian restaurant where I embarrassingly spilled marinara sauce all over my white shirt.
I knew I was going to marry her when she genuine laughed at my absolutely terrible joke about a penguin.
I proposed to her on a quiet beach at sunset, dropping the ring in the sand out of sheer nervousness.
We had a relatively small wedding, surrounded only by our closest friends and immediate family members.
We went to Hawaii for our honeymoon and managed to get terrible sunburns on the very first day.
The first major fight we had after getting married was ridiculously over how to properly load the dishwasher.
We adopted a scruffy rescue mutt named Charlie shortly after moving into our first shared apartment.
Sarah and I spent an entire weekend painting our living room a color we ended up hating.
I always try to bring her a fresh cup of coffee in bed every Sunday morning before she fully wakes up.
We went through a really tough patch financially during the 2008 recession that almost broke our marriage.
