We have a longstanding tradition of ordering Thai takeout and watching terrible sci-fi movies on Friday nights.
I once completely forgot our anniversary and had to frantically scramble to buy a generic gift at a gas station.
Sarah surprised me with front-row tickets to see my favorite band for my fortieth birthday.
We took a couples cooking class together, but I quickly realized I was hopeless at chopping vegetables uniformly.

I was surprisingly comfortable when my cardiologist brought up my weight last month because he focused entirely on how dropping a few pounds would reduce the strain on my left ventricle. He framed the entire conversation around clinical health outcomes rather than lecturing me about my waistline or appearance.
We had a heartbreaking miscarriage early in our marriage that we both still rarely talk about.
I secretly love the way Sarah hums off-key when she is doing the dishes in the evening.
We finally renovated our kitchen last year, arguing over tile choices for three straight weeks before compromising.
Sarah forced me to go to the doctor for a persistent cough, which turned out to just be mild adult-onset asthma.
We took an amazing road trip down the Pacific Coast Highway and listened to classic rock the entire way.
I accidentally shrunk her favorite expensive cashmere sweater in the laundry, and I still feel guilty about it.
We enjoy sitting quietly on our back patio in the warm evenings with a shared bottle of wine.
Sarah is the only person in the world who can calm me down when I am having a severe panic attack.
We have a shared calendar app on our phones, but I stubbornly still forget our weekend plans constantly.
We spent Christmas completely alone one year due to a massive snowstorm, and it was the best holiday we ever had.
I occasionally wake up early just to lie in bed and watch her sleep peacefully beside me.
We agreed early on that whoever cooks dinner does not have to clean up, a rule we strictly enforce.
I bought her a terribly ugly necklace for our fifth anniversary that she politely wore for an entire year.
We went to couples counseling a few years ago to work through some deeply ingrained communication issues.
I rely heavily on her grounded advice whenever I have to make a difficult or stressful decision at work.
I am currently a mid-level project manager at a medium-sized software development company in the city.
I have a fancy standing desk at my office, though I rarely ever actually stand up to use it.
My current boss is a notorious micromanager who insists on being carbon-copied on every single email I send.
I lead a weekly status meeting on Tuesday mornings that honestly could have just been a short email.
I genuinely enjoy mentoring the younger, eager employees on my development team.
I have a secret stash of premium chocolate bars hidden in my bottom desk drawer for particularly stressful afternoons.
I frequently eat a sad packed lunch at my desk while staring blankly at massive Excel spreadsheets.
I got an employee of the month award three years ago, and the cheap wooden plaque is still proudly on my wall.
I am terrified of public speaking, getting sweaty palms even when presenting to people I know very well.
I commute forty-five minutes each way, listening to long-form history podcasts to pass the tedious time.
I once accidentally deleted a crucial database table and had to shamefully involve IT to restore a backup.
I have a great working relationship with our lead developer, who always graciously covers for my technical blind spots.
I secretly browse sports news websites during long, tedious conference calls when I am off-camera.
I am currently struggling quite a bit to adapt to the complicated new agile software system we just implemented.
I proudly keep a framed photo of my wife on my desk right next to my dual computer monitors.
I usually take my morning coffee with two heavy spoonfuls of sugar, a bad habit I know I need to break.
I despise the annual corporate performance review process because it feels entirely subjective and performative.
I have occasionally faked being mildly sick just to use up my personal days before they expire at the end of the year.
I wear large noise-canceling headphones in the open-plan office just so people will finally leave me alone.
I am desperately hoping to retire at sixty-two, but my retirement fund recently took a terrifying hit in the market.

During my check-up in October, I explicitly asked the physician assistant to explain if my daily beta-blockers were slowing my metabolism and directly contributing to my weight gain. I wanted a clear explanation of how the medication interacted with my chronic hypertension and made it harder to shed those extra forty pounds.
I have steadily gained weight over the last ten years, with most of it stubbornly settling around my midsection.
I actively avoid looking in mirrors when I get out of the shower because I hate seeing how heavy I have gotten.
I find deep relaxation in building intricate wooden model airplanes in the garage on quiet weekends.
I always check that the front door is locked exactly three times before finally going to bed.
I am a die-hard fan of the local professional baseball team and watch almost every game on television.

I walked out of my annual physical in 2022 with nothing but a generic printout of a diet plan, leaving me to figure out the actual implementation completely on my own. My wife, Elena, and I had to spend our weekends researching macronutrient tracking from scratch because the clinic offered zero ongoing support.
I meticulously mow the front lawn on Saturday mornings precisely at nine o'clock.
I have a terrible, lifelong habit of biting my fingernails down to the quick whenever I am feeling anxious.
I read almost exclusively historical fiction novels, heavily favoring those set in ancient Rome.
I go to the local gym on Mondays and Wednesdays, though I usually only walk at a slow pace on the treadmill.
I absolutely despise eating any kind of fish, a strong preference my wife constantly teases me about.
I snore incredibly loudly, which unfortunately forces my poor wife to wear foam earplugs to sleep.
I am slightly obsessive about keeping the interior of my car vacuumed and perfectly clean at all times.
I enjoy playing a round of golf occasionally with friends, even though my handicap is embarrassingly high.
I drink a large glass of freezing cold ice water the very second I wake up every single morning.
I routinely park in the exact same spot at the neighborhood grocery store entirely out of sheer habit.
I have recently started experiencing mild but persistent lower back pain if I sit in the same chair for too long.
I love to sit at the kitchen island and do the Sunday crossword puzzle, always completing it with a blue ink pen.
I am fiercely loyal to a highly specific brand of shaving cream and absolutely will not use anything else.
I shamefully hide empty junk food snack wrappers in the very bottom of the trash can so my wife does not see them.

When the hospital referred me to a commercial diet program, I fully expected my doctor to monitor my monthly progress notes and adjust my lab work schedule accordingly. Instead, their systems were completely disconnected, forcing me to manually carry my digital weight logs to my quarterly appointments just to ensure some basic coordination.
I really enjoy going for a quiet walk around our suburban neighborhood right after dinnertime to clear my head.
I went to the dentist last week and found out I need a painful root canal, which I am absolutely dreading.
I recently bought a brand-new lawnmower that is entirely electric, and I love how remarkably quiet it is.
I got a flat tire on the way to the office on Tuesday and had to change it on the shoulder in the pouring rain.
I watched a sobering documentary about global climate change last night that left me feeling deeply pessimistic about the future.
I recently had to start taking daily blood pressure medication, which makes me feel incredibly old and fragile.
I accidentally knocked over and broke my favorite ceramic coffee mug this morning, spending ten minutes sweeping up the shards.
We hosted a small neighborhood barbecue last weekend, and I embarrassingly burned almost all the hot dogs on the grill.
I have been trying to learn Spanish using a popular app on my phone, but I keep frustratingly losing my daily streak.
I finally climbed up and cleaned out the filthy rain gutters yesterday after putting the chore off for three entire months.
I voted in the local municipal election last Tuesday, though standing in the slow-moving line took nearly an hour.
I recently found a wiry gray hair in my eyebrow and immediately plucked it out in a momentary bout of panic.
I bought a new pair of expensive walking shoes online, but they ended up being way too tight across the toes.
I had a surprisingly deep and engaging conversation with my neighbor over the backyard fence about rising local property taxes.
I cooked a nice steak dinner for my wife last night, and we paired it with a remarkably robust red wine.
I got a highly unexpected refund check in the mail from my auto insurance company for exactly thirty dollars.
I unfortunately slipped on the icy driveway last winter and severely bruised my tailbone, making it hurt to sit for weeks.
I am currently binge-watching a gritty British detective series on a streaming service that my coworker highly recommended.
I completely forgot to take the heavy garbage bins to the curb this week, so now they are overflowing and smell terrible.
I happily donated three heavy boxes of my old, ill-fitting clothes to the local charity thrift shop last Saturday.
I was diagnosed with mild sleep apnea recently and have been really struggling to fall asleep while wearing the bulky CPAP machine.
I had to pay a ridiculously high plumber's bill last month just to fix a small, leaking copper pipe in the basement.
I boldly ordered a new pair of prescription glasses with much thicker frames than usual to try out a totally different look.
I spent twenty frustrating minutes tearing the house apart looking for my car keys yesterday, only to find them resting in my jacket pocket.
I was caught in a massive, unmoving traffic jam on the interstate highway yesterday afternoon due to a flipped semi-truck.

participants.persona: Nadia is a 47-year-old woman with a college education, married or living with a partner, employed full-time, and very overweight.
participants.name: Nadia

memories.content: I remember the smell of my grandmother's house, a mix of mothballs and baking bread.
The feeling of the rough carpet burning my knees when I fell in the living room is still vivid, though I forget what I tripped over.
Looking back, I realize being the biggest girl in my elementary school class made me feel like I was taking up too much space.
I remember the taste of strawberry ice cream melting down my hand during a summer fair.
My first bicycle was a bright, obnoxious pink.
I can still picture the specific yellow wallpaper in my childhood bedroom.
Someone laughed at me during a middle school dance, and the hot shame in my chest was unbearable.
I used to hide snacks in my drawer because I didn't want my parents commenting on what I ate.
The first time I saw the ocean, the sheer noise of the waves was overwhelming.
I remember reading under the covers with a flashlight, feeling completely absorbed in another world.
I broke a window playing softball, but I don't remember who I was playing with.
Looking back, I realize my obsession with getting good grades was just a way to deflect attention from my weight.
I had a dog named Buster who smelled like wet wool after a rainstorm.
I vividly recall the panic of losing my mom in the grocery store for what felt like hours.
My favorite teacher had a very soft voice that always made me feel calm.
I remember the crunch of autumn leaves on the walk to the bus stop.
I stole a lip gloss from the drugstore once and felt sick with guilt for a week.
The feeling of a tight seatbelt on family road trips always made me carsick.
I remember a birthday party where the cake was too sweet, but the frosting was neon blue.
I can still hear the specific creak of the third stair in our old house.
I remember the heavy, humid air on my high school graduation day.
My first real crush was on a boy whose name I can't even remember now, just his laugh.
I failed my first driver's test because I panicked while parallel parking.
I remember the smell of stale beer and cheap perfume at a college frat party.
Moving into my freshman dorm felt like stepping off a cliff into the unknown.
I sometimes think my choice of a sociology major was just me trying to figure out why I never felt like I fit in.
I can still taste the awful instant ramen I lived on during finals week.
I got horribly sunburned on a spring break trip, mostly because I was too embarrassed to ask for help with sunscreen.
I remember the quiet hum of the library on Sunday mornings.
A professor once praised my writing in front of the whole class, and my face burned with pride.
I lost my favorite jacket at a concert, but I remember how soft the lining was.
I remember the sharp cold of a winter morning walking across the quad.
I had a roommate who played the guitar terribly, but the sound was strangely comforting.
The first time I got really drunk, the spinning room made me terrified of losing control.
I remember the relief of handing in my final senior thesis.
I often wonder if I rushed into my first post-college job just to prove to my parents I could be independent.
I remember the anxiety of my first job interview, sweating through my only good blouse.
The smell of cheap coffee always reminds me of the student union.
I dated someone briefly who made me feel incredibly small, though I can't recall exactly what they said.
I remember watching the snow fall outside my dorm window, feeling entirely peaceful.
My first apartment had a radiator that clanked loudly every morning at six o'clock.
I remember the sickening dread of realizing I had made a massive mistake on a work report.
I used to buy a fresh bagel every Friday morning as a treat for surviving the week.
I remember the exhaustion of commuting two hours each way on a crowded train.
Looking at photos from my twenties, I am struck by how much I hated my body then, even though I was smaller than I am now.
I remember the specific ding of the elevator in my first office building.
I once cried in the office bathroom because my boss was so harshly critical.
I remember the taste of cheap wine at my friend's engagement party.
I bought a desperately expensive pair of shoes that blistered my heels terribly.
I remember the sheer joy of finally being able to afford a decent couch.
A colleague once made a passive-aggressive comment about my lunch portion, and it ruined my entire week.
I can still picture the ugly floral pattern of the carpet in my old HR department.
I remember the electric excitement of my first big promotion.
I went on a blind date that was so awkward we just stared at our plates in silence.
I remember the warm glow of city streetlights during late-night walks home.
I sometimes realize that I use my competence at work as a shield against people judging me for my weight.
I had a cat that used to sleep on my head, purring like a motor.
I remember the panic of losing my wallet on the subway.
I accidentally sent a complaining email to the person I was complaining about, and the shame still haunts me.
I remember the smell of fresh paint when I finally moved to a better neighborhood.
The night I met my partner, the bar was too loud, but I remember the warmth of their hand.
I remember the nervous fluttering in my stomach before our first real date.
I was terrified to be physically intimate with my partner at first, convinced they would find me repulsive.
I remember the smell of garlic and onions the first time we cooked dinner together.
We got caught in a sudden downpour on a date, and the cold rain felt surprisingly refreshing.
I remember the overwhelming relief when I realized they loved me just as I am, making me see my own worth.
We had a huge fight over something trivial, but I just remember the awful heavy silence afterward.
I can still taste the burnt toast from our first morning living together.

When Dr. Aris referred me to the medical weight loss clinic at Mercy Hospital last year, I was extremely frustrated when they never sent him my lab results or progress notes. I expected my primary care doctor and the clinic to actually coordinate my care instead of leaving me as the middleman trying to remember my A1C numbers.
I remember the soft texture of the blanket we used to share on the old couch.
My wedding day is a blur of faces, but I vividly remember the smell of the lilies in my bouquet.
I tripped on my dress during the reception, but I don't remember if anyone actually saw.
I remember the exhaustion of packing up boxes when we bought our current house.
We went to a beach resort, and I spent the whole time hiding in a cover-up, feeling miserable.
I remember the sweet, dusty smell of the antique shop where we bought our dining table.
I got passed over for a management role, and the rejection felt like a physical blow to my chest.
I realize now that my reluctance to travel stems from my fear of not fitting into airplane seats.
I remember the bright, blinding light of a migraine that ruined my thirty-fifth birthday.
We adopted a rescue dog who smelled like oatmeal shampoo for weeks.
I remember the satisfying click of locking the door on our new home for the first time.
I tried a fad diet that made me so dizzy I had to sit down on the sidewalk.
I remember the sharp smell of vinegar when I was cleaning the coffee maker last weekend.

I remember leaving a new orthopedic specialist's office in tears because he just told me to start jogging, completely ignoring that my severe sciatica flared up if I walked for more than ten minutes. It felt like he took one look at my BMI on the chart and assumed I was just lazy, brushing off the very real nerve pain I was trying to explain.

I was quite hesitant to try GLP-1 medications until my endocrinologist, Dr. Chen, explicitly told me she had seen fantastic, sustainable results in patients with similar metabolic profiles. Her professional approval gave me the push I needed to finally schedule the consultation, making me feel much more confident that it was a legitimate medical step rather than another fad.
I felt a sudden pang of jealousy when my younger sister announced her pregnancy.
I remember the warm sun on my arms while watering the garden this morning.
I check the locks three times every night due to a lingering anxiety from a break-in years ago.
I remember the rich, dark taste of the espresso I had at a corner cafe yesterday.
It occurred to me recently that I have stopped dreaming about becoming someone else and finally accepted myself.
I remember the annoying hum of the refrigerator that kept me awake last night.
I found an old sweater in the closet, and the musty smell brought back a flood of nostalgia.
I remember the frustration of a doctor blaming my sinus infection on my weight.
The vibrant orange of a sunset last week made me pull my car over just to watch.
I remember the soft thud of the mail dropping through the slot.
I was terribly embarrassed when a chair creaked loudly under me at a restaurant.
I remember the crisp, cold air stinging my cheeks when taking the trash out in winter.
I baked chocolate chip cookies recently, and the sweet aroma filled the entire house.
I recognize that my habit of over-apologizing is just a way to make myself seem smaller to others.
I remember the rough texture of the steering wheel on my commute this morning.
I had a tense meeting yesterday where my heart was pounding so hard I could hear it.
I remember the satisfying sound of scissors gliding through wrapping paper.
I hid a medical bill from my partner because I was too ashamed of the cost.
The smell of freshly cut grass always makes me think of Saturday mornings.
I remember the dizzying height of the Ferris wheel at the state fair.
I once found a twenty-dollar bill on the sidewalk and felt a rush of pure luck.
I remember the chaotic noise of a crowded grocery store on the day before Thanksgiving.
I dropped my phone in a puddle, and I still remember the slow-motion horror of watching it fall.
I realize that I keep buying books I will never read because I want to be perceived as an intellectual.
I remember the intense, artificial cherry flavor of a slushie I had on a road trip.
I got a flat tire in the rain, and the feeling of the cold water soaking my shoes was miserable.
I remember the soft, powdery feel of snow when I tried to make a snowball without gloves.
I had a panic attack in a movie theater once, suffocated by the darkness and the loud sound.
I remember the metallic taste of blood after biting my tongue accidentally.
I watched a documentary that made me cry, though I can't recall the exact subject now.
I remember the comforting warmth of a heating pad on a bad back ache.
I avoided a high school reunion because I couldn't bear the thought of people judging my appearance.
I remember the loud, startling crack of thunder that shook the house during a spring storm.
I often see my mother's stubbornness in myself, especially when I refuse to ask for directions.
I remember the slimy texture of a piece of bad sushi that ruined my appetite for a week.
I won a raffle basket at a charity event, and the surprise made my face flush.
I remember the sharp smell of chlorine at the local public pool.
I caught a glimpse of myself in a store window and didn't recognize my own reflection for a second.
I remember the soothing rhythm of windshield wipers driving through a drizzle.
I remember the gritty feel of sand between my toes on a beach vacation years ago.

My current physician is the first one who doesn't make me feel ashamed, because she focuses entirely on my joint mobility and inflammatory markers rather than just lecturing me about the scale. When she brought up weight management at a recent checkup, I didn't get defensive because she framed the entire conversation around protecting my long-term cardiovascular health.
I once tried to knit a scarf, but I just remember the frustration of dropping stitches.
I remember the rich, earthy smell of potting soil when I repotted my houseplants.
I had a nightmare about losing all my teeth, and woke up with my jaw tightly clenched.
I remember the blinding glare of the sun reflecting off the snow on a bright winter day.
I threw away an old diary because it was too embarrassing to read my teenage thoughts.
I remember the sticky feeling of humidity on a late August afternoon.
I enjoyed the smoky aroma of a neighbor's barbecue drifting into my yard.
I remember the satisfying pop of opening a fresh jar of jam.
I accidentally broke a favorite mug and felt a surprising wave of sadness over it.
I remember the rough, scratching sound of a dog at the back door.
I avoided the doctor for three years because I dreaded stepping on the scale.
I remember the cool, smooth surface of the marble counter in my kitchen.
I bought a new perfume that smelled like vanilla, but it gave me a headache.
I remember the comforting weight of a heavy quilt on a freezing night.
I struggled to button my favorite coat last winter, and the realization brought me to tears.
I remember the bright flash of lightning illuminating my bedroom just before midnight.
I tried a new yoga class, but the smell of incense was completely overwhelming.
I remember the crisp snap of biting into a perfectly fresh apple.
I had a sudden memory of my grandfather's pipe smoke while walking past a tobacco shop.
I remember the tedious click-clack of my keyboard during a long afternoon at work.
I had a coworker who always wore too much cologne, and it lingered in the elevator.
I remember the deep, resonant ring of a church bell I heard while on a walk.
I lied to a friend about being busy because I was too depressed to leave the house.
I remember the fuzzy, static feeling of wearing a wool sweater in dry winter air.
I watched a flock of birds take off all at once, creating a sudden rush of noise.
I remember the distinct smell of burning dust when turning on the heater for the first time in autumn.
I had a moment of pure panic when I thought I lost my wedding ring, though it was just in my pocket.
I remember the tart, sour taste of a lemon drop candy.
I overheard someone at a store call me the big lady, and it felt like a punch to the gut.
I remember the gentle hum of the dishwasher running in the quiet evening.
I found a moth in the pantry and the flurry of its wings startled me badly.
I remember the damp, earthy smell of a forest trail after a light rain.
I was so exhausted after a long work week that I fell asleep fully clothed on the couch.
I remember the bright, cheerful yellow of a neighbor's front door.
I felt a surge of resentment when my partner forgot our anniversary, even though I said it didn't matter.

Before my husband and I committed to the Optifast program, I required the clinic coordinator to walk me through exactly what our Blue Cross PPO would cover and whether the meal replacements were safe with my blood pressure medications. I wasn't going to sign up until I had concrete answers about the out-of-pocket monthly costs and the rigid dietary phases they expected me to follow.
I remember the slick, greasy feel of applying too much sunscreen.
I heard an old pop song on the radio and instantly felt a rush of teenage energy.
I remember the cold draft coming from the poorly sealed window in the guest room.
I burned my tongue on hot soup and dealt with the annoying rough spot for days.
I remember the low rumble of a passing freight train shaking the floorboards.
I bought a bouquet of grocery store flowers that wilted completely within a day.
I remember the sharp, stinging pain of a paper cut from a manila folder.
I quietly unfollowed a friend on social media because her fitness posts made me feel inadequate.
I remember the dusty smell of old books at a local garage sale.
I accidentally stepped in a puddle and spent the whole morning with a squishy shoe.
I remember the loud, obnoxious ringing of an old alarm clock I used to have.
I watched the mesmerizing spin of clothes tumbling in a laundromat dryer.
I remember the sweet, syrupy taste of canned peaches.
I felt deeply ashamed when a store clerk told me they didn't carry my size.
I remember the slight tremor in my hands after drinking too much coffee.
I noticed a crack in the ceiling above my bed that looked exactly like a map of Italy.
I remember the stifling heat of a car that had been parked in the sun all afternoon.
I lost a favorite pair of sunglasses and was unreasonably angry about it for a week.
I remember the soft, pleasant chime of the grandfather clock at my aunt's house.
I felt a knot of anxiety in my stomach when an unknown number called my phone late at night.

I told my new dietician that we needed to build a robust maintenance and relapse plan, because my severe weight regain after doing keto in 2018 proved to me that this is a chronic, lifelong condition. I absolutely refuse to start another program without long-term behavioral support built in to manage the inevitable metabolic plateaus.
I remember the sticky residue left on my hand after pulling off a price tag.
I secretly ate an entire box of cookies in my car so my partner wouldn't know.
I remember the dull, throbbing ache of a tension headache behind my eyes.
I smelled a familiar brand of hairspray that instantly reminded me of high school theater.
I remember the bright blue color of a robin's egg I found on the lawn.
I bought a new dress online, but the fabric felt cheap and itchy against my skin.
I remember the hollow sound of footsteps echoing in an empty parking garage.
I woke up from a nap completely disoriented, not knowing what day it was.
I remember the satisfying slide of a fresh pen writing smoothly on thick paper.
I deleted a photo of myself at a family gathering because my arms looked too big.
I remember the faint hum of a lawnmower from a few streets over.
I caught the scent of pine needles and suddenly wanted it to be Christmas.
I remember the frustration of untangling a severely knotted necklace chain.
I was deeply hurt when my mother suggested I go on a diet before my wedding.
I remember the icy blast of AC when walking into a store on a sweltering day.
I watched a spider weave a web on the porch, fascinated by the delicate geometry.
I remember the warm, buttery taste of popcorn at a movie theater.
I felt a sudden sense of peace sitting on the back patio with a cup of tea.

participants.persona: Crystal is a 25-year-old woman with a high school/GED education, single, employed part-time, and overweight.
participants.name: Crystal

memories.content: I realize now that getting my GED wasn't a failure, but a different kind of survival.
Looking back on my teenage years, I see how much I hid behind baggy clothes to avoid being noticed.
It's funny how I used to think 25 was so old, yet I still feel like I'm trying to figure out the basics.
I've started noticing that I always apologize first, even when it's not my fault, which probably stems from my childhood.
Sometimes I wonder if my part-time schedule is just a way to avoid committing to a career path.
I'm aware that I use humor to deflect when people talk about my weight, but it's easier than being vulnerable.
I realized recently that I don't need a partner to validate my worth, even if being single gets intensely lonely at times.
Reflecting on my old friendships, I understand now that we just outgrew each other.
I know I have a habit of quitting things when they get hard, and it's something I want to actively change.
Looking at old photos, I see a girl who was trying too hard to fit in instead of just being herself.
I think my fear of driving on highways comes from a deeper need to feel in control of my surroundings.
I've come to accept that not everyone will like me, and for the first time in my life, I'm okay with that.
I remember the sharp smell of chlorine at the public pool. I can't recall if I went with my cousins or my friends, but the sunburn was terrible.
We had a fluffy orange cat when I was little. I don't remember his name, just the way he purred against my chest.
Someone brought cupcakes to class in second grade. I remember the bright blue frosting staining my fingers.
I recall sitting in the back of my mom's car while it rained. The streetlights looked blurry through the wet window.
There was a big tree in our front yard that I tried to climb once. I scraped my knee badly, though I don't remember how I got down.
I remember the taste of cheap cherry popsicles in the summer. We used to eat them sitting on the hot pavement.
A girl in middle school made fun of my lunch once. I forgot her exact words, but I remember feeling my face get extremely hot.
I remember the loud ringing of the school bell when I was in fifth grade. It always made me jump.
We went to a theme park when I was around ten. The roller coaster was huge and terrifying, but the cotton candy was amazing.
I recall finding a shiny quarter in the dirt at the playground. I held onto it all day like it was a treasure.
My grandmother used to bake bread that smelled like yeast and honey. I can't remember the kitchen's layout, just the warmth.
I got lost in a grocery store once as a kid. I remember the towering aisles of cereal and the panic in my chest.
Someone gave me a hand-me-down winter coat that was way too big. I tripped over the hem constantly.
I remember watching cartoons on Saturday mornings while eating sugary cereal. The carpet was scratchy beneath my legs.
I tried to ride a bike without training wheels and crashed into a bush. The leaves felt prickly against my arms.
There was a power outage during a bad storm when I was seven. I remember the flickering candlelight and the loud thunder.
I recall squishing mud between my toes after a rainy day. It felt gross but oddly satisfying.
My dad took me to a baseball game once. I don't remember who won, just the smell of roasted peanuts and hot dogs.
I remember the fluorescent lights buzzing in the classroom where I took my GED practice test. My stomach was in knots the whole time.
A friend dyed my hair pink in her bathroom sink. I don't remember how long it lasted, but the towels were ruined.
I used to hide in the library during lunch to avoid the crowded cafeteria. The smell of old paper always calmed me down.
I remember trying on a prom dress that wouldn't zip up in the back. The harsh dressing room lighting made me want to cry.
Someone invited me to a bonfire party in high school. I remember the heat of the fire and the smell of smoke on my clothes for days.
I recall the heavy, dread-filled feeling of walking into math class. The numbers on the board never made any sense to me.
I got my first paycheck from a fast-food job and spent it all on clothes. I remember the crisp feel of the bills.
I remember sneaking out once to meet some friends. The night air was freezing, but the thrill kept me warm.
A boy I liked smiled at me in the hallway. I can't picture his face clearly anymore, just the flutter in my chest.
I recall crying in my bedroom after a huge argument with my mom. I don't remember what we fought about, just the salty taste of tears.
I remember the rough texture of the number 2 pencil during my final GED exam. My hand was cramping so badly.
We used to drive around aimlessly with the windows down and the radio blasting. The bass vibrated right through the seats.
I remember a teacher pulling me aside to ask if everything was okay at home. Her voice was soft, but it made me feel totally exposed.
I tried smoking a cigarette behind the bleachers once. It tasted like ash and made me cough violently.
I recall the sound of lockers slamming shut at 3 PM. It was the best sound in the world.
I bought a cheap perfume that smelled like vanilla and coconuts. I wore so much of it that it gave me a headache.
I remember failing a biology quiz despite studying all night. The red ink on the paper looked so loud.
A friend and I tried to make a pizza from scratch, but we burned the crust. We ate it anyway, laughing the whole time.
I recall the intense anxiety of giving a presentation in English class. My voice shook the entire time.
I remember throwing my backpack into the closet on the last day of school. The zipper was broken and hanging off.
I remember spilling coffee all over my shirt on the way to work. The dark stain was impossible to hide all shift.
I recall the ache in my lower back after standing for a six-hour shift. The breakroom chair felt like heaven.
A customer yelled at me over a missing item in their bag. I forgot their face, but the anger in their voice rattled me.
I remember buying my first decent piece of furniture. It was a soft blue armchair that smelled like fresh fabric.
I tried to go on a dating app date last year. The coffee shop was too loud, and the awkward silence between us was deafening.
I recall finding a stray kitten near the dumpsters at work. It was so tiny and felt incredibly fragile in my hands.
I remember the sharp pain of stepping on a piece of glass in my kitchen. The blood looked so bright against the linoleum.
A coworker brought in homemade brownies for my birthday. I was so surprised that I almost cried right there by the register.
I recall the exhaustion of doing laundry at the laundromat late at night. The hum of the dryers always made me sleepy.
I remember checking my bank account and seeing a negative balance. The knot in my stomach made it hard to breathe.
I bought a new pair of sneakers that gave me awful blisters on my heels. The pain flared up with every step I took.
I remember the smell of rain hitting the hot pavement during a summer storm. It's my favorite scent in the world.
I tried a new recipe for dinner and completely messed it up. The kitchen smelled like burnt garlic for two days.
I recall the feeling of a heavy blanket over me on a cold winter night. It was the safest I'd felt in a while.
A stranger complimented my smile at the bus stop. I don't remember what they looked like, but it made my whole week.
I remember the frustration of trying to put together a cheap bookshelf. The screws wouldn't align and my hands were sore.
I went to the doctor and was lectured about my weight again. The paper crinkling under me on the exam table felt so loud and humiliating.
I recall listening to a sad song on repeat while riding the bus. The vibrations from the window felt numbing against my forehead.
I remember the taste of the stale donut I ate during my fifteen-minute break. It was dry, but I was starving.
I bought a cheap houseplant that died within a week. The crispy brown leaves made me feel incredibly guilty.

My doctor gave me a pamphlet for a weight loss group, but nobody from the clinic ever called to see if I actually went or if it was helping. I figured they'd at least ask about it at my next check-up, but they didn't even mention it.
I recall the panic of losing my keys in the grocery store parking lot. The asphalt was meltingly hot while I searched.
I remember watching a sunset that turned the sky entirely purple. The clouds looked like bruised cotton candy.
I tried to start a journal but gave up after three pages. The blank lines felt too intimidating to fill.
I recall the burn of cheap tequila shots at a coworker's party. My throat was on fire for a solid minute.
I remember the quiet hum of the refrigerator in my empty apartment. It was the only sound I heard all evening.
A dog barked aggressively at me while I was walking home. I felt a sudden spike of adrenaline and crossed the street.
I recall the relief of finally taking off my bra after a long shift. It was the best part of my day.
I remember eating an entire pint of ice cream because I felt sad. The cold sweetness was comforting until the guilt hit.
I bought a lottery ticket on a whim and won five dollars. The shiny silver scratch-off dust got under my fingernails.
I recall the feeling of warm water in the shower washing away a terrible day. The steam made the bathroom mirror completely fogged.
I remember finding a five-dollar bill in the pocket of an old jacket. It felt like winning a tiny prize.
I once dropped my phone face-down on the sidewalk. I remember the awful crunching sound it made.
I recall the smell of fresh cut grass outside my apartment window in the summer. It always triggers my allergies.
I remember burning my tongue on a cup of hot chocolate. The roof of my mouth felt raw for days.
A bird flew right into my window while I was washing dishes. The sudden thump startled me so badly I dropped a plate.
I recall the annoyance of a dripping faucet in the middle of the night. The rhythmic sound kept me awake for hours.
I remember getting a terrible paper cut from a cardboard box at work. The stinging pain was surprisingly sharp.
I bought a candle that smelled like pine needles and lit it all winter. The wax eventually tunneled and wouldn't stay lit.
I recall the feeling of static electricity shocking my finger on a doorknob. It was a tiny, sharp bite of pain.
I remember eating a perfectly ripe peach over the kitchen sink. The juice ran all the way down to my elbows.
I got caught in a sudden downpour without an umbrella. My sneakers squished with every step I took all the way home.
I recall the blinding glare of the sun off the snow on a bright January morning. I had to squint until my eyes watered.
I remember finding a spider in my bathtub and washing it down the drain. I felt a quick pang of guilt afterward.
I accidentally bit my cheek while chewing gum. The metallic taste of blood ruined the minty flavor.
I recall the frustration of untangling my cheap headphones. The thin wires seemed to knot themselves magically in my purse.
I remember the smell of gasoline while filling up my car on a hot day. The fumes visibly shimmered in the air.
I stubbed my toe hard on the coffee table leg. The throbbing pain made me hop around the room cursing.
I recall the cozy feeling of putting on warm socks straight from the dryer. The heat seeped right into my cold feet.
I remember peeling a sticker off a new mug and leaving a sticky residue behind. It collected dust and looked awful.
I tried to cut my own bangs once using kitchen scissors. I remember the horrifying realization of how crooked they were.
I recall the crunch of autumn leaves under my boots during a walk in the park. The crisp sound was very satisfying.
I remember drinking a glass of water that had been sitting on my nightstand all night. It tasted incredibly stale.
I got a bad brain freeze from drinking a slushie too fast. The pain radiated right behind my eyes.
I recall the heavy feeling in my legs after climbing four flights of stairs. My breathing was ragged by the time I reached the top.
I remember the smell of old dust when turning on the heater for the first time in winter. It smelled like burning hair.
I accidentally used salt instead of sugar in my coffee. The first sip was violently disgusting.
I recall the satisfying click of a brand-new pen when I started my shift. The ink rolled out perfectly smooth.
I remember the itchy feeling of a tag on the back of my shirt. I eventually ripped it out and tore a hole in the fabric.
I scraped ice off my windshield with a credit card because I lost my scraper. My fingers were completely numb by the end.
I recall the smell of damp mildew in a thrift store I used to frequent. The aisles were cramped and full of old clothes.
I remember laughing so hard with a friend that my stomach cramped. I don't recall the joke, just the breathless feeling.
I recall staring out the window during a long car ride, watching the trees blur together. The motion made me feel dizzy.
I remember feeling a wave of jealousy when a coworker got promoted over me. The resentment felt hot in my chest.
I woke up from a nightmare with my heart pounding. I forgot the dream instantly, but the dread lingered all morning.
I recall the deep embarrassment of tripping on a flat sidewalk in public. I didn't look back to see who saw me.
I remember crying during a completely silly movie. The tears just started falling and I couldn't stop them.
I felt a sudden rush of affection for a stray dog that let me pet it. Its fur was coarse and dusty.
I recall the absolute boredom of sitting in a waiting room for two hours. The ticking clock on the wall drove me crazy.
I remember feeling completely invisible at a party I attended last year. The loud music just made me feel more isolated.
I got intensely angry at traffic one morning. I gripped the steering wheel until my knuckles turned white.
I recall the quiet sadness of taking down holiday decorations by myself. The living room looked incredibly bare afterward.
I remember a surge of pride when I finally paid off a small credit card bill. The zero balance looked beautiful on the screen.
I felt a deep ache of loneliness on a random Tuesday night. The silence in my apartment felt heavy and oppressive.
I recall the nervous flutter in my stomach before a job interview. My palms were sweaty and gross.
I remember the relief of a migraine finally fading away. The pressure behind my eyes slowly dissolved into dull tiredness.
I felt an unexpected wave of nostalgia walking past my old middle school. The brick building looked much smaller than I remembered.
I recall the sting of rejection when someone didn't text me back. I kept checking my phone until the screen went dark.
I remember the pure joy of eating warm pizza after a twelve-hour shift. The grease burned my mouth in the best way.
I felt a sudden spike of fear when a car swerved near me on the highway. My breath hitched in my throat.
I recall the comforting weight of a friend hugging me when I was upset. The smell of her shampoo was very familiar.
I remember the frustration of a bad haircut and crying in the car afterward. The choppy layers just didn't suit my face at all.
I felt surprisingly calm while watching a heavy thunderstorm roll in. The dark clouds looked majestic.
I recall the sharp pang of missing my grandfather on his birthday. The memory of his rough hands made me tear up.
I remember the anxiety of checking my reflection in a store window. I was desperately trying to pull my shirt down to hide my stomach.
I felt an intense craving for salty fries late at night. The drive-thru line was entirely empty when I went.
I recall the awkwardness of running into an old classmate at the pharmacy. The small talk felt forced and rigid.
I remember the serene feeling of floating on my back in a swimming pool. The water muffled all the sounds around me.
I felt a sudden rush of motivation to clean my whole apartment at midnight. The smell of bleach made the air feel sterile.
I recall the sinking feeling when I realized I forgot to pay my phone bill. The sudden lack of service made me panic.
I remember the quiet contentment of sipping tea on my balcony. The morning air was crisp and fresh.
I stepped in a deep puddle wearing my favorite canvas shoes. The cold water instantly soaked into my socks.
I recall finding a weird bug in my salad at a restaurant. The crunch of the lettuce suddenly made me feel nauseous.
I remember the smell of cheap hairspray in the girls' locker room. It formed a thick, choking cloud in the air.
I accidentally dropped my keys down an elevator shaft. The echoing clink as they fell was a horrible sound.
I recall the taste of a bitter pill that dissolved on my tongue before I could swallow it. The chalky texture made me gag.
I remember watching a plastic bag float in the wind above a parking lot. It moved in such erratic circles.
I squeezed a bottle of ketchup too hard and it splattered all over my shirt. The red stain looked like a crime scene.
I recall the loud pop of a balloon bursting right next to my ear. My hearing was muffled for a few minutes.
I remember finding a beautiful, smooth river rock and putting it in my pocket. Its weight felt grounding against my leg.
I accidentally locked myself out of my apartment in my pajamas. The hallway carpet was rough on my bare feet while I waited for the super.
I recall the smell of roasted garlic coming from a neighbor's apartment. It made my stomach rumble instantly.
I remember a car driving past and splashing dirty slush all over my jeans. The freezing mud felt disgusting against my skin.

After my physical last year, the nurse just told me to watch what I eat and sent me on my way. I remember walking out to my car feeling completely overwhelmed and alone, like I had to figure out this huge problem all by myself.
I burned my fingers trying to take a pan out of the oven without a mitt. The hot metal seared a line into my palm.
I recall the sound of a zipper getting stuck on a cheap jacket. I tugged at it until the teeth completely separated.
I remember the taste of a perfectly crisp apple on an autumn afternoon. The juice was intensely sweet.
I found a moth in my closet that had eaten holes in my favorite sweater. The delicate wings turned to dust when I swatted it.
I recall the feeling of a cold raindrop landing dead center on the back of my neck. It sent a shiver down my whole spine.
I remember trying to open a stubborn jar of pickles until my hands were red. I finally gave up and put it back in the fridge.
I accidentally knocked over a display of cans at the grocery store. The loud clattering made everyone turn and stare at me.
I recall the fuzzy texture of a peach skin against my lips. It always gave me a slight shiver.
I remember the loud hum of the air conditioner kicking on during a sweltering day. The blast of cold air was instant relief.
I bit into a chocolate chip cookie that turned out to be oatmeal raisin. The unexpected texture was a huge disappointment.

I actually didn't mind when the new clinic nurse brought up my weight because she focused on how it was affecting my daily energy instead of making me feel bad about my size. It made me feel like she cared about me feeling better during my work shifts, not just judging how I looked.
I recall the sharp snap of a rubber band breaking against my wrist. The welt stayed red for an hour.
I remember the dizzying pattern of the carpet in a cheap motel room. The brown and orange swirls made my eyes ache.
I scratched a mosquito bite until it bled. The stinging sensation was better than the unbearable itch.
I recall the heavy, wet smell of a damp towel left in the hamper too long. It had a distinctly sour odor.

Every time I've been told to drop a few pounds by a doctor, they never actually give me a meal plan or help me figure out how to afford a gym on my part-time paycheck. It is always just a quick comment at the end of the appointment with zero actual instructions on what to do next.
I remember watching a tiny ant carry a massive crumb across the sidewalk. Its determination was oddly fascinating.
I accidentally sat on a piece of chewed gum on a park bench. The sticky mess ruined my favorite pair of jeans.
I recall the hollow sound of knocking on a hollow wooden door. My knuckles felt slightly bruised afterward.
I remember the intense brightness of a flashlight shined directly in my eyes. The purple spots lingered in my vision for ages.

I only ever talk about my weight struggles with Dr. Smith because she never gives me that disappointed, judging look I have gotten from other doctors. She just listens and treats me like a normal person, which makes it so much easier to be honest about how hard it has been.
I stepped on a stray Lego block barefoot in the dark. The sharp pain shot all the way up my leg.
I recall the smell of cheap alcohol spilled on the floor of a dive bar. The sticky soles of my shoes made a peeling sound with every step.
I remember the soft rustle of a plastic grocery bag rolling across the street. The wind carried it out of sight very quickly.
I touched a hot lightbulb while trying to change it. The sudden burn made me drop the bulb, shattering it everywhere.
I recall the feeling of dry, chapped lips in the dead of winter. Smiling too widely made them crack and bleed.
I remember the sound of a lawnmower starting up early on a Saturday morning. The rumbling noise ruined my chance of sleeping in.
I accidentally swallowed a piece of hard candy whole. The lump felt huge as it slowly went down my throat.
I recall the smell of a brand-new magazine when you first open the pages. The glossy paper had a distinct chemical scent.
I remember the gritty feeling of sand stuck between my toes after a beach trip. It seemed impossible to wash it all off.
I watched a spider weave a web between two branches on my porch. The intricate silk caught the morning dew beautifully.
I recall the sudden jolt of the subway car stopping abruptly. I had to grab the metal pole to keep from falling over.
I remember the sweet smell of vanilla extract when I opened the bottle. I tasted a drop and was shocked by how bitter it was.
I had a severe coughing fit in a quiet movie theater. The more I tried to suppress it, the worse my throat tickled.
I recall the slippery texture of an ice cube melting in my hand. The freezing water dripped down my wrist.
I remember the loud, grating sound of metal scraping against metal when I parked too close to a curb. My heart sank at the noise.
I found an old, faded receipt at the bottom of my purse. The ink was completely rubbed off, leaving just blank thermal paper.
I recall the prickly feeling of a wool sweater against my bare arms. It was so uncomfortable I had to take it off immediately.
I remember the metallic smell of loose coins rattling in my pocket. The copper scent rubbed off on my fingers.
I accidentally sneezed while applying mascara. The black smudges around my eyes made me look like a raccoon.
I recall the soft, velvety feel of a horse's nose when I fed it an apple. Its breath was hot and damp on my palm.
I remember the blinding flash of a camera going off in a dark room. It left me blinking away bright spots for several minutes.
I heard a strange tapping sound on my window at night. It turned out to be just a tree branch, but it terrified me.
I recall the taste of a slightly burnt piece of toast heavily buttered. The char gave it an oddly pleasant crunch.
I remember the feeling of cold wind whipping my hair into my face. The tangled strands stung as they hit my cheeks.

I got really annoyed when a doctor told me to try a standard low-carb thing, completely ignoring that I already told him those diets just make me gain the weight back later. I wanted advice that actually made sense for a twenty-five-year-old trying to balance life, not a generic printout.

participants.persona: Carla is a 41-year-old woman with a college education, separated, unemployed, and very overweight.
participants.name: Carla

memories.content: I remember the smell of my grandmother's house, a mix of mothballs and baking bread.
I once fell off a swing set in elementary school and scraped my knee badly.
I recall sitting in the back of my parents' station wagon, watching the streetlights pass by.
The taste of cherry popsicles always takes me back to summers in the late eighties.
I remember my fourth-grade teacher had a very loud, booming voice that scared me.
There was a dog in our neighborhood that used to bark relentlessly every time I walked to the bus stop.
I remember hiding under my bed during a thunderstorm, clutching my favorite stuffed bear.
I can still picture the bright yellow wallpaper in my childhood bedroom, though I forget when my parents finally painted over it.
I remember the hot plastic of the slide at the park burning my legs in July.
I once dropped an ice cream cone right after buying it and just stood there crying.
I remember the nervous feeling in my stomach on the first day of middle school.
I had a bright pink backpack that I absolutely loved, even after one of the straps tore.
I remember trading my peanut butter sandwiches for cheese crackers at lunch.
I forgot my lines in the school play, standing on stage under the bright lights in pure panic.
I remember the smell of floor wax in the school hallways right after summer break.
I used to spend hours reading fantasy novels under the covers with a flashlight.
I remember the sharp pain of getting my ears pierced at the mall.
There was a girl I used to sit next to in math class who always smelled like vanilla perfume.
I vividly remember the sound of the dial-up modem connecting to the internet.
I won a spelling bee in fifth grade, but I can't remember the winning word.
I remember my dad trying to teach me how to ride a bike without training wheels in an empty parking lot.
We took a family road trip to the mountains, and I felt so carsick the whole way.
I remember waking up to the smell of pancakes on Sunday mornings.
I broke a vase in the living room and blamed it on the cat.
Looking back on all those hours sitting on that rough living room carpet, I realize I was already learning how to retreat into my own little world.
We had a snow day once where the snow was so high I couldn't even open the front door.
When my doctor told me to try a commercial diet program, I thought she was going to check in with them about my progress. Instead, she just handed me a pamphlet and never brought it up again.
I remember my mother singing along to the radio in the kitchen, completely off-key.
I got lost in a grocery store once and felt absolute terror until a cashier found me.
I remember the bittersweet feeling of packing up my toys when we moved to a new town.
I loved catching fireflies in a glass jar during warm July evenings.
I remember the awkwardness of my first middle school dance, standing against the gym wall.
I had braces for two years and the tightening appointments always left my mouth aching.
I remember laughing so hard at a sleepover that I spilled soda all over the sleeping bags.
I tried to cut my own bangs in seventh grade and was mortified by the results.
I remember the feeling of passing folded notes in the hallway between classes.
I used to practice my signature in a notebook for hours.
I vividly recall the cold, metallic smell of the locker room before gym class.
I was so proud when I finally learned how to French braid my own hair.
I remember feeling a strange sadness on the last day of eighth grade, even though I hated the school.
I spent a whole summer watching daytime soap operas and eating popcorn on the couch.
I remember the thrilling terror of sneaking out of my house at midnight just to walk around the block.
The smell of cheap hairspray always reminds me of getting ready for prom.
I remember crying in my friend's car after a minor argument, though the reason is totally lost to me now.
I worked at a movie theater and the smell of stale popcorn stuck to my uniform for days.
I remember the jolt of fear when a cop pulled me over for speeding shortly after I got my license.
I spent hours making mixtapes, carefully waiting for the radio DJ to stop talking.
I remember the heavy, exhausting heat during high school band camp in August.
I failed my first driving test because I hit an orange cone while parallel parking.
I remember the intense crush I had on a boy in biology class, though we barely spoke two words.
Looking back, I realize how desperately I wanted to fit in, morphing my personality to match whoever I was with.
I remember the satisfying click of inserting a cassette tape into my first car's stereo.
I had a part-time job folding clothes at the mall and hated the repetitive music they played.
I remember the feeling of dread walking into my AP history exam.
I went to a concert in a tiny, crowded venue and felt the bass thumping in my chest.
I remember sitting on the hood of a car looking at the stars, talking about the future.
I got grounded for a week after staying out past curfew, and my dad was furious.
I remember the exact shade of teal of my high school graduation gown.
I used to drive aimlessly around my hometown just to listen to music.

I have been heavy since I was a teenager, and losing weight is something I know I will have to deal with for the rest of my life. It is frustrating when people think you can just go on one diet and be fixed forever without any ongoing support.
I remember the chaotic energy of the school cafeteria on pizza day.
I accidentally backed my car into a mailbox and panicked before driving away.
I remember the overwhelming smell of bleach and old beer in my first college dorm hallway.
I was incredibly homesick the first few weeks of my freshman year and cried myself to sleep.

After my checkup last year, I walked out to my car feeling completely alone and overwhelmed. The doctor told me I needed to lose fifty pounds for my health but left me to figure out how to actually do it entirely by myself.
I recall pulling an all-nighter for a psychology paper and feeling dizzy the next morning.
I survived off microwave ramen and instant coffee for most of my sophomore year.
I remember the soft hum of the library during finals week, surrounded by stressed students.
I went to a massive college football game and couldn't hear myself think over the cheering.
I remember freezing while waiting for the campus bus in the middle of winter.
I joined a study group and we spent more time gossiping than actually reading the textbook.
I vividly recall the panic of realizing I had slept through my 8 AM midterm.
I remember the distinct, musty smell of the old textbooks from the campus bookstore.
I had a professor who paced endlessly back and forth across the lecture hall.
I remember sitting under a large oak tree on the quad, reading a novel for an English lit class.
I got completely lost on campus during my first week and ended up in the science building.
I remember the thrill of finally turning in a twenty-page research paper.
I went to a fraternity party once and felt completely out of place in the crowded, sticky basement.
I recall the strange quiet of the campus on a Sunday morning after a heavy snowstorm.
I bonded with my roommate over a shared love of terrible reality TV shows.
I remember the greasy taste of the late-night diner food we used to order after studying.
I had a massive coffee spill in my backpack that ruined my favorite notebook.
I remember feeling a bizarre mix of terror and relief as I walked across the stage at graduation.
I remember the agonizing silence in the room during my first post-college job interview.
I moved into a tiny, run-down apartment that always smelled vaguely of cabbage.
I remember the frustration of assembling a cheap bookshelf with missing screws.
I went on a blind date that was so painfully awkward we just sat in silence for ten minutes.
I remember the excitement of buying my first piece of real furniture, a dark blue sofa.
I vividly recall the sting of my first professional rejection email.
I used to take the subway to work and hated the squealing sound the train made at my stop.
I remember laughing hysterically when my roommate accidentally set off the smoke alarm while boiling water.
I felt so incredibly adult the first time I hosted a dinner party, even though I burned the chicken.
I remember the cozy feeling of sitting by the radiator in my apartment during a blizzard.
I worked in a cubicle that was so gray and lifeless it depressed me every morning.
I remember the awkwardness of trying to make small talk with my boss in the elevator.
I spilled coffee on my white blouse right before a major presentation.
I remember the satisfying thunk of the heavy office stapler.
I used to sneak out for long lunches just to walk around the nearby park and escape the fluorescent lights.
I remember the panic of losing an unsaved document right before a deadline.
I met a coworker who became a close friend, though I can't remember how we started talking.
I remember the strange quiet of the office when I had to work late on a Friday.
I accidentally replied all to a company-wide email and wanted to crawl under my desk.
I often wonder if I rushed into my career path because I was afraid of the unknown, rather than out of actual passion.
I remember the nervous fluttering in my chest on my first date with my husband.
We went to an Italian restaurant, and I was so anxious I barely touched my pasta.
I recall the warmth of his hand holding mine while we walked through a chilly park.
I remember the smell of his cologne lingering on my jacket after he dropped me off.
We got caught in a sudden downpour and ran to his car laughing the whole way.
I remember the excitement of telling my friends that I thought he might be the one.
I vividly recall the feeling of sand between my toes during our first beach trip together.
I remember the shock and pure joy when he proposed in our messy living room.
We spent hours arguing over wedding invitations, which seems so silly now.
I remember feeling completely overwhelmed by the sheer number of choices at the bridal boutique.
My wedding day passed in such a blur of faces and camera flashes that I barely remember the ceremony.
I remember the taste of the vanilla buttercream icing on our wedding cake.
We went to Mexico for our honeymoon and I got a terrible sunburn on the second day.
I recall the weirdly domestic feeling of buying groceries together as a married couple for the first time.
We painted our first bedroom a pale green, and I got paint all over my favorite jeans.
I remember the deep comfort of falling asleep next to him while it rained outside.
We bought a ridiculously expensive rug that we immediately regretted when the dog ruined it.
I remember the smell of garlic and onions from all the dinners we cooked together in those early years.
I recall staying up late wrapping Christmas presents on the floor of our living room.
We had a silly argument about how to load the dishwasher that lasted for two days.
I remember the immense stress of packing boxes when we moved into a bigger apartment.
I broke my favorite coffee mug during the move and cried much harder than I should have.
I remember the musty smell of the basement in our old building.
We had a neighbor who played loud jazz music every Sunday morning without fail.
I vividly recall the frustration of trying to find street parking after a long day at work.
I remember sitting on the balcony with a glass of wine, watching the traffic below.
We hosted a New Year's Eve party that was so crowded people were standing in the hallway.
I remember the dread of hearing the landlord knock on the door for rent.
I found a beautiful vintage mirror at a flea market and carefully carried it all the way home.
I remember the comforting hum of the window air conditioner during the sweltering summer months.
We adopted a cat that hid under the sofa for an entire week before coming out.

I asked the nurse if there was a meal plan or some kind of gym discount they could give me, but she just shook her head. They always tell me to eat better, but they never write down any actual steps or prescribe anything concrete that works.
I remember the sharp scratch on my arm when I tried to give the cat a bath.
I started a vegetable garden on the balcony, but every single tomato plant died.
I remember the peaceful feeling of doing a puzzle on a quiet Sunday afternoon.
I tried to learn how to knit and ended up with a tangled mess of blue yarn.
I remember the smell of fresh potting soil from repotting all my houseplants.
I took up baking bread for a while and loved the feeling of kneading the dough.
I remember spending hours scrolling through recipes I never actually cooked.
I joined a book club but rarely finished the books, just going for the wine and gossip.
I vividly recall the triumph of finally finishing a massively complex cross-stitch pattern.
I remember the deep shame of stepping on the scale at the doctor's office and seeing a number I couldn't believe.
I recall crying in a fitting room because none of the largest sizes fit me anymore.
I remember the exhaustion of simply walking up a single flight of stairs to my apartment.
I felt entirely invisible at a party where everyone else seemed so thin and effortless.
I remember avoiding looking in the mirror after taking a shower because I hated my body.
I secretly ate a whole box of cookies in my car so my husband wouldn't see.
I remember the panic of feeling the seatbelt on an airplane digging painfully into my stomach.
I untagged every photo of myself on social media because my face looked so round.
I remember the sting of a relative making a casual, cruel joke about my portion size at Thanksgiving.
I realize now that my weight gain was a physical manifestation of the emotional walls I was building to protect myself.
I remember the cold knot in my stomach when HR called me into the conference room.
The hollow silence in my car after I packed up my desk and drove home jobless was deafening.

I actually felt pretty hopeful about joining that local clinic's weight program because Dr. Evans specifically said it would be perfect for me. Hearing him say he believed it would work made me feel confident enough to actually sign up.
I remember the paralyzing anxiety of watching my savings account drain week by week.
I snapped at a cashier over a coupon because I was so stressed about money.
I recall the shame of having to ask my parents for a loan at forty years old.
I spent weeks avoiding calls from friends because I didn't want to admit I was still unemployed.
I remember staring blankly at a job application, feeling entirely unqualified for anything.
I woke up with my heart pounding in the middle of the night, terrified about my future.
I remember the heavy, sinking depression that kept me in bed until noon on a Tuesday.
I lied in a job interview about why I left my last position, and my voice shook the entire time.
I remember the sheer volume of the screaming match we had in the kitchen that finally broke us.
I recall the physical ache in my chest when I realized my marriage was actually over.
I remember the eerie quiet of the house after he packed his bags and left for the first time.
I cried so hard on the bathroom floor that I threw up.
I remember the awkwardness of taking off my wedding ring and feeling the pale indent left behind.
I recall the bitter resentment I felt watching happy couples hold hands at the grocery store.
I avoided telling my mother we separated for three months because I couldn't bear her disappointment.
I remember sleeping on the edge of the bed out of habit, leaving his side completely empty.
I found one of his old t-shirts in the laundry and broke down completely.
I remember the detached, numb feeling of signing the preliminary separation papers.
These days, I remember the exact squeak the refrigerator door makes when I open it at night.
I watch daytime talk shows just to hear other people's voices in the background.
I remember the distinct smell of the generic brand of laundry detergent I buy now to save money.
I walked to the end of the driveway for the mail and was out of breath by the time I got back inside.
I remember the mild annoyance of the internet cutting out while I was applying for jobs.
I spend hours playing solitaire on my phone, totally zoning out from reality.
I remember the taste of the cold, leftover pizza I ate over the sink for dinner yesterday.
I sat on the porch watching a squirrel bury a nut, feeling strange envy for its simple purpose.
I remember the dull ache in my lower back that seems to be a permanent fixture now.
I had a sudden craving for a childhood candy that doesn't even exist anymore.
I remember the sound of the garbage truck waking me up far too early on a Wednesday.

I finally opened up about my binge eating because the new doctor did not give me that usual pitying look. She just listened without judging me, which made it so much easier to talk about how hard my weight has been to manage since my separation.
I found a twenty-dollar bill in an old winter coat and felt a brief rush of pure excitement.
I remember the annoying flicker of the hallway lightbulb that I've been too lazy to change.
I bought a cheap candle that smelled like synthetic pine and gave me a headache.
I remember the repetitive sound of rain hitting the metal awning outside my window.
I organized my entire spice cabinet alphabetically, just to feel a sense of control.
I remember the frustration of dropping my phone and checking frantically for a cracked screen.
I sat at a red light for entirely too long before realizing it had turned green.
I remember the rough texture of the cheap paper towels I've been buying lately.
I burned my tongue on a cup of hot tea and could barely taste anything for two days.
I remember watching the dust motes float in a beam of sunlight in my living room.
I had a dream about wandering through an empty supermarket, but I forgot the ending when I woke up.
I remember the sticky feeling on the floor of the local convenience store where I buy lotto tickets.
I saw a flock of birds take off all at once from a power line and felt a sudden, inexplicable sense of awe.

participants.persona: Rochelle is a 30-year-old woman with a college education, single, employed full-time, and overweight.
participants.name: Rochelle

memories.content: I realize now that my habit of using humor as a defense mechanism started when I was bullied about my weight in middle school.
Looking back at my twenties, I can see how much I settled for less in relationships just because I felt lucky to be chosen.
I finally understand why my mother was so strict about my grades; she wanted me to have the financial independence she never had.
Sometimes I catch myself apologizing for taking up space in a room, and I have to consciously remind myself that I deserve to be here.
I have noticed that I tend to bury myself in work projects whenever I feel lonely, which is probably why I have been promoted twice.
It took me years to recognize that my constant need to people-please was draining my own energy and leaving me exhausted.
I often reflect on how getting my college degree completely changed the trajectory of my life and gave me confidence I never thought I would possess.
I realize I buy clothes that are meant to hide my body rather than flatter it, and I am trying to change that mindset.
Thinking about my past friendships, I realize I am usually the one who reaches out first, which makes me wonder if they value me as much as I value them.
I am becoming aware that my fear of public speaking is actually rooted in a fear of being judged for my appearance rather than my words.
When I look at old photographs, I see a girl who was desperately trying to fit in, and it makes me appreciate the authenticity I have cultivated as I turned thirty.
I have started to see my single status not as a waiting period, but as a valuable time to figure out exactly what I want from my own life.
I remember the smell of crayons and floor wax on the first day of kindergarten.
My dad used to take me to get ice cream every Sunday afternoon when I was little.
I fell off my bike when I was seven and scraped my knee so badly it left a scar I still have.
My childhood dog, a golden retriever named Rusty, used to sleep at the foot of my bed.
I won the third-grade spelling bee by spelling the word accommodation correctly.
During middle school, I had a diary with a tiny padlock where I wrote all my secrets.
I felt incredibly embarrassed when my gym teacher pointed out that I was the slowest runner in the class.
I used to spend hours playing video games on our family desktop computer.
My grandmother taught me how to knit a scarf when I was ten years old.
I remember the anxiety of waiting for the school bus on cold winter mornings in middle school.
I got my first period at a friend sleepover and had to awkwardly ask her mom for supplies.
I spent my entire allowance on CDs at the mall when I was thirteen.
My high school history teacher always wore the most ridiculous patterned ties.
I remember the sinking feeling of getting a failing grade on my first algebra test.
I asked a boy to the dance and he laughed at me, which crushed my self-esteem for years.
I was part of the school yearbook committee and loved organizing the photo layouts.
My friends and I would drive around aimlessly in my beat-up car after getting our licenses.
I remember crying in the dressing room when trying on prom dresses because nothing fit my body right.
The first time I tried coffee was at a late-night diner with my high school friends.
I had an after-school job working the cash register at a local grocery store.

When I saw Dr. Evans for my annual physical last October, she told me to just watch my portions without offering a written meal plan or a referral to a dietitian. I left the clinic empty-handed, wishing she had given me a prescription or at least a structured follow-up schedule.

My weight has fluctuated constantly since I graduated from Penn State eight years ago, demonstrating that managing my BMI is a chronic, lifelong condition. Whenever I discuss my health with doctors, I insist on establishing long-term maintenance strategies and concrete relapse prevention plans.
I remember the excitement of receiving my college acceptance letter in the mail.
Moving into my college dorm freshman year was terrifying because I did not know anyone.
My freshman roommate used to set her alarm for 5 AM every day and it drove me crazy.
I practically lived in the campus library during finals week of my sophomore year.
I decided to major in Communications after taking an intro class that fascinated me.
I went to a party once, spilled my drink on my shirt, and left after twenty minutes.
I gained weight during my freshman year and felt so ashamed going home for Thanksgiving.
My favorite college professor always brought donuts for the class on midterm days.
I remember the thrill of finally turning twenty-one and going out to a real bar.
I met my best friend Maya during a group project in a public relations class.
We took a spontaneous road trip to the beach during spring break and got terrible sunburns.
I bombed a mock interview for a class assignment because my hands were shaking so badly.
I walked across the graduation stage feeling a mix of immense pride and total panic about the future.
My parents took me out to a fancy steakhouse to celebrate my college graduation.
My first apartment after college was a tiny studio that always smelled faintly of cabbage.
I spent my first post-grad summer applying to hundreds of entry-level jobs with no luck.
I remember the relief of getting the call offering me a position as an HR assistant.
I accidentally sent an email complaining about my boss to my boss during my first week of work.
I bought a real blazer for my first job and felt like a complete imposter wearing it.
I started packing my lunches to save money because my starting salary was so low.
I remember the awful blind date my aunt set me up on where the guy talked about his ex the whole time.
I adopted my cat, Barnaby, from a shelter when he was just a scrawny little kitten.
I signed up for a half-marathon, trained for two weeks, and completely gave up.
I remember the sheer panic of locking my keys in my car while it was still running.
I got a promotion to HR coordinator and finally felt like I had a real career path.
I was deeply hurt when a guy I had been dating for three months ghosted me without explanation.
I decided to try online dating but found the endless swiping exhausting and deleted the app.
I attended a coworker wedding and felt entirely out of place as the only single person at my table.
I took a pottery class on weekends for a few months and made several lopsided mugs.
I remember the frustration of a doctor blaming my sinus infection on my weight.
Maya and I have a tradition of ordering Thai food and watching cheesy romantic comedies every month.
I splurge on expensive skincare products because taking care of my skin makes me feel put together.
I was devastated when my grandfather passed away right before my twenty-fifth birthday.
I love reading psychological thrillers before bed, even though they sometimes give me nightmares.
I burned a Thanksgiving turkey so badly I had to order pizzas for my family.
I started listening to true crime podcasts during my morning commute to make the traffic bearable.
I remember finding my first gray hair in the bathroom mirror and staring at it for ten minutes.
I bought a bright red lipstick but never wore it out of the house because it felt too bold for me.
I negotiated my salary for the first time last year and was shocked when they agreed to my number.
I occasionally skip my friends group workouts because I feel self-conscious about my stamina.

When the clinic referred me to a commercial weight-loss group last spring, I fully expected my doctor to review my weekly progress logs during our visits. Instead, there was absolutely zero coordination or communication between my primary care office and the commercial program.
I always keep a stash of dark chocolate hidden in the bottom drawer of my office desk.
I felt a pang of jealousy when my younger sister announced she was engaged.
I spent an entire weekend watching a new series and never left my apartment.
I tried a trendy juice cleanse and made it exactly fourteen hours before eating a bagel.
I love the smell of rain hitting the hot pavement during summer thunderstorms.
I had a panic attack in a fitting room when I realized I had gone up another dress size.
I have a habit of leaving my clean laundry in the basket for days before folding it.
I accidentally killed every houseplant I bought until I finally settled for a plastic one.
